translation: Herein is contained the Commentary on the Vajracchedikā, called the Sun that Illuminates the Profound Meaning of the Excellent Path for Travelling to Freedom. Namo Mañjughoṣāya. I bow to the lord of sages, the lord of clouds, who has risen in the exceedingly vast, undefiled sky of the dharmakāya, is beautiful with the glory of the thunderous roar of profound emptiness, and makes the continuous rain of the two benefits descend upon the fields of the disciples. I respectfully bow at the feet of the noble Subhūti, prophesied as the supreme of those free from afflictions, who, as an arhat manifestation of the stable circle, questions the profound meaning and is skilled in giving all answers. I bow to the spiritual friends who came in succession, such as Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, and Candrakīrti, who were prophesied by the victorious ones to comment on the profound meaning, as well as the second victorious one, Lobsang, along with his spiritual sons, and so forth. Here, with faith, I shall explain as suitably as possible a commentary on the Prajñāpāramitā in Three Hundred Stanzas, which is renowned as the Vajracchedikā. Since this text primarily explains the meaning of selflessness and contains many repeated statements, and since apart from one Indian commentary there do not appear to be any Tibetan commentaries on it, although it seems difficult to explain exactly as it is, I shall explain it according to the capability of my own mind. This has three parts: the preliminaries, the main part, and the concluding stages.

source: དང་པོ་ནི། རྒྱ་གར་སྐད་དུ། ཨཱརྱ་བཛྲ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཏེ། དེ་བོད་སྐད་དུ་བསྒྱུར་ན། ཨཱརྱ་ནི་འཕགས་པ། །བཛྲ་ནི་རྡོ་རྗེ། ཙྪེ་ད་ཀ་ནི་གཅོད་པ། པྲཛྙཱ་ནི་ཤེས་རབ། པཱ་ར་ནི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ། ཨི་ཏ་ནི་ཕྱིན་པ། ནཱ་མ་ནི་ཞེས་བྱ་བ། མ་ཧཱ་ནི་ཆེན་པོ། ཡ་ན་ནི་ཐེག་པ། སཱུ་ཏྲ་ནི་མདོ་ཞེས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །འདིར་པཱ་ར་མི་ཏ་ཞེས་འབྱུང་བ་ནི། །པཱ་ར་དང་ཨི་ཏའི་བར་དུ་རྣམ་དབྱེ་གཉིས་པའི་ཨམ་བྱིན་ནས་ཨི་ཕྱིས་ཏེ་མ་ཨི་ལ་བྱིན་ནས་མཚམས་སྦྱར་བས་མི་ཏར་སོང་བའོ། །འདིའི་མཚན་དོན་བཤད་པ་ནི། །བརྒྱ་བྱིན་གྱི་ལག་གི་རྡོ་རྗེ་དེ་ཕྱིའི་དངོས་པོ་གཞན་གྱིས་གཞིག་པར་མི་ནུས་ཤིང༌། །དེ་ནི་བྲག་སོགས་ཀྱི་དངོས་པོ་གང་ལ་བསྣུན་ཀྱང་ཐལ་བར་བྱེད་ནུས་པ་ལྟར། གཞུང་འདིའི་བརྗོད་བྱ་དོན་གྱི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་སྟོང་ཉིད་རྟོགས་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེ་ལ་མི་མཐུན་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱིས་མི་ཚུགས་ཤིང༌། དེས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཐམས་ཅད་རྩད་ནས་གཅོད་པའི་དོན་ནོ། །
translation: The first: In the language of India, it is Āryavajra and so forth; when translated into the Tibetan language, ārya is 'noble', vajra is 'vajra', cchedaka is 'cutter', prajñā is 'wisdom', pāra is 'to the other side', ita is 'gone', nāma is 'called', mahā is 'great', yāna is 'vehicle', and sūtra translates as 'sūtra'. Here, regarding the occurrence of pāramitā: by adding the second case ending am between pāra and ita, deleting the i, and applying the ma to the i, through phonetic conjunction it becomes mita. The explanation of the meaning of this title is: just as the vajra in the hand of Śakra cannot be destroyed by other outer entities, and is capable of reducing to dust whatever entity it strikes, such as a rock, so too, the actual prajñāpāramitā, the expressed subject matter of this text, the pristine wisdom that realizes emptiness, cannot be harmed by discordant factors, and it cuts all afflictions and suffering from the root; such is the meaning.

The first: In the language of India, it is Āryavajra and so forth; when translated into the Tibetan language, ārya is 'noble', vajra is 'vajra', cchedaka is 'cutter', prajñā is 'wisdom', pāra is 'to the other side', ita is 'gone', nāma is 'called', mahā is 'great', yāna is 'vehicle', and sūtra translates as 'sūtra'. heading: གླེང་གཞི།
translation: The third, the prologue: "Thus did I, the compiler, hear at one time: the Bhagavān was residing in Śrāvastī, in Prince Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park, together as one with a great saṅgha of monks, one thousand two hundred and fifty śrāvakas, and exceedingly many bodhisattvas." Furthermore, among the six great cities in India such as Śrāvastī, this Śrāvastī belonged under the dominion of King Prasenajit, and there was an excellent pleasure grove with good ground called Prince Jeta's. At a time when a few years had passed since the Bhagavān became enlightened, the householder called Anāthapiṇḍada wished to establish a good, large vihāra as a place for the Bhagavān and his retinue to reside continuously; so he gave Prince Jeta many thousands of ounces of gold to cover the grove and bought that Jeta's Grove. Prince Jeta also offered a plot of land near the gateway to the Bhagavān, and in that grove, Anāthapiṇḍada, relying on Śāriputra, had divine and human builders construct an exceptionally exalted park, and when it was finished, the Bhagavān, knowing Prince Jeta's intention, bestowed the name of the vihāra correspondingly.

Herein is contained the Commentary on the Vajracchedikā, called the Sun that Illuminates the Profound Meaning of the Excellent Path for Travelling to Freedom. Namo Mañjughoṣāya. I bow to the lord of sages, the lord of clouds, who has risen in the exceedingly vast, undefiled sky of the dharmakāya, is beautiful with the glory of the thunderous roar of profound emptiness, and makes the continuous rain of the two benefits descend upon the fields of the disciples. I respectfully bow at the feet of the noble Subhūti, prophesied as the supreme of those free from afflictions, who, as an arhat manifestation of the stable circle, questions the profound meaning and is skilled in giving all answers. I bow to the spiritual friends who came in succession, such as Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, and Candrakīrti, who were prophesied by the victorious ones to comment on the profound meaning, as well as the second victorious one, Lobsang, along with his spiritual sons, and so forth. Here, with faith, I shall explain as suitably as possible a commentary on the Prajñāpāramitā in Three Hundred Stanzas, which is renowned as the Vajracchedikā. Since this text primarily explains the meaning of selflessness and contains many repeated statements, and since apart from one Indian commentary there do not appear to be any Tibetan commentaries on it, although it seems difficult to explain exactly as it is, I shall explain it according to the capability of my own mind. This has three parts: the preliminaries, the main part, and the concluding stages.

heading: གླེང་གཞི།
translation: This Anāthapiṇḍada was a holy great being who had intentionally taken birth for the sake of being the patron of the Teacher, and was capable of seeing the treasures of jewels in the water and underground, taking them at will, and enjoying them. Then, for the sake of the disciples, in the morning the Bhagavān put on his three dharma robes, took up his alms bowl, and went to the great city of Śrāvastī for the purpose of alms. Having received alms, he later returned and performed the act of partaking of the meal.

Herein is contained the Commentary on the Vajracchedikā, called the Sun that Illuminates the Profound Meaning of the Excellent Path for Travelling to Freedom. Namo Mañjughoṣāya. I bow to the lord of sages, the lord of clouds, who has risen in the exceedingly vast, undefiled sky of the dharmakāya, is beautiful with the glory of the thunderous roar of profound emptiness, and makes the continuous rain of the two benefits descend upon the fields of the disciples. I respectfully bow at the feet of the noble Subhūti, prophesied as the supreme of those free from afflictions, who, as an arhat manifestation of the stable circle, questions the profound meaning and is skilled in giving all answers. I bow to the spiritual friends who came in succession, such as Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, and Candrakīrti, who were prophesied by the victorious ones to comment on the profound meaning, as well as the second victorious one, Lobsang, along with his spiritual sons, and so forth. Here, with faith, I shall explain as suitably as possible a commentary on the Prajñāpāramitā in Three Hundred Stanzas, which is renowned as the Vajracchedikā. Since this text primarily explains the meaning of selflessness and contains many repeated statements, and since apart from one Indian commentary there do not appear to be any Tibetan commentaries on it, although it seems difficult to explain exactly as it is, I shall explain it according to the capability of my own mind. This has three parts: the preliminaries, the main part, and the concluding stages.

The first: In the language of India, it is Āryavajra and so forth; when translated into the Tibetan language, ārya is 'noble', vajra is 'vajra', cchedaka is 'cutter', prajñā is 'wisdom', pāra is 'to the other side', ita is 'gone', nāma is 'called', mahā is 'great', yāna is 'vehicle', and sūtra translates as 'sūtra'. Here, regarding the occurrence of pāramitā: by adding the second case ending am between pāra and ita, deleting the i, and applying the ma to the i, through phonetic conjunction it becomes mita. The explanation of the meaning of this title is: just as the vajra in the hand of Śakra cannot be destroyed by other outer entities, and is capable of reducing to dust whatever entity it strikes, such as a rock, so too, the actual prajñāpāramitā, the expressed subject matter of this text, the pristine wisdom that realizes emptiness, cannot be harmed by discordant factors, and it cuts all afflictions and suffering from the root; such is the meaning.

source: ཟས་ཕྱི་མ་ཕྱི་དྲོའི་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཟ་བ་སྤངས་ནས། ལྷུང་བཟེད་སོགས་བཞག་ནས་ཞབས་བཀྲུས་ཤིང་ བསིལ་ཏེ། གདན་བཤམས་པ་ཉིད་ལ་དཀྱིལ་མོ་ཀྲུང་བཅས་ནས་སྐུ་དྲང་པོར་སྲང་སྟེ། གཞུང་འདི་སྟོན་པར་འགྱུར་བ་མཁྱེན་པའི་དྲན་པ་མངོན་དུ་བཞག་ནས་བཞུགས་སོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ལ་འབྱོན་པ་ནི། རང་ཉིད་བསོད་སྙོམས་ ཀྱི་ཟས་ཟ་དགོས་པའི་ཆེད་མིན་གྱི། གདུལ་བྱ་ལ་ཚོགས་གསོག་པ་དང་ཆོས་སྟོན་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཆེད་དུའོ། །སངས་རྒྱས་ལ་ནི་བཀྲེས་སྐོམ་འབྱུང་མི་སྲིད་པར་གསེར་འོད་ལས་བཤད་ཅིང༌། གསོལ་དགོས་ནའང་རང་ཉིད་ནམ་མཁའ་མཛོད་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལ་དབང་བསྒྱུར་བས་ཡོ་བྱད་ཀྱིས་ཕོངས་པ་མི་སྲིད་ལ། ས་རྡོ་སོགས་གསེར་དངུལ་རིན་པོ་ཆེར་བསྒྱུར་ནུས་ཤིང༌། དེ་དག་དང་ཟས་དམན་པ་དག་ཀྱང་རོ་བརྒྱ་ལྡན་པའི་ཟས་སུ་བསྒྱུར་བ་དང༌། ཟས་ངན་པ་ཅི་འདྲ་བ་ཞིག་ཡིན་ཀྱང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞལ་དུ་བཞེས་པ་ན་རོ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་གཞན་གྱིས་མྱོང་བར་མི་འགྱུར་བ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཟས་སུ་འགྱུར་ཏེ། མངོན་རྟོགས་རྒྱན་ལས། འདི་ལ་རོ་མི་ཞིམ་པ་རོ་མཆོག་སྣང༌། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ཡང་དེའོ། །སྔོན་སྟོན་པས་ཟླ་བ་གསུམ་དུ་རྟ་ཆས་ཀྱི་ནས་གསོལ་དགོས་པའི་ཚུལ་བསྟན་པའི་ཚེ། ཀུན་དགའ་བོའི་བསམ་པ་ལ་སྟོན་པ་རྒྱལ་པོའི་རིགས་སུ་སྐྱེས་ཀྱང༌། ད་ལྟ་རྟ་ཆས་གསོལ་བའི་དུས་བྱུང་ངོ་སྙམ་དུ་ཡིད་སྐྱོ་བའི་ཚེ། སྟོན་པས་ཞལ་ནས་ནས་ཀྱི་འབྲུ་གཅིག་ཕྱུང་སྟེ་འདི་ཟོ་ཞིག་ཅེས་གསུངས་ནས་བྱིན་པས་ཀུན་དགའ་བོས་ཟོས་པ་ན་ཚིམ་སྟེ། དེ་ནས་ཉིན་ཞག་བདུན་དུ་ཟས་ཟ་དགོས་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་མ་སྐྱེས་པས་ངོ་མཚར་དུ་གྱུར་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །གསེར་འོད་ལས་སྟོན་པས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ལེན་པར་མཛད་ཅིང་གསོལ་བ་ལྟར་སྣང་ཡང་དོན་ལ་གསོལ་བ་མེད་ཅིང༌། བཤང་གཅི་ཡང་མེད་པར་བཤད་ལ། གསང་བ་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་པའི་མདོ་ལས། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་སྐུ་ནི་གསེར་གྱི་གར་བུ་ལྟ་བུ་སྟེ། སྐུ་ལ་ཁོང་སྟོང་དང་ཕོ་བ་ལོང་ག་རྒྱུ་མ་སོགས་ཀྱང་མེད་པར་བཤད་དེ་དོན་ལ་གནས་སོ། །
translation: Having abandoned eating the later meal, the afternoon alms, he set down his alms bowl and so forth, washed and cooled his feet, and crossing his legs in the lotus posture upon the seat that had been arranged, he straightened his body and sat, establishing mindfulness with the knowledge that he would teach this text. As for the Bhagavān going for alms, it was not because he himself needed to eat the alms food, but for the sake of the disciples accumulating merit, teaching the dharma, and so forth. As explained in the Suvarṇaprabhāsa, it is impossible for hunger and thirst to occur for a Buddha, and even if he needed to eat, since he himself masters the pristine wisdom of the sky treasury, he could not possibly be destitute of requisites; he is capable of transforming earth, stones, and so forth into gold, silver, and jewels, and he can transform those and inferior foods into food possessing a hundred tastes, and whatever kind of bad food it might be, when partaken of in the Buddha's mouth, it turns into food of perfect taste such as others would not experience; and this is the meaning of what is said in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "For him, unpalatable tastes appear as supreme tastes." Previously, when the Teacher demonstrated the manner of needing to eat horse-fodder barley for three months, Ānanda thought, "Although the Teacher was born in a royal caste, now the time to eat horse fodder has come," and while he was sorrowful, the Teacher brought forth a single grain of barley from his mouth, said "Eat this," and gave it to him; when Ānanda ate it, he was satisfied, and since for seven days and nights the notion of needing to eat food did not arise in him, he marvelled. In the Suvarṇaprabhāsa it is explained that although it appears that the Teacher takes and eats alms, in reality he does not eat, and he also has no feces or urine; and in the Acintyaguhyasūtra it is explained that the Tathāgata's body is like a solid block of gold, and his body has no hollows, stomach, large intestine, small intestine, and so forth; thus it accords with reality.

Herein is contained the Commentary on the Vajracchedikā, called the Sun that Illuminates the Profound Meaning of the Excellent Path for Travelling to Freedom. Namo Mañjughoṣāya. I bow to the lord of sages, the lord of clouds, who has risen in the exceedingly vast, undefiled sky of the dharmakāya, is beautiful with the glory of the thunderous roar of profound emptiness, and makes the continuous rain of the two benefits descend upon the fields of the disciples. I respectfully bow at the feet of the noble Subhūti, prophesied as the supreme of those free from afflictions, who, as an arhat manifestation of the stable circle, questions the profound meaning and is skilled in giving all answers. I bow to the spiritual friends who came in succession, such as Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, and Candrakīrti, who were prophesied by the victorious ones to comment on the profound meaning, as well as the second victorious one, Lobsang, along with his spiritual sons, and so forth. Here, with faith, I shall explain as suitably as possible a commentary on the Prajñāpāramitā in Three Hundred Stanzas, which is renowned as the Vajracchedikā. Since this text primarily explains the meaning of selflessness and contains many repeated statements, and since apart from one Indian commentary there do not appear to be any Tibetan commentaries on it, although it seems difficult to explain exactly as it is, I shall explain it according to the capability of my own mind. This has three parts: the preliminaries, the main part, and the concluding stages.

Prince Jeta also offered a plot of land near the gateway to the Bhagavān, and in that grove, Anāthapiṇḍada, relying on Śāriputra, had divine and human builders construct an exceptionally exalted park, and when it was finished, the Bhagavān, knowing Prince Jeta's intention, bestowed the name of the vihāra correspondingly.

Having abandoned eating the later meal, the afternoon alms, he set down his alms bowl and so forth, washed and cooled his feet, and crossing his legs in the lotus posture upon the seat that had been arranged, he straightened his body and sat, establishing mindfulness with the knowledge that he would teach this text. As for the Bhagavān going for alms, it was not because he himself needed to eat the alms food, but for the sake of the disciples accumulating merit, teaching the dharma, and so forth. As explained in the Suvarṇaprabhāsa, it is impossible for hunger and thirst to occur for a Buddha, and even if he needed to eat, since he himself masters the pristine wisdom of the sky treasury, he could not possibly be destitute of requisites; he is capable of transforming earth, stones, and so forth into gold, silver, and jewels, and he can transform those and inferior foods into food possessing a hundred tastes, and whatever kind of bad food it might be, when partaken of in the Buddha's mouth, it turns into food of perfect taste such as others would not experience; and this is the meaning of what is said in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "For him, unpalatable tastes appear as supreme tastes." Previously, when the Teacher demonstrated the manner of needing to eat horse-fodder barley for three months, Ānanda thought, "Although the Teacher was born in a royal caste, now the time to eat horse fodder has come," and while he was sorrowful, the Teacher brought forth a single grain of barley from his mouth, said "Eat this," and gave it to him; when Ānanda ate it, he was satisfied, and since for seven days and nights the notion of needing to eat food did not arise in him, he marvelled. In the Suvarṇaprabhāsa it is explained that although it appears that the Teacher takes and eats alms, in reality he does not eat, and he also has no feces or urine; and in the Acintyaguhyasūtra it is explained that the Tathāgata's body is like a solid block of gold, and his body has no hollows, stomach, large intestine, small intestine, and so forth; thus it accords with reality.

Having abandoned eating the later meal, the afternoon alms, he set down his alms bowl and so forth, washed and cooled his feet, and crossing his legs in the lotus posture upon the seat that had been arranged, he straightened his body and sat, establishing mindfulness with the knowledge that he would teach this text. As for the Bhagavān going for alms, it was not because he himself needed to eat the alms food, but for the sake of the disciples accumulating merit, teaching the dharma, and so forth. As explained in the Suvarṇaprabhāsa, it is impossible for hunger and thirst to occur for a Buddha, and even if he needed to eat, since he himself masters the pristine wisdom of the sky treasury, he could not possibly be destitute of requisites; he is capable of transforming earth, stones, and so forth into gold, silver, and jewels, and he can transform those and inferior foods into food possessing a hundred tastes, and whatever kind of bad food it might be, when partaken of in the Buddha's mouth, it turns into food of perfect taste such as others would not experience; and this is the meaning of what is said in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "For him, unpalatable tastes appear as supreme tastes." Previously, when the Teacher demonstrated the manner of needing to eat horse-fodder barley for three months, Ānanda thought, "Although the Teacher was born in a royal caste, now the time to eat horse fodder has come," and while he was sorrowful, the Teacher brought forth a single grain of barley from his mouth, said "Eat this," and gave it to him; when Ānanda ate it, he was satisfied, and since for seven days and nights the notion of needing to eat food did not arise in him, he marvelled. In the Suvarṇaprabhāsa it is explained that although it appears that the Teacher takes and eats alms, in reality he does not eat, and he also has no feces or urine; and in the Acintyaguhyasūtra it is explained that the Tathāgata's body is like a solid block of gold, and his body has no hollows, stomach, large intestine, small intestine, and so forth; thus it accords with reality.

Having abandoned eating the later meal, the afternoon alms, he set down his alms bowl and so forth, washed and cooled his feet, and crossing his legs in the lotus posture upon the seat that had been arranged, he straightened his body and sat, establishing mindfulness with the knowledge that he would teach this text. As for the Bhagavān going for alms, it was not because he himself needed to eat the alms food, but for the sake of the disciples accumulating merit, teaching the dharma, and so forth. As explained in the Suvarṇaprabhāsa, it is impossible for hunger and thirst to occur for a Buddha, and even if he needed to eat, since he himself masters the pristine wisdom of the sky treasury, he could not possibly be destitute of requisites; he is capable of transforming earth, stones, and so forth into gold, silver, and jewels, and he can transform those and inferior foods into food possessing a hundred tastes, and whatever kind of bad food it might be, when partaken of in the Buddha's mouth, it turns into food of perfect taste such as others would not experience; and this is the meaning of what is said in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "For him, unpalatable tastes appear as supreme tastes." Previously, when the Teacher demonstrated the manner of needing to eat horse-fodder barley for three months, Ānanda thought, "Although the Teacher was born in a royal caste, now the time to eat horse fodder has come," and while he was sorrowful, the Teacher brought forth a single grain of barley from his mouth, said "Eat this," and gave it to him; when Ānanda ate it, he was satisfied, and since for seven days and nights the notion of needing to eat food did not arise in him, he marvelled. In the Suvarṇaprabhāsa it is explained that although it appears that the Teacher takes and eats alms, in reality he does not eat, and he also has no feces or urine; and in the Acintyaguhyasūtra it is explained that the Tathāgata's body is like a solid block of gold, and his body has no hollows, stomach, large intestine, small intestine, and so forth; thus it accords with reality.

Prince Jeta also offered a plot of land near the gateway to the Bhagavān, and in that grove, Anāthapiṇḍada, relying on Śāriputra, had divine and human builders construct an exceptionally exalted park, and when it was finished, the Bhagavān, knowing Prince Jeta's intention, bestowed the name of the vihāra correspondingly.

Having abandoned eating the later meal, the afternoon alms, he set down his alms bowl and so forth, washed and cooled his feet, and crossing his legs in the lotus posture upon the seat that had been arranged, he straightened his body and sat, establishing mindfulness with the knowledge that he would teach this text. As for the Bhagavān going for alms, it was not because he himself needed to eat the alms food, but for the sake of the disciples accumulating merit, teaching the dharma, and so forth. As explained in the Suvarṇaprabhāsa, it is impossible for hunger and thirst to occur for a Buddha, and even if he needed to eat, since he himself masters the pristine wisdom of the sky treasury, he could not possibly be destitute of requisites; he is capable of transforming earth, stones, and so forth into gold, silver, and jewels, and he can transform those and inferior foods into food possessing a hundred tastes, and whatever kind of bad food it might be, when partaken of in the Buddha's mouth, it turns into food of perfect taste such as others would not experience; and this is the meaning of what is said in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "For him, unpalatable tastes appear as supreme tastes." Previously, when the Teacher demonstrated the manner of needing to eat horse-fodder barley for three months, Ānanda thought, "Although the Teacher was born in a royal caste, now the time to eat horse fodder has come," and while he was sorrowful, the Teacher brought forth a single grain of barley from his mouth, said "Eat this," and gave it to him; when Ānanda ate it, he was satisfied, and since for seven days and nights the notion of needing to eat food did not arise in him, he marvelled. In the Suvarṇaprabhāsa it is explained that although it appears that the Teacher takes and eats alms, in reality he does not eat, and he also has no feces or urine; and in the Acintyaguhyasūtra it is explained that the Tathāgata's body is like a solid block of gold, and his body has no hollows, stomach, large intestine, small intestine, and so forth; thus it accords with reality.

translation: Then, to state it by condensing the words: he addressed him, saying, 'Since you, the Bhagavān, have benefited the great bodhisattvas by performing as many supreme, excellent benefits for this and future lives through the dharma as there are, and furthermore, since you have perfectly entrusted the bodhisattvas with as many excellent perfect entrustments of the three types—of place, dharma, and command—as there are, Bhagavān, it is a great marvel,' and so forth. At a time when a few years had passed since the Bhagavān became enlightened, the householder called Anāthapiṇḍada wished to establish a good, large vihāra as a place for the Bhagavān and his retinue to reside continuously; so he gave Prince Jeta many thousands of ounces of gold to cover the grove and bought that Jeta's Grove. Prince Jeta also offered a plot of land near the gateway to the Bhagavān, and in that grove, Anāthapiṇḍada, relying on Śāriputra, had divine and human builders construct an exceptionally exalted park, and when it was finished, the Bhagavān, knowing Prince Jeta's intention, bestowed the name of the vihāra correspondingly.

Having abandoned eating the later meal, the afternoon alms, he set down his alms bowl and so forth, washed and cooled his feet, and crossing his legs in the lotus posture upon the seat that had been arranged, he straightened his body and sat, establishing mindfulness with the knowledge that he would teach this text. As for the Bhagavān going for alms, it was not because he himself needed to eat the alms food, but for the sake of the disciples accumulating merit, teaching the dharma, and so forth. As explained in the Suvarṇaprabhāsa, it is impossible for hunger and thirst to occur for a Buddha, and even if he needed to eat, since he himself masters the pristine wisdom of the sky treasury, he could not possibly be destitute of requisites; he is capable of transforming earth, stones, and so forth into gold, silver, and jewels, and he can transform those and inferior foods into food possessing a hundred tastes, and whatever kind of bad food it might be, when partaken of in the Buddha's mouth, it turns into food of perfect taste such as others would not experience; and this is the meaning of what is said in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "For him, unpalatable tastes appear as supreme tastes." Previously, when the Teacher demonstrated the manner of needing to eat horse-fodder barley for three months, Ānanda thought, "Although the Teacher was born in a royal caste, now the time to eat horse fodder has come," and while he was sorrowful, the Teacher brought forth a single grain of barley from his mouth, said "Eat this," and gave it to him; when Ānanda ate it, he was satisfied, and since for seven days and nights the notion of needing to eat food did not arise in him, he marvelled. In the Suvarṇaprabhāsa it is explained that although it appears that the Teacher takes and eats alms, in reality he does not eat, and he also has no feces or urine; and in the Acintyaguhyasūtra it is explained that the Tathāgata's body is like a solid block of gold, and his body has no hollows, stomach, large intestine, small intestine, and so forth; thus it accords with reality.

གསུམ་པ་གླེང་གཞི་ནི། གཞུང་འདི་སྐད་ཅེས་སྡུད་པ་པོ་བདག་གིས་ཐོས་པ་ནི་དུས་གཅིག་གི་ཚེ་ན། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་མཉན་ཡོད་ན་རྒྱལ་བུ་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཚལ་མགོན་མེད་ཟས་སྦྱིན་གྱི་ཀུན་དགའ་ར་བ་ན། དགེ་སློང་གི་དགེ་འདུན་ཆེན་པོ་ཉན་ཐོས་སྟོང་ཉིས་བརྒྱ་ལྔ་བཅུ་དང༌། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རབ་ཏུ་མང་པོ་དག་དང་ཐབས་གཅིག་སྟེ་ལྷན་ཅིག་ཏུ་བཞུགས་སོ། །དེ་ཡང་རྒྱ་གར་ན་མཉན་ཡོད་སོགས་གྲོང་ཁྱེར་ཆེན་པོ་དྲུག་ཡོད་པ་ལས། མཉན་ཡོད་འདི་རྒྱལ་པོ་གསལ་རྒྱལ་གྱི་མངའ་འོག་ཏུ་གཏོགས་ཤིང༌། དེར་རྒྱལ་བུ་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཅེས་བྱ་བའི་སྐྱེད་མོའི་ཚལ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ས་གཞི་བཟང་བ་ཞིག་ཡོད་དོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་སངས་རྒྱས་ནས་ལོ་ཆ་ཤས་སོང་བའི་སྐབས་ཤིག་ན་ཁྱིམ་བདག་མགོན་མེད་ཟས་སྦྱིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་འཁོར་བཅས་རྒྱུན་དུ་བཞུགས་པའི་གནས་གཙུག་ལག་ཁང་ཆེན་པོ་བཟང་བ་ཞིག་འདེབས་པར་འདོད་ནས། རྒྱལ་བུ་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ལ་ཚལ་དེ་གང་བའི་གསེར་སྲང་སྟོང་ཕྲག་དུ་མ་བྱིན་ནས་ རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཚལ་དེ་ཉོས་སོ། །རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་སྒོ་ཁང་ཕྱོགས་ནས་ས་དུམ་བུ་ཞིག་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་ཕུལ་ཏེ། ཚལ་དེར་མགོན་མེད་ཟས་སྦྱིན་གྱིས་ཤཱ་རིའི་བུ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ལྷ་མིའི་བཟོ་བོས་ཀུན་དགའ་ར་བ་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་པ་ཞིག་བཞེངས་ཏེ་ ཟིན་པ་ན་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་བསམ་པ་མཁྱེན་ནས། གཙུག་ལག་ཁང་གི་མིང་ཡང་དེ་བསྟུན་གྱིས་བཏགས་སོ། །

The third, the prologue: "Thus did I, the compiler, hear at one time: the Bhagavān was residing in Śrāvastī, in Prince Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada's Park, together as one with a great saṅgha of monks, one thousand two hundred and fifty śrāvakas, and exceedingly many bodhisattvas." Furthermore, among the six great cities in India such as Śrāvastī, this Śrāvastī belonged under the dominion of King Prasenajit, and there was an excellent pleasure grove with good ground called Prince Jeta's. At a time when a few years had passed since the Bhagavān became enlightened, the householder called Anāthapiṇḍada wished to establish a good, large vihāra as a place for the Bhagavān and his retinue to reside continuously; so he gave Prince Jeta many thousands of ounces of gold to cover the grove and bought that Jeta's Grove. Prince Jeta also offered a plot of land near the gateway to the Bhagavān, and in that grove, Anāthapiṇḍada, relying on Śāriputra, had divine and human builders construct an exceptionally exalted park, and when it was finished, the Bhagavān, knowing Prince Jeta's intention, bestowed the name of the vihāra correspondingly.

This Anāthapiṇḍada was a holy great being who had intentionally taken birth for the sake of being the patron of the Teacher, and was capable of seeing the treasures of jewels in the water and underground, taking them at will, and enjoying them. Then, for the sake of the disciples, in the morning the Bhagavān put on his three dharma robes, took up his alms bowl, and went to the great city of Śrāvastī for the purpose of alms. Having received alms, he later returned and performed the act of partaking of the meal.

ཟས་ཕྱི་མ་ཕྱི་དྲོའི་བསོད་སྙོམས་ཟ་བ་སྤངས་ནས། ལྷུང་བཟེད་སོགས་བཞག་ནས་ཞབས་བཀྲུས་ཤིང་ བསིལ་ཏེ། གདན་བཤམས་པ་ཉིད་ལ་དཀྱིལ་མོ་ཀྲུང་བཅས་ནས་སྐུ་དྲང་པོར་སྲང་སྟེ། གཞུང་འདི་སྟོན་པར་འགྱུར་བ་མཁྱེན་པའི་དྲན་པ་མངོན་དུ་བཞག་ནས་བཞུགས་སོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ལ་འབྱོན་པ་ནི། རང་ཉིད་བསོད་སྙོམས་ ཀྱི་ཟས་ཟ་དགོས་པའི་ཆེད་མིན་གྱི། གདུལ་བྱ་ལ་ཚོགས་གསོག་པ་དང་ཆོས་སྟོན་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཆེད་དུའོ། །སངས་རྒྱས་ལ་ནི་བཀྲེས་སྐོམ་འབྱུང་མི་སྲིད་པར་གསེར་འོད་ལས་བཤད་ཅིང༌། གསོལ་དགོས་ནའང་རང་ཉིད་ནམ་མཁའ་མཛོད་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལ་དབང་བསྒྱུར་བས་ཡོ་བྱད་ཀྱིས་ཕོངས་པ་མི་སྲིད་ལ། ས་རྡོ་སོགས་གསེར་དངུལ་རིན་པོ་ཆེར་བསྒྱུར་ནུས་ཤིང༌། དེ་དག་དང་ཟས་དམན་པ་དག་ཀྱང་རོ་བརྒྱ་ལྡན་པའི་ཟས་སུ་བསྒྱུར་བ་དང༌། ཟས་ངན་པ་ཅི་འདྲ་བ་ཞིག་ཡིན་ཀྱང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞལ་དུ་བཞེས་པ་ན་རོ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་གཞན་གྱིས་མྱོང་བར་མི་འགྱུར་བ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཟས་སུ་འགྱུར་ཏེ། མངོན་རྟོགས་རྒྱན་ལས། འདི་ལ་རོ་མི་ཞིམ་པ་རོ་མཆོག་སྣང༌། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ཡང་དེའོ། །སྔོན་སྟོན་པས་ཟླ་བ་གསུམ་དུ་རྟ་ཆས་ཀྱི་ནས་གསོལ་དགོས་པའི་ཚུལ་བསྟན་པའི་ཚེ། ཀུན་དགའ་བོའི་བསམ་པ་ལ་སྟོན་པ་རྒྱལ་པོའི་རིགས་སུ་སྐྱེས་ཀྱང༌། ད་ལྟ་རྟ་ཆས་གསོལ་བའི་དུས་བྱུང་ངོ་སྙམ་དུ་ཡིད་སྐྱོ་བའི་ཚེ། སྟོན་པས་ཞལ་ནས་ནས་ཀྱི་འབྲུ་གཅིག་ཕྱུང་སྟེ་འདི་ཟོ་ཞིག་ཅེས་གསུངས་ནས་བྱིན་པས་ཀུན་དགའ་བོས་ཟོས་པ་ན་ཚིམ་སྟེ། དེ་ནས་ཉིན་ཞག་བདུན་དུ་ཟས་ཟ་དགོས་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་མ་སྐྱེས་པས་ངོ་མཚར་དུ་གྱུར་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །གསེར་འོད་ལས་སྟོན་པས་བསོད་སྙོམས་ལེན་པར་མཛད་ཅིང་གསོལ་བ་ལྟར་སྣང་ཡང་དོན་ལ་གསོལ་བ་མེད་ཅིང༌། བཤང་གཅི་ཡང་མེད་པར་བཤད་ལ། གསང་བ་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་པའི་མདོ་ལས། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་སྐུ་ནི་གསེར་གྱི་གར་བུ་ལྟ་བུ་སྟེ། སྐུ་ལ་ཁོང་སྟོང་དང་ཕོ་བ་ལོང་ག་རྒྱུ་མ་སོགས་ཀྱང་མེད་པར་བཤད་དེ་དོན་ལ་གནས་སོ། །

Having abandoned eating the later meal, the afternoon alms, he set down his alms bowl and so forth, washed and cooled his feet, and crossing his legs in the lotus posture upon the seat that had been arranged, he straightened his body and sat, establishing mindfulness with the knowledge that he would teach this text. As for the Bhagavān going for alms, it was not because he himself needed to eat the alms food, but for the sake of the disciples accumulating merit, teaching the dharma, and so forth. As explained in the Suvarṇaprabhāsa, it is impossible for hunger and thirst to occur for a Buddha, and even if he needed to eat, since he himself masters the pristine wisdom of the sky treasury, he could not possibly be destitute of requisites; he is capable of transforming earth, stones, and so forth into gold, silver, and jewels, and he can transform those and inferior foods into food possessing a hundred tastes, and whatever kind of bad food it might be, when partaken of in the Buddha's mouth, it turns into food of perfect taste such as others would not experience; and this is the meaning of what is said in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "For him, unpalatable tastes appear as supreme tastes." Previously, when the Teacher demonstrated the manner of needing to eat horse-fodder barley for three months, Ānanda thought, "Although the Teacher was born in a royal caste, now the time to eat horse fodder has come," and while he was sorrowful, the Teacher brought forth a single grain of barley from his mouth, said "Eat this," and gave it to him; when Ānanda ate it, he was satisfied, and since for seven days and nights the notion of needing to eat food did not arise in him, he marvelled. In the Suvarṇaprabhāsa it is explained that although it appears that the Teacher takes and eats alms, in reality he does not eat, and he also has no feces or urine; and in the Acintyaguhyasūtra it is explained that the Tathāgata's body is like a solid block of gold, and his body has no hollows, stomach, large intestine, small intestine, and so forth; thus it accords with reality.

translation: For that reason, he said, "Listen well and hold it well in mind without forgetting," and "I will explain to you the three requested above, such as how one should abide." In reply, Subhūti said, "Bhagavān, it is so," and listened as the Bhagavān had instructed, and the Bhagavān spoke these words, explaining to Subhūti: Although this Subhūti merely adopted the guise of a śrāvaka, in reality he appears as an emanation of Mañjuśrī; and when the Teacher taught the prajñāpāramitā, Subhūti himself was appointed as the initial explainer of the prajñāpāramitā sūtra, which has a great underlying intention. Regarding the summary of the text, Ācārya Kamalaśīla explained eighteen topics, from generating bodhicitta, engaging in the pāramitās, and aspiring to attain the form body, up to the Buddha's perfect seeking; and he explains them by correlating the first sixteen of those with the stage of zealous application, the next one with the stage of pure noble resolve, and the eighteenth with the stage of a Buddha.

heading: བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ།
translation: Here, wishing to explain it somewhat condensed, the first, generating the mind toward awakening, is: 'Subhūti, here one who has entered the bodhisattva vehicle should think thus at the time of initially generating the mind: 'As to however many immeasurable and countless realms of sentient beings there are, when they are subsumed by the categorization of the classes of sentient beings by way of their mode of birth—whether born from eggs, or likewise the four of being born from a womb, from heat and moisture, and miraculously born; sentient beings with form who exist in the desire realm and form realm; those without form who exist in the formless realm; sentient beings with perception other than the sentient beings of Great Fruit and the Peak of Existence; the sentient beings of a part of Great Fruit who are without perception; and the sentient beings born in the Peak of Existence who are without gross perception but not without subtle perception; in short, to whatever extent the realm of sentient beings is imputed by the designation of the name "sentient being"—I shall lead all of them entirely to perfect nirvāṇa in the expanse of non-abiding nirvāṇa that is without any remainder of the two obscurations and the aggregates of suffering.' Thinking thus, one should generate the mind. To summarize the meaning, it is generating the mind for the sake of all those sentient beings attaining the non-abiding nirvāṇa, the dharmakāya of a Buddha, the svabhāvikakāya. Having first brought forth great compassion that wishes to save all sentient beings from whatever applicable forms of the three sufferings, one newly generates the mind that wishes to establish them in ultimate nirvāṇa, and if it is one that has already been generated previously, one makes that generated mind vivid and causes it to increase further.

heading: སྐྱེ་གནས་བཞི།
translation: Among the four modes of birth, egg-birth exists among humans, nāgas, birds, and so forth, and womb-birth exists among humans, animals, and also hungry ghosts. As for heat-birth, although there are many external entities such as crops and so forth, among humans it is like the Crown-born King (Māndhātā), and it includes most insects that are born in the summer season. Miraculous birth exists among the humans of the first eon, gods, hell-beings, intermediate state beings, asuras, and also animals. As for egg-birth among humans, it is just as it is explained that during the time of the Teacher, from the upāsikā Viśākhā came many eggs, and from those came many sons. The above is the manner of generating relative bodhicitta, and within that there are the two, aspiring mind and engaging mind; I think this primarily intends the stages of accumulation and preparation. For the defining characteristic of generating the mind to be perfectly complete, merely wishing to establish others in buddhahood is not sufficient; a wish for oneself to attain buddhahood is also definitely required. Therefore Maitreya said, "Generating the mind is the wish for perfect, complete awakening for the sake of others," which explains that saying "for the sake of others" is the wish to establish others in nirvāṇa, and saying "the wish for complete awakening" means a wish for oneself to attain complete awakening is required.

Here, wishing to explain it somewhat condensed, the first, generating the mind toward awakening, is: 'Subhūti, here one who has entered the bodhisattva vehicle should think thus at the time of initially generating the mind: 'As to however many immeasurable and countless realms of sentient beings there are, when they are subsumed by the categorization of the classes of sentient beings by way of their mode of birth—whether born from eggs, or likewise the four of being born from a womb, from heat and moisture, and miraculously born; sentient beings with form who exist in the desire realm and form realm; those without form who exist in the formless realm; sentient beings with perception other than the sentient beings of Great Fruit and the Peak of Existence; the sentient beings of a part of Great Fruit who are without perception; and the sentient beings born in the Peak of Existence who are without gross perception but not without subtle perception; in short, to whatever extent the realm of sentient beings is imputed by the designation of the name "sentient being"—I shall lead all of them entirely to perfect nirvāṇa in the expanse of non-abiding nirvāṇa that is without any remainder of the two obscurations and the aggregates of suffering.' Thinking thus, one should generate the mind. To summarize the meaning, it is generating the mind for the sake of all those sentient beings attaining the non-abiding nirvāṇa, the dharmakāya of a Buddha, the svabhāvikakāya. Having first brought forth great compassion that wishes to save all sentient beings from whatever applicable forms of the three sufferings, one newly generates the mind that wishes to establish them in ultimate nirvāṇa, and if it is one that has already been generated previously, one makes that generated mind vivid and causes it to increase further.

heading: སྐྱེ་གནས་བཞི།
translation: In order to teach that this generation of the mind must be embraced by the view realizing selflessness, one should wish to entirely establish limitless sentient beings in non-abiding nirvāṇa in that way, and generate the mind thinking, "Even if they are so established, ultimately no sentient being whatsoever will have attained perfect nirvāṇa." Regarding the occurrence of the word "sorrow" here, sorrow is the two, karma and afflictions, as well as suffering; and passing beyond (bzlas/'das) that is nirvāṇa, which is being liberated or having passed beyond karma, afflictions, and suffering. Therefore, saying "passed beyond" (bzlas/'das) comes to mean both nirvāṇa and establishing them in it. This text teaches a concordant ultimate generation of the mind for ordinary beings, and it also teaches the actual ultimate generation of the mind, which exists only in noble ones.

དེ་ནས་ཚིག་སྣ་བསྡུས་ཏེ་བརྗོད་ན། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་རྣམས་ལ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་འདི་ཕྱི་རྣམས་ལ་ཕན་གདགས་པའི་དམ་པ་མཆོག་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་ཅིག་མཛད་ནས་ཕན་གདགས་པ་དང༌། ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ལ་གནས་དང་ཆོས་དང་བཀར་གདགས་པའི་ཡོངས་སུ་གཏད་པ་རྣམ་པ་གསུམ་གྱི་དམ་པ་ཇི་སྙེད་པས་ཡོངས་སུ་གཏད་པར་མཛད་ན། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ངོ་མཚར་ཆེ་སོགས་ཞེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །དེ་ལ་གནས་ནི་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་ལ་གཏད་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་ནི་དེས་ཕན་འདོགས་བྱེད་དུ་བཅུག་པ་དང༌། བཀར་བཏགས་པ་ནི་བྱང་སེམས་ཁྱེད་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་སེམས་ཅན་ལ་ཕན་གདགས་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་གཏད་པ་སྟེ་སློབ་དཔོན་ཀཱ་མ་ལ་ཤཱིའི་དགོངས་པའོ། །

Then, to state it by condensing the words: he addressed him, saying, 'Since you, the Bhagavān, have benefited the great bodhisattvas by performing as many supreme, excellent benefits for this and future lives through the dharma as there are, and furthermore, since you have perfectly entrusted the bodhisattvas with as many excellent perfect entrustments of the three types—of place, dharma, and command—as there are, Bhagavān, it is a great marvel,' and so forth. Regarding that, place is entrusting to a spiritual friend, dharma is causing them to benefit, and command is entrusting them by saying, 'You bodhisattvas must benefit sentient beings'; this is the intention of Ācārya Kamalaśīla.

[2-4] source:
ཞུས་ཚུལ་དངོས་ནི་ བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཐེག་པ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་ཞུགས་པས་ཇི་ལྟར་གནས་པར་བགྱི། ཇི་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བགྱི། ཇི་ལྟར་སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བར་བགྱི་ཞེས་དོན་ཚན་གསུམ་ཞུས་སོ། །གཉིས་པ་ལན་ལ།

The actual manner of questioning: he asked three points, saying, 'Bhagavān, how should one who has correctly entered the bodhisattva vehicle abide? How should they practice? How should they thoroughly control their mind?' The second, regarding the replies:

[2-5] source:
བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་དེ་ལྟར་ཞུས་པ་ལ་ཐུགས་དགྱེས་ནས་ལེགས་སོ་དང་དེ་ཡིན་པའི་བདེན་ཁ་གནང་སྟེ། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ལ་ཕན་གདགས་པ་དང༌། ཡོངས་སུ་གཏད་པར་ཞལ་གྱིས་བཞེས་སོ། །

Being pleased with what Subhūti had thus asked the Bhagavān, he granted his affirmation, saying "Excellent!" and that it is so, and acknowledged that the Tathāgata benefits and perfectly entrusts the bodhisattvas.

[2-6] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་དེའི་ཕྱིར་ན། ལེགས་པར་ཉོན་ལ་ལེགས་པར་ཡིད་ལ་མི་བརྗེད་པར་ཟུངས་ཤིག་ཅེས་དང༌། གོང་དུ་ཞུས་པའི་ཇི་ལྟར་གནས་པར་བྱ་བ་སོགས་གསུམ་ཁྱོད་ལ་བཤད་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས། ལན་ལ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དེ་དེ་བཞིན་ནོ་ཞེས་གསོལ་ནས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་མཉན་པ་དང༌། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་འཆད་པར་འགྱུར་བ་འདི་སྐད་ཅེས་བཀའ་སྩལ་ཏོ། །རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་བཟུང་བ་ཙམ་མ་གཏོགས། དོན་ལ་འཇམ་དཔལ་གྱི་སྤྲུལ་པར་སྣང་ལ། སྟོན་པས་ཡུམ་གསུངས་པའི་ཚེ་རབ་འབྱོར་ཉིད་ཡུམ་གྱི་མདོ་ཐོག་མར་འཆད་པ་པོར་བསྐོས་ཏེ་དགོངས་གཞི་ཆེའོ། །གཞུང་གི་བསྡུས་དོན་ལ་སློབ་དཔོན་ཀཱ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལས། སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དང༌། ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བ་དང༌། གཟུགས་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདུན་པ་ནས། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་བཙལ་བའི་བར་བཅྭོ་བརྒྱད་བཤད་ཅིང༌། དེའི་དང་པོ་བཅུ་དྲུག་ནི་མོས་སྤྱོད་ཀྱི་ས་དང༌། དེ་ནས་གཅིག་ནི་ལྷག་བསམ་དག་པའི་ས་དང༌། བཙྭོ་བརྒྱད་པ་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ས་དང་སྦྱར་ནས་འཆད་དོ། །

For that reason, he said, "Listen well and hold it well in mind without forgetting," and "I will explain to you the three requested above, such as how one should abide." In reply, Subhūti said, "Bhagavān, it is so," and listened as the Bhagavān had instructed, and the Bhagavān spoke these words, explaining to Subhūti: Although this Subhūti merely adopted the guise of a śrāvaka, in reality he appears as an emanation of Mañjuśrī; and when the Teacher taught the prajñāpāramitā, Subhūti himself was appointed as the initial explainer of the prajñāpāramitā sūtra, which has a great underlying intention. Regarding the summary of the text, Ācārya Kamalaśīla explained eighteen topics, from generating bodhicitta, engaging in the pāramitās, and aspiring to attain the form body, up to the Buddha's perfect seeking; and he explains them by correlating the first sixteen of those with the stage of zealous application, the next one with the stage of pure noble resolve, and the eighteenth with the stage of a Buddha.

[2-7] source:
འདིར་ཅུང་ཟད་བསྡུས་ནས་འཆད་པར་འདོད་པས་དང་པོ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་ནི། རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ལ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཐེག་པ་ལ་ཞུགས་པས་ཐོག་མར་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པའི་ཚེ་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ། བདག་གིས་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་ཁམས་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་ཅིང་གྲངས་མེད་པ་ཞིག་ཡོད་པ་ཇི་ཙམ་པ་དེ་རྣམས་སྐྱེ་གནས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་རིགས་སུ་བསྡུ་བས་བསྡུས་པ་ན། སྒོ་ང་ལས་སྐྱེས་པའམ། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་མངལ་དང༌། དྲོད་གཤེར་དང༌། རྫུས་ཏེ་སྐྱེས་པ་བཞི་དང༌། འདོད་ཁམས་དང་གཟུགས་ཁམས་ན་ཡོད་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་གཟུགས་ཅན་དང༌། གཟུགས་མེད་ན་ཡོད་པའི་གཟུགས་ཅན་མ་ཡིན་པ་དང༌། འབྲས་བུ་ཆེ་བ་དང་སྲིད་རྩེའི་སེམས་ཅན་ལས་གཞན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཅན་གྱི་སེམས་ཅན་དང༌། འབྲས་བུ་ཆེ་བའི་ཕྱོགས་གཅིག་གི་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་པ་དང༌། སྲིད་རྩེར་སྐྱེས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་འདུ་ཤེས་རགས་པ་མེད་ཅིང་ཕྲ་བ་མེད་པའང་མ་ཡིན་པ་སྟེ། མདོར་ན་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་ཁམས་ཅི་ཙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཅན་ཞེས་མིང་གིས་གདགས་པས་བཏགས་པ་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་སྒྲིབ་གཉིས་དང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ལྷག་མ་མེད་པའི་མི་གནས་པའི་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པའི་དབྱིངས་སུ་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་བཟླའོ་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པར་བྱའོ། །དོན་བསྡུ་ན་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་མི་གནས་པའི་མྱང་འདས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པའི་ཆེད་དུ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པའོ། །སེམས་ཅན་ཀུན་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གསུམ་པོ་ཅི་རིགས་ལས་སྐྱོབ་འདོད་ཀྱི་སྙིང་རྗེ་ཆེན་པོ་སྔོན་དུ་བཏང་ནས་མྱང་འདས་མཐར་ཐུག་ལ་འགོད་འདོད་ཀྱི་སེམས་གསར་དུ་བསྐྱེད་པ་དང༌། སྔར་བསྐྱེད་ཟིན་པ་ཞིག་ཡིན་ན་ནི་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་གསལ་བཏབ་སྟེ་གོང་འཕེལ་དུ་བྱེད་པའོ། །

Here, wishing to explain it somewhat condensed, the first, generating the mind toward awakening, is: 'Subhūti, here one who has entered the bodhisattva vehicle should think thus at the time of initially generating the mind: 'As to however many immeasurable and countless realms of sentient beings there are, when they are subsumed by the categorization of the classes of sentient beings by way of their mode of birth—whether born from eggs, or likewise the four of being born from a womb, from heat and moisture, and miraculously born; sentient beings with form who exist in the desire realm and form realm; those without form who exist in the formless realm; sentient beings with perception other than the sentient beings of Great Fruit and the Peak of Existence; the sentient beings of a part of Great Fruit who are without perception; and the sentient beings born in the Peak of Existence who are without gross perception but not without subtle perception; in short, to whatever extent the realm of sentient beings is imputed by the designation of the name "sentient being"—I shall lead all of them entirely to perfect nirvāṇa in the expanse of non-abiding nirvāṇa that is without any remainder of the two obscurations and the aggregates of suffering.' Thinking thus, one should generate the mind. To summarize the meaning, it is generating the mind for the sake of all those sentient beings attaining the non-abiding nirvāṇa, the dharmakāya of a Buddha, the svabhāvikakāya. Having first brought forth great compassion that wishes to save all sentient beings from whatever applicable forms of the three sufferings, one newly generates the mind that wishes to establish them in ultimate nirvāṇa, and if it is one that has already been generated previously, one makes that generated mind vivid and causes it to increase further.

heading: ལྟ་བའི་དགག་བྱ་བཤད་པ།
source: སློབ་དཔོན་ཀཱ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལས། སྐབས་འདིར་ལྟ་བའི་སྐོར་མང་པོ་ཞིག་བཤད་ཅིང༌། དེ་ཡང་འདིའི་གཞུང་འོག་མ་རྣམས་ནི་སྟོང་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ལྟ་བ་དང་སྦྱར་ནས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ཤེས་པ་ལ་དགོས་པའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ་ཡིན་པས་གལ་ཆེ་ཡང༌། འདིར་མང་དུ་འགྱུར་དོགས་ནས་བསྡུས་ཏེ་མཚོན་ཙམ་བརྗོད་ན། ཀུན་བྱང་གི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་ཐ་སྙད་ཙམ་དུ་ཡོད་པར་འཇོག་གི །དོན་དམ་དཔྱོད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་རིགས་པས་དཔྱད་ནས་དཔྱད་མི་བཟོད་ཅིང་བཏགས་དོན་མི་རྙེད་དེ། དེ་ལ་དགག་བྱ་ངོས་ཟིན་ན་འགོག་སླ་བས་ཐོག་མར་དགག་བྱ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཡིན་བརྗོད་ན། དགག་བྱ་ལ་སྤྱིར་འདོད་ཚུལ་མང་ཡང་འདིར་དབུ་མ་ཐལ་འགྱུར་བའི་ལུགས་ལྟར་བཤད་པར་བྱའོ། །དེ་ཡང་མདོ་ལས། དེ་དག་རྟོག་པའི་དབང་གིས་བཞག་པ་ཡིན། །ཞེས་དང༌། བཞི་བརྒྱ་པའི་འགྲེལ་པ་ལས། རྟོག་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཁོ་ནས་ཡོད་པ་ཉིད་དང་ཞེས་སོགས་དང༌། རྗེས་དགོངས་པ་རབ་གསལ་ལས། ཆོས་རྣམས་རྟོག་པའི་དབང་གིས་བཞག་པར་གསུངས་ཏེ། ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རྟོག་པས་བཏགས་ པ་ཙམ་དང་རྟོག་པའི་དབང་གིས་བཞག་པར་གསུངས་པ་མང་ངོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར། ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རྟོག་པས་བཏགས་པའི་དཔེ་ནི། ཐག་པ་ཁྲ་བོ་ཡུལ་མི་གསལ་བ་ན་གནས་པའི་ཚེ་ཁ་ཅིག་ལ་འདི་སྦྲུལ་ལོ་སྙམ་པའི་བློ་འབྱུང་ངོ༌། །དེའི་ཚེ་ཐག་པ་དེའི་ཚོགས་པ་དང་ཆ་ཤས་གང་ཡང་སྦྲུལ་དུ་མེད་ཀྱང༌། དེ་ལ་སྦྲུལ་ལོ་སྙམ་པའི་སྦྲུལ་ནི་རྟོག་པས་བཏགས་པ་ཙམ་དུ་འཆར་རོ། །
translation: Master Kamalaśīla explained a great deal concerning the view in this context, and since this was done for the sake of needing to know the meaning of the subsequent passages of this text being taught in conjunction with the view of emptiness, it is important; yet, fearing that it would become too much here, if I state just an illustration by summarizing it: all phenomena of affliction and purification are posited as existing merely conventionally, but when analyzed by reasoning that analyzes the ultimate, they cannot withstand analysis and their designated referents are not found; and regarding that, since the object of refutation is easy to refute if it is recognized, if I first state what the object of refutation is like: although there are generally many ways of asserting the object of refutation, here I shall explain it according to the system of the Prāsaṅgika Mādhyamaka. Furthermore, as it is stated in a sūtra, "Those are posited by the power of conception"; and in the commentary on the Catuḥśataka, "They exist only through the existence of conception," and so forth; and by the Lord in the Illumination of the Thought, "It is taught that phenomena are posited by the power of conception, so there are many statements that all phenomena are merely designated by conception and posited by the power of conception"; just as it is stated there, an example of all phenomena being designated by conception is: when a speckled rope is situated in a dim place, the mind arises in someone thinking, "This is a snake." At that time, although neither the collection of that rope nor any of its parts is a snake, the snake of thinking "This is a snake" regarding it appears as merely designated by conception.

Here, wishing to explain it somewhat condensed, the first, generating the mind toward awakening, is: 'Subhūti, here one who has entered the bodhisattva vehicle should think thus at the time of initially generating the mind: 'As to however many immeasurable and countless realms of sentient beings there are, when they are subsumed by the categorization of the classes of sentient beings by way of their mode of birth—whether born from eggs, or likewise the four of being born from a womb, from heat and moisture, and miraculously born; sentient beings with form who exist in the desire realm and form realm; those without form who exist in the formless realm; sentient beings with perception other than the sentient beings of Great Fruit and the Peak of Existence; the sentient beings of a part of Great Fruit who are without perception; and the sentient beings born in the Peak of Existence who are without gross perception but not without subtle perception; in short, to whatever extent the realm of sentient beings is imputed by the designation of the name "sentient being"—I shall lead all of them entirely to perfect nirvāṇa in the expanse of non-abiding nirvāṇa that is without any remainder of the two obscurations and the aggregates of suffering.' Thinking thus, one should generate the mind. To summarize the meaning, it is generating the mind for the sake of all those sentient beings attaining the non-abiding nirvāṇa, the dharmakāya of a Buddha, the svabhāvikakāya. Having first brought forth great compassion that wishes to save all sentient beings from whatever applicable forms of the three sufferings, one newly generates the mind that wishes to establish them in ultimate nirvāṇa, and if it is one that has already been generated previously, one makes that generated mind vivid and causes it to increase further.

Among the four modes of birth, egg-birth exists among humans, nāgas, birds, and so forth, and womb-birth exists among humans, animals, and also hungry ghosts. As for heat-birth, although there are many external entities such as crops and so forth, among humans it is like the Crown-born King (Māndhātā), and it includes most insects that are born in the summer season. Miraculous birth exists among the humans of the first eon, gods, hell-beings, intermediate state beings, asuras, and also animals. As for egg-birth among humans, it is just as it is explained that during the time of the Teacher, from the upāsikā Viśākhā came many eggs, and from those came many sons. The above is the manner of generating relative bodhicitta, and within that there are the two, aspiring mind and engaging mind; I think this primarily intends the stages of accumulation and preparation. For the defining characteristic of generating the mind to be perfectly complete, merely wishing to establish others in buddhahood is not sufficient; a wish for oneself to attain buddhahood is also definitely required. Therefore Maitreya said, "Generating the mind is the wish for perfect, complete awakening for the sake of others," which explains that saying "for the sake of others" is the wish to establish others in nirvāṇa, and saying "the wish for complete awakening" means a wish for oneself to attain complete awakening is required.

In order to teach that this generation of the mind must be embraced by the view realizing selflessness, one should wish to entirely establish limitless sentient beings in non-abiding nirvāṇa in that way, and generate the mind thinking, "Even if they are so established, ultimately no sentient being whatsoever will have attained perfect nirvāṇa." Regarding the occurrence of the word "sorrow" here, sorrow is the two, karma and afflictions, as well as suffering; and passing beyond (bzlas/'das) that is nirvāṇa, which is being liberated or having passed beyond karma, afflictions, and suffering. Therefore, saying "passed beyond" (bzlas/'das) comes to mean both nirvāṇa and establishing them in it. This text teaches a concordant ultimate generation of the mind for ordinary beings, and it also teaches the actual ultimate generation of the mind, which exists only in noble ones.

heading: ལྟ་བའི་དགག་བྱ་བཤད་པ།
source: དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཕུང་པོ་འདི་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ངའོ་སྙམ་དུ་འབྱུང་ཡང༌། ཕུང་པོའི་ཚོགས་པ་དང་རྒྱུན་དང་ཆ་ཤས་གང་ཡང་ངའི་མཚན་གཞིར་འཇོག་རྒྱུ་མེད་ཅིང༌། ཕུང་པོ་ལས་ངོ་བོ་ཐ་དད་པ་གཞན་ཞིག་ཀྱང་ངའི་མཚན་གཞིར་བཟུང་དུ་མེད་པས། ང་དེ་ནི་ཕུང་པོ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་བཏགས་པ་ཙམ་ཡིན་གྱི། རང་གི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་དོ། །དེ་ལྟར་ཡང་འཕགས་པའི་རིན་ཆེན་འཕྲེང་བ་ལས། སྐྱེས་བུ་ས་མིན་ཆུ་མ་ཡིན། །མེ་མིན་རླུང་མིན་ནམ་མཁའ་མིན། །རྣམ་ཤེས་མ་ཡིན་ཀུན་མིན་ན། །དེ་ལས་གཞན་པའི་སྐྱེས་བུ་གང༌། །ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། ས་མིན་ནས་རྣམ་ཤེས་མིན་ཞེས་པས་སྐྱེས་བུའི་ཁམས་དྲུག་གི་ཆ་ཤས་རེ་རེ་བ་དང༌། ཀུན་མིན་ཞེས་པས་ཁམས་དྲུག་གི་ཚོགས་པ་སྐྱེས་བུའི་བདག་ཏུ་འཇོག་པ་བཀག་ཅིང༌། རྐང་པ་ཕྱི་མས་ཁམས་རྣམས་ལས་ངོ་བོ་ཐ་དད་པའི་བདག་བཀག་གོ །འོ་ན་སྐྱེས་བུ་སྟེ་གང་ཟག་ཇི་ལྟར་འཇོག་པ་ཡང་དེ་ཉིད་ལས། སྐྱེས་བུ་ཁམས་དྲུག་འདུས་པའི་ཕྱིར། །ཡང་དག་མ་ཡིན་ཇི་ལྟ་བར། །དེ་བཞིན་ཁམས་ནི་རེ་རེ་ཡང༌། འདུས་ཕྱིར་ཡང་དག་ཉིད་དུ་མིན། །ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། རྒྱུ་མཚན་དེས་ན་སྐྱེས་བུ་ནི་རང་གི་ཁམས་དྲུག་འདུས་པའི་སྟེང་ དུ་བཏགས་པ་ཙམ་མ་གཏོགས། ཡང་དག་པར་མ་གྲུབ་བོ། །དེ་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་དུ་ཁམས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་རང་རང་གི་ཆ་ཤས་འདུས་པ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་བཏགས་པ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཡང་དག་པར་མ་གྲུབ་ཅེས་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
translation: Likewise, although the thought "I" arises in dependence upon these aggregates, neither the collection, nor the continuum, nor any part of the aggregates exists to be posited as the basis of characteristics of "I," and another entity different from the aggregates cannot be apprehended as the basis of characteristics of "I" either; therefore, that "I" is merely designated in dependence upon the aggregates, but is not established by its own intrinsic nature. Thus also it is said in the Noble One's Ratnāvalī: "A person is not earth, not water, not fire, not wind, not space, not consciousness, and not all of them; what person is there other than these?" Saying "not earth" through to "not consciousness" refutes positing each individual part of the six elements of a person as the self of a person, saying "not all of them" refutes positing the collection of the six elements as the self of a person, and the last line refutes a self with an entity different from the elements. Well then, as to how a person, an individual, is posited, from that same text it is said: "Because a person is an assembly of the six elements, it is not perfectly real; just as that is so, likewise each element is also not perfectly real, because it is an assembly." For that reason, other than a person being merely designated upon the assembly of its own six elements, it is not perfectly established. It demonstrates that just as that is so, the elements are also not perfectly established, because they are designated in dependence upon the assembly of their own respective parts.

Here, wishing to explain it somewhat condensed, the first, generating the mind toward awakening, is: 'Subhūti, here one who has entered the bodhisattva vehicle should think thus at the time of initially generating the mind: 'As to however many immeasurable and countless realms of sentient beings there are, when they are subsumed by the categorization of the classes of sentient beings by way of their mode of birth—whether born from eggs, or likewise the four of being born from a womb, from heat and moisture, and miraculously born; sentient beings with form who exist in the desire realm and form realm; those without form who exist in the formless realm; sentient beings with perception other than the sentient beings of Great Fruit and the Peak of Existence; the sentient beings of a part of Great Fruit who are without perception; and the sentient beings born in the Peak of Existence who are without gross perception but not without subtle perception; in short, to whatever extent the realm of sentient beings is imputed by the designation of the name "sentient being"—I shall lead all of them entirely to perfect nirvāṇa in the expanse of non-abiding nirvāṇa that is without any remainder of the two obscurations and the aggregates of suffering.' Thinking thus, one should generate the mind. To summarize the meaning, it is generating the mind for the sake of all those sentient beings attaining the non-abiding nirvāṇa, the dharmakāya of a Buddha, the svabhāvikakāya. Having first brought forth great compassion that wishes to save all sentient beings from whatever applicable forms of the three sufferings, one newly generates the mind that wishes to establish them in ultimate nirvāṇa, and if it is one that has already been generated previously, one makes that generated mind vivid and causes it to increase further.

སྐྱེ་གནས་བཞི་ལས་སྒོང་སྐྱེས་ནི། མི་དང་ཀླུ་དང་བྱ་སོགས་ལ་ཡོད་ཅིང༌། མངལ་སྐྱེས་ནི་མི་དང་དུད་འགྲོ་དང་ཡི་དྭགས་ལའང་ཡོད་དོ། །དྲོད་སྐྱེས་ལ་ཕྱིའི་དངོས་པོ་ལོ་ཏོག་སོགས་མང་ཡང་མི་ལ་རྒྱལ་པོ་སྤྱི་བོ་སྐྱེས་ལྟ་བུ་དང་དབྱར་དུས་སུ་སྐྱེས་པའི་འབུ་སྲིན་ཕལ་ཆེར་རོ། །བརྫུས་སྐྱེས་ནི་བསྐལ་པ་དང་པོའི་མི་རྣམས་དང་ལྷ་དང་དམྱལ་བ་པ་རྣམས་དང་བར་དོ་བ་དང་ལྷ་མིན་དུད་འགྲོ་ལའང་ཡོད་དོ། །མི་ལ་སྒོང་སྐྱེས་ནི་སྟོན་པའི་དུས་སུ་དགེ་བསྙེན་ས་ག་མ་ལས་སྒོ་ང་མང་པོ་དང་དེ་ལས་བུ་མང་པོ་ཞིག་བྱུང་བར་བཤད་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །གོང་གི་དེ་ནི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་པའི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་ཚུལ་ཡིན་ལ། དེ་ལ་སྨོན་སེམས་དང་འཇུག་སེམས་གཉིས་ཏེ། གཙོ་བོར་ཚོགས་སྦྱོར་གྱི་གནས་སྐབས་ལ་དགོངས་པར་སེམས་སོ། །སེམས་བསྐྱེད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པ་ལ་གཞན་སངས་རྒྱས་ལ་འགོད་འདོད་ཙམ་གྱིས་མི་ཆོག་གི །རང་ཡང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐོབ་འདོད་ཅིག་ངེས་པར་དགོས་སོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར་བྱམས་པས། སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་ནི་གཞན་དོན་ཕྱིར། །ཡང་དག་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་འདོད། །ཅེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། གཞན་དོན་ཕྱིར་ཞེས་པས་གཞན་མྱང་འདས་ལ་འགོད་འདོད་དང༌། རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་འདོད་ཅེས་རང་རྫོགས་བྱང་ཐོབ་འདོད་ཅིག་དགོས་ཞེས་བཤད་དོ། །

Among the four modes of birth, egg-birth exists among humans, nāgas, birds, and so forth, and womb-birth exists among humans, animals, and also hungry ghosts. As for heat-birth, although there are many external entities such as crops and so forth, among humans it is like the Crown-born King (Māndhātā), and it includes most insects that are born in the summer season. Miraculous birth exists among the humans of the first eon, gods, hell-beings, intermediate state beings, asuras, and also animals. As for egg-birth among humans, it is just as it is explained that during the time of the Teacher, from the upāsikā Viśākhā came many eggs, and from those came many sons. The above is the manner of generating relative bodhicitta, and within that there are the two, aspiring mind and engaging mind; I think this primarily intends the stages of accumulation and preparation. For the defining characteristic of generating the mind to be perfectly complete, merely wishing to establish others in buddhahood is not sufficient; a wish for oneself to attain buddhahood is also definitely required. Therefore Maitreya said, "Generating the mind is the wish for perfect, complete awakening for the sake of others," which explains that saying "for the sake of others" is the wish to establish others in nirvāṇa, and saying "the wish for complete awakening" means a wish for oneself to attain complete awakening is required.

[2-9] translation already produced for this document:
In order to teach that this generation of the mind must be embraced by the view realizing selflessness, one should wish to entirely establish limitless sentient beings in non-abiding nirvāṇa in that way, and generate the mind thinking, "Even if they are so established, ultimately no sentient being whatsoever will have attained perfect nirvāṇa." Regarding the occurrence of the word "sorrow" here, sorrow is the two, karma and afflictions, as well as suffering; and passing beyond (bzlas/'das) that is nirvāṇa, which is being liberated or having passed beyond karma, afflictions, and suffering. Therefore, saying "passed beyond" (bzlas/'das) comes to mean both nirvāṇa and establishing them in it. This text teaches a concordant ultimate generation of the mind for ordinary beings, and it also teaches the actual ultimate generation of the mind, which exists only in noble ones.

heading: ལྟ་བའི་དགག་བྱ་བཤད་པ།
translation: Likewise, one applies this to say that all phenomena of the aggregates and so forth are also not independently established, because they are designated in dependence upon their own respective parts and collections. One's own aggregate of form is designated in dependence upon the five limbs and so forth, and the limbs too are designated in dependence upon the aggregates which possess the parts and their own directional parts, and the secondary limbs such as fingers are also designated in dependence upon their own possessors of parts and their parts, and a vase is designated upon its own lip, base, belly, and so forth, and the lip, base, and so forth are also designated in dependence upon their own parts and the vase which possesses the parts; applying this to forms and so forth, consciousnesses too are designated in dependence upon earlier and later moments and their objects and so forth, and unconditioned phenomena too are designated in dependence upon their own individual bases of designation; this has been explained extensively elsewhere. Therefore, since there is no phenomenon that is not dependently arisen and not dependently designated, existing without being dependently designated is the measure of the object of refutation that is an extreme held by imputation. Thus also it is said in the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā: "Because there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not dependently arisen, therefore there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not empty." In short, although the self or person is not found when its designated referent is sought, conventionally agent and action are tenable like an illusion or an emanation; likewise, it is similar for all phenomena too, as it is said in the Saṃcayagāthā: "Just as the self is, so should all sentient beings be known;

[2-9] translation already produced for this document:
In order to teach that this generation of the mind must be embraced by the view realizing selflessness, one should wish to entirely establish limitless sentient beings in non-abiding nirvāṇa in that way, and generate the mind thinking, "Even if they are so established, ultimately no sentient being whatsoever will have attained perfect nirvāṇa." Regarding the occurrence of the word "sorrow" here, sorrow is the two, karma and afflictions, as well as suffering; and passing beyond (bzlas/'das) that is nirvāṇa, which is being liberated or having passed beyond karma, afflictions, and suffering. Therefore, saying "passed beyond" (bzlas/'das) comes to mean both nirvāṇa and establishing them in it. This text teaches a concordant ultimate generation of the mind for ordinary beings, and it also teaches the actual ultimate generation of the mind, which exists only in noble ones.

Master Kamalaśīla explained a great deal concerning the view in this context, and since this was done for the sake of needing to know the meaning of the subsequent passages of this text being taught in conjunction with the view of emptiness, it is important; yet, fearing that it would become too much here, if I state just an illustration by summarizing it: all phenomena of affliction and purification are posited as existing merely conventionally, but when analyzed by reasoning that analyzes the ultimate, they cannot withstand analysis and their designated referents are not found; and regarding that, since the object of refutation is easy to refute if it is recognized, if I first state what the object of refutation is like: although there are generally many ways of asserting the object of refutation, here I shall explain it according to the system of the Prāsaṅgika Mādhyamaka. Furthermore, as it is stated in a sūtra, "Those are posited by the power of conception"; and in the commentary on the Catuḥśataka, "They exist only through the existence of conception," and so forth; and by the Lord in the Illumination of the Thought, "It is taught that phenomena are posited by the power of conception, so there are many statements that all phenomena are merely designated by conception and posited by the power of conception"; just as it is stated there, an example of all phenomena being designated by conception is: when a speckled rope is situated in a dim place, the mind arises in someone thinking, "This is a snake." At that time, although neither the collection of that rope nor any of its parts is a snake, the snake of thinking "This is a snake" regarding it appears as merely designated by conception.

Likewise, although the thought "I" arises in dependence upon these aggregates, neither the collection, nor the continuum, nor any part of the aggregates exists to be posited as the basis of characteristics of "I," and another entity different from the aggregates cannot be apprehended as the basis of characteristics of "I" either; therefore, that "I" is merely designated in dependence upon the aggregates, but is not established by its own intrinsic nature. Thus also it is said in the Noble One's Ratnāvalī: "A person is not earth, not water, not fire, not wind, not space, not consciousness, and not all of them; what person is there other than these?" Saying "not earth" through to "not consciousness" refutes positing each individual part of the six elements of a person as the self of a person, saying "not all of them" refutes positing the collection of the six elements as the self of a person, and the last line refutes a self with an entity different from the elements. Well then, as to how a person, an individual, is posited, from that same text it is said: "Because a person is an assembly of the six elements, it is not perfectly real; just as that is so, likewise each element is also not perfectly real, because it is an assembly." For that reason, other than a person being merely designated upon the assembly of its own six elements, it is not perfectly established. It demonstrates that just as that is so, the elements are also not perfectly established, because they are designated in dependence upon the assembly of their own respective parts.

source: སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ཅི་འདྲ་དེ་འདྲར་ཆོས་ཀུན་ཤེས། །ཞེས་དང༌། ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་རྒྱལ་པོ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། ཇི་ལྟར་ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་བདག་གི་འདུ་ཤེས་ནི། །ཤེས་པ་དེ་བཞིན་ཀུན་ལ་བློས་སྦྱར་བྱ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་སྦྱིན་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཐ་སྙད་བཏགས་པ་ཙམ་དུ་ཡོད་པ་མ་གཏོགས། རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་དགོས་པ་ལ་དགོངས་ནས་དངོས་པོ་ཅི་ལ་ཡང་མི་གནས་པར་སྦྱིན་པ་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་སོགས་གསུངས་སོ། །གནད་ཆེ་བ་འདི་ཤེས་དགོས་ཏེ། ཇི་སྲིད་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པ་ལས་མ་གྲོལ་ཅིང་སྟོང་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་མ་རྟོགས་པར་དེ་སྲིད་དུ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་དངོས་སུ་རྗེས་སུ་བཟུང་ཡང་ཐར་པ་ཐོབ་མི་ནུས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། མགོན་པོ་ཀླུ་སྒྲུབ་ཀྱིས། གང་དག་སྟོང་ཉིད་མི་ཤེས་པ། །དེ་དག་ཐར་པ་བསྟེན་མ་ཡིན། །འགྲོ་དྲུག་སྲིད་པའི་བཙོན་རར་ནི། །རྨོངས་པ་དེ་དག་འཁོར་བར་འགྱུར། །ཞེས་གསུངས་ཤིང༌། འཕགས་པ་ལྷས་ཀྱང༌། དངོས་པོའི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཅན་ལ་ཐར་པ་མེད་ཅེས་བཤད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང༌། གཞན་ཡང་མང་ངོ༌། །
translation: just as all sentient beings are, so should all phenomena be known"; and from the Samādhirāja too it is said: "Just as you know the perception of self, likewise you should apply the mind to all." Likewise, intending that one must know that phenomena such as generosity too, other than existing as merely conventionally designated, are empty of inherent nature, it is said "one should give generosity without abiding in any entity whatsoever" and so forth. One must know this great essential point: as long as one is not freed from being bound by apprehension of true existence and has not realized the meaning of emptiness, for that long, even if directly accepted by a buddha, one is incapable of attaining liberation; because the Protector Nāgārjuna said: "Those who do not know emptiness do not resort to liberation; those deluded ones will cycle in the prison of existence of the six migrations," and because Āryadeva also explained, "There is no liberation for one who has perception of entities," and there are many others as well.

In order to teach that this generation of the mind must be embraced by the view realizing selflessness, one should wish to entirely establish limitless sentient beings in non-abiding nirvāṇa in that way, and generate the mind thinking, "Even if they are so established, ultimately no sentient being whatsoever will have attained perfect nirvāṇa." Regarding the occurrence of the word "sorrow" here, sorrow is the two, karma and afflictions, as well as suffering; and passing beyond (bzlas/'das) that is nirvāṇa, which is being liberated or having passed beyond karma, afflictions, and suffering. Therefore, saying "passed beyond" (bzlas/'das) comes to mean both nirvāṇa and establishing them in it. This text teaches a concordant ultimate generation of the mind for ordinary beings, and it also teaches the actual ultimate generation of the mind, which exists only in noble ones.

Master Kamalaśīla explained a great deal concerning the view in this context, and since this was done for the sake of needing to know the meaning of the subsequent passages of this text being taught in conjunction with the view of emptiness, it is important; yet, fearing that it would become too much here, if I state just an illustration by summarizing it: all phenomena of affliction and purification are posited as existing merely conventionally, but when analyzed by reasoning that analyzes the ultimate, they cannot withstand analysis and their designated referents are not found; and regarding that, since the object of refutation is easy to refute if it is recognized, if I first state what the object of refutation is like: although there are generally many ways of asserting the object of refutation, here I shall explain it according to the system of the Prāsaṅgika Mādhyamaka. Furthermore, as it is stated in a sūtra, "Those are posited by the power of conception"; and in the commentary on the Catuḥśataka, "They exist only through the existence of conception," and so forth; and by the Lord in the Illumination of the Thought, "It is taught that phenomena are posited by the power of conception, so there are many statements that all phenomena are merely designated by conception and posited by the power of conception"; just as it is stated there, an example of all phenomena being designated by conception is: when a speckled rope is situated in a dim place, the mind arises in someone thinking, "This is a snake." At that time, although neither the collection of that rope nor any of its parts is a snake, the snake of thinking "This is a snake" regarding it appears as merely designated by conception.

Likewise, although the thought "I" arises in dependence upon these aggregates, neither the collection, nor the continuum, nor any part of the aggregates exists to be posited as the basis of characteristics of "I," and another entity different from the aggregates cannot be apprehended as the basis of characteristics of "I" either; therefore, that "I" is merely designated in dependence upon the aggregates, but is not established by its own intrinsic nature. Thus also it is said in the Noble One's Ratnāvalī: "A person is not earth, not water, not fire, not wind, not space, not consciousness, and not all of them; what person is there other than these?" Saying "not earth" through to "not consciousness" refutes positing each individual part of the six elements of a person as the self of a person, saying "not all of them" refutes positing the collection of the six elements as the self of a person, and the last line refutes a self with an entity different from the elements. Well then, as to how a person, an individual, is posited, from that same text it is said: "Because a person is an assembly of the six elements, it is not perfectly real; just as that is so, likewise each element is also not perfectly real, because it is an assembly." For that reason, other than a person being merely designated upon the assembly of its own six elements, it is not perfectly established. It demonstrates that just as that is so, the elements are also not perfectly established, because they are designated in dependence upon the assembly of their own respective parts.

In order to teach that this generation of the mind must be embraced by the view realizing selflessness, one should wish to entirely establish limitless sentient beings in non-abiding nirvāṇa in that way, and generate the mind thinking, "Even if they are so established, ultimately no sentient being whatsoever will have attained perfect nirvāṇa." Regarding the occurrence of the word "sorrow" here, sorrow is the two, karma and afflictions, as well as suffering; and passing beyond (bzlas/'das) that is nirvāṇa, which is being liberated or having passed beyond karma, afflictions, and suffering. Therefore, saying "passed beyond" (bzlas/'das) comes to mean both nirvāṇa and establishing them in it. This text teaches a concordant ultimate generation of the mind for ordinary beings, and it also teaches the actual ultimate generation of the mind, which exists only in noble ones.

Thus also it is said in the Noble One's Ratnāvalī: "A person is not earth, not water, not fire, not wind, not space, not consciousness, and not all of them; what person is there other than these?" Saying "not earth" through to "not consciousness" refutes positing each individual part of the six elements of a person as the self of a person, saying "not all of them" refutes positing the collection of the six elements as the self of a person, and the last line refutes a self with an entity different from the elements. For that reason, other than a person being merely designated upon the assembly of its own six elements, it is not perfectly established. It demonstrates that just as that is so, the elements are also not perfectly established, because they are designated in dependence upon the assembly of their own respective parts.

heading: ལྟ་བའི་དགག་བྱ་བཤད་པ།
translation: Why is that? If any bodhisattva engages in the perception of a sentient being as true as a sentient being, or engages in the perception as a living soul, that is, as possessing a living soul, or if the perception of a person as true, the apprehension of true existence, arises and engages, it is because that one is not suitable to be called a bodhisattva who knows the lack of true existence. Regarding what is said in the Madhyamakāvatāra that if the ultimate bodhicitta has not arisen in the mind-stream, one is not called an ultimate bodhisattva, that is the meaning of not being called an ultimate bodhisattva if one has never directly realized emptiness; whereas here, since there are bodhisattvas on the two paths of accumulation and preparation, it is explained from that perspective. The meaning of the word "sentient being" is possessing an intention that is entirely tormented in saṃsāra; and "living soul" is abiding until the completion of the homogenous similar lot of this life; and "person" is expressed by way of the mind-stream being filled with inferior latencies and falling into saṃsāra; and although "self" does not appear here, because it will appear below, "self" has the meaning of the basis for the arising of the apprehension of "I" thinking "I"—as is explained in the Annotated Commentary on the Śikṣāsamuccaya. Although those are synonyms for a person, if it is a person, it is not necessarily pervaded by possessing all those above word meanings, and between a sentient being and a person too, there is a difference in the breadth of their pervasion.

Likewise, one applies this to say that all phenomena of the aggregates and so forth are also not independently established, because they are designated in dependence upon their own respective parts and collections. One's own aggregate of form is designated in dependence upon the five limbs and so forth, and the limbs too are designated in dependence upon the aggregates which possess the parts and their own directional parts, and the secondary limbs such as fingers are also designated in dependence upon their own possessors of parts and their parts, and a vase is designated upon its own lip, base, belly, and so forth, and the lip, base, and so forth are also designated in dependence upon their own parts and the vase which possesses the parts; applying this to forms and so forth, consciousnesses too are designated in dependence upon earlier and later moments and their objects and so forth, and unconditioned phenomena too are designated in dependence upon their own individual bases of designation; this has been explained extensively elsewhere. Therefore, since there is no phenomenon that is not dependently arisen and not dependently designated, existing without being dependently designated is the measure of the object of refutation that is an extreme held by imputation. Thus also it is said in the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā: "Because there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not dependently arisen, therefore there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not empty." In short, although the self or person is not found when its designated referent is sought, conventionally agent and action are tenable like an illusion or an emanation; likewise, it is similar for all phenomena too, as it is said in the Saṃcayagāthā: "Just as the self is, so should all sentient beings be known;
