source: དེ་ལྟར་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་ནས་སྤྱོད་པ་ལ་སློབ་ཚུལ་ནི། སྦྱིན་པས་མཚོན་ནས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གཞན་རྣམས་ལའང་སློབ་པར་སྟོན་པས་དང་པོ་སྦྱིན་པ་ནི། ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་དངོས་པོ་ལ་མི་གནས་པར་སྦྱིན་པ་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་པའི་ དངོས་པོ་ནི་སྦྱིན་བྱའི་དངོས་པོ་སྟེ་དེ་དང་སྦྱིན་པ་དང་གང་ལ་སྦྱིན་པའི་འཁོར་གསུམ་གྱི་དངོས་པོ་གསུམ་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་མི་གནས་པར་སྦྱིན་པ་བྱེད་པའོ། །དེ་ནི་བྱམས་སྨོན་ལས། དངོས་པོ་ཀུན་ལ་མི་གནས་པར། །སེར་སྣ་མ་མཆིས་སྦྱིན་གཏོང་ཤོག །ཅེས་དང༌། གང་གིས་སྦྱིན་པ་གང་ལ་སྦྱིན། །སྦྱིན་པ་ཇི་ལྟར་མི་དམིགས་པའི། །སྦྱིན་པ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་དང༌། དབུ་མ་འཇུག་པ་ལས། སྦྱིན་པ་སྦྱིན་བྱ་ལེན་པོ་གཏོང་པོས་སྟོང༌། །འཇིག་རྟེན་འདས་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་ཅེས་བྱ། །གསུམ་པོ་དག་ལ་ཆགས་སྐྱེས་གྱུར་པ་དེ། །འཇིག་རྟེན་པ་ཡི་ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་ཅེས་བསྟན། །ཞེས་སྦྱིན་པའི་འཁོར་གསུམ་བདེན་མེད་དུ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཟིན་པའི་སྦྱིན་པ་དེ་འཇིག་རྟེན་ལས་འདས་པའི་སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དང༌། དེས་མ་ཟིན་པའི་སྦྱིན་པ་འཇིག་རྟེན་པའི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དུ་བཤད་དེ། སྔ་མ་འཕགས་པ་དང་ཕྱི་མ་སོ་སྐྱེ་ལ་ཡོད་པའོ། །ལམ་མ་ཞུགས་ན་སྦྱིན་པ་ཡོད་ཀྱང་སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་མེད་ཅིང་གཞན་ལྔ་ལའང་འདྲའོ། །སྦྱིན་པ་སྦྱིན་པ་ལ་བརྩོན་པ་ལྟ་བུ་ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་གནས་པར་བྱ་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་དང༌། དེའི་འཁོར་གསུམ་ལ་བདེན་པར་མི་ཞེན་པ་ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་དང༌། བདེན་མེད་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་བློ་ལ་སེམས་རྩེ་གཅིག་ཏུ་བྱེད་པ་ནི་སེམས་རབ་ཏུ་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་དུ་བཤད་དེ། ཕར་ཕྱིན་གཞན་ལའང་སྦྱར་བར་བྱའོ། །
translation: As for the way of training in conduct after having generated bodhicitta in that way: illustrating with generosity, it shows that one trains in the other perfections as well, so first, regarding generosity: "Moreover, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give generosity without abiding in entities"; here "entities" means the entity to be given, and it means giving generosity without abiding through clinging to true existence in the three entities of the three spheres—that, the act of giving, and to whom it is given. That is as it is said in Maitreya's Praṇidhāna: "Without abiding in any entities, may I give generosity without miserliness," and "Whoever gives, to whom it is given, and the generosity: the generosity wherein they are not apprehended in any way"; and from the Madhyamakāvatāra: "Generosity empty of given, receiver, and giver is called a supramundane perfection. When attachment to those three arises, it is taught as a mundane perfection"; thus, generosity endowed with the wisdom that directly realizes the three spheres of generosity as lacking true existence is explained as the supramundane perfection of generosity, and generosity not endowed with that is explained as the mundane perfection, the former existing in noble ones and the latter in ordinary beings. If one has not entered the path, even though one has generosity, one does not have the perfection of generosity, and it is similar for the other five too. Striving in giving generosity, for example, is explained as the meaning of "how should one abide", and not clinging to its three spheres as truly existent as the meaning of "how should one practice", and one-pointedly concentrating the mind on the awareness that realizes the lack of true existence as the meaning of "how should the mind be thoroughly controlled", and one should apply this to the other perfections as well.

Likewise, one applies this to say that all phenomena of the aggregates and so forth are also not independently established, because they are designated in dependence upon their own respective parts and collections. One's own aggregate of form is designated in dependence upon the five limbs and so forth, and the limbs too are designated in dependence upon the aggregates which possess the parts and their own directional parts, and the secondary limbs such as fingers are also designated in dependence upon their own possessors of parts and their parts, and a vase is designated upon its own lip, base, belly, and so forth, and the lip, base, and so forth are also designated in dependence upon their own parts and the vase which possesses the parts; applying this to forms and so forth, consciousnesses too are designated in dependence upon earlier and later moments and their objects and so forth, and unconditioned phenomena too are designated in dependence upon their own individual bases of designation; this has been explained extensively elsewhere. Therefore, since there is no phenomenon that is not dependently arisen and not dependently designated, existing without being dependently designated is the measure of the object of refutation that is an extreme held by imputation. Thus also it is said in the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā: "Because there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not dependently arisen, therefore there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not empty." Why is that? If any bodhisattva engages in the perception of a sentient being as true as a sentient being, or engages in the perception as a living soul, that is, as possessing a living soul, or if the perception of a person as true, the apprehension of true existence, arises and engages, it is because that one is not suitable to be called a bodhisattva who knows the lack of true existence. Regarding what is said in the Madhyamakāvatāra that if the ultimate bodhicitta has not arisen in the mind-stream, one is not called an ultimate bodhisattva, that is the meaning of not being called an ultimate bodhisattva if one has never directly realized emptiness; whereas here, since there are bodhisattvas on the two paths of accumulation and preparation, it is explained from that perspective. The meaning of the word "sentient being" is possessing an intention that is entirely tormented in saṃsāra; and "living soul" is abiding until the completion of the homogenous similar lot of this life; and "person" is expressed by way of the mind-stream being filled with inferior latencies and falling into saṃsāra; and although "self" does not appear here, because it will appear below, "self" has the meaning of the basis for the arising of the apprehension of "I" thinking "I"—as is explained in the Annotated Commentary on the Śikṣāsamuccaya. Although those are synonyms for a person, if it is a person, it is not necessarily pervaded by possessing all those above word meanings, and between a sentient being and a person too, there is a difference in the breadth of their pervasion.

Likewise, one applies this to say that all phenomena of the aggregates and so forth are also not independently established, because they are designated in dependence upon their own respective parts and collections. One's own aggregate of form is designated in dependence upon the five limbs and so forth, and the limbs too are designated in dependence upon the aggregates which possess the parts and their own directional parts, and the secondary limbs such as fingers are also designated in dependence upon their own possessors of parts and their parts, and a vase is designated upon its own lip, base, belly, and so forth, and the lip, base, and so forth are also designated in dependence upon their own parts and the vase which possesses the parts; applying this to forms and so forth, consciousnesses too are designated in dependence upon earlier and later moments and their objects and so forth, and unconditioned phenomena too are designated in dependence upon their own individual bases of designation; this has been explained extensively elsewhere. Therefore, since there is no phenomenon that is not dependently arisen and not dependently designated, existing without being dependently designated is the measure of the object of refutation that is an extreme held by imputation. Thus also it is said in the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā: "Because there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not dependently arisen, therefore there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not empty." In short, although the self or person is not found when its designated referent is sought, conventionally agent and action are tenable like an illusion or an emanation; likewise, it is similar for all phenomena too, as it is said in the Saṃcayagāthā: "Just as the self is, so should all sentient beings be known;

just as all sentient beings are, so should all phenomena be known"; and from the Samādhirāja too it is said: "Just as you know the perception of self, likewise you should apply the mind to all." Likewise, intending that one must know that phenomena such as generosity too, other than existing as merely conventionally designated, are empty of inherent nature, it is said "one should give generosity without abiding in any entity whatsoever" and so forth. One must know this great essential point: as long as one is not freed from being bound by apprehension of true existence and has not realized the meaning of emptiness, for that long, even if directly accepted by a buddha, one is incapable of attaining liberation; because the Protector Nāgārjuna said: "Those who do not know emptiness do not resort to liberation; those deluded ones will cycle in the prison of existence of the six migrations," and because Āryadeva also explained, "There is no liberation for one who has perception of entities," and there are many others as well.

Why is that? If any bodhisattva engages in the perception of a sentient being as true as a sentient being, or engages in the perception as a living soul, that is, as possessing a living soul, or if the perception of a person as true, the apprehension of true existence, arises and engages, it is because that one is not suitable to be called a bodhisattva who knows the lack of true existence. Regarding what is said in the Madhyamakāvatāra that if the ultimate bodhicitta has not arisen in the mind-stream, one is not called an ultimate bodhisattva, that is the meaning of not being called an ultimate bodhisattva if one has never directly realized emptiness; whereas here, since there are bodhisattvas on the two paths of accumulation and preparation, it is explained from that perspective. The meaning of the word "sentient being" is possessing an intention that is entirely tormented in saṃsāra; and "living soul" is abiding until the completion of the homogenous similar lot of this life; and "person" is expressed by way of the mind-stream being filled with inferior latencies and falling into saṃsāra; and although "self" does not appear here, because it will appear below, "self" has the meaning of the basis for the arising of the apprehension of "I" thinking "I"—as is explained in the Annotated Commentary on the Śikṣāsamuccaya. Although those are synonyms for a person, if it is a person, it is not necessarily pervaded by possessing all those above word meanings, and between a sentient being and a person too, there is a difference in the breadth of their pervasion.

translation: Explaining this slightly differentiated, it is said "one should give generosity without abiding through clinging to true existence in form, and in sound, and smell, and taste, and tactile object, and phenomena too," where forms are external forms, the objects of eye-consciousness, and sounds are objects of the ear, smells are objects of the nose, tastes are objects of the tongue, tactile objects are objects of the body, and phenomena are objects of the mental consciousness, which are all phenomena however they are and however many they are. Subhūti, since all phenomena, other than existing as merely conventionally designated, do not have even an atom of inherent establishment, apprehending them as inherently established is to cling perversely, so a bodhisattva must absolutely not abide in a perception that apprehends signs, clinging to them as inherently established. "Apprehending signs" is a synonym for the apprehension of true existence; an example of the great fault of being bound by the apprehension of true existence will be explained below.

Why is that? If any bodhisattva engages in the perception of a sentient being as true as a sentient being, or engages in the perception as a living soul, that is, as possessing a living soul, or if the perception of a person as true, the apprehension of true existence, arises and engages, it is because that one is not suitable to be called a bodhisattva who knows the lack of true existence. Regarding what is said in the Madhyamakāvatāra that if the ultimate bodhicitta has not arisen in the mind-stream, one is not called an ultimate bodhisattva, that is the meaning of not being called an ultimate bodhisattva if one has never directly realized emptiness; whereas here, since there are bodhisattvas on the two paths of accumulation and preparation, it is explained from that perspective. The meaning of the word "sentient being" is possessing an intention that is entirely tormented in saṃsāra; and "living soul" is abiding until the completion of the homogenous similar lot of this life; and "person" is expressed by way of the mind-stream being filled with inferior latencies and falling into saṃsāra; and although "self" does not appear here, because it will appear below, "self" has the meaning of the basis for the arising of the apprehension of "I" thinking "I"—as is explained in the Annotated Commentary on the Śikṣāsamuccaya. Although those are synonyms for a person, if it is a person, it is not necessarily pervaded by possessing all those above word meanings, and between a sentient being and a person too, there is a difference in the breadth of their pervasion.

heading: ཕྱིན་དྲུག་གི་སྤྱོད་པ་ལ་སློབ་ཚུལ།
translation: Although great merit arises from generosity and so forth that is bound by the apprehension of true existence, to show that it is certain that the merit is extraordinarily great if one practices generosity and so forth by way of being free from being bound by the apprehension of true existence: "Why is that? Subhūti, if any bodhisattva gives generosity without abiding, the limit and measure of the greatness of that heap of merit is not easy for others to apprehend, because it is difficult."

Likewise, one applies this to say that all phenomena of the aggregates and so forth are also not independently established, because they are designated in dependence upon their own respective parts and collections. One's own aggregate of form is designated in dependence upon the five limbs and so forth, and the limbs too are designated in dependence upon the aggregates which possess the parts and their own directional parts, and the secondary limbs such as fingers are also designated in dependence upon their own possessors of parts and their parts, and a vase is designated upon its own lip, base, belly, and so forth, and the lip, base, and so forth are also designated in dependence upon their own parts and the vase which possesses the parts; applying this to forms and so forth, consciousnesses too are designated in dependence upon earlier and later moments and their objects and so forth, and unconditioned phenomena too are designated in dependence upon their own individual bases of designation; this has been explained extensively elsewhere. Therefore, since there is no phenomenon that is not dependently arisen and not dependently designated, existing without being dependently designated is the measure of the object of refutation that is an extreme held by imputation. Thus also it is said in the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā: "Because there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not dependently arisen, therefore there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not empty." Why is that? If any bodhisattva engages in the perception of a sentient being as true as a sentient being, or engages in the perception as a living soul, that is, as possessing a living soul, or if the perception of a person as true, the apprehension of true existence, arises and engages, it is because that one is not suitable to be called a bodhisattva who knows the lack of true existence. Regarding what is said in the Madhyamakāvatāra that if the ultimate bodhicitta has not arisen in the mind-stream, one is not called an ultimate bodhisattva, that is the meaning of not being called an ultimate bodhisattva if one has never directly realized emptiness; whereas here, since there are bodhisattvas on the two paths of accumulation and preparation, it is explained from that perspective. The meaning of the word "sentient being" is possessing an intention that is entirely tormented in saṃsāra; and "living soul" is abiding until the completion of the homogenous similar lot of this life; and "person" is expressed by way of the mind-stream being filled with inferior latencies and falling into saṃsāra; and although "self" does not appear here, because it will appear below, "self" has the meaning of the basis for the arising of the apprehension of "I" thinking "I"—as is explained in the Annotated Commentary on the Śikṣāsamuccaya. Although those are synonyms for a person, if it is a person, it is not necessarily pervaded by possessing all those above word meanings, and between a sentient being and a person too, there is a difference in the breadth of their pervasion.

Likewise, one applies this to say that all phenomena of the aggregates and so forth are also not independently established, because they are designated in dependence upon their own respective parts and collections. One's own aggregate of form is designated in dependence upon the five limbs and so forth, and the limbs too are designated in dependence upon the aggregates which possess the parts and their own directional parts, and the secondary limbs such as fingers are also designated in dependence upon their own possessors of parts and their parts, and a vase is designated upon its own lip, base, belly, and so forth, and the lip, base, and so forth are also designated in dependence upon their own parts and the vase which possesses the parts; applying this to forms and so forth, consciousnesses too are designated in dependence upon earlier and later moments and their objects and so forth, and unconditioned phenomena too are designated in dependence upon their own individual bases of designation; this has been explained extensively elsewhere. Therefore, since there is no phenomenon that is not dependently arisen and not dependently designated, existing without being dependently designated is the measure of the object of refutation that is an extreme held by imputation. Thus also it is said in the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā: "Because there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not dependently arisen, therefore there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not empty." In short, although the self or person is not found when its designated referent is sought, conventionally agent and action are tenable like an illusion or an emanation; likewise, it is similar for all phenomena too, as it is said in the Saṃcayagāthā: "Just as the self is, so should all sentient beings be known;

just as all sentient beings are, so should all phenomena be known"; and from the Samādhirāja too it is said: "Just as you know the perception of self, likewise you should apply the mind to all." Likewise, intending that one must know that phenomena such as generosity too, other than existing as merely conventionally designated, are empty of inherent nature, it is said "one should give generosity without abiding in any entity whatsoever" and so forth. One must know this great essential point: as long as one is not freed from being bound by apprehension of true existence and has not realized the meaning of emptiness, for that long, even if directly accepted by a buddha, one is incapable of attaining liberation; because the Protector Nāgārjuna said: "Those who do not know emptiness do not resort to liberation; those deluded ones will cycle in the prison of existence of the six migrations," and because Āryadeva also explained, "There is no liberation for one who has perception of entities," and there are many others as well.

Why is that? If any bodhisattva engages in the perception of a sentient being as true as a sentient being, or engages in the perception as a living soul, that is, as possessing a living soul, or if the perception of a person as true, the apprehension of true existence, arises and engages, it is because that one is not suitable to be called a bodhisattva who knows the lack of true existence. Regarding what is said in the Madhyamakāvatāra that if the ultimate bodhicitta has not arisen in the mind-stream, one is not called an ultimate bodhisattva, that is the meaning of not being called an ultimate bodhisattva if one has never directly realized emptiness; whereas here, since there are bodhisattvas on the two paths of accumulation and preparation, it is explained from that perspective. The meaning of the word "sentient being" is possessing an intention that is entirely tormented in saṃsāra; and "living soul" is abiding until the completion of the homogenous similar lot of this life; and "person" is expressed by way of the mind-stream being filled with inferior latencies and falling into saṃsāra; and although "self" does not appear here, because it will appear below, "self" has the meaning of the basis for the arising of the apprehension of "I" thinking "I"—as is explained in the Annotated Commentary on the Śikṣāsamuccaya. Although those are synonyms for a person, if it is a person, it is not necessarily pervaded by possessing all those above word meanings, and between a sentient being and a person too, there is a difference in the breadth of their pervasion.

As for the way of training in conduct after having generated bodhicitta in that way: illustrating with generosity, it shows that one trains in the other perfections as well, so first, regarding generosity: "Moreover, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give generosity without abiding in entities"; here "entities" means the entity to be given, and it means giving generosity without abiding through clinging to true existence in the three entities of the three spheres—that, the act of giving, and to whom it is given. That is as it is said in Maitreya's Praṇidhāna: "Without abiding in any entities, may I give generosity without miserliness," and "Whoever gives, to whom it is given, and the generosity: the generosity wherein they are not apprehended in any way"; and from the Madhyamakāvatāra: "Generosity empty of given, receiver, and giver is called a supramundane perfection. When attachment to those three arises, it is taught as a mundane perfection"; thus, generosity endowed with the wisdom that directly realizes the three spheres of generosity as lacking true existence is explained as the supramundane perfection of generosity, and generosity not endowed with that is explained as the mundane perfection, the former existing in noble ones and the latter in ordinary beings. If one has not entered the path, even though one has generosity, one does not have the perfection of generosity, and it is similar for the other five too. Striving in giving generosity, for example, is explained as the meaning of "how should one abide", and not clinging to its three spheres as truly existent as the meaning of "how should one practice", and one-pointedly concentrating the mind on the awareness that realizes the lack of true existence as the meaning of "how should the mind be thoroughly controlled", and one should apply this to the other perfections as well.

translation: "Subhūti, what do you think of this?" means: Subhūti, how do you think, that is, consider, about this point? When asked, "The two kinds of form body of a Tathāgata are indeed endowed with the perfection of the major and minor marks, but do you think that one should view, that is, assert, [him] as a Tathāgata merely by there being the perfection of the major and minor marks?", Subhūti replied, "Bhagavān, he is not to be viewed like that." Slightly differentiating it: one does not view [him] as a Tathāgata merely by there being the perfection of the major and minor marks. "Why is that? Because whatever perfection of the major and minor marks of the form body the Tathāgata has spoken of, that itself is spoken of as existing conventionally like an illusion, but ultimately the perfection of the major and minor marks does not exist," he replied.

Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the sūtra, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names and technical terms in standard Sanskrit transliteration (Subhūti, Tathāgata, Dīpaṃkara, prajñāpāramitā) rather than translating them. Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own. Begin directly with the translation: do not write any introductory sentence such as "Here is the translation". Render each source line as exactly one line of continuous English prose, even where the source contains verse stanzas or lists; do not break it into several lines.

[2-16] translation already produced for this document:
As for the way of training in conduct after having generated bodhicitta in that way: illustrating with generosity, it shows that one trains in the other perfections as well, so first, regarding generosity: "Moreover, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give generosity without abiding in entities"; here "entities" means the entity to be given, and it means giving generosity without abiding through clinging to true existence in the three entities of the three spheres—that, the act of giving, and to whom it is given. That is as it is said in Maitreya's Praṇidhāna: "Without abiding in any entities, may I give generosity without miserliness," and "Whoever gives, to whom it is given, and the generosity: the generosity wherein they are not apprehended in any way"; and from the Madhyamakāvatāra: "Generosity empty of given, receiver, and giver is called a supramundane perfection. When attachment to those three arises, it is taught as a mundane perfection"; thus, generosity endowed with the wisdom that directly realizes the three spheres of generosity as lacking true existence is explained as the supramundane perfection of generosity, and generosity not endowed with that is explained as the mundane perfection, the former existing in noble ones and the latter in ordinary beings. If one has not entered the path, even though one has generosity, one does not have the perfection of generosity, and it is similar for the other five too. Striving in giving generosity, for example, is explained as the meaning of "how should one abide", and not clinging to its three spheres as truly existent as the meaning of "how should one practice", and one-pointedly concentrating the mind on the awareness that realizes the lack of true existence as the meaning of "how should the mind be thoroughly controlled", and one should apply this to the other perfections as well.

ཅུང་ཟད་ཕྱེ་སྟེ་བཤད་པ་ནི་གཟུགས་ལ་དང་སྒྲ་དང་དྲི་དང་རོ་དང་རེག་བྱ་དང་ཆོས་ལ་ཡང་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་མི་གནས་པར་སྦྱིན་པ་བྱའོ་ཞེས་པ་སྟེ། གཟུགས་ནི་ཕྱི་རོལ་གྱི་གཟུགས་མིག་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཡུལ་རྣམས་དང༌། སྒྲ་ནི་རྣ་བའི་ཡུལ། དྲི་ནི་སྣའི་ཡུལ། རོ་ནི་ལྕེའི་ཡུལ། རེག་བྱ་ནི་ལུས་ཀྱི་ཡུལ། ཆོས་ནི་ཡིད་ཀྱི་ཡུལ་ཏེ། ཇི་ལྟ་ཇི་སྙེད་པའི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་དོ། །རབ་འབྱོར་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཐ་སྙད་བཏགས་པ་ཙམ་དུ་ཡོད་པ་མ་གཏོགས། རང་བཞིན་གྱི་གྲུབ་པ་རྡུལ་ཙམ་ཡང་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རང་བཞིན་གྱི་གྲུབ་པར་འཛིན་པ་ནི་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཏུ་ཞེན་པ་ཡིན་པས། ཅི་ནས་ཀྱང་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་གྲུབ་པར་ཞེན་པའི་མཚན་མར་འཛིན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་ལ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་གནས་པར་མི་བྱའོ། །མཚན་མར་འཛིན་པ་ནི་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱི་མིང་གི་རྣམ་གྲངས་ཏེ། བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་ན་སྐྱོན་ཆེ་བའི་དཔེ་འོག་ཏུ་འཆད་དོ། །
[2-18] translation already produced for this document:
Explaining this slightly differentiated, it is said "one should give generosity without abiding through clinging to true existence in form, and in sound, and smell, and taste, and tactile object, and phenomena too," where forms are external forms, the objects of eye-consciousness, and sounds are objects of the ear, smells are objects of the nose, tastes are objects of the tongue, tactile objects are objects of the body, and phenomena are objects of the mental consciousness, which are all phenomena however they are and however many they are. Subhūti, since all phenomena, other than existing as merely conventionally designated, do not have even an atom of inherent establishment, apprehending them as inherently established is to cling perversely, so a bodhisattva must absolutely not abide in a perception that apprehends signs, clinging to them as inherently established. "Apprehending signs" is a synonym for the apprehension of true existence; an example of the great fault of being bound by the apprehension of true existence will be explained below.

heading: སྦྱིན་སོགས་ལས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་པར་བསྟན་པ།
translation: To show that the major and minor marks of the form body are false conventional modes of being that arise from a collection of conditions, like a drawn image, and are not a true nature, the Bhagavān said to Subhūti: "As much as there is the perfection of marks, to that extent there is falsity." If one asks, "If so, what is not false?", as much as the perfections of the major and minor marks lack true existence, to that extent it is not false but true; thus, one should view a Tathāgata as not having truly established marks and signs.

As for the way of training in conduct after having generated bodhicitta in that way: illustrating with generosity, it shows that one trains in the other perfections as well, so first, regarding generosity: "Moreover, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give generosity without abiding in entities"; here "entities" means the entity to be given, and it means giving generosity without abiding through clinging to true existence in the three entities of the three spheres—that, the act of giving, and to whom it is given. That is as it is said in Maitreya's Praṇidhāna: "Without abiding in any entities, may I give generosity without miserliness," and "Whoever gives, to whom it is given, and the generosity: the generosity wherein they are not apprehended in any way"; and from the Madhyamakāvatāra: "Generosity empty of given, receiver, and giver is called a supramundane perfection. When attachment to those three arises, it is taught as a mundane perfection"; thus, generosity endowed with the wisdom that directly realizes the three spheres of generosity as lacking true existence is explained as the supramundane perfection of generosity, and generosity not endowed with that is explained as the mundane perfection, the former existing in noble ones and the latter in ordinary beings. If one has not entered the path, even though one has generosity, one does not have the perfection of generosity, and it is similar for the other five too. Striving in giving generosity, for example, is explained as the meaning of "how should one abide", and not clinging to its three spheres as truly existent as the meaning of "how should one practice", and one-pointedly concentrating the mind on the awareness that realizes the lack of true existence as the meaning of "how should the mind be thoroughly controlled", and one should apply this to the other perfections as well.

Explaining this slightly differentiated, it is said "one should give generosity without abiding through clinging to true existence in form, and in sound, and smell, and taste, and tactile object, and phenomena too," where forms are external forms, the objects of eye-consciousness, and sounds are objects of the ear, smells are objects of the nose, tastes are objects of the tongue, tactile objects are objects of the body, and phenomena are objects of the mental consciousness, which are all phenomena however they are and however many they are. Subhūti, since all phenomena, other than existing as merely conventionally designated, do not have even an atom of inherent establishment, apprehending them as inherently established is to cling perversely, so a bodhisattva must absolutely not abide in a perception that apprehends signs, clinging to them as inherently established. "Apprehending signs" is a synonym for the apprehension of true existence; an example of the great fault of being bound by the apprehension of true existence will be explained below.

translation: This clears away the two extremes regarding the form body, because since the form body and its major and minor marks exist in the manner of being empty as false conventions, it clears away deprecation, and since it is taught that there are no truly established marks and signs, it clears away the extreme of exaggeration. Of those, the former teaches the form body and the latter teaches the dharma body, and principally the essence body.

As for the way of training in conduct after having generated bodhicitta in that way: illustrating with generosity, it shows that one trains in the other perfections as well, so first, regarding generosity: "Moreover, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give generosity without abiding in entities"; here "entities" means the entity to be given, and it means giving generosity without abiding through clinging to true existence in the three entities of the three spheres—that, the act of giving, and to whom it is given. That is as it is said in Maitreya's Praṇidhāna: "Without abiding in any entities, may I give generosity without miserliness," and "Whoever gives, to whom it is given, and the generosity: the generosity wherein they are not apprehended in any way"; and from the Madhyamakāvatāra: "Generosity empty of given, receiver, and giver is called a supramundane perfection. When attachment to those three arises, it is taught as a mundane perfection"; thus, generosity endowed with the wisdom that directly realizes the three spheres of generosity as lacking true existence is explained as the supramundane perfection of generosity, and generosity not endowed with that is explained as the mundane perfection, the former existing in noble ones and the latter in ordinary beings. If one has not entered the path, even though one has generosity, one does not have the perfection of generosity, and it is similar for the other five too. Striving in giving generosity, for example, is explained as the meaning of "how should one abide", and not clinging to its three spheres as truly existent as the meaning of "how should one practice", and one-pointedly concentrating the mind on the awareness that realizes the lack of true existence as the meaning of "how should the mind be thoroughly controlled", and one should apply this to the other perfections as well.

Explaining this slightly differentiated, it is said "one should give generosity without abiding through clinging to true existence in form, and in sound, and smell, and taste, and tactile object, and phenomena too," where forms are external forms, the objects of eye-consciousness, and sounds are objects of the ear, smells are objects of the nose, tastes are objects of the tongue, tactile objects are objects of the body, and phenomena are objects of the mental consciousness, which are all phenomena however they are and however many they are. Subhūti, since all phenomena, other than existing as merely conventionally designated, do not have even an atom of inherent establishment, apprehending them as inherently established is to cling perversely, so a bodhisattva must absolutely not abide in a perception that apprehends signs, clinging to them as inherently established. "Apprehending signs" is a synonym for the apprehension of true existence; an example of the great fault of being bound by the apprehension of true existence will be explained below.

translation: As for asking, "Will there appear in the future sentient beings who believe in and are devoted to this sūtra that explains such dharma and form bodies?", Subhūti asked: "Bhagavān, in the future time, in the final five hundred years, when the holy dharma is thoroughly destroyed," and so forth; in reply, the Bhagavān saying, "Subhūti, do not speak thus," means "Do not ask out of harboring doubts about whether or not such individuals will appear in the future."

As for the way of training in conduct after having generated bodhicitta in that way: illustrating with generosity, it shows that one trains in the other perfections as well, so first, regarding generosity: "Moreover, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give generosity without abiding in entities"; here "entities" means the entity to be given, and it means giving generosity without abiding through clinging to true existence in the three entities of the three spheres—that, the act of giving, and to whom it is given. That is as it is said in Maitreya's Praṇidhāna: "Without abiding in any entities, may I give generosity without miserliness," and "Whoever gives, to whom it is given, and the generosity: the generosity wherein they are not apprehended in any way"; and from the Madhyamakāvatāra: "Generosity empty of given, receiver, and giver is called a supramundane perfection. When attachment to those three arises, it is taught as a mundane perfection"; thus, generosity endowed with the wisdom that directly realizes the three spheres of generosity as lacking true existence is explained as the supramundane perfection of generosity, and generosity not endowed with that is explained as the mundane perfection, the former existing in noble ones and the latter in ordinary beings. If one has not entered the path, even though one has generosity, one does not have the perfection of generosity, and it is similar for the other five too. Striving in giving generosity, for example, is explained as the meaning of "how should one abide", and not clinging to its three spheres as truly existent as the meaning of "how should one practice", and one-pointedly concentrating the mind on the awareness that realizes the lack of true existence as the meaning of "how should the mind be thoroughly controlled", and one should apply this to the other perfections as well.

Explaining this slightly differentiated, it is said "one should give generosity without abiding through clinging to true existence in form, and in sound, and smell, and taste, and tactile object, and phenomena too," where forms are external forms, the objects of eye-consciousness, and sounds are objects of the ear, smells are objects of the nose, tastes are objects of the tongue, tactile objects are objects of the body, and phenomena are objects of the mental consciousness, which are all phenomena however they are and however many they are. Subhūti, since all phenomena, other than existing as merely conventionally designated, do not have even an atom of inherent establishment, apprehending them as inherently established is to cling perversely, so a bodhisattva must absolutely not abide in a perception that apprehends signs, clinging to them as inherently established. "Apprehending signs" is a synonym for the apprehension of true existence; an example of the great fault of being bound by the apprehension of true existence will be explained below.

translation: "Subhūti, even in the future time when the holy dharma will be destroyed, great bodhisattvas endowed with the training in higher ethical discipline, and endowed with the qualities of the training in higher meditative concentration, and endowed with the training in higher wisdom, that is, endowed with the three trainings, will definitely appear; and it is not that those great bodhisattvas have venerated and generated roots of virtue under merely a single Buddha in the past, but I know that they have venerated and generated roots of virtue under many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas." As for what Kamalaśīla calls "the final five hundred", a collection of five hundreds is five hundred, and the "five periods of five hundred" from the explanation "since it is renowned that the Bhagavān's teaching remains for five periods of five hundred" means the teaching remains for two thousand five hundred years. Regarding the measure of the duration of the teaching, there are many different ways of explaining it in the sūtras and commentaries: there are also explanations that the Sage's teaching remains for one thousand, two thousand, two thousand five hundred, and five thousand years, but their intended meanings do not contradict one another. The way they are not contradictory is that some intend the time of fruition and practice, and some intend the time of transmission, and some are evidently spoken from the perspective of the Noble Land. Such bodhisattvas are, for example, the Six Ornaments of Jambudvīpa in the Noble Land and so forth, and in Tibet, for example, Sakya Paṇḍita, Butön, and the Lord and his spiritual sons.

As for the way of training in conduct after having generated bodhicitta in that way: illustrating with generosity, it shows that one trains in the other perfections as well, so first, regarding generosity: "Moreover, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give generosity without abiding in entities"; here "entities" means the entity to be given, and it means giving generosity without abiding through clinging to true existence in the three entities of the three spheres—that, the act of giving, and to whom it is given. That is as it is said in Maitreya's Praṇidhāna: "Without abiding in any entities, may I give generosity without miserliness," and "Whoever gives, to whom it is given, and the generosity: the generosity wherein they are not apprehended in any way"; and from the Madhyamakāvatāra: "Generosity empty of given, receiver, and giver is called a supramundane perfection. When attachment to those three arises, it is taught as a mundane perfection"; thus, generosity endowed with the wisdom that directly realizes the three spheres of generosity as lacking true existence is explained as the supramundane perfection of generosity, and generosity not endowed with that is explained as the mundane perfection, the former existing in noble ones and the latter in ordinary beings. If one has not entered the path, even though one has generosity, one does not have the perfection of generosity, and it is similar for the other five too. Striving in giving generosity, for example, is explained as the meaning of "how should one abide", and not clinging to its three spheres as truly existent as the meaning of "how should one practice", and one-pointedly concentrating the mind on the awareness that realizes the lack of true existence as the meaning of "how should the mind be thoroughly controlled", and one should apply this to the other perfections as well.

Explaining this slightly differentiated, it is said "one should give generosity without abiding through clinging to true existence in form, and in sound, and smell, and taste, and tactile object, and phenomena too," where forms are external forms, the objects of eye-consciousness, and sounds are objects of the ear, smells are objects of the nose, tastes are objects of the tongue, tactile objects are objects of the body, and phenomena are objects of the mental consciousness, which are all phenomena however they are and however many they are. Subhūti, since all phenomena, other than existing as merely conventionally designated, do not have even an atom of inherent establishment, apprehending them as inherently established is to cling perversely, so a bodhisattva must absolutely not abide in a perception that apprehends signs, clinging to them as inherently established. "Apprehending signs" is a synonym for the apprehension of true existence; an example of the great fault of being bound by the apprehension of true existence will be explained below.

"Subhūti, what do you think of this?" means: Subhūti, how do you think, that is, consider, about this point? When asked, "The two kinds of form body of a Tathāgata are indeed endowed with the perfection of the major and minor marks, but do you think that one should view, that is, assert, [him] as a Tathāgata merely by there being the perfection of the major and minor marks?", Subhūti replied, "Bhagavān, he is not to be viewed like that." Slightly differentiating it: one does not view [him] as a Tathāgata merely by there being the perfection of the major and minor marks. "Why is that? Because whatever perfection of the major and minor marks of the form body the Tathāgata has spoken of, that itself is spoken of as existing conventionally like an illusion, but ultimately the perfection of the major and minor marks does not exist," he replied.

To show that the major and minor marks of the form body are false conventional modes of being that arise from a collection of conditions, like a drawn image, and are not a true nature, the Bhagavān said to Subhūti: "As much as there is the perfection of marks, to that extent there is falsity." If one asks, "If so, what is not false?", as much as the perfections of the major and minor marks lack true existence, to that extent it is not false but true; thus, one should view a Tathāgata as not having truly established marks and signs.

[2-26] source:
རབ་འབྱོར་མ་འོངས་པའི་དུས་སུ་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་འཇིག་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཚེ་ན་ཡང༌། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ལྷག་པ་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་བསླབ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང༌། ལྷག་པ་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་གྱི་བསླབ་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང༌། ལྷག་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་བསླབ་པ་སྟེ་བསླབ་པ་གསུམ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དག་ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་སྟེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་སྔོན་སངས་རྒྱས་གཅིག་ཙམ་ལ་བསྙེན་བཀུར་ཞིང་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པ་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། སངས་རྒྱས་འབུམ་ཕྲག་དུ་མ་ལ་བསྙེན་བཀུར་ཞིང་དགེ་རྩ་བསྐྱེད་པ་ཡིན་པར་ངས་མཁྱེན་ཏོ་ཞེས་པའོ། །ཀཱ་ཤཱིས་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཐ་མ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་ལྔའི་ཚོགས་ནི་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་སྟེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་བསྟན་པ་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་ལྔའི་བར་དུ་གནས་ཞེས་གྲགས་པས་ཞེས་བཤད་པའི་ ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་ལྔ་ནི་ལོ་ཉིས་སྟོང་ལྔ་བརྒྱའི་བར་དུ་བསྟན་པ་གནས་ཞེས་པའོ། །བསྟན་པའི་གནས་ཚད་ལ་མདོ་དང་དགོངས་འགྲེལ་དག་ལས་བཤད་ཚུལ་མི་འདྲ་བ་མང་སྟེ། ཐུབ་པའི་བསྟན་པ་ལོ་སྟོང་དང་ཉིས་སྟོང་དང་ཉིས་སྟོང་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་དང་ལྔ་སྟོང་དུ་གནས་པར་བཤད་པའང་ཡོད་དེ་དགོངས་པ་ནི་མི་འགལ་ལོ། །མི་འགལ་བའི་ཚུལ་ནི་འགའ་ཞིག་འབྲས་བུ་དང་སྒྲུབ་པའི་དུས་དང་འགའ་ཞིག་ནི་ལུང་གི་དུས་ལ་དགོངས་ཤིང༌། ལ་ལ་ནི་འཕགས་ཡུལ་གྱི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པར་མངོན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ནི་འཕགས་ཡུལ་གྱི་འཛམ་གླིང་རྒྱན་དྲུག་ལྟ་བུ་སོགས་དང༌། བོད་དུ་ནི་ས་པཎ་དང་བུ་སྟོན་དང་རྗེ་ཡབ་སྲས་ལྟ་བུའོ། །
[2-26] translation already produced for this document:
"Subhūti, even in the future time when the holy dharma will be destroyed, great bodhisattvas endowed with the training in higher ethical discipline, and endowed with the qualities of the training in higher meditative concentration, and endowed with the training in higher wisdom, that is, endowed with the three trainings, will definitely appear; and it is not that those great bodhisattvas have venerated and generated roots of virtue under merely a single Buddha in the past, but I know that they have venerated and generated roots of virtue under many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas." As for what Kamalaśīla calls "the final five hundred", a collection of five hundreds is five hundred, and the "five periods of five hundred" from the explanation "since it is renowned that the Bhagavān's teaching remains for five periods of five hundred" means the teaching remains for two thousand five hundred years. Regarding the measure of the duration of the teaching, there are many different ways of explaining it in the sūtras and commentaries: there are also explanations that the Sage's teaching remains for one thousand, two thousand, two thousand five hundred, and five thousand years, but their intended meanings do not contradict one another. The way they are not contradictory is that some intend the time of fruition and practice, and some intend the time of transmission, and some are evidently spoken from the perspective of the Noble Land. Such bodhisattvas are, for example, the Six Ornaments of Jambudvīpa in the Noble Land and so forth, and in Tibet, for example, Sakya Paṇḍita, Butön, and the Lord and his spiritual sons.

translation: If one asks the reason, "Why is that?", it is because those bodhisattvas will not engage in manifest conceptions that truly apprehend a self, a sentient being, a living being, and an individual. The meanings of the words "self", "individual", and so forth are as explained above; Kamalaśīla [states], "Apprehending that a self exists by thinking 'I am' is the conception of a self.

Work: རྡོར་གཅོད་ཀྱི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཐར་པར་བགྲོད་པའི་ལམ་བཟང་ཟབ་དོན་གསལ་བའི་ཉི་མ། (The Sun that Illuminates the Profound Meaning of the Excellent Path for Travelling to Freedom), author: ཅོ་ནེ་གྲགས་པ་བཤད་སྒྲུབ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[2-21] source:
སྦྱིན་སོགས་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ལས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གཟུགས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་པར་འགྱུར་ ཞིང༌། གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ནི་མཚན་དཔེས་བརྒྱན་པའོ། །
[2-21] translation already produced for this document:
From the collection of merit of generosity and so forth, the form body of a Buddha is accomplished, and the form body is adorned with the major and minor marks.

[2-22] source:
རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཅི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཞེས་པ་ནི། རབ་འབྱོར་ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་དོན་འདི་ལ་ཇི་ལྟར་ཡིན་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པ་སྟེ་བསམ། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ནི་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཡིན་མོད། འོན་ཀྱང་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཡོད་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་ལྟ་བ་སྟེ་འདོད་པར་བྱ་བ་ཡིན་སྙམ་འཾ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དེ་ནི་དེ་ལྟར་བལྟ་བ་མ་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་གསོལ་ཏེ། ཅུང་ཟད་དབྱེ་བ་ནི་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཡོད་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་བལྟ་བར་མི་བགྱིད་དེ། དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེ་ན། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུའི་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་གང་གསུངས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟར་ཡོད་པར་གསུངས་ཀྱི། དོན་དམ་པར་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་མ་མཆིས་པའི་སླད་དུའོ་ཞེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །
[2-22] translation already produced for this document:
"Subhūti, what do you think of this?" means: Subhūti, how do you think, that is, consider, about this point? When asked, "The two kinds of form body of a Tathāgata are indeed endowed with the perfection of the major and minor marks, but do you think that one should view, that is, assert, [him] as a Tathāgata merely by there being the perfection of the major and minor marks?", Subhūti replied, "Bhagavān, he is not to be viewed like that." Slightly differentiating it: one does not view [him] as a Tathāgata merely by there being the perfection of the major and minor marks. "Why is that? Because whatever perfection of the major and minor marks of the form body the Tathāgata has spoken of, that itself is spoken of as existing conventionally like an illusion, but ultimately the perfection of the major and minor marks does not exist," he replied.

[2-23] source:
གཟུགས་སྐུའི་མཚན་དཔེ་རྣམས་ནི་རི་མོས་བྲིས་པའི་གཟུགས་བརྙན་ལྟར་རྐྱེན་ཚོགས་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་བརྫུན་པའི་གནས་ཚུལ་ཡིན་གྱི། བདེན་པའི་རང་བཞིན་མིན་ནོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་ཅི་ཙམ་དུ་མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དེ་ཙམ་དུ་བརྫུན་ནོ་ཞེས་གསུངས། འོ་ན་མི་བརྫུན་པ་གང་ཞེ་ན། ཇི་ཙམ་དུ་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་རྣམས་བདེན་པར་མེད་པ་དེ་ཙམ་ནི་མི་བརྫུན་ཞིང་བདེན་ཏེ། དེ་ལྟར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པའི་མཚན་དང་མཚན་མ་མེད་པར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །
[2-23] translation already produced for this document:
To show that the major and minor marks of the form body are false conventional modes of being that arise from a collection of conditions, like a drawn image, and are not a true nature, the Bhagavān said to Subhūti: "As much as there is the perfection of marks, to that extent there is falsity." If one asks, "If so, what is not false?", as much as the perfections of the major and minor marks lack true existence, to that extent it is not false but true; thus, one should view a Tathāgata as not having truly established marks and signs.

[2-24] source:
འདིས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་ལ་མཐའ་གཉིས་སེལ་ཏེ། གཟུགས་སྐུ་དང་དེའི་མཚན་དཔེ་རྣམས་ཀུན་རྫོབ་བརྫུན་པའི་སྟོང་ཚུལ་དུ་ཡོད་པས་སྐུར་འདེབས་སེལ་ཞིང༌། བདེན་གྲུབ་ཀྱི་མཚན་དང་མཚན་མ་མེད་པར་བསྟན་པས་སྒྲོ་འདོགས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་སེལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེའི་སྔ་མས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་དང་ཕྱི་མས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་བསྟན་ཏེ་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་སྐུ་གཙོ་ཆེའོ། །
[2-24] translation already produced for this document:
This clears away the two extremes regarding the form body, because since the form body and its major and minor marks exist in the manner of being empty as false conventions, it clears away deprecation, and since it is taught that there are no truly established marks and signs, it clears away the extreme of exaggeration. Of those, the former teaches the form body and the latter teaches the dharma body, and principally the essence body.

[2-25] source:
དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཆོས་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་བཤད་པའི་མདོ་འདི་ལ་ཡིད་ཆེས་ཤིང་མོས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་མ་འོངས་པ་འབྱུང་ངམ་ཞེས་པ་ནི། རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་མ་འོངས་པའི་དུས་ལྔ་བརྒྱའི་ཐ་མ་ལ་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་རབ་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་འཇིག་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ན་སོགས་ཏེ། ལན་དུ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ཁྱོད་དེ་སྐད་མ་ཟེར་ཅིག་ཅེས་པ་ནི་ཁྱོད་མ་འོངས་པ་ན་དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་གང་ཟག་འབྱུང་མི་འབྱུང་ལ་དོགས་པ་མ་ཟ་ནས་མ་འདྲི་ཞིག་ཅེས་པའི་དོན་ནོ། །
[2-25] translation already produced for this document:
As for asking, "Will there appear in the future sentient beings who believe in and are devoted to this sūtra that explains such dharma and form bodies?", Subhūti asked: "Bhagavān, in the future time, in the final five hundred years, when the holy dharma is thoroughly destroyed," and so forth; in reply, the Bhagavān saying, "Subhūti, do not speak thus," means "Do not ask out of harboring doubts about whether or not such individuals will appear in the future."

[2-26] source:
རབ་འབྱོར་མ་འོངས་པའི་དུས་སུ་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་འཇིག་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཚེ་ན་ཡང༌། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ལྷག་པ་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་བསླབ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང༌། ལྷག་པ་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་གྱི་བསླབ་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང༌། ལྷག་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་བསླབ་པ་སྟེ་བསླབ་པ་གསུམ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དག་ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་སྟེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་སྔོན་སངས་རྒྱས་གཅིག་ཙམ་ལ་བསྙེན་བཀུར་ཞིང་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པ་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། སངས་རྒྱས་འབུམ་ཕྲག་དུ་མ་ལ་བསྙེན་བཀུར་ཞིང་དགེ་རྩ་བསྐྱེད་པ་ཡིན་པར་ངས་མཁྱེན་ཏོ་ཞེས་པའོ། །ཀཱ་ཤཱིས་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཐ་མ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་ལྔའི་ཚོགས་ནི་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་སྟེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་བསྟན་པ་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་ལྔའི་བར་དུ་གནས་ཞེས་གྲགས་པས་ཞེས་བཤད་པའི་ ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་ལྔ་ནི་ལོ་ཉིས་སྟོང་ལྔ་བརྒྱའི་བར་དུ་བསྟན་པ་གནས་ཞེས་པའོ། །བསྟན་པའི་གནས་ཚད་ལ་མདོ་དང་དགོངས་འགྲེལ་དག་ལས་བཤད་ཚུལ་མི་འདྲ་བ་མང་སྟེ། ཐུབ་པའི་བསྟན་པ་ལོ་སྟོང་དང་ཉིས་སྟོང་དང་ཉིས་སྟོང་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་དང་ལྔ་སྟོང་དུ་གནས་པར་བཤད་པའང་ཡོད་དེ་དགོངས་པ་ནི་མི་འགལ་ལོ། །མི་འགལ་བའི་ཚུལ་ནི་འགའ་ཞིག་འབྲས་བུ་དང་སྒྲུབ་པའི་དུས་དང་འགའ་ཞིག་ནི་ལུང་གི་དུས་ལ་དགོངས་ཤིང༌། ལ་ལ་ནི་འཕགས་ཡུལ་གྱི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པར་མངོན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ནི་འཕགས་ཡུལ་གྱི་འཛམ་གླིང་རྒྱན་དྲུག་ལྟ་བུ་སོགས་དང༌། བོད་དུ་ནི་ས་པཎ་དང་བུ་སྟོན་དང་རྗེ་ཡབ་སྲས་ལྟ་བུའོ། །
[2-26] translation already produced for this document:
"Subhūti, even in the future time when the holy dharma will be destroyed, great bodhisattvas endowed with the training in higher ethical discipline, and endowed with the qualities of the training in higher meditative concentration, and endowed with the training in higher wisdom, that is, endowed with the three trainings, will definitely appear; and it is not that those great bodhisattvas have venerated and generated roots of virtue under merely a single Buddha in the past, but I know that they have venerated and generated roots of virtue under many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas." As for what Kamalaśīla calls "the final five hundred", a collection of five hundreds is five hundred, and the "five periods of five hundred" from the explanation "since it is renowned that the Bhagavān's teaching remains for five periods of five hundred" means the teaching remains for two thousand five hundred years. Regarding the measure of the duration of the teaching, there are many different ways of explaining it in the sūtras and commentaries: there are also explanations that the Sage's teaching remains for one thousand, two thousand, two thousand five hundred, and five thousand years, but their intended meanings do not contradict one another. The way they are not contradictory is that some intend the time of fruition and practice, and some intend the time of transmission, and some are evidently spoken from the perspective of the Noble Land. Such bodhisattvas are, for example, the Six Ornaments of Jambudvīpa in the Noble Land and so forth, and in Tibet, for example, Sakya Paṇḍita, Butön, and the Lord and his spiritual sons.

heading: སྦྱིན་སོགས་ལས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་པར་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Apprehending that there is 'mine' is the conception of a sentient being. Thoroughly apprehending that very self for as long as a lifetime lasts is the conception of a living being. Apprehending it as transmigrating again and again into the transmigratory realms is the apprehension of an individual," he explained, and the meaning of apprehending "mine" is slightly different from the former [explanation]. The non-engagement of such coarse conceptions is intended for the occasion of having realized selflessness.

"Subhūti, even in the future time when the holy dharma will be destroyed, great bodhisattvas endowed with the training in higher ethical discipline, and endowed with the qualities of the training in higher meditative concentration, and endowed with the training in higher wisdom, that is, endowed with the three trainings, will definitely appear; and it is not that those great bodhisattvas have venerated and generated roots of virtue under merely a single Buddha in the past, but I know that they have venerated and generated roots of virtue under many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas." As for what Kamalaśīla calls "the final five hundred", a collection of five hundreds is five hundred, and the "five periods of five hundred" from the explanation "since it is renowned that the Bhagavān's teaching remains for five periods of five hundred" means the teaching remains for two thousand five hundred years. Regarding the measure of the duration of the teaching, there are many different ways of explaining it in the sūtras and commentaries: there are also explanations that the Sage's teaching remains for one thousand, two thousand, two thousand five hundred, and five thousand years, but their intended meanings do not contradict one another. The way they are not contradictory is that some intend the time of fruition and practice, and some intend the time of transmission, and some are evidently spoken from the perspective of the Noble Land. Such bodhisattvas are, for example, the Six Ornaments of Jambudvīpa in the Noble Land and so forth, and in Tibet, for example, Sakya Paṇḍita, Butön, and the Lord and his spiritual sons.

heading: སྦྱིན་སོགས་ལས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་པར་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Not only do they not engage through adherence to true existence as a self and so forth, they do not engage in the conception of form and so forth being true as conventional phenomena, nor do they engage through adherence to true existence in the conception of them not existing as phenomena; they will not engage in having such conceptions, nor in lacking conceptions.

"Subhūti, what do you think of this?" means: Subhūti, how do you think, that is, consider, about this point? When asked, "The two kinds of form body of a Tathāgata are indeed endowed with the perfection of the major and minor marks, but do you think that one should view, that is, assert, [him] as a Tathāgata merely by there being the perfection of the major and minor marks?", Subhūti replied, "Bhagavān, he is not to be viewed like that." [2-26] translation already produced for this document:
"Subhūti, even in the future time when the holy dharma will be destroyed, great bodhisattvas endowed with the training in higher ethical discipline, and endowed with the qualities of the training in higher meditative concentration, and endowed with the training in higher wisdom, that is, endowed with the three trainings, will definitely appear; and it is not that those great bodhisattvas have venerated and generated roots of virtue under merely a single Buddha in the past, but I know that they have venerated and generated roots of virtue under many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas." As for what Kamalaśīla calls "the final five hundred", a collection of five hundreds is five hundred, and the "five periods of five hundred" from the explanation "since it is renowned that the Bhagavān's teaching remains for five periods of five hundred" means the teaching remains for two thousand five hundred years. Regarding the measure of the duration of the teaching, there are many different ways of explaining it in the sūtras and commentaries: there are also explanations that the Sage's teaching remains for one thousand, two thousand, two thousand five hundred, and five thousand years, but their intended meanings do not contradict one another. The way they are not contradictory is that some intend the time of fruition and practice, and some intend the time of transmission, and some are evidently spoken from the perspective of the Noble Land. Such bodhisattvas are, for example, the Six Ornaments of Jambudvīpa in the Noble Land and so forth, and in Tibet, for example, Sakya Paṇḍita, Butön, and the Lord and his spiritual sons.

"Subhūti, what do you think of this?" means: Subhūti, how do you think, that is, consider, about this point? When asked, "The two kinds of form body of a Tathāgata are indeed endowed with the perfection of the major and minor marks, but do you think that one should view, that is, assert, [him] as a Tathāgata merely by there being the perfection of the major and minor marks?", Subhūti replied, "Bhagavān, he is not to be viewed like that." Slightly differentiating it: one does not view [him] as a Tathāgata merely by there being the perfection of the major and minor marks. "Why is that? Because whatever perfection of the major and minor marks of the form body the Tathāgata has spoken of, that itself is spoken of as existing conventionally like an illusion, but ultimately the perfection of the major and minor marks does not exist," he replied.

To show that the major and minor marks of the form body are false conventional modes of being that arise from a collection of conditions, like a drawn image, and are not a true nature, the Bhagavān said to Subhūti: "As much as there is the perfection of marks, to that extent there is falsity." If one asks, "If so, what is not false?", as much as the perfections of the major and minor marks lack true existence, to that extent it is not false but true; thus, one should view a Tathāgata as not having truly established marks and signs.

[2-26] translation already produced for this document:
"Subhūti, even in the future time when the holy dharma will be destroyed, great bodhisattvas endowed with the training in higher ethical discipline, and endowed with the qualities of the training in higher meditative concentration, and endowed with the training in higher wisdom, that is, endowed with the three trainings, will definitely appear; and it is not that those great bodhisattvas have venerated and generated roots of virtue under merely a single Buddha in the past, but I know that they have venerated and generated roots of virtue under many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas." As for what Kamalaśīla calls "the final five hundred", a collection of five hundreds is five hundred, and the "five periods of five hundred" from the explanation "since it is renowned that the Bhagavān's teaching remains for five periods of five hundred" means the teaching remains for two thousand five hundred years. Regarding the measure of the duration of the teaching, there are many different ways of explaining it in the sūtras and commentaries: there are also explanations that the Sage's teaching remains for one thousand, two thousand, two thousand five hundred, and five thousand years, but their intended meanings do not contradict one another. The way they are not contradictory is that some intend the time of fruition and practice, and some intend the time of transmission, and some are evidently spoken from the perspective of the Noble Land. Such bodhisattvas are, for example, the Six Ornaments of Jambudvīpa in the Noble Land and so forth, and in Tibet, for example, Sakya Paṇḍita, Butön, and the Lord and his spiritual sons.

translation: Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, one should not wrongly grasp dharma, because one should not grasp non-dharma either," if it is explained that "dharma" means not wrongly grasping the holy dharma of scriptural transmission through adherence to true existence, and "non-dharma" means not grasping what is not the holy dharma, such as non-Buddhist texts and so forth, it appears that this requires investigation.

"Subhūti, what do you think of this?" means: Subhūti, how do you think, that is, consider, about this point? When asked, "The two kinds of form body of a Tathāgata are indeed endowed with the perfection of the major and minor marks, but do you think that one should view, that is, assert, [him] as a Tathāgata merely by there being the perfection of the major and minor marks?", Subhūti replied, "Bhagavān, he is not to be viewed like that." Slightly differentiating it: one does not view [him] as a Tathāgata merely by there being the perfection of the major and minor marks. "Why is that? [2-26] translation already produced for this document:
"Subhūti, even in the future time when the holy dharma will be destroyed, great bodhisattvas endowed with the training in higher ethical discipline, and endowed with the qualities of the training in higher meditative concentration, and endowed with the training in higher wisdom, that is, endowed with the three trainings, will definitely appear; and it is not that those great bodhisattvas have venerated and generated roots of virtue under merely a single Buddha in the past, but I know that they have venerated and generated roots of virtue under many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas." As for what Kamalaśīla calls "the final five hundred", a collection of five hundreds is five hundred, and the "five periods of five hundred" from the explanation "since it is renowned that the Bhagavān's teaching remains for five periods of five hundred" means the teaching remains for two thousand five hundred years. Regarding the measure of the duration of the teaching, there are many different ways of explaining it in the sūtras and commentaries: there are also explanations that the Sage's teaching remains for one thousand, two thousand, two thousand five hundred, and five thousand years, but their intended meanings do not contradict one another. The way they are not contradictory is that some intend the time of fruition and practice, and some intend the time of transmission, and some are evidently spoken from the perspective of the Noble Land. Such bodhisattvas are, for example, the Six Ornaments of Jambudvīpa in the Noble Land and so forth, and in Tibet, for example, Sakya Paṇḍita, Butön, and the Lord and his spiritual sons.

heading: སྦྱིན་སོགས་ལས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་པར་བསྟན་པ།
translation: For that reason, the Tathāgata, intending that principle, stated: "This dharma discourse of scriptural transmission is like a raft; just as one knows that a raft is not needed when one has crossed to the other side of the water, for noble ones who have reached the culmination, if even dharmas such as the collections of scriptural transmissions, which are the methods for attaining the result, are to be cast aside and abandoned at the time of attaining the result, let alone casting aside what are not holy dharmas, which is established as a basis." That means that at the time of attaining the result, since the purpose has been accomplished, there is no need for such scriptural transmissions for one's own sake, and that one does not depend on them.

རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཅི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཞེས་པ་ནི། རབ་འབྱོར་ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་དོན་འདི་ལ་ཇི་ལྟར་ཡིན་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པ་སྟེ་བསམ། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ནི་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཡིན་མོད། འོན་ཀྱང་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཡོད་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་ལྟ་བ་སྟེ་འདོད་པར་བྱ་བ་ཡིན་སྙམ་འཾ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དེ་ནི་དེ་ལྟར་བལྟ་བ་མ་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་གསོལ་ཏེ། ཅུང་ཟད་དབྱེ་བ་ནི་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཡོད་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་བལྟ་བར་མི་བགྱིད་དེ། དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེ་ན། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུའི་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་གང་གསུངས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟར་ཡོད་པར་གསུངས་ཀྱི། དོན་དམ་པར་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་མ་མཆིས་པའི་སླད་དུའོ་ཞེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །

"Subhūti, what do you think of this?" means: Subhūti, how do you think, that is, consider, about this point? When asked, "The two kinds of form body of a Tathāgata are indeed endowed with the perfection of the major and minor marks, but do you think that one should view, that is, assert, [him] as a Tathāgata merely by there being the perfection of the major and minor marks?", Subhūti replied, "Bhagavān, he is not to be viewed like that." Slightly differentiating it: one does not view [him] as a Tathāgata merely by there being the perfection of the major and minor marks. "Why is that? Because whatever perfection of the major and minor marks of the form body the Tathāgata has spoken of, that itself is spoken of as existing conventionally like an illusion, but ultimately the perfection of the major and minor marks does not exist," he replied.

[2-23] source:

To show that the major and minor marks of the form body are false conventional modes of being that arise from a collection of conditions, like a drawn image, and are not a true nature, the Bhagavān said to Subhūti: "As much as there is the perfection of marks, to that extent there is falsity." If one asks, "If so, what is not false?", as much as the perfections of the major and minor marks lack true existence, to that extent it is not false but true; thus, one should view a Tathāgata as not having truly established marks and signs.

[2-26] source:
རབ་འབྱོར་མ་འོངས་པའི་དུས་སུ་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་འཇིག་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཚེ་ན་ཡང༌། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ལྷག་པ་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་བསླབ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང༌། ལྷག་པ་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་གྱི་བསླབ་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང༌། ལྷག་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་བསླབ་པ་སྟེ་བསླབ་པ་གསུམ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དག་ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་སྟེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་སྔོན་སངས་རྒྱས་གཅིག་ཙམ་ལ་བསྙེན་བཀུར་ཞིང་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པ་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། སངས་རྒྱས་འབུམ་ཕྲག་དུ་མ་ལ་བསྙེན་བཀུར་ཞིང་དགེ་རྩ་བསྐྱེད་པ་ཡིན་པར་ངས་མཁྱེན་ཏོ་ཞེས་པའོ། །ཀཱ་ཤཱིས་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཐ་མ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་ལྔའི་ཚོགས་ནི་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་སྟེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་བསྟན་པ་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་ལྔའི་བར་དུ་གནས་ཞེས་གྲགས་པས་ཞེས་བཤད་པའི་ ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་ལྔ་ནི་ལོ་ཉིས་སྟོང་ལྔ་བརྒྱའི་བར་དུ་བསྟན་པ་གནས་ཞེས་པའོ། །བསྟན་པའི་གནས་ཚད་ལ་མདོ་དང་དགོངས་འགྲེལ་དག་ལས་བཤད་ཚུལ་མི་འདྲ་བ་མང་སྟེ། ཐུབ་པའི་བསྟན་པ་ལོ་སྟོང་དང་ཉིས་སྟོང་དང་ཉིས་སྟོང་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་དང་ལྔ་སྟོང་དུ་གནས་པར་བཤད་པའང་ཡོད་དེ་དགོངས་པ་ནི་མི་འགལ་ལོ། །མི་འགལ་བའི་ཚུལ་ནི་འགའ་ཞིག་འབྲས་བུ་དང་སྒྲུབ་པའི་དུས་དང་འགའ་ཞིག་ནི་ལུང་གི་དུས་ལ་དགོངས་ཤིང༌། ལ་ལ་ནི་འཕགས་ཡུལ་གྱི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པར་མངོན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ནི་འཕགས་ཡུལ་གྱི་འཛམ་གླིང་རྒྱན་དྲུག་ལྟ་བུ་སོགས་དང༌། བོད་དུ་ནི་ས་པཎ་དང་བུ་སྟོན་དང་རྗེ་ཡབ་སྲས་ལྟ་བུའོ། །
[2-26] translation already produced for this document:
"Subhūti, even in the future time when the holy dharma will be destroyed, great bodhisattvas endowed with the training in higher ethical discipline, and endowed with the qualities of the training in higher meditative concentration, and endowed with the training in higher wisdom, that is, endowed with the three trainings, will definitely appear; and it is not that those great bodhisattvas have venerated and generated roots of virtue under merely a single Buddha in the past, but I know that they have venerated and generated roots of virtue under many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas." As for what Kamalaśīla calls "the final five hundred", a collection of five hundreds is five hundred, and the "five periods of five hundred" from the explanation "since it is renowned that the Bhagavān's teaching remains for five periods of five hundred" means the teaching remains for two thousand five hundred years. Regarding the measure of the duration of the teaching, there are many different ways of explaining it in the sūtras and commentaries: there are also explanations that the Sage's teaching remains for one thousand, two thousand, two thousand five hundred, and five thousand years, but their intended meanings do not contradict one another. The way they are not contradictory is that some intend the time of fruition and practice, and some intend the time of transmission, and some are evidently spoken from the perspective of the Noble Land. Such bodhisattvas are, for example, the Six Ornaments of Jambudvīpa in the Noble Land and so forth, and in Tibet, for example, Sakya Paṇḍita, Butön, and the Lord and his spiritual sons.

translation: Furthermore, when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "Do you think that there is any dharma that the Tathāgata has manifestly completely awakened to as unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening, and any dharma that he has spoken and taught?", Subhūti said in reply, "According to how I understand, that is, comprehend and know, the meaning spoken by the Bhagavān, ultimately there is no dharma whatsoever that has been awakened to and taught."
