Work: རྡོར་གཅོད་ཀྱི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཐར་པར་བགྲོད་པའི་ལམ་བཟང་ཟབ་དོན་གསལ་བའི་ཉི་མ། (The Sun that Illuminates the Profound Meaning of the Excellent Path for Travelling to Freedom), author: ཅོ་ནེ་གྲགས་པ་བཤད་སྒྲུབ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[2-21] source:
སྦྱིན་སོགས་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ལས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གཟུགས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་པར་འགྱུར་ ཞིང༌། གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ནི་མཚན་དཔེས་བརྒྱན་པའོ། །
[2-21] translation already produced for this document:
From the collection of merit of generosity and so forth, the form body of a Buddha is accomplished, and the form body is adorned with the major and minor marks.

[2-22] source:
རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཅི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཞེས་པ་ནི། རབ་འབྱོར་ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་དོན་འདི་ལ་ཇི་ལྟར་ཡིན་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་པ་སྟེ་བསམ། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ནི་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཡིན་མོད། འོན་ཀྱང་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཡོད་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་ལྟ་བ་སྟེ་འདོད་པར་བྱ་བ་ཡིན་སྙམ་འཾ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དེ་ནི་དེ་ལྟར་བལྟ་བ་མ་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་གསོལ་ཏེ། ཅུང་ཟད་དབྱེ་བ་ནི་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཡོད་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་བལྟ་བར་མི་བགྱིད་དེ། དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེ་ན། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུའི་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་གང་གསུངས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟར་ཡོད་པར་གསུངས་ཀྱི། དོན་དམ་པར་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་མ་མཆིས་པའི་སླད་དུའོ་ཞེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །
[2-22] translation already produced for this document:
"Subhūti, what do you think of this?" means: Subhūti, how do you think, that is, consider, about this point? When asked, "The two kinds of form body of a Tathāgata are indeed endowed with the perfection of the major and minor marks, but do you think that one should view, that is, assert, [him] as a Tathāgata merely by there being the perfection of the major and minor marks?", Subhūti replied, "Bhagavān, he is not to be viewed like that." Slightly differentiating it: one does not view [him] as a Tathāgata merely by there being the perfection of the major and minor marks. "Why is that? Because whatever perfection of the major and minor marks of the form body the Tathāgata has spoken of, that itself is spoken of as existing conventionally like an illusion, but ultimately the perfection of the major and minor marks does not exist," he replied.

[2-23] source:
གཟུགས་སྐུའི་མཚན་དཔེ་རྣམས་ནི་རི་མོས་བྲིས་པའི་གཟུགས་བརྙན་ལྟར་རྐྱེན་ཚོགས་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་བརྫུན་པའི་གནས་ཚུལ་ཡིན་གྱི། བདེན་པའི་རང་བཞིན་མིན་ནོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་ཅི་ཙམ་དུ་མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དེ་ཙམ་དུ་བརྫུན་ནོ་ཞེས་གསུངས། འོ་ན་མི་བརྫུན་པ་གང་ཞེ་ན། ཇི་ཙམ་དུ་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་རྣམས་བདེན་པར་མེད་པ་དེ་ཙམ་ནི་མི་བརྫུན་ཞིང་བདེན་ཏེ། དེ་ལྟར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པའི་མཚན་དང་མཚན་མ་མེད་པར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །
[2-23] translation already produced for this document:
To show that the major and minor marks of the form body are false conventional modes of being that arise from a collection of conditions, like a drawn image, and are not a true nature, the Bhagavān said to Subhūti: "As much as there is the perfection of marks, to that extent there is falsity." If one asks, "If so, what is not false?", as much as the perfections of the major and minor marks lack true existence, to that extent it is not false but true; thus, one should view a Tathāgata as not having truly established marks and signs.

[2-24] source:
འདིས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་ལ་མཐའ་གཉིས་སེལ་ཏེ། གཟུགས་སྐུ་དང་དེའི་མཚན་དཔེ་རྣམས་ཀུན་རྫོབ་བརྫུན་པའི་སྟོང་ཚུལ་དུ་ཡོད་པས་སྐུར་འདེབས་སེལ་ཞིང༌། བདེན་གྲུབ་ཀྱི་མཚན་དང་མཚན་མ་མེད་པར་བསྟན་པས་སྒྲོ་འདོགས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་སེལ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེའི་སྔ་མས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་དང་ཕྱི་མས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་བསྟན་ཏེ་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་སྐུ་གཙོ་ཆེའོ། །
[2-24] translation already produced for this document:
This clears away the two extremes regarding the form body, because since the form body and its major and minor marks exist in the manner of being empty as false conventions, it clears away deprecation, and since it is taught that there are no truly established marks and signs, it clears away the extreme of exaggeration. Of those, the former teaches the form body and the latter teaches the dharma body, and principally the essence body.

[2-25] source:
དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཆོས་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་བཤད་པའི་མདོ་འདི་ལ་ཡིད་ཆེས་ཤིང་མོས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་མ་འོངས་པ་འབྱུང་ངམ་ཞེས་པ་ནི། རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་མ་འོངས་པའི་དུས་ལྔ་བརྒྱའི་ཐ་མ་ལ་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་རབ་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་འཇིག་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ན་སོགས་ཏེ། ལན་དུ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ཁྱོད་དེ་སྐད་མ་ཟེར་ཅིག་ཅེས་པ་ནི་ཁྱོད་མ་འོངས་པ་ན་དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་གང་ཟག་འབྱུང་མི་འབྱུང་ལ་དོགས་པ་མ་ཟ་ནས་མ་འདྲི་ཞིག་ཅེས་པའི་དོན་ནོ། །
[2-25] translation already produced for this document:
As for asking, "Will there appear in the future sentient beings who believe in and are devoted to this sūtra that explains such dharma and form bodies?", Subhūti asked: "Bhagavān, in the future time, in the final five hundred years, when the holy dharma is thoroughly destroyed," and so forth; in reply, the Bhagavān saying, "Subhūti, do not speak thus," means "Do not ask out of harboring doubts about whether or not such individuals will appear in the future."

[2-26] source:
རབ་འབྱོར་མ་འོངས་པའི་དུས་སུ་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་འཇིག་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཚེ་ན་ཡང༌། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ལྷག་པ་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་བསླབ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང༌། ལྷག་པ་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་གྱི་བསླབ་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང༌། ལྷག་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་བསླབ་པ་སྟེ་བསླབ་པ་གསུམ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དག་ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་སྟེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་སྔོན་སངས་རྒྱས་གཅིག་ཙམ་ལ་བསྙེན་བཀུར་ཞིང་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པ་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། སངས་རྒྱས་འབུམ་ཕྲག་དུ་མ་ལ་བསྙེན་བཀུར་ཞིང་དགེ་རྩ་བསྐྱེད་པ་ཡིན་པར་ངས་མཁྱེན་ཏོ་ཞེས་པའོ། །ཀཱ་ཤཱིས་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཐ་མ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་ལྔའི་ཚོགས་ནི་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་སྟེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་བསྟན་པ་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་ལྔའི་བར་དུ་གནས་ཞེས་གྲགས་པས་ཞེས་བཤད་པའི་ ལྔ་བརྒྱ་ཕྲག་ལྔ་ནི་ལོ་ཉིས་སྟོང་ལྔ་བརྒྱའི་བར་དུ་བསྟན་པ་གནས་ཞེས་པའོ། །བསྟན་པའི་གནས་ཚད་ལ་མདོ་དང་དགོངས་འགྲེལ་དག་ལས་བཤད་ཚུལ་མི་འདྲ་བ་མང་སྟེ། ཐུབ་པའི་བསྟན་པ་ལོ་སྟོང་དང་ཉིས་སྟོང་དང་ཉིས་སྟོང་ལྔ་བརྒྱ་དང་ལྔ་སྟོང་དུ་གནས་པར་བཤད་པའང་ཡོད་དེ་དགོངས་པ་ནི་མི་འགལ་ལོ། །མི་འགལ་བའི་ཚུལ་ནི་འགའ་ཞིག་འབྲས་བུ་དང་སྒྲུབ་པའི་དུས་དང་འགའ་ཞིག་ནི་ལུང་གི་དུས་ལ་དགོངས་ཤིང༌། ལ་ལ་ནི་འཕགས་ཡུལ་གྱི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པར་མངོན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ནི་འཕགས་ཡུལ་གྱི་འཛམ་གླིང་རྒྱན་དྲུག་ལྟ་བུ་སོགས་དང༌། བོད་དུ་ནི་ས་པཎ་དང་བུ་སྟོན་དང་རྗེ་ཡབ་སྲས་ལྟ་བུའོ། །
[2-26] translation already produced for this document:
"Subhūti, even in the future time when the holy dharma will be destroyed, great bodhisattvas endowed with the training in higher ethical discipline, and endowed with the qualities of the training in higher meditative concentration, and endowed with the training in higher wisdom, that is, endowed with the three trainings, will definitely appear; and it is not that those great bodhisattvas have venerated and generated roots of virtue under merely a single Buddha in the past, but I know that they have venerated and generated roots of virtue under many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas." As for what Kamalaśīla calls "the final five hundred", a collection of five hundreds is five hundred, and the "five periods of five hundred" from the explanation "since it is renowned that the Bhagavān's teaching remains for five periods of five hundred" means the teaching remains for two thousand five hundred years. Regarding the measure of the duration of the teaching, there are many different ways of explaining it in the sūtras and commentaries: there are also explanations that the Sage's teaching remains for one thousand, two thousand, two thousand five hundred, and five thousand years, but their intended meanings do not contradict one another. The way they are not contradictory is that some intend the time of fruition and practice, and some intend the time of transmission, and some are evidently spoken from the perspective of the Noble Land. Such bodhisattvas are, for example, the Six Ornaments of Jambudvīpa in the Noble Land and so forth, and in Tibet, for example, Sakya Paṇḍita, Butön, and the Lord and his spiritual sons.

heading: སྦྱིན་སོགས་ལས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་པར་བསྟན་པ།
translation: If it is asked what the reason for that is: Even though it is explained that the Tathāgata manifestly realized it himself conventionally and awakened to it manifestly completely, or taught dharma conventionally, ultimately there is nothing that has been awakened to and no dharma whatsoever that has been taught by him, and their reality of emptiness of true existence cannot be grasped by a concordant conventional mind as it exists from the perspective of a noble one's meditative equipoise. It cannot be expressed by words in an unelaborated manner, because ultimately they are not dharma, and conventionally they are not non-dharma, that is, they are not non-existent; for that reason.

Furthermore, when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "Do you think that there is any dharma that the Tathāgata has manifestly completely awakened to as unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening, and any dharma that he has spoken and taught?", Subhūti said in reply, "According to how I understand, that is, comprehend and know, the meaning spoken by the Bhagavān, ultimately there is no dharma whatsoever that has been awakened to and taught."

heading: སྦྱིན་སོགས་ལས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་པར་བསྟན་པ།
translation: If it is asked what the reason for that is: he said in reply, "Because noble individuals are distinguished, that is, posited, by having manifestly realized the unconditioned reality, the emptiness of inherent existence of all phenomena." These [statements] are intended for the freedom from elaboration from the perspective of the exalted wisdom of the noble ones' meditative equipoise. Although it is necessary to assert that Tathāgatas have awakened conventionally, regarding their not having awakened ultimately: as stated above, except for being merely imputed in dependence upon their own aggregates, the Tathāgata is neither each individual undefiled aggregate of theirs, nor the collection, nor anything essentially different from those, because the protector Nāgārjuna stated in the twenty-second chapter of the Fundamental [Treatise on] Wisdom: "The Tathāgata is not the aggregates. He is not other than the aggregates. The aggregates are not in him, he is not in them. The Tathāgata does not possess the aggregates. What Tathāgata exists?" and "Without depending on the aggregates, there is no Tathāgata whatsoever." Here, rendering it into the first two lines of the text is for the sake of easy understanding. Thus, although his awakening and having awakened exist conventionally, they do not exist inherently; this is merely an illustration. The way that the dharma taught by him also does not exist inherently is from the Sūtra of Inconceivable Secrets: "The Tathāgata has not spoken even a single syllable.

heading: སྦྱིན་སོགས་ལས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་པར་བསྟན་པ།
translation: [and] will not speak." The meaning of this is from the twenty-fifth chapter of the Fundamental [Treatise on] Wisdom: "Elaborations are pacified and peaceful, and all apprehensions are pacified; the Buddhas have not taught any dharma whatsoever, to anyone, anywhere." In the commentary on that by Je [Tsongkhapa]: "When the Buddha Bhagavān passes beyond sorrow, where all elaborations are pacified, and dwells in the manner of not abiding in signs regarding the peaceful nature, at that time, because all apprehensions that apprehend signs are pacified and unapprehended, in terms of that, the Buddhas have not taught any thoroughly afflicted or completely purified dharma whatsoever, anywhere in the realms of gods or realms of humans," and "If it is asked, 'If the Buddha did not teach dharma to anyone, how do these various conventional expressions of the scriptures manifest?', he stated, '[Thinking] "The teacher taught dharma to us" arises from the own conceptions of those to be trained who, possessing the sleep of ignorance, are like dreamers dreaming;'" and it also appears in the Noble Sūtra Requested by Gaganagañja, so it is a point that is difficult to realize. As explained here, the meaning of the statement below as well that the Buddha did not teach dharma should be known. In short, "they are not dharma" refutes the extreme of permanence, and "they are not non-dharma" refutes the extreme of annihilation; having abandoned the two extremes of superimposition and deprecation, by [the statement] "noble individuals" and so forth, it is stated that great noble individuals are conventionally posited as manifestly realizing the reality of conditioned phenomena and manifestly actualizing nirvāṇa.

That means that at the time of attaining the result, since the purpose has been accomplished, there is no need for such scriptural transmissions for one's own sake, and that one does not depend on them.

[2-34] source:

[2-34] translation already produced for this document:
Furthermore, when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "Do you think that there is any dharma that the Tathāgata has manifestly completely awakened to as unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening, and any dharma that he has spoken and taught?", Subhūti said in reply, "According to how I understand, that is, comprehend and know, the meaning spoken by the Bhagavān, ultimately there is no dharma whatsoever that has been awakened to and taught."

heading: སྦྱིན་སོགས་ལས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་པར་བསྟན་པ།
source: དེ་ལྟར་སངས་རྒྱས་པ་དང་ཆོས་བསྟན་པ་སོགས་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་དོན་དམ་པར་མེད་ཀྱང་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཡོད་པས་སྦྱིན་པ་བྱིན་པ་ལས་ བསོད་ནམས་ཆེན་པོ་འབྱུང་མོད། དེ་ལས་ཀྱང་ཆོས་འདི་ལ་ཐོས་བསམ་སྒོམ་པའི་ཉམས་ལེན་བྱས་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་ལྷག་པར་ཆེའོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་ཁྱོད་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས། རིགས་ཀྱི་བུ་དང་བུ་མོ་གང་ ལ་ལ་ཞིག་གིས། ཇི་སྐད་དུ་མཛོད་ལས། གླིང་བཞི་པ་དང་ཉི་ཟླ་དང༌། །རི་རབ་དང་ནི་འདོད་ལྷ་དང༌། །ཚངས་པའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་སྟོང་ལ་ནི། །སྟོང་ནི་སྤྱི་ཕུད་ཡིན་པར་འདོད། །དེ་སྟོང་ལ་ནི་སྟོང་གཉིས་པ། །བར་མའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཁམས་ཡིན་ནོ། ། དེ་སྟོང་ལ་ནི་སྟོང་གསུམ་མོ། །
translation: Thus, although all phenomena such as having awakened and having taught dharma do not exist ultimately, because they exist conventionally, a great deal of merit indeed arises from giving generosity. Showing that the merit of having engaged in the practice of listening, reflecting, and meditating upon this dharma is exceptionally greater even than that: the Bhagavān [asked] Subhūti, "What do you think of this? If some son of noble family or daughter of noble family..." As it is stated in the Treasury: "A thousand [sets] of the four continents, suns and moons, / Mount Merus, desire realm gods, / and Brahmā worlds / is asserted to be a first-order thousand. / A thousand of those is a second-order thousand, / a middle world system. / A thousand of those is a third-order thousand."

[2-35] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེ་ན། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་རང་གིས་མངོན་དུ་བྱས་ཤིང༌། མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་པའམ། ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཆོས་བསྟན་པའོ་ཞེས་བཤད་ཀྱང་དོན་དམ་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་པ་དང་དེས་བསྟན་པའི་ཆོས་དེ་གང་ཡང་མེད་ཅིང་དེ་དག་གི་བདེན་སྟོང་ཆོས་ཉིད་དེ་འཕགས་པའི་མཉམ་གཞག་གི་གཟིགས་ངོ་ ན་ཡོད་པ་ལྟར་ཐ་སྙད་པའི་བློ་དོན་མཐུན་གྱིས་གཟུང་དུ་མ་མཆིས། ཚིག་གིས་སྤྲོས་མེད་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་དུ་བརྗོད་དུ་མ་མཆིས་ཏེ། དེ་དག་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་ཆོས་ཀྱང་མ་ལགས། ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཆོས་མ་མཆིས་པ་སྟེ་མེད་པ་ཡང་མ་ལགས་པའི་སླད་དུ་སྟེ་ དེའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །

If it is asked what the reason for that is: Even though it is explained that the Tathāgata manifestly realized it himself conventionally and awakened to it manifestly completely, or taught dharma conventionally, ultimately there is nothing that has been awakened to and no dharma whatsoever that has been taught by him, and their reality of emptiness of true existence cannot be grasped by a concordant conventional mind as it exists from the perspective of a noble one's meditative equipoise. As explained here, the meaning of the statement below as well that the Buddha did not teach dharma should be known. In short, "they are not dharma" refutes the extreme of permanence, and "they are not non-dharma" refutes the extreme of annihilation; having abandoned the two extremes of superimposition and deprecation, by [the statement] "noble individuals" and so forth, it is stated that great noble individuals are conventionally posited as manifestly realizing the reality of conditioned phenomena and manifestly actualizing nirvāṇa.

heading: སྦྱིན་སོགས་ལས་གཟུགས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་པར་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Just as it appears [there], he asked whether, having filled this great trichiliocosm with the seven precious substances—gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, emerald, sapphire, and red pearl—and given it as a gift to others, they would generate a great heap of merit. In reply, Subhūti stated that it would be a great heap of merit, and replied, "That heap of merit is posited as existing merely conventionally, like a dream and an illusion; however, that very heap of merit is not established as a heap ultimately, and conventionally the Tathāgata has designated and spoken of it as a 'heap of merit, a heap of merit'." This teaches the manner in which it is necessary to assert that although white and black actions, both those done previously and those to be done later, do not exist because the past has ceased and the future has not currently arisen, they must be asserted to exist in general, and the result must be asserted to arise from their very connection to the mental continuum of the agent, and so forth, making it a somewhat difficult point. The occurrence of [the word] "stanza" is intended to mean that although this is not a stanza in the Tibetan language, it is capable of being arranged as a stanza in the Sanskrit language. "Taking up" refers to holding the words in mind, and it is also permissible to apply it to having the physical volume in hand; "reciting aloud" and "perfectly explaining" refer to reciting the words and properly explaining [them]; and "teaching" is explained as properly teaching the meaning, and this is done from the perspective of what is primary.

If it is asked what the reason for that is: he said in reply, "Because noble individuals are distinguished, that is, posited, by having manifestly realized the unconditioned reality, the emptiness of inherent existence of all phenomena." These [statements] are intended for the freedom from elaboration from the perspective of the exalted wisdom of the noble ones' meditative equipoise. Although it is necessary to assert that Tathāgatas have awakened conventionally, regarding their not having awakened ultimately: as stated above, except for being merely imputed in dependence upon their own aggregates, the Tathāgata is neither each individual undefiled aggregate of theirs, nor the collection, nor anything essentially different from those, because the protector Nāgārjuna stated in the twenty-second chapter of the Fundamental [Treatise on] Wisdom: "The Tathāgata is not the aggregates. He is not other than the aggregates. The aggregates are not in him, he is not in them. The Tathāgata does not possess the aggregates. What Tathāgata exists?" and "Without depending on the aggregates, there is no Tathāgata whatsoever." Here, rendering it into the first two lines of the text is for the sake of easy understanding. Thus, although his awakening and having awakened exist conventionally, they do not exist inherently; this is merely an illustration. The way that the dharma taught by him also does not exist inherently is from the Sūtra of Inconceivable Secrets: "The Tathāgata has not spoken even a single syllable.

The meaning of this is from the twenty-fifth chapter of the Fundamental [Treatise on] Wisdom: "Elaborations are pacified and peaceful, and all apprehensions are pacified; the Buddhas have not taught any dharma whatsoever, to anyone, anywhere." In the commentary on that by Je [Tsongkhapa]: "When the Buddha Bhagavān passes beyond sorrow, where all elaborations are pacified, and dwells in the manner of not abiding in signs regarding the peaceful nature, at that time, because all apprehensions that apprehend signs are pacified and unapprehended, in terms of that, the Buddhas have not taught any thoroughly afflicted or completely purified dharma whatsoever, anywhere in the realms of gods or realms of humans," and "If it is asked, 'If the Buddha did not teach dharma to anyone, how do these various conventional expressions of the scriptures manifest?', he stated, '[Thinking] "The teacher taught dharma to us" arises from the own conceptions of those to be trained who, possessing the sleep of ignorance, are like dreamers dreaming;'" and it also appears in the Noble Sūtra Requested by Gaganagañja, so it is a point that is difficult to realize. As explained here, the meaning of the statement below as well that the Buddha did not teach dharma should be known. In short, "they are not dharma" refutes the extreme of permanence, and "they are not non-dharma" refutes the extreme of annihilation; having abandoned the two extremes of superimposition and deprecation, by [the statement] "noble individuals" and so forth, it is stated that great noble individuals are conventionally posited as manifestly realizing the reality of conditioned phenomena and manifestly actualizing nirvāṇa.

If it is asked what the reason for that is: he said in reply, "Because noble individuals are distinguished, that is, posited, by having manifestly realized the unconditioned reality, the emptiness of inherent existence of all phenomena." These [statements] are intended for the freedom from elaboration from the perspective of the exalted wisdom of the noble ones' meditative equipoise. Although it is necessary to assert that Tathāgatas have awakened conventionally, regarding their not having awakened ultimately: as stated above, except for being merely imputed in dependence upon their own aggregates, the Tathāgata is neither each individual undefiled aggregate of theirs, nor the collection, nor anything essentially different from those, because the protector Nāgārjuna stated in the twenty-second chapter of the Fundamental [Treatise on] Wisdom: "The Tathāgata is not the aggregates. He is not other than the aggregates. The aggregates are not in him, he is not in them. The Tathāgata does not possess the aggregates. What Tathāgata exists?" and "Without depending on the aggregates, there is no Tathāgata whatsoever." Here, rendering it into the first two lines of the text is for the sake of easy understanding. Thus, although his awakening and having awakened exist conventionally, they do not exist inherently; this is merely an illustration. As explained here, the meaning of the statement below as well that the Buddha did not teach dharma should be known. In short, "they are not dharma" refutes the extreme of permanence, and "they are not non-dharma" refutes the extreme of annihilation; having abandoned the two extremes of superimposition and deprecation, by [the statement] "noble individuals" and so forth, it is stated that great noble individuals are conventionally posited as manifestly realizing the reality of conditioned phenomena and manifestly actualizing nirvāṇa.

As explained here, the meaning of the statement below as well that the Buddha did not teach dharma should be known. In short, "they are not dharma" refutes the extreme of permanence, and "they are not non-dharma" refutes the extreme of annihilation; having abandoned the two extremes of superimposition and deprecation, by [the statement] "noble individuals" and so forth, it is stated that great noble individuals are conventionally posited as manifestly realizing the reality of conditioned phenomena and manifestly actualizing nirvāṇa.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: The Stream-Enterer not apprehending it as true and thinking, "I have obtained the result," is done from the perspective of having refuted the object of true grasping, but it does not teach that innate grasping is also non-existent. This is just as it is stated, "By this, the latter ones are also to be understood." The meaning is that it teaches that in order to obtain the true cessation that is the result of separation for the four such as the Stream-Enterer, one must certainly realize emptiness, and it is explained that with regard to that, having realized a lack of true existence, one must refute the conceived object of true grasping.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: Therefore, having or not having experienced the refutation of the conceived object of true grasping is posited by way of having or not having experienced the realization of a lack of true existence; as long as, when engaging in analyzing whether any basis is truly established or not, one is unable to pass beyond clinging to it as true, for that long one is unable to refute the conceived object of true grasping, and thus one is posited as being bound by true grasping. Likewise, this is just as was stated having applied it to the three—the Once-Returner, the Non-Returner, and the Arhat—and the meaning is just as before. Because there is a pair—the enterer and the one abiding in the result—for each of the four such as the Stream-Enterer, if differentiated individually they are the eight individuals, and if each pair is combined they become the four pairs of beings. Although there are many explanations regarding these four, just as an illustration: the true cessation that is the result of the ascetic practice of a Stream-Enterer is posited by way of having abandoned the three fetters abandoned by seeing; therefore, having obtained such a result, abiding in it is the Stream-Enterer abiding in the result, and striving and entering for the sake of obtaining it is called its enterer; and the three fetters are the view of the transitory collection, holding ethical discipline and observances as supreme, and afflicted doubt. Although there is an innate view of the transitory collection, here it is the artificial one. The result of a Once-Returner is posited from the perspective of having abandoned the sixth degree of desire realm afflictions; abiding in that is its one abiding in the result, and entering by striving for the sake of obtaining it is its enterer.

Just as it appears [there], he asked whether, having filled this great trichiliocosm with the seven precious substances—gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, emerald, sapphire, and red pearl—and given it as a gift to others, they would generate a great heap of merit. In reply, Subhūti stated that it would be a great heap of merit, and replied, "That heap of merit is posited as existing merely conventionally, like a dream and an illusion; however, that very heap of merit is not established as a heap ultimately, and conventionally the Tathāgata has designated and spoken of it as a 'heap of merit, a heap of merit'." This teaches the manner in which it is necessary to assert that although white and black actions, both those done previously and those to be done later, do not exist because the past has ceased and the future has not currently arisen, they must be asserted to exist in general, and the result must be asserted to arise from their very connection to the mental continuum of the agent, and so forth, making it a somewhat difficult point. The occurrence of [the word] "stanza" is intended to mean that although this is not a stanza in the Tibetan language, it is capable of being arranged as a stanza in the Sanskrit language. "Taking up" refers to holding the words in mind, and it is also permissible to apply it to having the physical volume in hand; "reciting aloud" and "perfectly explaining" refer to reciting the words and properly explaining [them]; and "teaching" is explained as properly teaching the meaning, and this is done from the perspective of what is primary.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: The result of a Non-Returner is posited from the perspective of having abandoned the ninth degree of desire realm afflictions; abiding in that and entering for its sake are its one abiding in the result and its enterer. The result of an Arhat is posited from the perspective of having abandoned the ninth degree of afflictions of the peak of existence; abiding in that result and entering for the sake of obtaining it are the Arhat abiding in the result and its enterer; and it appears that if done in detail, much would need to be explained. The meaning of a Once-Returner is that they still need to take birth one time in the desire realm, and a Non-Returner is that they do not need to take it. Furthermore, there is the way that the result of a Once-Returner is posited by way of having abandoned the five lower fetters, namely the three fetters, longing for sense pleasures, and malice, and the result of a Non-Returner is posited by way of having abandoned a portion of attachment, excitement, pride, and ignorance of the upper two realms; and these are only śrāvakas, and here in the Prāsaṅgika system they are all noble ones, whereas in the system of the Abhidharmasamuccaya there are ordinary beings among the enterers to stream-entry, but all the others are noble ones. In short, those four such as the Stream-Enterer do not cling as true to the obtainer and the result to be obtained, and although they may have innate true grasping, it is not the case that they have not refuted its conceived object, because for all of them the realization of emptiness has gone before.

As for the reason: although that Stream-Enterer ultimately has not entered into any object to be entered, because they have entered the stream of the path to liberation conventionally, they are called a 'Stream-Enterer'. Ultimately they have not entered anything, and they have not entered forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and dharmas having apprehended them ultimately.

[2-45] source:
རྗེས་འཇུག་པའི་ཊཱིཀ་ཆེན་དུ་སྐབས་འདི་དྲངས་ཏེ། རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་ཀྱིས་ཐོབ་མཁན་དང་ཐོབ་བྱའི་འབྲས་བུ་བདེན་པར་བཟུང་ནས། བདག་གིས་རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་ཐོབ་བོ་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ན། དེ་ཉིད་དེ་ཡི་བདག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་པས་གང་ཟག་དང་འབྲས་བུ་བདེན་འཛིན་བདག་འཛིན་དུ་གསུངས་པའི་དང་པོ་ནི། གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་འཛིན་དང༌། གཉིས་པ་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདག་འཛིན་ནོ། །
[2-45] translation already produced for this document:
Quoting this context in the Great Commentary that follows, it states, "If a Stream-Enterer, having apprehended the obtainer and the result to be obtained as true, were to think, 'I have obtained stream-entry', that very thing would become their grasping at a self"; and since this teaches that grasping at the person and the result as true is grasping at a self, the first is grasping at the self of persons, and the second is grasping at the self of phenomena.

[2-46] source:
རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་ཀྱིས་བདེན་པར་བཟུང་ནས་བདག་གིས་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་བོ་སྙམ་དུ་མི་འཛིན་པ་ནི། བདེན་འཛིན་གྱི་ཡུལ་སུན་ཕྱུང་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། ལྷན་སྐྱེས་ཀྱི་འཛིན་པ་ཡང་མེད་པར་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེས་ནི་ཕྱི་མ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཤེས་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །དོན་ནི་རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་སོགས་ བཞིའི་བྲལ་བའི་འབྲས་བུ་འགོག་བདེན་ཐོབ་པ་ལ་སྟོང་ཉིད་ངེས་པར་རྟོགས་དགོས་པར་བསྟན་ཅིང༌། དེ་ལ་བདེན་མེད་རྟོགས་ནས་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱི་ཞེན་ཡུལ་སུན་འབྱིན་དགོས་པར་བཤད་པའོ། །
[2-46] translation already produced for this document:
The Stream-Enterer not apprehending it as true and thinking, "I have obtained the result," is done from the perspective of having refuted the object of true grasping, but it does not teach that innate grasping is also non-existent. This is just as it is stated, "By this, the latter ones are also to be understood." The meaning is that it teaches that in order to obtain the true cessation that is the result of separation for the four such as the Stream-Enterer, one must certainly realize emptiness, and it is explained that with regard to that, having realized a lack of true existence, one must refute the conceived object of true grasping.

[2-47] source:
དེས་ན་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱི་ ཞེན་ཡུལ་སུན་འབྱིན་མྱོང་མ་མྱོང་ནི་བདེན་མེད་རྟོགས་མྱོང་མ་མྱོང་བའི་སྒོ་ནས་འཇོག་སྟེ། ཇི་སྲིད་གཞི་གང་ལ་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་བམ་མ་གྲུབ་སྙམ་དུ་དཔྱོད་པ་ཞུགས་པ་ན་བདེན་ཞེན་ལས་འདའ་མི་ནུས་པའི་བར་དེ་སྲིད་དུ་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱི་ཞེན་ཡུལ་ སུན་འབྱིན་མི་ནུས་པས་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པར་འཇོག་གོ །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ལན་ཅིག་ཕྱིར་འོང་བ་དང་ཕྱིར་མི་འོང་བ་དང་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་གསུམ་ལ་སྦྱར་ནས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་ཏེ་དོན་ནི་སྔར་ལྟར་རོ། །རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་སོགས་བཞི་ལ་ཞུགས་པ་དང་ འབྲས་གནས་ཟུང་རེ་ཡོད་པས་སོ་སོར་ཕྱེ་ན་གང་ཟག་ཡ་བརྒྱད་དང༌། ཟུང་རེ་བསྡོམས་ན་སྐྱེས་བུ་ཟུང་བཞིར་འགྱུར་རོ། །འདིའི་བཞི་ལ་བཤད་པ་མང་དུ་ཡོད་ཀྱང་མཚོན་ཙམ་ནི་རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་དགེ་སྦྱོང་ཚུལ་གྱི་འབྲས་བུ་འགོག་བདེན་ནི་ མཐོང་སྤངས་ཀུན་སྦྱོར་གསུམ་སྤངས་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བཞག་པས། དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་འབྲས་བུ་དེ་ཐོབ་ནས་དེ་ལ་གནས་པ་ལ་ནི་རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་འབྲས་གནས་དང༌། དེ་ཐོབ་ཕྱིར་དུ་འབད་ཅིང་ཞུགས་པ་ལ་དེའི་ཞུགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་ཞིང༌། ཀུན་སྦྱོར་གསུམ་ནི། འཇིག་ལྟ་དང་ཚུལ་ཞུགས་མཆོག་འཛིན་དང་ཐེ་ཚོམ་ཉོན་མོངས་ཅན་ནོ། །འཇིག་ལྟ་ལ་ལྷན་སྐྱེས་ཡོད་ཀྱང་འདིར་ཀུན་བཏགས་སོ། །ཕྱིར་འོང་གི་འབྲས་བུ་ནི་འདོད་ཉོན་དྲུག་པ་སྤངས་པའི་ཆ་ནས་འཇོག་ཅིང༌། དེ་ལ་གནས་པ་ནི་དེའི་ འབྲས་གནས་དང༌། དེ་ཐོབ་ཕྱིར་དུ་བརྩོན་པས་འཇུག་པ་ནི་དེའི་ཞུགས་པའོ། །
[2-47] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, having or not having experienced the refutation of the conceived object of true grasping is posited by way of having or not having experienced the realization of a lack of true existence; as long as, when engaging in analyzing whether any basis is truly established or not, one is unable to pass beyond clinging to it as true, for that long one is unable to refute the conceived object of true grasping, and thus one is posited as being bound by true grasping. Likewise, this is just as was stated having applied it to the three—the Once-Returner, the Non-Returner, and the Arhat—and the meaning is just as before. Because there is a pair—the enterer and the one abiding in the result—for each of the four such as the Stream-Enterer, if differentiated individually they are the eight individuals, and if each pair is combined they become the four pairs of beings. Although there are many explanations regarding these four, just as an illustration: the true cessation that is the result of the ascetic practice of a Stream-Enterer is posited by way of having abandoned the three fetters abandoned by seeing; therefore, having obtained such a result, abiding in it is the Stream-Enterer abiding in the result, and striving and entering for the sake of obtaining it is called its enterer; and the three fetters are the view of the transitory collection, holding ethical discipline and observances as supreme, and afflicted doubt. Although there is an innate view of the transitory collection, here it is the artificial one. The result of a Once-Returner is posited from the perspective of having abandoned the sixth degree of desire realm afflictions; abiding in that is its one abiding in the result, and entering by striving for the sake of obtaining it is its enterer.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: Then Subhūti said, 'Although I am conventionally an Arhat who has abandoned afflictions, I do not apprehend it as true, thinking "I am an Arhat,"' and 'If I were to apprehend it like that, I would also become afflicted, and thus I would not be an Arhat.'

[2-42] source:
ཐ་སྙད་དུ་དེ་ལྟར་ཡིན་ཀྱང་དོན་དམ་པར་ ཐོབ་པར་བྱར་མེད་དེ། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སྟོབས་བཅུ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དེ་དག་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་བཏགས་པ་ཙམ་མ་གཏོགས། དོན་དམ་པར་དེ་དག་མེད་པར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་པ་དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། འོན་ཀྱང་ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཙམ་དུ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ལ་དེ་དང་དེར་ཐ་སྙད་གདགས་སོ་ཞེས་པའོ། །
[2-42] translation already produced for this document:
Although it is like that conventionally, ultimately there is nothing to be obtained, because the Tathāgata has stated that "the dharmas of the Buddha", namely the ten powers of the Buddha and so forth, do not exist ultimately, except for being merely imputed conventionally; nevertheless, it means that the dharmas of the Buddha are designated as such and such merely relatively.

[2-43] source:
ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་འབྲས་བུ་གང་ཐོབ་པ་དེ་ཡང་བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་ནས་ཐོབ་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། དེ་མ་རྟོགས་པར་ཐོབ་པར་མི་ནུས་སོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། རབ་འབྱོར་རྒྱུན་ཏུ་ཞུགས་པས་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་བདག་གི་རྒྱུན་ཏུ་ཞུགས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་བོ་སྙམ་དུ་བདེན་པར་ཞེན་ཅིང་སེམས་སྙམ་མམ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ན། རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་དེ་ནི་མ་ལགས་སོ། །
[2-43] translation already produced for this document:
Teaching that even the results that the noble śrāvakas obtain are obtained having realized selflessness, and cannot be obtained without realizing it: when [the Bhagavān] asked, "Subhūti, does a Stream-Enterer think like this, clinging to it as true, 'I have obtained the result of a Stream-Enterer'?" Subhūti replied, "That is not so."

[2-44] source:

[2-47] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, having or not having experienced the refutation of the conceived object of true grasping is posited by way of having or not having experienced the realization of a lack of true existence; as long as, when engaging in analyzing whether any basis is truly established or not, one is unable to pass beyond clinging to it as true, for that long one is unable to refute the conceived object of true grasping, and thus one is posited as being bound by true grasping. Likewise, this is just as was stated having applied it to the three—the Once-Returner, the Non-Returner, and the Arhat—and the meaning is just as before. Because there is a pair—the enterer and the one abiding in the result—for each of the four such as the Stream-Enterer, if differentiated individually they are the eight individuals, and if each pair is combined they become the four pairs of beings. Although there are many explanations regarding these four, just as an illustration: the true cessation that is the result of the ascetic practice of a Stream-Enterer is posited by way of having abandoned the three fetters abandoned by seeing; therefore, having obtained such a result, abiding in it is the Stream-Enterer abiding in the result, and striving and entering for the sake of obtaining it is called its enterer; and the three fetters are the view of the transitory collection, holding ethical discipline and observances as supreme, and afflicted doubt. Although there is an innate view of the transitory collection, here it is the artificial one. The result of a Once-Returner is posited from the perspective of having abandoned the sixth degree of desire realm afflictions; abiding in that is its one abiding in the result, and entering by striving for the sake of obtaining it is its enterer.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: He explained, 'I am an Arhat, because the Bhagavān has conventionally prophesied of me: "The son of noble family Subhūti is the supreme of those without afflictions," but because I do not abide in anything ultimately, he does not prophesy me as "abiding without afflictions", because ultimately the object to be abided in, the act of abiding, and the abider are none of them established'; and this accords with the Prāsaṅgikas asserting true grasping as an affliction.

Teaching that even the results that the noble śrāvakas obtain are obtained having realized selflessness, and cannot be obtained without realizing it: when [the Bhagavān] asked, "Subhūti, does a Stream-Enterer think like this, clinging to it as true, 'I have obtained the result of a Stream-Enterer'?" Subhūti replied, "That is not so."

[2-44] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་ལ་རྒྱུན་ཏུ་ཞུགས་པ་དེ་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་འཇུག་བྱ་གང་ལ་ཡང་ཞུགས་པ་མ་མཆིས་ཀྱང༌། ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཐར་པའི་ལམ་རྒྱུན་ལ་ཞུགས་པས་ན་རྒྱུན་ཏུ་ཞུགས་པ་ཞེས་བགྱིའོ། །དོན་དམ་པར་གང་ལ་ཡང་མ་ཞུགས་ཤིང་གཟུགས་དང་སྒྲ་དང་དྲི་དང་རོ་དང་རེག་བྱ་དང་ཆོས་རྣམས་ལ་ཡང་དོན་དམ་པར་བཟུང་ནས་ཞུགས་པ་མ་ལགས་སོ། །
[2-44] translation already produced for this document:
As for the reason: although that Stream-Enterer ultimately has not entered into any object to be entered, because they have entered the stream of the path to liberation conventionally, they are called a 'Stream-Enterer'. Ultimately they have not entered anything, and they have not entered forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangible objects, and dharmas having apprehended them ultimately.

[2-45] source:
རྗེས་འཇུག་པའི་ཊཱིཀ་ཆེན་དུ་སྐབས་འདི་དྲངས་ཏེ། རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་ཀྱིས་ཐོབ་མཁན་དང་ཐོབ་བྱའི་འབྲས་བུ་བདེན་པར་བཟུང་ནས། བདག་གིས་རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་ཐོབ་བོ་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ན། དེ་ཉིད་དེ་ཡི་བདག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་པས་གང་ཟག་དང་འབྲས་བུ་བདེན་འཛིན་བདག་འཛིན་དུ་གསུངས་པའི་དང་པོ་ནི། གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་འཛིན་དང༌། གཉིས་པ་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདག་འཛིན་ནོ། །
[2-45] translation already produced for this document:
Quoting this context in the Great Commentary that follows, it states, "If a Stream-Enterer, having apprehended the obtainer and the result to be obtained as true, were to think, 'I have obtained stream-entry', that very thing would become their grasping at a self"; and since this teaches that grasping at the person and the result as true is grasping at a self, the first is grasping at the self of persons, and the second is grasping at the self of phenomena.

[2-46] source:
རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་ཀྱིས་བདེན་པར་བཟུང་ནས་བདག་གིས་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་བོ་སྙམ་དུ་མི་འཛིན་པ་ནི། བདེན་འཛིན་གྱི་ཡུལ་སུན་ཕྱུང་བའི་དབང་དུ་མཛད་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། ལྷན་སྐྱེས་ཀྱི་འཛིན་པ་ཡང་མེད་པར་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེས་ནི་ཕྱི་མ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཤེས་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །དོན་ནི་རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་སོགས་ བཞིའི་བྲལ་བའི་འབྲས་བུ་འགོག་བདེན་ཐོབ་པ་ལ་སྟོང་ཉིད་ངེས་པར་རྟོགས་དགོས་པར་བསྟན་ཅིང༌། དེ་ལ་བདེན་མེད་རྟོགས་ནས་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱི་ཞེན་ཡུལ་སུན་འབྱིན་དགོས་པར་བཤད་པའོ། །
[2-46] translation already produced for this document:
The Stream-Enterer not apprehending it as true and thinking, "I have obtained the result," is done from the perspective of having refuted the object of true grasping, but it does not teach that innate grasping is also non-existent. This is just as it is stated, "By this, the latter ones are also to be understood." The meaning is that it teaches that in order to obtain the true cessation that is the result of separation for the four such as the Stream-Enterer, one must certainly realize emptiness, and it is explained that with regard to that, having realized a lack of true existence, one must refute the conceived object of true grasping.

[2-47] source:
དེས་ན་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱི་ ཞེན་ཡུལ་སུན་འབྱིན་མྱོང་མ་མྱོང་ནི་བདེན་མེད་རྟོགས་མྱོང་མ་མྱོང་བའི་སྒོ་ནས་འཇོག་སྟེ། ཇི་སྲིད་གཞི་གང་ལ་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་བམ་མ་གྲུབ་སྙམ་དུ་དཔྱོད་པ་ཞུགས་པ་ན་བདེན་ཞེན་ལས་འདའ་མི་ནུས་པའི་བར་དེ་སྲིད་དུ་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱི་ཞེན་ཡུལ་ སུན་འབྱིན་མི་ནུས་པས་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པར་འཇོག་གོ །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ལན་ཅིག་ཕྱིར་འོང་བ་དང་ཕྱིར་མི་འོང་བ་དང་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་གསུམ་ལ་སྦྱར་ནས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་ཏེ་དོན་ནི་སྔར་ལྟར་རོ། །རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་སོགས་བཞི་ལ་ཞུགས་པ་དང་ འབྲས་གནས་ཟུང་རེ་ཡོད་པས་སོ་སོར་ཕྱེ་ན་གང་ཟག་ཡ་བརྒྱད་དང༌། ཟུང་རེ་བསྡོམས་ན་སྐྱེས་བུ་ཟུང་བཞིར་འགྱུར་རོ། །འདིའི་བཞི་ལ་བཤད་པ་མང་དུ་ཡོད་ཀྱང་མཚོན་ཙམ་ནི་རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་དགེ་སྦྱོང་ཚུལ་གྱི་འབྲས་བུ་འགོག་བདེན་ནི་ མཐོང་སྤངས་ཀུན་སྦྱོར་གསུམ་སྤངས་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བཞག་པས། དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་འབྲས་བུ་དེ་ཐོབ་ནས་དེ་ལ་གནས་པ་ལ་ནི་རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་འབྲས་གནས་དང༌། དེ་ཐོབ་ཕྱིར་དུ་འབད་ཅིང་ཞུགས་པ་ལ་དེའི་ཞུགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་ཞིང༌། ཀུན་སྦྱོར་གསུམ་ནི། འཇིག་ལྟ་དང་ཚུལ་ཞུགས་མཆོག་འཛིན་དང་ཐེ་ཚོམ་ཉོན་མོངས་ཅན་ནོ། །འཇིག་ལྟ་ལ་ལྷན་སྐྱེས་ཡོད་ཀྱང་འདིར་ཀུན་བཏགས་སོ། །ཕྱིར་འོང་གི་འབྲས་བུ་ནི་འདོད་ཉོན་དྲུག་པ་སྤངས་པའི་ཆ་ནས་འཇོག་ཅིང༌། དེ་ལ་གནས་པ་ནི་དེའི་ འབྲས་གནས་དང༌། དེ་ཐོབ་ཕྱིར་དུ་བརྩོན་པས་འཇུག་པ་ནི་དེའི་ཞུགས་པའོ། །
[2-47] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, having or not having experienced the refutation of the conceived object of true grasping is posited by way of having or not having experienced the realization of a lack of true existence; as long as, when engaging in analyzing whether any basis is truly established or not, one is unable to pass beyond clinging to it as true, for that long one is unable to refute the conceived object of true grasping, and thus one is posited as being bound by true grasping. Likewise, this is just as was stated having applied it to the three—the Once-Returner, the Non-Returner, and the Arhat—and the meaning is just as before. Because there is a pair—the enterer and the one abiding in the result—for each of the four such as the Stream-Enterer, if differentiated individually they are the eight individuals, and if each pair is combined they become the four pairs of beings. Although there are many explanations regarding these four, just as an illustration: the true cessation that is the result of the ascetic practice of a Stream-Enterer is posited by way of having abandoned the three fetters abandoned by seeing; therefore, having obtained such a result, abiding in it is the Stream-Enterer abiding in the result, and striving and entering for the sake of obtaining it is called its enterer; and the three fetters are the view of the transitory collection, holding ethical discipline and observances as supreme, and afflicted doubt. Although there is an innate view of the transitory collection, here it is the artificial one. The result of a Once-Returner is posited from the perspective of having abandoned the sixth degree of desire realm afflictions; abiding in that is its one abiding in the result, and entering by striving for the sake of obtaining it is its enterer.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།

translation: Teaching that not only do the object to be obtained, the act of obtaining, and the obtainer not exist ultimately, but ultimately there is also no dharma to be taken up: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, 'Do you think there is any dharma that I, the Tathāgata, ultimately took up from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in the past?', Subhūti replied, 'There is not.' Specifically mentioning the name of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara here is for the sake of remembering his kindness, because in the past when the Teacher became the youth Dharmamegha, in dependence on being blessed by the Buddha Dīpaṃkara he obtained the great acceptance that dharmas are non-arising, and upon actualizing the eighth ground, Dīpaṃkara prophesied to him, 'In the future time you will become the Buddha named Śākyamuni'; and this will be explained below. As for obtaining the great acceptance that dharmas are non-arising: because, having abandoned afflictions, one has obtained mastery in habituating to the non-conceptual pristine awareness that directly realizes the entire dharmatā, which is all dharmas being empty by nature, therefore, not only during the state of meditative equipoise, but also during post-meditation, all conditioned dharmas will appear exclusively as empty of true existence, like illusions. Because, through obtaining the acceptance that dharmas are non-arising, he directly saw all dharmas as lacking true existence, and saw whatever was prophesied, the result to be obtained, and becoming a Buddha all to be empty by nature, he had no clinging, thinking that he had taken up any truly established dharma from Dīpaṃkara.

Therefore, having or not having experienced the refutation of the conceived object of true grasping is posited by way of having or not having experienced the realization of a lack of true existence; as long as, when engaging in analyzing whether any basis is truly established or not, one is unable to pass beyond clinging to it as true, for that long one is unable to refute the conceived object of true grasping, and thus one is posited as being bound by true grasping. Because there is a pair—the enterer and the one abiding in the result—for each of the four such as the Stream-Enterer, if differentiated individually they are the eight individuals, and if each pair is combined they become the four pairs of beings. Although there are many explanations regarding these four, just as an illustration: the true cessation that is the result of the ascetic practice of a Stream-Enterer is posited by way of having abandoned the three fetters abandoned by seeing; therefore, having obtained such a result, abiding in it is the Stream-Enterer abiding in the result, and striving and entering for the sake of obtaining it is called its enterer; and the three fetters are the view of the transitory collection, holding ethical discipline and observances as supreme, and afflicted doubt. Although there is an innate view of the transitory collection, here it is the artificial one. The result of a Once-Returner is posited from the perspective of having abandoned the sixth degree of desire realm afflictions; abiding in that is its one abiding in the result, and entering by striving for the sake of obtaining it is its enterer.

translation: Furthermore, at the time of prophesying, the Buddha who is prophesied does not exist, and the person at the time of prophesying also does not exist at the time of having become a Buddha after being prophesied, but conventionally the persons from being prophesied to become a Buddha up to having become a Buddha are one continuum, and without differentiating the "I"s of past and future times, there is a general "I" that follows all the past and future "I"s, so with this in mind he prophesied: "You will become that Buddha in the future." For example, although the "I"s of past and future lives and of the early and later parts of this life are not this "I" of the present time, one is able to conventionally designate "I did it" for what they did, and "I will do it" for what they will do. Likewise, it is like when saying "I will make such and such a house, hat, clothes, shoes, and so forth", although the house and so forth do not exist at the time of speaking, one speaks thinking of what will occur in the future; so although it occurs merely conventionally, it does not arise by nature. If it were to arise by nature, one would have to assert that the house and so forth exist even at the time of thinking "I will make a house and so forth", but they do not. Intending such, the Sūtra Requested by Anavatapta states: "Whatever is born from conditions is unborn; it does not have the nature of birth. Whatever depends on conditions is explained to be empty; whoever knows emptiness is conscientious." And the previously explained reasonings establishing the lack of true existence should be applied here as well. If one understands well the way that although results arise from causes they do not arise by nature, one will understand the way that agents and actions are viable in the Mādhyamika system of emptiness of nature, and one will also find the Mādhyamika path of the union of appearance and emptiness.

The result of a Non-Returner is posited from the perspective of having abandoned the ninth degree of desire realm afflictions; abiding in that and entering for its sake are its one abiding in the result and its enterer. The result of an Arhat is posited from the perspective of having abandoned the ninth degree of afflictions of the peak of existence; abiding in that result and entering for the sake of obtaining it are the Arhat abiding in the result and its enterer; and it appears that if done in detail, much would need to be explained. The meaning of a Once-Returner is that they still need to take birth one time in the desire realm, and a Non-Returner is that they do not need to take it. Furthermore, there is the way that the result of a Once-Returner is posited by way of having abandoned the five lower fetters, namely the three fetters, longing for sense pleasures, and malice, and the result of a Non-Returner is posited by way of having abandoned a portion of attachment, excitement, pride, and ignorance of the upper two realms; and these are only śrāvakas, and here in the Prāsaṅgika system they are all noble ones, whereas in the system of the Abhidharmasamuccaya there are ordinary beings among the enterers to stream-entry, but all the others are noble ones. In short, those four such as the Stream-Enterer do not cling as true to the obtainer and the result to be obtained, and although they may have innate true grasping, it is not the case that they have not refuted its conceived object, because for all of them the realization of emptiness has gone before.

བདག་ནི་ དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བདག་ལ་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་རིགས་ཀྱི་བུ་རབ་འབྱོར་ནི་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མེད་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་མཆོག་ཏུ་ལུང་བསྟན་ལ། དོན་དམ་པར་ཅི་ལ་ཡང་མི་གནས་པས་ན་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མེད་པར་གནས་པར་ཞེས་ལུང་ མི་སྟོན་ཏེ། དོན་དམ་པར་གནས་བྱ་དང་གནས་བྱེད་དང་གནས་པ་པོ་གང་ཡང་མ་གྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེས་བཤད་དེ། ཐལ་འགྱུར་བས་བདེན་འཛིན་ཉོན་མོངས་སུ་བཞེད་པ་དང་མཐུན་ནོ། །

དོན་དམ་པར་ཐོབ་བྱ་དང་ཐོབ་བྱེད་དང་ཐོབ་མཁན་ རྣམས་མེད་པར་མ་ཟད། དོན་དམ་པར་བླང་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་ཀྱང་མེད་ཅེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ངས་སྔོན་སངས་རྒྱས་མར་མེ་མཛད་ལས་དོན་དམ་པར་གང་བླངས་པའི་ཆོས་དེ་གང་ཡང་ ཡོད་སྙམ་མམ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་དེ་མ་མཆིས་སོ་ཞེས་ལན་ཕུལ། འདིར་སྒོས་སུ་སངས་རྒྱས་མར་མེ་མཛད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ནས་སྨོས་པ་ནི། སྟོན་པས་སྔོན་གཞོན་ནུ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྤྲིན་དུ་གྱུར་པའི་ཚེ། སངས་རྒྱས་མར་མེ་ མཛད་ཀྱིས་བྱིན་གྱིས་བརླབས་པ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཆོས་ལ་བཟོད་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ཐོབ་ཅིང༌། ས་བརྒྱད་པ་མངོན་དུ་མཛད་པ་ན་མར་མེ་མཛད་ཀྱིས་ཁྱོད་ལ་མ་འོངས་པའི་དུས་སུ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཤཱཀྱ་ཐུབ་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་ལུང་བསྟན་པའི་བཀའ་དྲིན་དྲན་པའི་ཆེད་དེ་འོག་ཏུ་བཤད་པར་བྱའོ། །མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཆོས་ལ་བཟོད་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ཐོབ་པ་ནི། ཉོན་མོངས་སྤངས་ཤིང་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པའི་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐའ་དག་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་མི་རྟོག་ཡེ་ཤེས་ ལ་གོམས་པ་དབང་བསྒྱུར་ཐོབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་མཉམ་གཞག་གི་གནས་སྐབས་སུ་མ་ཟད། རྗེས་ཐོབ་ཀྱི་སྐབས་སུ་ཡང་འདུས་བྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་སྟོང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་འབའ་ཞིག་ཏུ་སྣང་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཆོས་ལ་བཟོད་པ་ཐོབ་པས་ ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་མེད་དུ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གཟིགས་ཤིང་གང་ལུང་བསྟན་པ་དང་ཐོབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་འཚང་རྒྱ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པར་གཟིགས་པས། མར་མེ་མཛད་ལས་བདེན་གྲུབ་ཀྱི་ཆོས་གང་ཡང་བླངས་སྙམ་ དུ་ཞེན་པ་མེད་དོ། །
[2-51] translation already produced for this document:
Teaching that not only do the object to be obtained, the act of obtaining, and the obtainer not exist ultimately, but ultimately there is also no dharma to be taken up: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, 'Do you think there is any dharma that I, the Tathāgata, ultimately took up from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in the past?', Subhūti replied, 'There is not.' Specifically mentioning the name of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara here is for the sake of remembering his kindness, because in the past when the Teacher became the youth Dharmamegha, in dependence on being blessed by the Buddha Dīpaṃkara he obtained the great acceptance that dharmas are non-arising, and upon actualizing the eighth ground, Dīpaṃkara prophesied to him, 'In the future time you will become the Buddha named Śākyamuni'; and this will be explained below. As for obtaining the great acceptance that dharmas are non-arising: because, having abandoned afflictions, one has obtained mastery in habituating to the non-conceptual pristine awareness that directly realizes the entire dharmatā, which is all dharmas being empty by nature, therefore, not only during the state of meditative equipoise, but also during post-meditation, all conditioned dharmas will appear exclusively as empty of true existence, like illusions. Because, through obtaining the acceptance that dharmas are non-arising, he directly saw all dharmas as lacking true existence, and saw whatever was prophesied, the result to be obtained, and becoming a Buddha all to be empty by nature, he had no clinging, thinking that he had taken up any truly established dharma from Dīpaṃkara.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: Teaching that in order to thus become a Buddha one needs to accomplish the pure field where one will become a Buddha: the Bhagavān said to Subhūti, "If any bodhisattva thinks and says with true grasping, 'I will ultimately accomplish the arrays of the field,' that statement speaks what is untrue."

The result of a Non-Returner is posited from the perspective of having abandoned the ninth degree of desire realm afflictions; abiding in that and entering for its sake are its one abiding in the result and its enterer. The result of an Arhat is posited from the perspective of having abandoned the ninth degree of afflictions of the peak of existence; abiding in that result and entering for the sake of obtaining it are the Arhat abiding in the result and its enterer; and it appears that if done in detail, much would need to be explained. The meaning of a Once-Returner is that they still need to take birth one time in the desire realm, and a Non-Returner is that they do not need to take it. Furthermore, there is the way that the result of a Once-Returner is posited by way of having abandoned the five lower fetters, namely the three fetters, longing for sense pleasures, and malice, and the result of a Non-Returner is posited by way of having abandoned a portion of attachment, excitement, pride, and ignorance of the upper two realms; and these are only śrāvakas, and here in the Prāsaṅgika system they are all noble ones, whereas in the system of the Abhidharmasamuccaya there are ordinary beings among the enterers to stream-entry, but all the others are noble ones. In short, those four such as the Stream-Enterer do not cling as true to the obtainer and the result to be obtained, and although they may have innate true grasping, it is not the case that they have not refuted its conceived object, because for all of them the realization of emptiness has gone before.

Teaching that not only do the object to be obtained, the act of obtaining, and the obtainer not exist ultimately, but ultimately there is also no dharma to be taken up: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, 'Do you think there is any dharma that I, the Tathāgata, ultimately took up from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in the past?', Subhūti replied, 'There is not.' Specifically mentioning the name of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara here is for the sake of remembering his kindness, because in the past when the Teacher became the youth Dharmamegha, in dependence on being blessed by the Buddha Dīpaṃkara he obtained the great acceptance that dharmas are non-arising, and upon actualizing the eighth ground, Dīpaṃkara prophesied to him, 'In the future time you will become the Buddha named Śākyamuni'; and this will be explained below. As for obtaining the great acceptance that dharmas are non-arising: because, having abandoned afflictions, one has obtained mastery in habituating to the non-conceptual pristine awareness that directly realizes the entire dharmatā, which is all dharmas being empty by nature, therefore, not only during the state of meditative equipoise, but also during post-meditation, all conditioned dharmas will appear exclusively as empty of true existence, like illusions. Because, through obtaining the acceptance that dharmas are non-arising, he directly saw all dharmas as lacking true existence, and saw whatever was prophesied, the result to be obtained, and becoming a Buddha all to be empty by nature, he had no clinging, thinking that he had taken up any truly established dharma from Dīpaṃkara.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: The reason for that is because the Tathāgata has taught that the perfect arrays of the field that is the place of becoming a Buddha are illusory arrays that have arisen from the gathering of multiple causes and conditions, but ultimately those arrays do not exist; however, since they exist to the perspective of an unexamined and unanalyzed mind, they are conventionally called "the arrays of the field." Not only Buddha fields, but all arrays of the environment and its inhabitants are designated upon the gathering of multiple parts, like a house and so forth. If all of them are broken down by reasoning down to the smallest particle, they will become nothing whatsoever; this is merely an illustration.

The result of an Arhat is posited from the perspective of having abandoned the ninth degree of afflictions of the peak of existence; abiding in that result and entering for the sake of obtaining it are the Arhat abiding in the result and its enterer; and it appears that if done in detail, much would need to be explained. The meaning of a Once-Returner is that they still need to take birth one time in the desire realm, and a Non-Returner is that they do not need to take it. Furthermore, there is the way that the result of a Once-Returner is posited by way of having abandoned the five lower fetters, namely the three fetters, longing for sense pleasures, and malice, and the result of a Non-Returner is posited by way of having abandoned a portion of attachment, excitement, pride, and ignorance of the upper two realms; and these are only śrāvakas, and here in the Prāsaṅgika system they are all noble ones, whereas in the system of the Abhidharmasamuccaya there are ordinary beings among the enterers to stream-entry, but all the others are noble ones. In short, those four such as the Stream-Enterer do not cling as true to the obtainer and the result to be obtained, and although they may have innate true grasping, it is not the case that they have not refuted its conceived object, because for all of them the realization of emptiness has gone before.

Teaching that not only do the object to be obtained, the act of obtaining, and the obtainer not exist ultimately, but ultimately there is also no dharma to be taken up: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, 'Do you think there is any dharma that I, the Tathāgata, ultimately took up from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in the past?', Subhūti replied, 'There is not.' Specifically mentioning the name of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara here is for the sake of remembering his kindness, because in the past when the Teacher became the youth Dharmamegha, in dependence on being blessed by the Buddha Dīpaṃkara he obtained the great acceptance that dharmas are non-arising, and upon actualizing the eighth ground, Dīpaṃkara prophesied to him, 'In the future time you will become the Buddha named Śākyamuni'; and this will be explained below. As for obtaining the great acceptance that dharmas are non-arising: because, having abandoned afflictions, one has obtained mastery in habituating to the non-conceptual pristine awareness that directly realizes the entire dharmatā, which is all dharmas being empty by nature, therefore, not only during the state of meditative equipoise, but also during post-meditation, all conditioned dharmas will appear exclusively as empty of true existence, like illusions. Because, through obtaining the acceptance that dharmas are non-arising, he directly saw all dharmas as lacking true existence, and saw whatever was prophesied, the result to be obtained, and becoming a Buddha all to be empty by nature, he had no clinging, thinking that he had taken up any truly established dharma from Dīpaṃkara.

The result of a Non-Returner is posited from the perspective of having abandoned the ninth degree of desire realm afflictions; abiding in that and entering for its sake are its one abiding in the result and its enterer. The result of an Arhat is posited from the perspective of having abandoned the ninth degree of afflictions of the peak of existence; abiding in that result and entering for the sake of obtaining it are the Arhat abiding in the result and its enterer; and it appears that if done in detail, much would need to be explained. The meaning of a Once-Returner is that they still need to take birth one time in the desire realm, and a Non-Returner is that they do not need to take it. Furthermore, there is the way that the result of a Once-Returner is posited by way of having abandoned the five lower fetters, namely the three fetters, longing for sense pleasures, and malice, and the result of a Non-Returner is posited by way of having abandoned a portion of attachment, excitement, pride, and ignorance of the upper two realms; and these are only śrāvakas, and here in the Prāsaṅgika system they are all noble ones, whereas in the system of the Abhidharmasamuccaya there are ordinary beings among the enterers to stream-entry, but all the others are noble ones. In short, those four such as the Stream-Enterer do not cling as true to the obtainer and the result to be obtained, and although they may have innate true grasping, it is not the case that they have not refuted its conceived object, because for all of them the realization of emptiness has gone before.

[2-49] source:
དེ་ནས་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་བདག་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཉོན་མོངས་སྤངས་པའི་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ལགས་ཀྱང༌། བདག་གིས་བདག་ནི་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་བདེན་པར་མི་འཛིན་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་དང༌། གལ་ཏེ་དེ་ལྟར་འཛིན་ན་ནི་བདག་ཀྱང་ཉོན་མོངས་ཅན་དུ་འགྱུར་བས་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་མ་ཡིན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[2-49] translation already produced for this document:
Then Subhūti said, 'Although I am conventionally an Arhat who has abandoned afflictions, I do not apprehend it as true, thinking "I am an Arhat,"' and 'If I were to apprehend it like that, I would also become afflicted, and thus I would not be an Arhat.'

[2-50] source:
བདག་ནི་ དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བདག་ལ་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་རིགས་ཀྱི་བུ་རབ་འབྱོར་ནི་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མེད་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་མཆོག་ཏུ་ལུང་བསྟན་ལ། དོན་དམ་པར་ཅི་ལ་ཡང་མི་གནས་པས་ན་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མེད་པར་གནས་པར་ཞེས་ལུང་ མི་སྟོན་ཏེ། དོན་དམ་པར་གནས་བྱ་དང་གནས་བྱེད་དང་གནས་པ་པོ་གང་ཡང་མ་གྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེས་བཤད་དེ། ཐལ་འགྱུར་བས་བདེན་འཛིན་ཉོན་མོངས་སུ་བཞེད་པ་དང་མཐུན་ནོ། །

He explained, 'I am an Arhat, because the Bhagavān has conventionally prophesied of me: "The son of noble family Subhūti is the supreme of those without afflictions," but because I do not abide in anything ultimately, he does not prophesy me as "abiding without afflictions", because ultimately the object to be abided in, the act of abiding, and the abider are none of them established'; and this accords with the Prāsaṅgikas asserting true grasping as an affliction.

[2-51] source:
དོན་དམ་པར་ཐོབ་བྱ་དང་ཐོབ་བྱེད་དང་ཐོབ་མཁན་ རྣམས་མེད་པར་མ་ཟད། དོན་དམ་པར་བླང་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་ཀྱང་མེད་ཅེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ངས་སྔོན་སངས་རྒྱས་མར་མེ་མཛད་ལས་དོན་དམ་པར་གང་བླངས་པའི་ཆོས་དེ་གང་ཡང་ ཡོད་སྙམ་མམ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་དེ་མ་མཆིས་སོ་ཞེས་ལན་ཕུལ། འདིར་སྒོས་སུ་སངས་རྒྱས་མར་མེ་མཛད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ནས་སྨོས་པ་ནི། སྟོན་པས་སྔོན་གཞོན་ནུ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྤྲིན་དུ་གྱུར་པའི་ཚེ། སངས་རྒྱས་མར་མེ་ མཛད་ཀྱིས་བྱིན་གྱིས་བརླབས་པ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཆོས་ལ་བཟོད་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ཐོབ་ཅིང༌། ས་བརྒྱད་པ་མངོན་དུ་མཛད་པ་ན་མར་མེ་མཛད་ཀྱིས་ཁྱོད་ལ་མ་འོངས་པའི་དུས་སུ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཤཱཀྱ་ཐུབ་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་ལུང་བསྟན་པའི་བཀའ་དྲིན་དྲན་པའི་ཆེད་དེ་འོག་ཏུ་བཤད་པར་བྱའོ། །མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཆོས་ལ་བཟོད་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ཐོབ་པ་ནི། ཉོན་མོངས་སྤངས་ཤིང་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པའི་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐའ་དག་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་མི་རྟོག་ཡེ་ཤེས་ ལ་གོམས་པ་དབང་བསྒྱུར་ཐོབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་མཉམ་གཞག་གི་གནས་སྐབས་སུ་མ་ཟད། རྗེས་ཐོབ་ཀྱི་སྐབས་སུ་ཡང་འདུས་བྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་སྟོང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་འབའ་ཞིག་ཏུ་སྣང་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཆོས་ལ་བཟོད་པ་ཐོབ་པས་ ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་མེད་དུ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གཟིགས་ཤིང་གང་ལུང་བསྟན་པ་དང་ཐོབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་འཚང་རྒྱ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པར་གཟིགས་པས། མར་མེ་མཛད་ལས་བདེན་གྲུབ་ཀྱི་ཆོས་གང་ཡང་བླངས་སྙམ་ དུ་ཞེན་པ་མེད་དོ། །
[2-51] translation already produced for this document:
Teaching that not only do the object to be obtained, the act of obtaining, and the obtainer not exist ultimately, but ultimately there is also no dharma to be taken up: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, 'Do you think there is any dharma that I, the Tathāgata, ultimately took up from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in the past?', Subhūti replied, 'There is not.' Specifically mentioning the name of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara here is for the sake of remembering his kindness, because in the past when the Teacher became the youth Dharmamegha, in dependence on being blessed by the Buddha Dīpaṃkara he obtained the great acceptance that dharmas are non-arising, and upon actualizing the eighth ground, Dīpaṃkara prophesied to him, 'In the future time you will become the Buddha named Śākyamuni'; and this will be explained below. As for obtaining the great acceptance that dharmas are non-arising: because, having abandoned afflictions, one has obtained mastery in habituating to the non-conceptual pristine awareness that directly realizes the entire dharmatā, which is all dharmas being empty by nature, therefore, not only during the state of meditative equipoise, but also during post-meditation, all conditioned dharmas will appear exclusively as empty of true existence, like illusions. Because, through obtaining the acceptance that dharmas are non-arising, he directly saw all dharmas as lacking true existence, and saw whatever was prophesied, the result to be obtained, and becoming a Buddha all to be empty by nature, he had no clinging, thinking that he had taken up any truly established dharma from Dīpaṃkara.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: They should generate the mind without abiding in anything ultimately and without abiding with true grasping in any dharma of form, sound, and so forth.

[2-48] source:
ཕྱི་མི་འོང་གི་འབྲས་བུ་ནི་འདོད་ཉོན་དགུ་པ་སྤངས་པའི་ཆ་ནས་འཇོག་ཅིང༌། དེ་ལ་གནས་པ་དང་དེའི་ཆེད་དུ་ཞུགས་པ་ནི་འབྲས་གནས་དང་ཞུགས་པའོ། །དགྲ་བཅོམ་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ནི་སྲིད་རྩེའི་ཉོན་མོངས་དགུ་པ་སྤངས་པའི་ཆ་ནས་འཇོག་ཅིང༌། འབྲས་བུ་དེ་ལ་གནས་པ་དང་དེ་ཐོབ་ཕྱིར་ཞུགས་པ་ནི་དགྲ་བཅོམ་འབྲས་གནས་དང་ཞུགས་པ་སྟེ་ཞིབ་ན་མང་དུ་བཤད་དགོས་པར་སྣང་ངོ༌། །ལན་ཅིག་ཕྱིར་འོང་བའི་དོན་ནི་འདོད་ཁམས་སུ་ད་དུང་སྐྱེ་བ་ལན་གཅིག་ལེན་དགོས་པ་དང༌། ཕྱིར་མི་འོང་བ་ནི་དེ་ལེན་མི་དགོས་པའོ། །གཞན་ཡང་ཕྱིར་འོང་གི་འབྲས་བུ་ནི། ཀུན་སྦྱོར་གསུམ་དང་འདོད་པ་ལ་འདུན་པ་དང་གནོད་སེམས་ཏེ་ཐ་མའི་ཆ་མཐུན་ལྔ་སྤངས་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་འཇོག་པ་དང༌། ཕྱིར་མི་འོང་གི་འབྲས་བུ་ནི་ཁམས་གོང་མ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་འདོད་ཆགས་དང་རྒོད་པ་དང་ང་རྒྱལ་དང་མ་རིག་པའི་ཕྱོགས་གཅིག་སྤངས་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་འཇོག་ཚུལ་ཡོད་ཅིང༌། འདི་དག་རྣམས་ཉན་ཐོས་ཁོ་ན་སྟེ། འདིར་ཐལ་འགྱུར་བའི་ལུགས་སུ་ཐམས་ཅད་འཕགས་པ་ཡིན་ལ། ཀུན་བཏུས་ཀྱི་ལུགས་ལ་རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་ཞུགས་པ་ལ་སོ་སྐྱེ་ཡོད་ཀྱང་གཞན་ཐམས་ཅད་འཕགས་པའོ། །མདོར་ན་རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་སོགས་བཞི་པོ་དེས་ཐོབ་མཁན་དང་ཐོབ་བྱའི་འབྲས་བུ་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་མི་བྱེད་ཅིང༌། བདེན་འཛིན་ལྷན་སྐྱེས་ཡོད་སྲིད་ཀྱང་དེའི་ཞེན་ཡུལ་སུན་མ་ཕྱུང་བ་ནི་མེད་དེ། དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་སྟོང་ཉིད་རྟོགས་པ་སྔོན་དུ་སོང་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[2-48] translation already produced for this document:
The result of a Non-Returner is posited from the perspective of having abandoned the ninth degree of desire realm afflictions; abiding in that and entering for its sake are its one abiding in the result and its enterer. The result of an Arhat is posited from the perspective of having abandoned the ninth degree of afflictions of the peak of existence; abiding in that result and entering for the sake of obtaining it are the Arhat abiding in the result and its enterer; and it appears that if done in detail, much would need to be explained. The meaning of a Once-Returner is that they still need to take birth one time in the desire realm, and a Non-Returner is that they do not need to take it. Furthermore, there is the way that the result of a Once-Returner is posited by way of having abandoned the five lower fetters, namely the three fetters, longing for sense pleasures, and malice, and the result of a Non-Returner is posited by way of having abandoned a portion of attachment, excitement, pride, and ignorance of the upper two realms; and these are only śrāvakas, and here in the Prāsaṅgika system they are all noble ones, whereas in the system of the Abhidharmasamuccaya there are ordinary beings among the enterers to stream-entry, but all the others are noble ones. In short, those four such as the Stream-Enterer do not cling as true to the obtainer and the result to be obtained, and although they may have innate true grasping, it is not the case that they have not refuted its conceived object, because for all of them the realization of emptiness has gone before.

དེ་ནས་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་བདག་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཉོན་མོངས་སྤངས་པའི་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ལགས་ཀྱང༌། བདག་གིས་བདག་ནི་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་བདེན་པར་མི་འཛིན་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་དང༌། གལ་ཏེ་དེ་ལྟར་འཛིན་ན་ནི་བདག་ཀྱང་ཉོན་མོངས་ཅན་དུ་འགྱུར་བས་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་མ་ཡིན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །

Then Subhūti said, 'Although I am conventionally an Arhat who has abandoned afflictions, I do not apprehend it as true, thinking "I am an Arhat,"' and 'If I were to apprehend it like that, I would also become afflicted, and thus I would not be an Arhat.'

[2-50] source:
བདག་ནི་ དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་བདག་ལ་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་རིགས་ཀྱི་བུ་རབ་འབྱོར་ནི་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མེད་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་མཆོག་ཏུ་ལུང་བསྟན་ལ། དོན་དམ་པར་ཅི་ལ་ཡང་མི་གནས་པས་ན་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་མེད་པར་གནས་པར་ཞེས་ལུང་ མི་སྟོན་ཏེ། དོན་དམ་པར་གནས་བྱ་དང་གནས་བྱེད་དང་གནས་པ་པོ་གང་ཡང་མ་གྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེས་བཤད་དེ། ཐལ་འགྱུར་བས་བདེན་འཛིན་ཉོན་མོངས་སུ་བཞེད་པ་དང་མཐུན་ནོ། །

He explained, 'I am an Arhat, because the Bhagavān has conventionally prophesied of me: "The son of noble family Subhūti is the supreme of those without afflictions," but because I do not abide in anything ultimately, he does not prophesy me as "abiding without afflictions", because ultimately the object to be abided in, the act of abiding, and the abider are none of them established'; and this accords with the Prāsaṅgikas asserting true grasping as an affliction.

[2-51] source:
དོན་དམ་པར་ཐོབ་བྱ་དང་ཐོབ་བྱེད་དང་ཐོབ་མཁན་ རྣམས་མེད་པར་མ་ཟད། དོན་དམ་པར་བླང་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་ཀྱང་མེད་ཅེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ངས་སྔོན་སངས་རྒྱས་མར་མེ་མཛད་ལས་དོན་དམ་པར་གང་བླངས་པའི་ཆོས་དེ་གང་ཡང་ ཡོད་སྙམ་མམ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་དེ་མ་མཆིས་སོ་ཞེས་ལན་ཕུལ། འདིར་སྒོས་སུ་སངས་རྒྱས་མར་མེ་མཛད་ཀྱི་མཚན་ནས་སྨོས་པ་ནི། སྟོན་པས་སྔོན་གཞོན་ནུ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྤྲིན་དུ་གྱུར་པའི་ཚེ། སངས་རྒྱས་མར་མེ་ མཛད་ཀྱིས་བྱིན་གྱིས་བརླབས་པ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཆོས་ལ་བཟོད་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ཐོབ་ཅིང༌། ས་བརྒྱད་པ་མངོན་དུ་མཛད་པ་ན་མར་མེ་མཛད་ཀྱིས་ཁྱོད་ལ་མ་འོངས་པའི་དུས་སུ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཤཱཀྱ་ཐུབ་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་ལུང་བསྟན་པའི་བཀའ་དྲིན་དྲན་པའི་ཆེད་དེ་འོག་ཏུ་བཤད་པར་བྱའོ། །མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཆོས་ལ་བཟོད་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ཐོབ་པ་ནི། ཉོན་མོངས་སྤངས་ཤིང་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པའི་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐའ་དག་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་མི་རྟོག་ཡེ་ཤེས་ ལ་གོམས་པ་དབང་བསྒྱུར་ཐོབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་མཉམ་གཞག་གི་གནས་སྐབས་སུ་མ་ཟད། རྗེས་ཐོབ་ཀྱི་སྐབས་སུ་ཡང་འདུས་བྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་སྟོང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་འབའ་ཞིག་ཏུ་སྣང་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཆོས་ལ་བཟོད་པ་ཐོབ་པས་ ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་མེད་དུ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གཟིགས་ཤིང་གང་ལུང་བསྟན་པ་དང་ཐོབ་པར་བྱ་བ་དང་འཚང་རྒྱ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པར་གཟིགས་པས། མར་མེ་མཛད་ལས་བདེན་གྲུབ་ཀྱི་ཆོས་གང་ཡང་བླངས་སྙམ་ དུ་ཞེན་པ་མེད་དོ། །
[2-51] translation already produced for this document:
Teaching that not only do the object to be obtained, the act of obtaining, and the obtainer not exist ultimately, but ultimately there is also no dharma to be taken up: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, 'Do you think there is any dharma that I, the Tathāgata, ultimately took up from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in the past?', Subhūti replied, 'There is not.' Specifically mentioning the name of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara here is for the sake of remembering his kindness, because in the past when the Teacher became the youth Dharmamegha, in dependence on being blessed by the Buddha Dīpaṃkara he obtained the great acceptance that dharmas are non-arising, and upon actualizing the eighth ground, Dīpaṃkara prophesied to him, 'In the future time you will become the Buddha named Śākyamuni'; and this will be explained below. As for obtaining the great acceptance that dharmas are non-arising: because, having abandoned afflictions, one has obtained mastery in habituating to the non-conceptual pristine awareness that directly realizes the entire dharmatā, which is all dharmas being empty by nature, therefore, not only during the state of meditative equipoise, but also during post-meditation, all conditioned dharmas will appear exclusively as empty of true existence, like illusions. Because, through obtaining the acceptance that dharmas are non-arising, he directly saw all dharmas as lacking true existence, and saw whatever was prophesied, the result to be obtained, and becoming a Buddha all to be empty by nature, he had no clinging, thinking that he had taken up any truly established dharma from Dīpaṃkara.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
source: ཕྱིའི་ ཞིང་གི་བཀོད་པ་ལྟ་བུར་མ་ཟད། བཅུད་ཀྱི་གང་ཟག་གི་ལུས་ཀྱི་བཀོད་པ་ཡང་རྐྱེན་ཚོགས་པ་ཙམ་ལས་དོན་དམ་པར་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། རབ་འབྱོར་དཔེར་ན་སྐྱེས་བུ་ཞིག་ལུས་རིའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་རི་རབ་ཙམ་དུ་གྱུར་ན་ལུས་དེ་ཆེ་བ་ཡིན་ སྙམ་མམ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། ལན་དུ་ལུས་དེ་ཆེ་བར་ཞུས་ཤིང༌། ལུས་དེ་ཉིད་ཆ་དུ་མ་ཚོགས་པའི་ཕུང་པོ་ཐ་སྙད་ཙམ་དུ་ཡོད་ཀྱི། ཆ་ལ་མ་བལྟོས་པའི་དངོས་པོ་སྟེ་ངོ་བོར་མེད་པར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་ཏེ། འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཐ་སྙད་ དུ་ལུས་དེ་ལ་ཆེའོ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །དེས་ན་དོན་དམ་པར་ལུས་སུ་གྲུབ་པ་མ་མཆིས་པའི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་པའི་ལུས་དེ་ལ་ལུས་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །ལུས་ཆེ་བས་མཚོན་ནས་གཟུགས་ཆེ་ཆུང་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་དེ་དང་འདྲ་བར་སྦྱར་རོ། །དེ་ལྟར་གསུངས་པ་ནི་སྣོད་བཅུད་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པར་སྒོམ་པའི་ཚུལ་བཤད་པའོ། །
translation: Teaching that not only is the array of the outer field like that, but the array of the body of the persons who are its inhabitants is also merely a gathering of conditions and not ultimately established: when he asked, "Subhūti, for example, if a person's body became as large as the king of mountains, Sumeru, do you think that body would be large?", he replied that that body would be large; and the Tathāgata taught that that body itself exists merely as a conventionality, an aggregate of multiple gathered parts, but does not exist as an entity, i.e., an essence, that does not depend on parts; so in worldly convention that body is called "large." Therefore, that conventional body, which is not ultimately established as a body, is called a "body." By the illustration of a large body, all large and small forms should be applied similarly. Speaking like that explains the way to meditate that the entire environment and inhabitants are empty by nature.

The result of a Non-Returner is posited from the perspective of having abandoned the ninth degree of desire realm afflictions; abiding in that and entering for its sake are its one abiding in the result and its enterer. The result of an Arhat is posited from the perspective of having abandoned the ninth degree of afflictions of the peak of existence; abiding in that result and entering for the sake of obtaining it are the Arhat abiding in the result and its enterer; and it appears that if done in detail, much would need to be explained. The meaning of a Once-Returner is that they still need to take birth one time in the desire realm, and a Non-Returner is that they do not need to take it. Furthermore, there is the way that the result of a Once-Returner is posited by way of having abandoned the five lower fetters, namely the three fetters, longing for sense pleasures, and malice, and the result of a Non-Returner is posited by way of having abandoned a portion of attachment, excitement, pride, and ignorance of the upper two realms; and these are only śrāvakas, and here in the Prāsaṅgika system they are all noble ones, whereas in the system of the Abhidharmasamuccaya there are ordinary beings among the enterers to stream-entry, but all the others are noble ones. In short, those four such as the Stream-Enterer do not cling as true to the obtainer and the result to be obtained, and although they may have innate true grasping, it is not the case that they have not refuted its conceived object, because for all of them the realization of emptiness has gone before.

He explained, 'I am an Arhat, because the Bhagavān has conventionally prophesied of me: "The son of noble family Subhūti is the supreme of those without afflictions," but because I do not abide in anything ultimately, he does not prophesy me as "abiding without afflictions", because ultimately the object to be abided in, the act of abiding, and the abider are none of them established'; and this accords with the Prāsaṅgikas asserting true grasping as an affliction.
