Teaching that not only do the object to be obtained, the act of obtaining, and the obtainer not exist ultimately, but ultimately there is also no dharma to be taken up: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, 'Do you think there is any dharma that I, the Tathāgata, ultimately took up from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in the past?', Subhūti replied, 'There is not.' Specifically mentioning the name of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara here is for the sake of remembering his kindness, because in the past when the Teacher became the youth Dharmamegha, in dependence on being blessed by the Buddha Dīpaṃkara he obtained the great acceptance that dharmas are non-arising, and upon actualizing the eighth ground, Dīpaṃkara prophesied to him, 'In the future time you will become the Buddha named Śākyamuni'; and this will be explained below. As for obtaining the great acceptance that dharmas are non-arising: because, having abandoned afflictions, one has obtained mastery in habituating to the non-conceptual pristine awareness that directly realizes the entire dharmatā, which is all dharmas being empty by nature, therefore, not only during the state of meditative equipoise, but also during post-meditation, all conditioned dharmas will appear exclusively as empty of true existence, like illusions. Because, through obtaining the acceptance that dharmas are non-arising, he directly saw all dharmas as lacking true existence, and saw whatever was prophesied, the result to be obtained, and becoming a Buddha all to be empty by nature, he had no clinging, thinking that he had taken up any truly established dharma from Dīpaṃkara.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: The example for teaching the benefits of meditating like that: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "If there were exactly as many Gaṅgā rivers as there are grains of sand in the Gaṅgā river, would the grains of sand of those be many in number?", he replied, "If those Gaṅgā rivers themselves are many, what need is there to mention that their grains of sand are many, so there is no need to state it." Then the Bhagavān said to Subhūti, "You should generate inclination, i.e., desire, and you should comprehend that meaning."

Furthermore, at the time of prophesying, the Buddha who is prophesied does not exist, and the person at the time of prophesying also does not exist at the time of having become a Buddha after being prophesied, but conventionally the persons from being prophesied to become a Buddha up to having become a Buddha are one continuum, and without differentiating the "I"s of past and future times, there is a general "I" that follows all the past and future "I"s, so with this in mind he prophesied: "You will become that Buddha in the future." For example, although the "I"s of past and future lives and of the early and later parts of this life are not this "I" of the present time, one is able to conventionally designate "I did it" for what they did, and "I will do it" for what they will do. Likewise, it is like when saying "I will make such and such a house, hat, clothes, shoes, and so forth", although the house and so forth do not exist at the time of speaking, one speaks thinking of what will occur in the future; so although it occurs merely conventionally, it does not arise by nature. If it were to arise by nature, one would have to assert that the house and so forth exist even at the time of thinking "I will make a house and so forth", but they do not. Intending such, the Sūtra Requested by Anavatapta states: "Whatever is born from conditions is unborn; it does not have the nature of birth. Whatever depends on conditions is explained to be empty; whoever knows emptiness is conscientious." And the previously explained reasonings establishing the lack of true existence should be applied here as well. If one understands well the way that although results arise from causes they do not arise by nature, one will understand the way that agents and actions are viable in the Mādhyamika system of emptiness of nature, and one will also find the Mādhyamika path of the union of appearance and emptiness.

དེ་ལྟར་འཚང་རྒྱ་ བ་ལ་གང་དུ་འཚང་རྒྱ་བའི་ཞིང་དག་པ་སྒྲུབ་དགོས་པར་སྟོན་པ་ནི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ལ་ལ་ཞིག་བདག་གིས་ཞིང་བཀོད་པ་རྣམས་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་དོན་དམ་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱའོ་སྙམ་ ཞིང་ཟེར་ན། ཚིག་དེ་ནི་མི་བདེན་པར་སྨྲ་བའོ། །
[2-53] translation already produced for this document:
Teaching that in order to thus become a Buddha one needs to accomplish the pure field where one will become a Buddha: the Bhagavān said to Subhūti, "If any bodhisattva thinks and says with true grasping, 'I will ultimately accomplish the arrays of the field,' that statement speaks what is untrue."

[2-54] source:
དེའི་རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི། འཚང་རྒྱ་བའི་གནས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་གི་བཀོད་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་རྣམས་ནི་རྒྱུ་རྐྱེན་དུ་མ་ཚོགས་ནས་བྱུང་བ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུའི་བཀོད་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། དོན་དམ་པར་བཀོད་པ་དེ་དག་མེད་པར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། འོན་ཀྱང་མ་བརྟག་མ་དཔྱད་པའི་བློ་ངོ་ན་ཡོད་པས་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཞིང་གི་བཀོད་པ་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་དུ་མ་ཟད། སྣོད་བཅུད་ཀྱི་བཀོད་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་ ཆ་ཤས་དུ་མ་ཚོགས་པ་ལ་བཏགས་པ་སྟེ། ཁང་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་རིགས་པས་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་བར་བཤིག་ན་ཅི་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་པའི་བར་འགྱུར་ཏེ་མཚོན་ཙམ་མོ། །
[2-54] translation already produced for this document:
The reason for that is because the Tathāgata has taught that the perfect arrays of the field that is the place of becoming a Buddha are illusory arrays that have arisen from the gathering of multiple causes and conditions, but ultimately those arrays do not exist; however, since they exist to the perspective of an unexamined and unanalyzed mind, they are conventionally called "the arrays of the field." Not only Buddha fields, but all arrays of the environment and its inhabitants are designated upon the gathering of multiple parts, like a house and so forth. If all of them are broken down by reasoning down to the smallest particle, they will become nothing whatsoever; this is merely an illustration.

[2-55] source:
དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞིང་གི་ བཀོད་པ་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བ་ན་འདི་ལྟར་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་མི་གནས་པར་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པར་བྱའོ། །
[2-55] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, when a bodhisattva is to accomplish the array of a field, they should generate the mind without abiding with true grasping like this.

[2-56] source:
དོན་དམ་པར་ཅི་ལ་ཡང་མི་གནས་ཤིང་གཟུགས་སྒྲ་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་གང་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་མི་གནས་པར་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པར་བྱའོ། །

They should generate the mind without abiding in anything ultimately and without abiding with true grasping in any dharma of form, sound, and so forth.

[2-57] source:
ཕྱིའི་ ཞིང་གི་བཀོད་པ་ལྟ་བུར་མ་ཟད། བཅུད་ཀྱི་གང་ཟག་གི་ལུས་ཀྱི་བཀོད་པ་ཡང་རྐྱེན་ཚོགས་པ་ཙམ་ལས་དོན་དམ་པར་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། རབ་འབྱོར་དཔེར་ན་སྐྱེས་བུ་ཞིག་ལུས་རིའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་རི་རབ་ཙམ་དུ་གྱུར་ན་ལུས་དེ་ཆེ་བ་ཡིན་ སྙམ་མམ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། ལན་དུ་ལུས་དེ་ཆེ་བར་ཞུས་ཤིང༌། ལུས་དེ་ཉིད་ཆ་དུ་མ་ཚོགས་པའི་ཕུང་པོ་ཐ་སྙད་ཙམ་དུ་ཡོད་ཀྱི། ཆ་ལ་མ་བལྟོས་པའི་དངོས་པོ་སྟེ་ངོ་བོར་མེད་པར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་ཏེ། འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཐ་སྙད་ དུ་ལུས་དེ་ལ་ཆེའོ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །དེས་ན་དོན་དམ་པར་ལུས་སུ་གྲུབ་པ་མ་མཆིས་པའི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་པའི་ལུས་དེ་ལ་ལུས་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །ལུས་ཆེ་བས་མཚོན་ནས་གཟུགས་ཆེ་ཆུང་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་དེ་དང་འདྲ་བར་སྦྱར་རོ། །དེ་ལྟར་གསུངས་པ་ནི་སྣོད་བཅུད་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པར་སྒོམ་པའི་ཚུལ་བཤད་པའོ། །
[2-57] translation already produced for this document:
Teaching that not only is the array of the outer field like that, but the array of the body of the persons who are its inhabitants is also merely a gathering of conditions and not ultimately established: when he asked, "Subhūti, for example, if a person's body became as large as the king of mountains, Sumeru, do you think that body would be large?", he replied that that body would be large; and the Tathāgata taught that that body itself exists merely as a conventionality, an aggregate of multiple gathered parts, but does not exist as an entity, i.e., an essence, that does not depend on parts; so in worldly convention that body is called "large." Therefore, that conventional body, which is not ultimately established as a body, is called a "body." By the illustration of a large body, all large and small forms should be applied similarly. Speaking like that explains the way to meditate that the entire environment and inhabitants are empty by nature.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: In reply to the question, "If any man or woman were to fill world systems equal in number to the grains of sand of those Gaṅgā rivers with the seven precious substances like gold, silver, and so forth as explained before, and give them as an offering to the Tathāgatas, would their merit be many?", he replied that it would be very many. Regarding what is called the "Gaṅgā river", there appear to be two ways: asserting it to be the Gaṅgā river flowing from Lake Anavatapta, and asserting it to be the great ocean; and regarding the "sand", there also appear to be two ways: taking it as the universally known sand, and taking it as the particles of water drops.

Furthermore, at the time of prophesying, the Buddha who is prophesied does not exist, and the person at the time of prophesying also does not exist at the time of having become a Buddha after being prophesied, but conventionally the persons from being prophesied to become a Buddha up to having become a Buddha are one continuum, and without differentiating the "I"s of past and future times, there is a general "I" that follows all the past and future "I"s, so with this in mind he prophesied: "You will become that Buddha in the future." For example, although the "I"s of past and future lives and of the early and later parts of this life are not this "I" of the present time, one is able to conventionally designate "I did it" for what they did, and "I will do it" for what they will do. Likewise, it is like when saying "I will make such and such a house, hat, clothes, shoes, and so forth", although the house and so forth do not exist at the time of speaking, one speaks thinking of what will occur in the future; so although it occurs merely conventionally, it does not arise by nature. If it were to arise by nature, one would have to assert that the house and so forth exist even at the time of thinking "I will make a house and so forth", but they do not. Intending such, the Sūtra Requested by Anavatapta states: "Whatever is born from conditions is unborn; it does not have the nature of birth. Whatever depends on conditions is explained to be empty; whoever knows emptiness is conscientious." And the previously explained reasonings establishing the lack of true existence should be applied here as well. If one understands well the way that although results arise from causes they do not arise by nature, one will understand the way that agents and actions are viable in the Mādhyamika system of emptiness of nature, and one will also find the Mādhyamika path of the union of appearance and emptiness.

The reason for that is because the Tathāgata has taught that the perfect arrays of the field that is the place of becoming a Buddha are illusory arrays that have arisen from the gathering of multiple causes and conditions, but ultimately those arrays do not exist; however, since they exist to the perspective of an unexamined and unanalyzed mind, they are conventionally called "the arrays of the field." Not only Buddha fields, but all arrays of the environment and its inhabitants are designated upon the gathering of multiple parts, like a house and so forth. If all of them are broken down by reasoning down to the smallest particle, they will become nothing whatsoever; this is merely an illustration.

Teaching that not only is the array of the outer field like that, but the array of the body of the persons who are its inhabitants is also merely a gathering of conditions and not ultimately established: when he asked, "Subhūti, for example, if a person's body became as large as the king of mountains, Sumeru, do you think that body would be large?", he replied that that body would be large; and the Tathāgata taught that that body itself exists merely as a conventionality, an aggregate of multiple gathered parts, but does not exist as an entity, i.e., an essence, that does not depend on parts; so in worldly convention that body is called "large." Therefore, that conventional body, which is not ultimately established as a body, is called a "body." By the illustration of a large body, all large and small forms should be applied similarly. Speaking like that explains the way to meditate that the entire environment and inhabitants are empty by nature.

Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the sūtra, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names and technical terms in standard Sanskrit transliteration (Subhūti, Tathāgata, Dīpaṃkara, prajñāpāramitā) rather than translating them. Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own. Begin directly with the translation: do not write any introductory sentence such as "Here is the translation". Render each source line as exactly one line of continuous English prose, even where the source contains verse stanzas or lists; do not break it into several lines.

Work: རྡོར་གཅོད་ཀྱི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཐར་པར་བགྲོད་པའི་ལམ་བཟང་ཟབ་དོན་གསལ་བའི་ཉི་མ། (The Sun that Illuminates the Profound Meaning of the Excellent Path for Travelling to Freedom), author: ཅོ་ནེ་གྲགས་པ་བཤད་སྒྲུབ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

དེ་ཡང་ལུང་སྟོན་པའི་དུས་སུ་གང་དུ་ལུང་བསྟན་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་དེ་མེད་ཅིང༌། ལུང་བསྟན་པའི་དུས་ཀྱི་གང་ཟག་དེ་ལུང་བསྟན་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་པའི་ཚེ་ཡང་མེད་ཀྱང༌། ཐ་སྙད་དུ་འཚང་རྒྱ་བར་ལུང་བསྟན་པ་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་ པའི་བར་གྱི་གང་ཟག་རྣམས་རྒྱུད་གཅིག་ཡིན་ཞིང༌། དུས་སྔ་ཕྱིའི་ང་རྣམས་སོ་སོར་མ་ཕྱེ་བར་སྔ་ཕྱིའི་ང་ཀུན་ལ་རྗེས་སུ་འགྲོ་བའི་ང་སྤྱི་ཞིག་ཡོད་པས་དེ་ལ་དགོངས་ནས་ཁྱོད་མ་འོངས་པ་ན་སངས་རྒྱས་དེར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་ལུང་བསྟན་པའོ། །དཔེར་ན་ སྐྱེ་བ་སྔ་ཕྱི་རྣམས་དང་ཚེ་སྟོད་སྨད་ཀྱི་ང་རྣམས་ད་ལྟའི་དུས་ཀྱི་ང་འདི་མིན་ཡང་དེ་དག་གིས་བྱས་པ་ལ་ངས་བྱས་སོ་ཞེས་དང༌། དེ་དག་གིས་བྱེད་པ་ཡང་ངས་བྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་ཐ་སྙད་འདོགས་ནུས་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ངས་ཁང་པ་དང་ཞྭ་གོས་ལྷམ་སོགས་འདི་དང་འདི་བྱའོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པའི་དུས་སུ་ཁང་པ་སོགས་མེད་ཀྱང་མ་འོངས་པ་ན་འབྱུང་འགྱུར་ལ་བསམས་ཏེ་བརྗོད་པ་ལྟ་བུ་སྟེ། ཐ་སྙད་ཙམ་དུ་འབྱུང་ཡང་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་དོ། །རང་བཞིན་ གྱིས་སྐྱེ་ན་ནི་ཁང་པ་སོགས་བྱའོ་སྙམ་པའི་དུས་ནའང་ཁང་པ་སོགས་ཡོད་ཅེས་འདོད་དགོས་ཀྱང་དེ་མེད་དོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་དགོངས་ནས། མ་དྲོས་པས་ཞུས་པའི་མདོ་ལས། གང་ཞིག་རྐྱེན་ལས་སྐྱེས་པ་དེ་མ་སྐྱེས། །དེ་ལ་སྐྱེ་བའི་རང་ བཞིན་ཡོད་མ་ཡིན། །རྐྱེན་ལ་རག་ལས་གང་དེ་སྟོང་པར་བཤད། །གང་ཞིག་སྟོང་ཉིད་ཤེས་དེ་བག་ཡོད་ཡིན། །ཞེས་གསུངས་ཤིང༌། སྔར་བཤད་པའི་བདེན་མེད་སྒྲུབ་པའི་རིགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་འདིར་ཡང་སྦྱར་རོ། །རྒྱུ་ལས་འབྲས་ བུ་རྣམས་སྐྱེ་ཡང་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཚུལ་དེ་བཞིན་ལེགས་པར་ཤེས་ན་དབུ་མའི་ལུགས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་གྱི་སྟོང་པ་ལ་བྱ་བྱེད་འཐད་ཚུལ་ཤེས་ཤིང༌། སྣང་སྟོང་ཟུང་འཇུག་གི་དབུ་མའི་ལམ་ཡང་རྙེད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[2-52] translation already produced for this document:
Furthermore, at the time of prophesying, the Buddha who is prophesied does not exist, and the person at the time of prophesying also does not exist at the time of having become a Buddha after being prophesied, but conventionally the persons from being prophesied to become a Buddha up to having become a Buddha are one continuum, and without differentiating the "I"s of past and future times, there is a general "I" that follows all the past and future "I"s, so with this in mind he prophesied: "You will become that Buddha in the future." For example, although the "I"s of past and future lives and of the early and later parts of this life are not this "I" of the present time, one is able to conventionally designate "I did it" for what they did, and "I will do it" for what they will do. Likewise, it is like when saying "I will make such and such a house, hat, clothes, shoes, and so forth", although the house and so forth do not exist at the time of speaking, one speaks thinking of what will occur in the future; so although it occurs merely conventionally, it does not arise by nature. If it were to arise by nature, one would have to assert that the house and so forth exist even at the time of thinking "I will make a house and so forth", but they do not. Intending such, the Sūtra Requested by Anavatapta states: "Whatever is born from conditions is unborn; it does not have the nature of birth. Whatever depends on conditions is explained to be empty; whoever knows emptiness is conscientious." And the previously explained reasonings establishing the lack of true existence should be applied here as well. If one understands well the way that although results arise from causes they do not arise by nature, one will understand the way that agents and actions are viable in the Mādhyamika system of emptiness of nature, and one will also find the Mādhyamika path of the union of appearance and emptiness.

དེའི་རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི། འཚང་རྒྱ་བའི་གནས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་གི་བཀོད་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་རྣམས་ནི་རྒྱུ་རྐྱེན་དུ་མ་ཚོགས་ནས་བྱུང་བ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུའི་བཀོད་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། དོན་དམ་པར་བཀོད་པ་དེ་དག་མེད་པར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། འོན་ཀྱང་མ་བརྟག་མ་དཔྱད་པའི་བློ་ངོ་ན་ཡོད་པས་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཞིང་གི་བཀོད་པ་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་དུ་མ་ཟད། སྣོད་བཅུད་ཀྱི་བཀོད་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་ ཆ་ཤས་དུ་མ་ཚོགས་པ་ལ་བཏགས་པ་སྟེ། ཁང་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་རིགས་པས་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་བར་བཤིག་ན་ཅི་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་པའི་བར་འགྱུར་ཏེ་མཚོན་ཙམ་མོ། །

The reason for that is because the Tathāgata has taught that the perfect arrays of the field that is the place of becoming a Buddha are illusory arrays that have arisen from the gathering of multiple causes and conditions, but ultimately those arrays do not exist; however, since they exist to the perspective of an unexamined and unanalyzed mind, they are conventionally called "the arrays of the field." Not only Buddha fields, but all arrays of the environment and its inhabitants are designated upon the gathering of multiple parts, like a house and so forth. If all of them are broken down by reasoning down to the smallest particle, they will become nothing whatsoever; this is merely an illustration.

Teaching that not only is the array of the outer field like that, but the array of the body of the persons who are its inhabitants is also merely a gathering of conditions and not ultimately established: when he asked, "Subhūti, for example, if a person's body became as large as the king of mountains, Sumeru, do you think that body would be large?", he replied that that body would be large; and the Tathāgata taught that that body itself exists merely as a conventionality, an aggregate of multiple gathered parts, but does not exist as an entity, i.e., an essence, that does not depend on parts; so in worldly convention that body is called "large." Therefore, that conventional body, which is not ultimately established as a body, is called a "body." By the illustration of a large body, all large and small forms should be applied similarly. source: ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་རྣམ་གྲངས་སྟོན་ཏེ། འདོན་པ་སོགས་ལས་ཕན་ཡོན་དེ་ལྟར་འབྱུང་བར་མ་ཟད། གཞུང་འདི་ལེགས་པར་འདོན་པ་དང་འདིའི་དོན་སྟོན་ཅིང་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པའི་ས་ཕྱོགས་སམ་གནས་དེ་ནི་གཞན་གྱི་མཆོད་པའི་རྟེན་དུ་འགྱུར་བ་ཡིན་པས། དེ་ལྟ་ན་གཞུང་འདིའི་ཚིག་བློ་ལ་ལེན་ཅིང་ འཛིན་པ་དང༌། གླེགས་བམ་འཆང་བ་དང༌། དེ་ཀློག་པ་དང༌། དེའི་དོན་ཀུན་ཆུབ་པ་སྟེ་ཤེས་པ་དང༌། དོན་ཚུལ་བཞིན་དུ་ཉམས་ལེན་གྱིས་ཡིད་ལ་བྱེད་པའི་གང་ཟག་དེ་ནི་ངོ་མཚར་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ལྟ་ཅི་སྨོས་ཏེ། ས་ཕྱོགས་དེ་ན་ སྟོན་པ་སངས་རྒྱས་སམ་བླ་མ་སྐྱེས་བུ་དམ་པ་གང་ཡང་རུང་བ་གནས་སོ། །
translation: Teaching the enumeration with "Moreover, Subhūti" and so forth: not only do such benefits arise from reciting and so forth, but the location or place where one recites this text well, teaches its meaning, and practices it becomes an object of offering for others; so if that is the case, what need is there to mention that the person who takes the words of this text to mind and retains them, carries a volume of it, reads it, comprehends—i.e., knows—all its meaning, and takes the meaning to mind by practicing it properly will become endowed with supreme wonder? In that place dwells either the Teacher Buddha or a guru who is a holy being, whichever it may be.

Furthermore, at the time of prophesying, the Buddha who is prophesied does not exist, and the person at the time of prophesying also does not exist at the time of having become a Buddha after being prophesied, but conventionally the persons from being prophesied to become a Buddha up to having become a Buddha are one continuum, and without differentiating the "I"s of past and future times, there is a general "I" that follows all the past and future "I"s, so with this in mind he prophesied: "You will become that Buddha in the future." For example, although the "I"s of past and future lives and of the early and later parts of this life are not this "I" of the present time, one is able to conventionally designate "I did it" for what they did, and "I will do it" for what they will do. Likewise, it is like when saying "I will make such and such a house, hat, clothes, shoes, and so forth", although the house and so forth do not exist at the time of speaking, one speaks thinking of what will occur in the future; so although it occurs merely conventionally, it does not arise by nature. If it were to arise by nature, one would have to assert that the house and so forth exist even at the time of thinking "I will make a house and so forth", but they do not. Intending such, the Sūtra Requested by Anavatapta states: "Whatever is born from conditions is unborn; it does not have the nature of birth. Whatever depends on conditions is explained to be empty; whoever knows emptiness is conscientious." And the previously explained reasonings establishing the lack of true existence should be applied here as well. If one understands well the way that although results arise from causes they do not arise by nature, one will understand the way that agents and actions are viable in the Mādhyamika system of emptiness of nature, and one will also find the Mādhyamika path of the union of appearance and emptiness.

[2-57] translation already produced for this document:
Teaching that not only is the array of the outer field like that, but the array of the body of the persons who are its inhabitants is also merely a gathering of conditions and not ultimately established: when he asked, "Subhūti, for example, if a person's body became as large as the king of mountains, Sumeru, do you think that body would be large?", he replied that that body would be large; and the Tathāgata taught that that body itself exists merely as a conventionality, an aggregate of multiple gathered parts, but does not exist as an entity, i.e., an essence, that does not depend on parts; so in worldly convention that body is called "large." Therefore, that conventional body, which is not ultimately established as a body, is called a "body." By the illustration of a large body, all large and small forms should be applied similarly. Speaking like that explains the way to meditate that the entire environment and inhabitants are empty by nature.

translation: Then when Subhūti asked, "What is the name of this text?", the Bhagavān replied, "The name of this text is the prajñāpāramitā, so bear its name like that"; this designates the expressing text with the name of what is expressed, because it teaches by taking the prajñāpāramitā of the expressed meaning as what is to be expressed. By illustrating with the name of the prajñāpāramitā, this also teaches the other pāramitās.

Furthermore, at the time of prophesying, the Buddha who is prophesied does not exist, and the person at the time of prophesying also does not exist at the time of having become a Buddha after being prophesied, but conventionally the persons from being prophesied to become a Buddha up to having become a Buddha are one continuum, and without differentiating the "I"s of past and future times, there is a general "I" that follows all the past and future "I"s, so with this in mind he prophesied: "You will become that Buddha in the future." For example, although the "I"s of past and future lives and of the early and later parts of this life are not this "I" of the present time, one is able to conventionally designate "I did it" for what they did, and "I will do it" for what they will do. Likewise, it is like when saying "I will make such and such a house, hat, clothes, shoes, and so forth", although the house and so forth do not exist at the time of speaking, one speaks thinking of what will occur in the future; so although it occurs merely conventionally, it does not arise by nature. If it were to arise by nature, one would have to assert that the house and so forth exist even at the time of thinking "I will make a house and so forth", but they do not. Intending such, the Sūtra Requested by Anavatapta states: "Whatever is born from conditions is unborn; it does not have the nature of birth. Whatever depends on conditions is explained to be empty; whoever knows emptiness is conscientious." And the previously explained reasonings establishing the lack of true existence should be applied here as well. If one understands well the way that although results arise from causes they do not arise by nature, one will understand the way that agents and actions are viable in the Mādhyamika system of emptiness of nature, and one will also find the Mādhyamika path of the union of appearance and emptiness.

The reason for that is because the Tathāgata has taught that the perfect arrays of the field that is the place of becoming a Buddha are illusory arrays that have arisen from the gathering of multiple causes and conditions, but ultimately those arrays do not exist; however, since they exist to the perspective of an unexamined and unanalyzed mind, they are conventionally called "the arrays of the field." Not only Buddha fields, but all arrays of the environment and its inhabitants are designated upon the gathering of multiple parts, like a house and so forth. If all of them are broken down by reasoning down to the smallest particle, they will become nothing whatsoever; this is merely an illustration.

[2-57] translation already produced for this document:
Teaching that not only is the array of the outer field like that, but the array of the body of the persons who are its inhabitants is also merely a gathering of conditions and not ultimately established: when he asked, "Subhūti, for example, if a person's body became as large as the king of mountains, Sumeru, do you think that body would be large?", he replied that that body would be large; and the Tathāgata taught that that body itself exists merely as a conventionality, an aggregate of multiple gathered parts, but does not exist as an entity, i.e., an essence, that does not depend on parts; so in worldly convention that body is called "large." Therefore, that conventional body, which is not ultimately established as a body, is called a "body." By the illustration of a large body, all large and small forms should be applied similarly. Speaking like that explains the way to meditate that the entire environment and inhabitants are empty by nature.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: That very prajñāpāramitā which the Tathāgata taught is not ultimately established as a pāramitā; therefore, it is conventionally designated as the "prajñāpāramitā." All such explanations of not existing ultimately but existing conventionally teach the Mādhyamika path of the union of the two truths that has abandoned the two extremes; that also teaches that both being empty of nature and existing conventionally gather simultaneously upon a single basis. The meaning of the term "pāramitā" is both causing one to go to the other shore of the ocean of saṃsāra and having already gone to it; according to the former, it exists on the path of training, and the latter exists on the ground of a Buddha, which is synonymous with omniscience. Merely regarding what is expressed by the term "prajñāpāramitā", there are many, such as the prajñāpāramitā of nature, of text, of path, and of result, so although one needs to know the distinctions, they are not stated here. In short, this prajñāpāramitā—where the exalted wisdom realizing emptiness that is embraced by bodhicitta is taught as the prajñāpāramitā—is the special method that leads the first five pāramitās, such as the pāramitā of generosity, to the ground of a Buddha; this will be explained.

[2-52] translation already produced for this document:
Furthermore, at the time of prophesying, the Buddha who is prophesied does not exist, and the person at the time of prophesying also does not exist at the time of having become a Buddha after being prophesied, but conventionally the persons from being prophesied to become a Buddha up to having become a Buddha are one continuum, and without differentiating the "I"s of past and future times, there is a general "I" that follows all the past and future "I"s, so with this in mind he prophesied: "You will become that Buddha in the future." For example, although the "I"s of past and future lives and of the early and later parts of this life are not this "I" of the present time, one is able to conventionally designate "I did it" for what they did, and "I will do it" for what they will do. Likewise, it is like when saying "I will make such and such a house, hat, clothes, shoes, and so forth", although the house and so forth do not exist at the time of speaking, one speaks thinking of what will occur in the future; so although it occurs merely conventionally, it does not arise by nature. If it were to arise by nature, one would have to assert that the house and so forth exist even at the time of thinking "I will make a house and so forth", but they do not. Intending such, the Sūtra Requested by Anavatapta states: "Whatever is born from conditions is unborn; it does not have the nature of birth. Whatever depends on conditions is explained to be empty; whoever knows emptiness is conscientious." And the previously explained reasonings establishing the lack of true existence should be applied here as well. If one understands well the way that although results arise from causes they do not arise by nature, one will understand the way that agents and actions are viable in the Mādhyamika system of emptiness of nature, and one will also find the Mādhyamika path of the union of appearance and emptiness.

The reason for that is because the Tathāgata has taught that the perfect arrays of the field that is the place of becoming a Buddha are illusory arrays that have arisen from the gathering of multiple causes and conditions, but ultimately those arrays do not exist; however, since they exist to the perspective of an unexamined and unanalyzed mind, they are conventionally called "the arrays of the field." Not only Buddha fields, but all arrays of the environment and its inhabitants are designated upon the gathering of multiple parts, like a house and so forth. If all of them are broken down by reasoning down to the smallest particle, they will become nothing whatsoever; this is merely an illustration.

[2-57] translation already produced for this document:
Teaching that not only is the array of the outer field like that, but the array of the body of the persons who are its inhabitants is also merely a gathering of conditions and not ultimately established: when he asked, "Subhūti, for example, if a person's body became as large as the king of mountains, Sumeru, do you think that body would be large?", he replied that that body would be large; and the Tathāgata taught that that body itself exists merely as a conventionality, an aggregate of multiple gathered parts, but does not exist as an entity, i.e., an essence, that does not depend on parts; so in worldly convention that body is called "large." Therefore, that conventional body, which is not ultimately established as a body, is called a "body." By the illustration of a large body, all large and small forms should be applied similarly. Speaking like that explains the way to meditate that the entire environment and inhabitants are empty by nature.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: When it is explained that the prajñāpāramitā is taught by the phrase, "That which is taught as the prajñāpāramitā here", if one thinks, "Well then, is there another dharma that was ultimately taught by the Tathāgata?", teaching that there is not: when asked, "Do you think there is any such dharma?", Subhūti offered the reply, "Any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has taught does not ultimately exist", which is similar to the earlier explanation of the meaning of the statement that the Tathāgata has not taught a dharma.
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Diamond Sūtra (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the sūtra, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names and technical terms in standard Sanskrit transliteration (Subhūti, Tathāgata, Dīpaṃkara, prajñāpāramitā) rather than translating them. Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own. Begin directly with the translation: do not write any introductory sentence such as "Here is the translation". Render each source line as exactly one line of continuous English prose, even where the source contains verse stanzas or lists; do not break it into several lines.

Work: རྡོར་གཅོད་ཀྱི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཐར་པར་བགྲོད་པའི་ལམ་བཟང་ཟབ་དོན་གསལ་བའི་ཉི་མ། (The Sun that Illuminates the Profound Meaning of the Excellent Path for Travelling to Freedom), author: ཅོ་ནེ་གྲགས་པ་བཤད་སྒྲུབ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[2-58] source:
དེ་ལྟར་བསྒོམས་པའི་ཕན་ཡོན་སྟོན་པ་ལ་དཔེ་ནི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་གངྒཱའི་ཀླུང་གི་བྱེ་མ་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་ གངྒཱའི་ཀླུང་ཡང་དེ་སྙེད་ཁོ་ནར་གྱུར་ན། དེ་དག་གི་བྱེ་མ་དེ་དག་གྲངས་མང་ངམ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། ལན་ལ་གངྒཱའི་ཀླུང་དེ་དག་ཉིད་ཀྱང་མང་ན་དེ་དག་གི་བྱེ་མ་རྣམས་མང་བ་ལྟ་སྨོས་ཀྱང་ཅི་འཚལ་ཏེ་བརྗོད་མི་དགོས་སོ་ཞེས་གསོལ། དེ་ནས་ བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་ཁྱོད་མོས་པ་སྟེ་འདོད་པ་བསྐྱེད་པ་དང་ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་དོན་དེ་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་པར་བྱའོ། །
[2-58] translation already produced for this document:
The example for teaching the benefits of meditating like that: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "If there were exactly as many Gaṅgā rivers as there are grains of sand in the Gaṅgā river, would the grains of sand of those be many in number?", he replied, "If those Gaṅgā rivers themselves are many, what need is there to mention that their grains of sand are many, so there is no need to state it." Then the Bhagavān said to Subhūti, "You should generate inclination, i.e., desire, and you should comprehend that meaning."

[2-59] source:
གངྒཱའི་ཀླུང་དེ་དག་གི་བྱེ་མ་ཇི་སྙེད་པའི་གྲངས་ཀྱི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་རྣམས་སྐྱེས་པའམ་བུད་མེད་གང་གིས་ གསེར་དངུལ་སོགས་སྔར་བཤད་པ་ལྟར་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྣ་བདུན་གྱིས་གང་བར་བྱས་ཏེ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་རྣམས་ལ་མཆོད་དེ་སྦྱིན་པ་བྱིན་ན་བསོད་ནམས་མང་ངམ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པའི་ལན་དུ་ཆེས་མང་བར་ཞུས་སོ། །གངྒཱའི་ཀླུང་ཞེས་པ་ནི་མ་ དྲོས་མཚོ་ནས་འབབ་པའི་ཆུ་བོ་གངྒཱ་ལ་བཞེད་པ་དང༌། རྒྱ་མཚོ་ཆེན་པོ་ལ་བཞེད་པའི་ཚུལ་གཉིས་དང༌། བྱེ་མ་ཡང་བྱེ་མ་ཡོངས་གྲགས་དང༌། ཆུའི་ཐིགས་པའི་རྡུལ་ལ་བྱེད་པའི་ཚུལ་གཉིས་སྣང་ངོ༌། །
[2-59] translation already produced for this document:
In reply to the question, "If any man or woman were to fill world systems equal in number to the grains of sand of those Gaṅgā rivers with the seven precious substances like gold, silver, and so forth as explained before, and give them as an offering to the Tathāgatas, would their merit be many?", he replied that it would be very many. Regarding what is called the "Gaṅgā river", there appear to be two ways: asserting it to be the Gaṅgā river flowing from Lake Anavatapta, and asserting it to be the great ocean; and regarding the "sand", there also appear to be two ways: taking it as the universally known sand, and taking it as the particles of water drops.

[2-60] source:
དཔེ་བཤད་པ་དེ་ལས་གཞུང་འདི་ འདོན་ཅིང་ཉན་སེམས་བསྒོམས་པའི་ཕན་ཡོན་ལྷག་པར་ཆེའོ་ཞེས་པ་ནི། གང་གིས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་ལས༌ཐ་ན་ཞེས་པ་ནི་མ་ཐའོ། །གཞན་ནི་སྔར་ལྟར་རོ། །
[2-60] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the statement that the benefits of reciting this text, listening to it, thinking about it, and meditating on it are exceptionally greater than the explained example: "Whoever... from this dharma discourse, even at a minimum" means at the very least. The rest is as before.

[2-61] source:
ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་རྣམ་གྲངས་སྟོན་ཏེ། འདོན་པ་སོགས་ལས་ཕན་ཡོན་དེ་ལྟར་འབྱུང་བར་མ་ཟད། གཞུང་འདི་ལེགས་པར་འདོན་པ་དང་འདིའི་དོན་སྟོན་ཅིང་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པའི་ས་ཕྱོགས་སམ་གནས་དེ་ནི་གཞན་གྱི་མཆོད་པའི་རྟེན་དུ་འགྱུར་བ་ཡིན་པས། དེ་ལྟ་ན་གཞུང་འདིའི་ཚིག་བློ་ལ་ལེན་ཅིང་ འཛིན་པ་དང༌། གླེགས་བམ་འཆང་བ་དང༌། དེ་ཀློག་པ་དང༌། དེའི་དོན་ཀུན་ཆུབ་པ་སྟེ་ཤེས་པ་དང༌། དོན་ཚུལ་བཞིན་དུ་ཉམས་ལེན་གྱིས་ཡིད་ལ་བྱེད་པའི་གང་ཟག་དེ་ནི་ངོ་མཚར་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ལྟ་ཅི་སྨོས་ཏེ། ས་ཕྱོགས་དེ་ན་ སྟོན་པ་སངས་རྒྱས་སམ་བླ་མ་སྐྱེས་བུ་དམ་པ་གང་ཡང་རུང་བ་གནས་སོ། །
[2-61] translation already produced for this document:
Teaching the enumeration with "Moreover, Subhūti" and so forth: not only do such benefits arise from reciting and so forth, but the location or place where one recites this text well, teaches its meaning, and practices it becomes an object of offering for others; so if that is the case, what need is there to mention that the person who takes the words of this text to mind and retains them, carries a volume of it, reads it, comprehends—i.e., knows—all its meaning, and takes the meaning to mind by practicing it properly will become endowed with supreme wonder? In that place dwells either the Teacher Buddha or a guru who is a holy being, whichever it may be.

[2-62] source:
དེ་ནས་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་གཞུང་འདིའི་མིང་ཅི་ལྟར་ལགས་ཞེས་ཞུས་པ་ན། ལན་དུ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་འདིའི་མིང་ལ་གཞུང་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་ སྟེ་འདིའི་མིང་དེ་ལྟར་ཟུངས་ཤིག་ཅེས་པ་ནི། བརྗོད་བྱ་དོན་གྱི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་བརྗོད་བྱར་བྱས་ནས་སྟོན་པས་རྗོད་བྱེད་གཞུང་ལ་བརྗོད་བྱའི་མིང་གིས་བཏགས་པའོ། །འདིས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་མིང་གིས་མཚོན་ཏེ་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གཞན་ཡང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[2-62] translation already produced for this document:
Then when Subhūti asked, "What is the name of this text?", the Bhagavān replied, "The name of this text is the prajñāpāramitā, so bear its name like that"; this designates the expressing text with the name of what is expressed, because it teaches by taking the prajñāpāramitā of the expressed meaning as what is to be expressed. By illustrating with the name of the prajñāpāramitā, this also teaches the other pāramitās.

[2-63] source:
དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་གང་གསུངས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་དོན་དམ་པར་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་ཅིང༌། དེས་ན་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་འདོགས་སོ། །དོན་དམ་པར་མེད་ཅིང་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཡོད་པར་ བཤད་པ་འདི་འདྲ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་མཐའ་གཉིས་སྤངས་པའི་བདེན་གཉིས་ཟུང་དུ་འཇུག་པའི་དབུ་མའི་ལམ་སྟོན་ཏེ། དེ་ཡང་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པ་དང་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཡོད་པ་གཉིས་དུས་གཅིག་ཏུ་གཞི་གཅིག་གི་སྟེང་དུ་འདུ་བར་སྟོན་པའོ། །ཕར་ཕྱིན་ཞེས་པའི་སྒྲ་དོན་ནི། འཁོར་བའི་རྒྱ་མཚོའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པར་བྱེད་པ་དང་ཕྱིན་ཟིན་པའི་དོན་ཏེ། སྔ་མ་ལྟར་ན་སློབ་ལམ་ན་ཡོད་ཅིང༌། ཕྱི་མ་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ས་ན་ཡོད་དེ་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་དང་དོན་གཅིག་གོ །ཤེར་ ཕྱིན་ཀྱི་སྒྲས་བརྗོད་པ་ཙམ་ལ་ནི། རང་བཞིན་དང་གཞུང་དང་ལམ་དང་འབྲས་བུའི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལྟ་བུ་མང་སྟེ་ཁྱད་པར་ཤེས་དགོས་ཀྱང་མ་བརྗོད་དོ། །མདོར་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཟིན་པའི་སྟོང་ཉིད་རྟོགས་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ དུ་གསུངས་པའི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་འདི་ནི་སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་སོགས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དང་པོ་ལྔ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སར་འཁྲིད་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཐབས་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་ཡིན་ཏེ་འཆད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[2-63] translation already produced for this document:
That very prajñāpāramitā which the Tathāgata taught is not ultimately established as a pāramitā; therefore, it is conventionally designated as the "prajñāpāramitā." All such explanations of not existing ultimately but existing conventionally teach the Mādhyamika path of the union of the two truths that has abandoned the two extremes; that also teaches that both being empty of nature and existing conventionally gather simultaneously upon a single basis. The meaning of the term "pāramitā" is both causing one to go to the other shore of the ocean of saṃsāra and having already gone to it; according to the former, it exists on the path of training, and the latter exists on the ground of a Buddha, which is synonymous with omniscience. Merely regarding what is expressed by the term "prajñāpāramitā", there are many, such as the prajñāpāramitā of nature, of text, of path, and of result, so although one needs to know the distinctions, they are not stated here. In short, this prajñāpāramitā—where the exalted wisdom realizing emptiness that is embraced by bodhicitta is taught as the prajñāpāramitā—is the special method that leads the first five pāramitās, such as the pāramitā of generosity, to the ground of a Buddha; this will be explained.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: Then, teaching that subtle particles and world systems accumulated from subtle particles are not ultimately established: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "Are however many particles of earth there are in a three-thousandfold world system many?", in reply he stated, "They are many," and "Those subtle particles of earth, whatever they are, the Tathāgata has taught that they are not ultimately established as particles; since they do not exist ultimately but exist conventionally, they are therefore called 'particles of earth'."

[2-63] translation already produced for this document:
That very prajñāpāramitā which the Tathāgata taught is not ultimately established as a pāramitā; therefore, it is conventionally designated as the "prajñāpāramitā." All such explanations of not existing ultimately but existing conventionally teach the Mādhyamika path of the union of the two truths that has abandoned the two extremes; that also teaches that both being empty of nature and existing conventionally gather simultaneously upon a single basis. The meaning of the term "pāramitā" is both causing one to go to the other shore of the ocean of saṃsāra and having already gone to it; according to the former, it exists on the path of training, and the latter exists on the ground of a Buddha, which is synonymous with omniscience. Merely regarding what is expressed by the term "prajñāpāramitā", there are many, such as the prajñāpāramitā of nature, of text, of path, and of result, so although one needs to know the distinctions, they are not stated here. In short, this prajñāpāramitā—where the exalted wisdom realizing emptiness that is embraced by bodhicitta is taught as the prajñāpāramitā—is the special method that leads the first five pāramitās, such as the pāramitā of generosity, to the ground of a Buddha; this will be explained.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: Therefore, as for whatever world systems accumulated from subtle particles there are, that is because the Tathāgata has taught that they too are not ultimately established as world systems; therefore, they are conventionally called "world systems."

[2-63] translation already produced for this document:
That very prajñāpāramitā which the Tathāgata taught is not ultimately established as a pāramitā; therefore, it is conventionally designated as the "prajñāpāramitā." All such explanations of not existing ultimately but existing conventionally teach the Mādhyamika path of the union of the two truths that has abandoned the two extremes; that also teaches that both being empty of nature and existing conventionally gather simultaneously upon a single basis. The meaning of the term "pāramitā" is both causing one to go to the other shore of the ocean of saṃsāra and having already gone to it; according to the former, it exists on the path of training, and the latter exists on the ground of a Buddha, which is synonymous with omniscience. Merely regarding what is expressed by the term "prajñāpāramitā", there are many, such as the prajñāpāramitā of nature, of text, of path, and of result, so although one needs to know the distinctions, they are not stated here. In short, this prajñāpāramitā—where the exalted wisdom realizing emptiness that is embraced by bodhicitta is taught as the prajñāpāramitā—is the special method that leads the first five pāramitās, such as the pāramitā of generosity, to the ground of a Buddha; this will be explained.

heading: ཉན་ཐོས་འཕགས་པ་ཞུགས་གནས་བརྒྱད།
translation: As for merely a fraction of the reasoning that they are not ultimately established: world systems accumulated from subtle particles are merely designated upon the assembly of subtle particles, but there is no separate thing called a "world system" as the individual subtle particles, their collection, or an entity distinct from them; for example, just as a vase is designated upon the collection of the vase's lip, base, belly, and so forth. Does a single subtle particle have the six directions of the four cardinal directions and above and below, or not? If it does, then because it would be larger than its own six directional parts, it would lack the meaning of being "subtle"; if it does not have those six directions, then because it lacks the capacity to occupy space, it would absurdly follow that the particle is not physical and it would also become a non-entity. Therefore, since a single subtle particle cannot exist in isolation, it must depend on collecting and assembling with others, so a subtle particle is not independently established; and because it is not established, it is said that the gross particles accumulated from it are also not independently established. In short, it is explained to meditate on emptiness by understanding that subtle particles do not truly exist as a singular nature, and world systems are not truly established as the nature of a multiple collection. Master Kamalaśīla explained that the world system in this context is intended as the world of sentient beings: the impure world system that is the basis where sentient beings dwell.

[2-58] translation already produced for this document:
The example for teaching the benefits of meditating like that: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "If there were exactly as many Gaṅgā rivers as there are grains of sand in the Gaṅgā river, would the grains of sand of those be many in number?", he replied, "If those Gaṅgā rivers themselves are many, what need is there to mention that their grains of sand are many, so there is no need to state it." Then the Bhagavān said to Subhūti, "You should generate inclination, i.e., desire, and you should comprehend that meaning."

Regarding the statement that the benefits of reciting this text, listening to it, thinking about it, and meditating on it are exceptionally greater than the explained example: "Whoever... from this dharma discourse, even at a minimum" means at the very least. The rest is as before.

ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་རྣམ་གྲངས་སྟོན་ཏེ། འདོན་པ་སོགས་ལས་ཕན་ཡོན་དེ་ལྟར་འབྱུང་བར་མ་ཟད། གཞུང་འདི་ལེགས་པར་འདོན་པ་དང་འདིའི་དོན་སྟོན་ཅིང་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པའི་ས་ཕྱོགས་སམ་གནས་དེ་ནི་གཞན་གྱི་མཆོད་པའི་རྟེན་དུ་འགྱུར་བ་ཡིན་པས། དེ་ལྟ་ན་གཞུང་འདིའི་ཚིག་བློ་ལ་ལེན་ཅིང་ འཛིན་པ་དང༌། གླེགས་བམ་འཆང་བ་དང༌། དེ་ཀློག་པ་དང༌། དེའི་དོན་ཀུན་ཆུབ་པ་སྟེ་ཤེས་པ་དང༌། དོན་ཚུལ་བཞིན་དུ་ཉམས་ལེན་གྱིས་ཡིད་ལ་བྱེད་པའི་གང་ཟག་དེ་ནི་ངོ་མཚར་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་བ་ལྟ་ཅི་སྨོས་ཏེ། ས་ཕྱོགས་དེ་ན་ སྟོན་པ་སངས་རྒྱས་སམ་བླ་མ་སྐྱེས་བུ་དམ་པ་གང་ཡང་རུང་བ་གནས་སོ། །
[2-61] translation already produced for this document:
Teaching the enumeration with "Moreover, Subhūti" and so forth: not only do such benefits arise from reciting and so forth, but the location or place where one recites this text well, teaches its meaning, and practices it becomes an object of offering for others; so if that is the case, what need is there to mention that the person who takes the words of this text to mind and retains them, carries a volume of it, reads it, comprehends—i.e., knows—all its meaning, and takes the meaning to mind by practicing it properly will become endowed with supreme wonder? In that place dwells either the Teacher Buddha or a guru who is a holy being, whichever it may be.

[2-62] source:
དེ་ནས་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་གཞུང་འདིའི་མིང་ཅི་ལྟར་ལགས་ཞེས་ཞུས་པ་ན། ལན་དུ་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་འདིའི་མིང་ལ་གཞུང་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་ སྟེ་འདིའི་མིང་དེ་ལྟར་ཟུངས་ཤིག་ཅེས་པ་ནི། བརྗོད་བྱ་དོན་གྱི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་བརྗོད་བྱར་བྱས་ནས་སྟོན་པས་རྗོད་བྱེད་གཞུང་ལ་བརྗོད་བྱའི་མིང་གིས་བཏགས་པའོ། །འདིས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་མིང་གིས་མཚོན་ཏེ་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གཞན་ཡང་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[2-62] translation already produced for this document:
Then when Subhūti asked, "What is the name of this text?", the Bhagavān replied, "The name of this text is the prajñāpāramitā, so bear its name like that"; this designates the expressing text with the name of what is expressed, because it teaches by taking the prajñāpāramitā of the expressed meaning as what is to be expressed. By illustrating with the name of the prajñāpāramitā, this also teaches the other pāramitās.

[2-63] source:
དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་གང་གསུངས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་དོན་དམ་པར་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་ཅིང༌། དེས་ན་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཞེས་འདོགས་སོ། །དོན་དམ་པར་མེད་ཅིང་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཡོད་པར་ བཤད་པ་འདི་འདྲ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་མཐའ་གཉིས་སྤངས་པའི་བདེན་གཉིས་ཟུང་དུ་འཇུག་པའི་དབུ་མའི་ལམ་སྟོན་ཏེ། དེ་ཡང་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པ་དང་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཡོད་པ་གཉིས་དུས་གཅིག་ཏུ་གཞི་གཅིག་གི་སྟེང་དུ་འདུ་བར་སྟོན་པའོ། །ཕར་ཕྱིན་ཞེས་པའི་སྒྲ་དོན་ནི། འཁོར་བའི་རྒྱ་མཚོའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པར་བྱེད་པ་དང་ཕྱིན་ཟིན་པའི་དོན་ཏེ། སྔ་མ་ལྟར་ན་སློབ་ལམ་ན་ཡོད་ཅིང༌། ཕྱི་མ་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ས་ན་ཡོད་དེ་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་དང་དོན་གཅིག་གོ །ཤེར་ ཕྱིན་ཀྱི་སྒྲས་བརྗོད་པ་ཙམ་ལ་ནི། རང་བཞིན་དང་གཞུང་དང་ལམ་དང་འབྲས་བུའི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལྟ་བུ་མང་སྟེ་ཁྱད་པར་ཤེས་དགོས་ཀྱང་མ་བརྗོད་དོ། །མདོར་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཟིན་པའི་སྟོང་ཉིད་རྟོགས་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ དུ་གསུངས་པའི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་འདི་ནི་སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་སོགས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དང་པོ་ལྔ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སར་འཁྲིད་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཐབས་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་ཡིན་ཏེ་འཆད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[2-63] translation already produced for this document:
That very prajñāpāramitā which the Tathāgata taught is not ultimately established as a pāramitā; therefore, it is conventionally designated as the "prajñāpāramitā." All such explanations of not existing ultimately but existing conventionally teach the Mādhyamika path of the union of the two truths that has abandoned the two extremes; that also teaches that both being empty of nature and existing conventionally gather simultaneously upon a single basis. The meaning of the term "pāramitā" is both causing one to go to the other shore of the ocean of saṃsāra and having already gone to it; according to the former, it exists on the path of training, and the latter exists on the ground of a Buddha, which is synonymous with omniscience. Merely regarding what is expressed by the term "prajñāpāramitā", there are many, such as the prajñāpāramitā of nature, of text, of path, and of result, so although one needs to know the distinctions, they are not stated here. In short, this prajñāpāramitā—where the exalted wisdom realizing emptiness that is embraced by bodhicitta is taught as the prajñāpāramitā—is the special method that leads the first five pāramitās, such as the pāramitā of generosity, to the ground of a Buddha; this will be explained.

heading: མཚན་དང་དཔེ་བྱད།
source: དེ་ནས་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་སུ་མ་ཟད། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གཟུགས་སྐུ་དང་དེའི་མཚན་དཔེ་ཡང་དོན་དམ་པར་མ་གྲུབ་ཅེས་པ་ནི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་སྐྱེས་བུ་ཆེན་པོ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་མཚན་སུམ་ཅུ་རྩ་གཉིས་པོ་དེ་དག་ཚོགས་པའི་སྐུ་ཙམ་ཞིག་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་བལྟ་བ་སྟེ་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་སྙམ་མམ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་དེ་མ་ལགས་ཏེ། རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་སྐྱེས་བུ་ཆེན་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཚན་སོ་གཉིས་པོ་གང་དག་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཡོད་པར་གསུངས་པ་དེ་དག་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་མཚན་མ་མཆིས་པར་གསུངས་པའི་སླད་དུ་སྟེ་ཞེས་སྒྲོ་འདོགས་རྟག་མཐའ་བཀག་ཅིང༌། དེས་ན་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་དེ་དག་ལ་སྐྱེས་བུ་ཆེན་པོའི་མཚན་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱའོ་ཞེས་པས་སྐུར་འདེབས་ཆད་མཐའ་བཀག་པ་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་གཞན་ལ་ཡང་འདྲའོ། །མཚན་བསྟན་པའི་ཤུགས་ལ་དཔེ་བྱད་བརྒྱད་ཅུ་ཡང་བསྟན་ཏེ། དཔེ་བྱད་རྣམས་ནི་མཚན་གྱི་འཁོར་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །མཚན་ སོ་གཉིས་ནི་མངོན་རྟོགས་རྒྱན་ལས། ཕྱག་ཞབས་འཁོར་ལོའི་མཚན་དང་རུས་སྦས་ཞབས། །ཞེས་སོགས་དང༌། དཔེ་བྱད་བརྒྱད་ཅུ་ནི། ཐུབ་པའི་སེན་མོ་ཟངས་མདོག་དང༌། །ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གཟུགས་སྐུ་གཉིས་ལ་མཚན་དཔེ་གསལ་རྫོགས་ཡོད་པར་མཐོང་བ་ན་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་སངས་རྒྱས་ནི་མཚན་དཔེ་འདི་ཙམ་གྱི་སྒོ་ནས་འཇོག་གམ་སྙམ་ན། དེ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ལ་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ མངོན་དུ་བྱས་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་ཀྱི། མཚན་དཔེ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་སྐུ་ཐོབ་པ་ཙམ་གྱི་སྒོ་ནས་བཞག་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས། གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་བརྙེས་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ གྲངས་སུ་མི་འགྲོ་ཡི། རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཉིད་བརྙེས་པས་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་གྲངས་སུ་འགྲོའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །སྐུ་མཚན་དཔེས་བརྒྱན་པའི་གཟུགས་སྐུ་མཐོང་ནས་དེ་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་ཕྱག་ འཚལ་བ་སོགས་ལེགས་པའི་ལམ་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་བསྡུས་པ་ཡིན་མོད། གང་དག་ང་ལ་གཟུགས་སུ་མཐོང༌། །ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱི་སྐབས་སུ་འཆད་པ་ལྟར་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པའི་སྐྱོན་ཅན་ཡིན་ཏེ། མངོན་ རྟོགས་རྒྱན་ལས་ཀྱང༌། རྒྱལ་ལ་སོགས་ལ་ཆགས་པ་ཕྲ། །ཞེས་པའི་སྐབས་སུ་ཚུལ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱི་ཆགས་པའི་སྐྱོན་ཡོད་པར་བཤད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །སྐབས་འདིར་བདེན་འཛིན་ནི་མ་རིག་པར་འདོད་དགོས་པས། མ་རིག་པས ཀུན་ནས་བསླངས་ཏེ་དགེ་བའི་ལས་བསགས་ནས་འཁོར་བས་བསྡུས་པའི་མངོན་མཐོ་དང༌། མི་དགེ་བའི་ལས་བསགས་ན་ནི་ངན་འགྲོའི་ལུས་འགྲུབ་པར་གཞུང་དུ་མ་ལས་བཤད་དོ། །གཞུང་འདི་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་དེ་ལྟར་དག་མ་དག་གི
translation: Then, as for [the teaching] that not only world systems, but also the form bodies of a Buddha and their marks and signs are not ultimately established: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "Do you think that the Tathāgata should be seen—that is, apprehended—as merely a body that is the collection of those thirty-two marks of a great being of the Tathāgata?", Subhūti replied, "That is not so. The reason is that whatever thirty-two marks of a great being of the Buddha were taught by the Tathāgata to exist conventionally, those were taught as not ultimately existing as marks," which refutes the extreme of permanence of superimposition, and by the phrase, "therefore they are conventionally called 'marks of a great being'," the extreme of nihilism of deprecation is refuted; this is similar for others as well. By the force of teaching the marks, the eighty signs are also taught, because the signs are the retinue of the marks. The thirty-two marks are as taught in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "The marks of wheels on the hands and feet, and feet like a tortoise," and so forth; and the eighty signs are as taught by "The Sage's nails are copper-colored," and so forth. If one thinks, upon seeing that the marks and signs are clear and complete on the two form bodies of a Buddha, through attachment to true existence, "Is the Buddha posited merely by these marks and signs?", that is not so, because the two form bodies of a Buddha are called the Tathāgata by way of having actualized the dharmakāya, but they are not posited merely by way of obtaining a body possessing the marks and signs. For, as taught in the Aṣṭasāhasrikā: "By finding a form body, one is not counted as being called a Tathāgata; rather, by finding omniscience of all aspects, one is counted as being called a Tathāgata." Seeing a form body adorned with the marks and signs of a body and paying homage to it and so forth with attachment to its true existence is indeed subsumed by the collection of merit of the excellent path, but it is flawed by being bound by apprehending true existence, as will be explained in the context of "Those who see me as form," and so forth; because it is also explained in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra in the context of "Attachment to the Jinas and so forth is subtle," that such a manner has the flaw of attachment to true existence. In this context, apprehending true existence must be asserted as ignorance, and it is explained in many texts that if one accumulates virtuous karma motivated by ignorance, one accomplishes higher realms subsumed by saṃsāra, and if one accumulates non-virtuous karma, one accomplishes the bodies of bad migrations. The meaning of the term "pāramitā" is both causing one to go to the other shore of the ocean of saṃsāra and having already gone to it; according to the former, it exists on the path of training, and the latter exists on the ground of a Buddha, which is synonymous with omniscience. [2-67] translation already produced for this document:
As for merely a fraction of the reasoning that they are not ultimately established: world systems accumulated from subtle particles are merely designated upon the assembly of subtle particles, but there is no separate thing called a "world system" as the individual subtle particles, their collection, or an entity distinct from them; for example, just as a vase is designated upon the collection of the vase's lip, base, belly, and so forth. Does a single subtle particle have the six directions of the four cardinal directions and above and below, or not? If it does, then because it would be larger than its own six directional parts, it would lack the meaning of being "subtle"; if it does not have those six directions, then because it lacks the capacity to occupy space, it would absurdly follow that the particle is not physical and it would also become a non-entity. Therefore, since a single subtle particle cannot exist in isolation, it must depend on collecting and assembling with others, so a subtle particle is not independently established; and because it is not established, it is said that the gross particles accumulated from it are also not independently established. In short, it is explained to meditate on emptiness by understanding that subtle particles do not truly exist as a singular nature, and world systems are not truly established as the nature of a multiple collection. Master Kamalaśīla explained that the world system in this context is intended as the world of sentient beings: the impure world system that is the basis where sentient beings dwell.

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Showing that if one knows and meditates on all phenomena as empty of nature, the benefits are great: the Bhagavān said to Subhūti that even more than whatever person were to give away their own bodies as gifts in number equal to the sand grains of the river Gaṅgā, if one were to apprehend merely a four-line stanza from this dharma discourse, and teach it to others and meditate on it, the merit is exceedingly greater. Although this also intends the arising of benefits like those stated by Āryadeva: "Those with small merit will not even have doubts about this dharma; even just having entertained a doubt will tear cyclic existence to shreds", yet in order that future disciples of inferior intellect who possess faith may generate enthusiasm for the benefits and engage in the text through hearing and contemplating, it is stated in the manner of praise that if one merely apprehends and recites a four-line stanza, such vast benefits will arise; and the actual intended meaning is that from the prajñāpāramitā of the meaning thus taught, one will completely obtain such benefits, but from merely reading the text, one will not completely obtain them, aside from a fraction of such benefits. This principle must also be known in other such contexts.
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Diamond Sūtra (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the sūtra, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names and technical terms in standard Sanskrit transliteration (Subhūti, Tathāgata, Dīpaṃkara, prajñāpāramitā) rather than translating them. Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own. Begin directly with the translation: do not write any introductory sentence such as "Here is the translation". Render each source line as exactly one line of continuous English prose, even where the source contains verse stanzas or lists; do not break it into several lines.

[2-66] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, as for whatever world systems accumulated from subtle particles there are, that is because the Tathāgata has taught that they too are not ultimately established as world systems; therefore, they are conventionally called "world systems."

[2-67] source:
དེ་དག་དོན་དམ་པར་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་པའི་རིགས་པ་ཕྱོགས་ཙམ་ནི། རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་བསགས་པའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་འདུས་པའི་སྟེང་དུ་བཏགས་པ་ཙམ་ཡིན་གྱི། རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རེ་རེ་བ་དང་ ཚོགས་པ་དང་དེ་ལས་དོན་གཞན་ན་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་ཞེས་པ་ཞིག་ལོགས་སུ་མེད་དེ། དཔེར་ན་བུམ་པའི་མཆུ་ཞབས་ལྟོ་བ་སོགས་ཚོགས་པ་ལ་བུམ་པར་བཏགས་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་གཅིག་ལ་ཕྱོགས་བཞི་དང་སྟེང་ འོག་གི་ཕྱོགས་དྲུག་ཡོད་དམ་མེད། ཡོད་ན་དེ་རང་གི་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱི་ཆ་དྲུག་ལས་ཆེ་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་དོན་མེད་ལ། དེའི་ཕྱོགས་དྲུག་མེད་ན་ནི་གོ་ས་མནོན་པའི་ནུས་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ན་རྡུལ་གཟུགས་ཅན་མ་ཡིན་པར་ ཐལ་ཞིང་དངོས་མེད་དུའང་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེས་ན་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་གཅིག་ནི་ཡན་གར་དུ་གནས་མི་ནུས་པས་གཞན་དང་ཚོགས་ཤིང་འདུས་པ་ལ་ལྟོས་དགོས་པས་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་རང་དབང་གིས་མ་གྲུབ་ཅིང༌། དེ་མ་གྲུབ་པས་དེ་བསགས་པའི་རྡུལ་རགས་པའང་རང་དབང་གིས་མ་གྲུབ་ཅེས་བྱའོ། །མདོར་ན་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ནི་གཅིག་གི་རང་བཞིན་དུ་བདེན་པར་མེད་ཅིང༌། འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་ནི་དུ་མ་ཚོགས་པའི་རང་བཞིན་དུ་བདེན་པར་མ་གྲུབ་ཅེས་སྟོང་ཉིད་བསྒོམ་པར་བཤད་པའོ། །སློབ་དཔོན་ཀ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལས་འདིའི་སྐབས་ཀྱི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་ནི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ལ་དགོངས་པར་བཤད་དེ། སེམས་ཅན་གནས་པའི་གཞི་མ་དག་པའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་སོ། །
[2-67] translation already produced for this document:
As for merely a fraction of the reasoning that they are not ultimately established: world systems accumulated from subtle particles are merely designated upon the assembly of subtle particles, but there is no separate thing called a "world system" as the individual subtle particles, their collection, or an entity distinct from them; for example, just as a vase is designated upon the collection of the vase's lip, base, belly, and so forth. Does a single subtle particle have the six directions of the four cardinal directions and above and below, or not? If it does, then because it would be larger than its own six directional parts, it would lack the meaning of being "subtle"; if it does not have those six directions, then because it lacks the capacity to occupy space, it would absurdly follow that the particle is not physical and it would also become a non-entity. Therefore, since a single subtle particle cannot exist in isolation, it must depend on collecting and assembling with others, so a subtle particle is not independently established; and because it is not established, it is said that the gross particles accumulated from it are also not independently established. In short, it is explained to meditate on emptiness by understanding that subtle particles do not truly exist as a singular nature, and world systems are not truly established as the nature of a multiple collection. Master Kamalaśīla explained that the world system in this context is intended as the world of sentient beings: the impure world system that is the basis where sentient beings dwell.

Then, as for [the teaching] that not only world systems, but also the form bodies of a Buddha and their marks and signs are not ultimately established: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "Do you think that the Tathāgata should be seen—that is, apprehended—as merely a body that is the collection of those thirty-two marks of a great being of the Tathāgata?", Subhūti replied, "That is not so. The reason is that whatever thirty-two marks of a great being of the Buddha were taught by the Tathāgata to exist conventionally, those were taught as not ultimately existing as marks," which refutes the extreme of permanence of superimposition, and by the phrase, "therefore they are conventionally called 'marks of a great being'," the extreme of nihilism of deprecation is refuted; this is similar for others as well. By the force of teaching the marks, the eighty signs are also taught, because the signs are the retinue of the marks. The thirty-two marks are as taught in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "The marks of wheels on the hands and feet, and feet like a tortoise," and so forth; and the eighty signs are as taught by "The Sage's nails are copper-colored," and so forth. If one thinks, upon seeing that the marks and signs are clear and complete on the two form bodies of a Buddha, through attachment to true existence, "Is the Buddha posited merely by these marks and signs?", that is not so, because the two form bodies of a Buddha are called the Tathāgata by way of having actualized the dharmakāya, but they are not posited merely by way of obtaining a body possessing the marks and signs. For, as taught in the Aṣṭasāhasrikā: "By finding a form body, one is not counted as being called a Tathāgata; rather, by finding omniscience of all aspects, one is counted as being called a Tathāgata." Seeing a form body adorned with the marks and signs of a body and paying homage to it and so forth with attachment to its true existence is indeed subsumed by the collection of merit of the excellent path, but it is flawed by being bound by apprehending true existence, as will be explained in the context of "Those who see me as form," and so forth; because it is also explained in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra in the context of "Attachment to the Jinas and so forth is subtle," that such a manner has the flaw of attachment to true existence. In this context, apprehending true existence must be asserted as ignorance, and it is explained in many texts that if one accumulates virtuous karma motivated by ignorance, one accomplishes higher realms subsumed by saṃsāra, and if one accumulates non-virtuous karma, one accomplishes the bodies of bad migrations. As for merely a fraction of the reasoning that they are not ultimately established: world systems accumulated from subtle particles are merely designated upon the assembly of subtle particles, but there is no separate thing called a "world system" as the individual subtle particles, their collection, or an entity distinct from them; for example, just as a vase is designated upon the collection of the vase's lip, base, belly, and so forth. Does a single subtle particle have the six directions of the four cardinal directions and above and below, or not? If it does, then because it would be larger than its own six directional parts, it would lack the meaning of being "subtle"; if it does not have those six directions, then because it lacks the capacity to occupy space, it would absurdly follow that the particle is not physical and it would also become a non-entity. Therefore, since a single subtle particle cannot exist in isolation, it must depend on collecting and assembling with others, so a subtle particle is not independently established; and because it is not established, it is said that the gross particles accumulated from it are also not independently established. In short, it is explained to meditate on emptiness by understanding that subtle particles do not truly exist as a singular nature, and world systems are not truly established as the nature of a multiple collection. Master Kamalaśīla explained that the world system in this context is intended as the world of sentient beings: the impure world system that is the basis where sentient beings dwell.

translation: "I, Subhūti, since the time noble wisdom was born in myself, have not heard this dharma discourse; not only that, but I have never heard this before." This does not mean that Subhūti had not heard such things before, but rather it shows that such a profound dharma of the prajñāpāramitā is difficult for others to hear.

[2-67] translation already produced for this document:
As for merely a fraction of the reasoning that they are not ultimately established: world systems accumulated from subtle particles are merely designated upon the assembly of subtle particles, but there is no separate thing called a "world system" as the individual subtle particles, their collection, or an entity distinct from them; for example, just as a vase is designated upon the collection of the vase's lip, base, belly, and so forth. Does a single subtle particle have the six directions of the four cardinal directions and above and below, or not? If it does, then because it would be larger than its own six directional parts, it would lack the meaning of being "subtle"; if it does not have those six directions, then because it lacks the capacity to occupy space, it would absurdly follow that the particle is not physical and it would also become a non-entity. Therefore, since a single subtle particle cannot exist in isolation, it must depend on collecting and assembling with others, so a subtle particle is not independently established; and because it is not established, it is said that the gross particles accumulated from it are also not independently established. In short, it is explained to meditate on emptiness by understanding that subtle particles do not truly exist as a singular nature, and world systems are not truly established as the nature of a multiple collection. Master Kamalaśīla explained that the world system in this context is intended as the world of sentient beings: the impure world system that is the basis where sentient beings dwell.

Then, as for [the teaching] that not only world systems, but also the form bodies of a Buddha and their marks and signs are not ultimately established: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "Do you think that the Tathāgata should be seen—that is, apprehended—as merely a body that is the collection of those thirty-two marks of a great being of the Tathāgata?", Subhūti replied, "That is not so. The reason is that whatever thirty-two marks of a great being of the Buddha were taught by the Tathāgata to exist conventionally, those were taught as not ultimately existing as marks," which refutes the extreme of permanence of superimposition, and by the phrase, "therefore they are conventionally called 'marks of a great being'," the extreme of nihilism of deprecation is refuted; this is similar for others as well. By the force of teaching the marks, the eighty signs are also taught, because the signs are the retinue of the marks. The thirty-two marks are as taught in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "The marks of wheels on the hands and feet, and feet like a tortoise," and so forth; and the eighty signs are as taught by "The Sage's nails are copper-colored," and so forth. If one thinks, upon seeing that the marks and signs are clear and complete on the two form bodies of a Buddha, through attachment to true existence, "Is the Buddha posited merely by these marks and signs?", that is not so, because the two form bodies of a Buddha are called the Tathāgata by way of having actualized the dharmakāya, but they are not posited merely by way of obtaining a body possessing the marks and signs. For, as taught in the Aṣṭasāhasrikā: "By finding a form body, one is not counted as being called a Tathāgata; rather, by finding omniscience of all aspects, one is counted as being called a Tathāgata." Seeing a form body adorned with the marks and signs of a body and paying homage to it and so forth with attachment to its true existence is indeed subsumed by the collection of merit of the excellent path, but it is flawed by being bound by apprehending true existence, as will be explained in the context of "Those who see me as form," and so forth; because it is also explained in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra in the context of "Attachment to the Jinas and so forth is subtle," that such a manner has the flaw of attachment to true existence. In this context, apprehending true existence must be asserted as ignorance, and it is explained in many texts that if one accumulates virtuous karma motivated by ignorance, one accomplishes higher realms subsumed by saṃsāra, and if one accumulates non-virtuous karma, one accomplishes the bodies of bad migrations. translation: As for the manner of being a great wonder: those sentient beings who, with respect to the words and meaning of this sūtra being taught, will generate the right perception free from attachment to true existence—those sentient beings, because they place predispositions for liberation and lay hold of a great cause for obtaining Buddhahood, will be endowed with a supreme great wonder.

As for merely a fraction of the reasoning that they are not ultimately established: world systems accumulated from subtle particles are merely designated upon the assembly of subtle particles, but there is no separate thing called a "world system" as the individual subtle particles, their collection, or an entity distinct from them; for example, just as a vase is designated upon the collection of the vase's lip, base, belly, and so forth. Does a single subtle particle have the six directions of the four cardinal directions and above and below, or not? If it does, then because it would be larger than its own six directional parts, it would lack the meaning of being "subtle"; if it does not have those six directions, then because it lacks the capacity to occupy space, it would absurdly follow that the particle is not physical and it would also become a non-entity. Therefore, since a single subtle particle cannot exist in isolation, it must depend on collecting and assembling with others, so a subtle particle is not independently established; and because it is not established, it is said that the gross particles accumulated from it are also not independently established. In short, it is explained to meditate on emptiness by understanding that subtle particles do not truly exist as a singular nature, and world systems are not truly established as the nature of a multiple collection. Master Kamalaśīla explained that the world system in this context is intended as the world of sentient beings: the impure world system that is the basis where sentient beings dwell.

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Whatever is explained as "the right perception" is because of the absence of the perception of being attached to true existence; therefore, the Tathāgata has taught that the perception which is without attachment to true existence and realizes the lack of true existence is called "the right perception".

[2-67] translation already produced for this document:
As for merely a fraction of the reasoning that they are not ultimately established: world systems accumulated from subtle particles are merely designated upon the assembly of subtle particles, but there is no separate thing called a "world system" as the individual subtle particles, their collection, or an entity distinct from them; for example, just as a vase is designated upon the collection of the vase's lip, base, belly, and so forth. Does a single subtle particle have the six directions of the four cardinal directions and above and below, or not? If it does, then because it would be larger than its own six directional parts, it would lack the meaning of being "subtle"; if it does not have those six directions, then because it lacks the capacity to occupy space, it would absurdly follow that the particle is not physical and it would also become a non-entity. Therefore, since a single subtle particle cannot exist in isolation, it must depend on collecting and assembling with others, so a subtle particle is not independently established; and because it is not established, it is said that the gross particles accumulated from it are also not independently established. In short, it is explained to meditate on emptiness by understanding that subtle particles do not truly exist as a singular nature, and world systems are not truly established as the nature of a multiple collection. Master Kamalaśīla explained that the world system in this context is intended as the world of sentient beings: the impure world system that is the basis where sentient beings dwell.

Then, as for [the teaching] that not only world systems, but also the form bodies of a Buddha and their marks and signs are not ultimately established: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "Do you think that the Tathāgata should be seen—that is, apprehended—as merely a body that is the collection of those thirty-two marks of a great being of the Tathāgata?", Subhūti replied, "That is not so. The reason is that whatever thirty-two marks of a great being of the Buddha were taught by the Tathāgata to exist conventionally, those were taught as not ultimately existing as marks," which refutes the extreme of permanence of superimposition, and by the phrase, "therefore they are conventionally called 'marks of a great being'," the extreme of nihilism of deprecation is refuted; this is similar for others as well. By the force of teaching the marks, the eighty signs are also taught, because the signs are the retinue of the marks. The thirty-two marks are as taught in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "The marks of wheels on the hands and feet, and feet like a tortoise," and so forth; and the eighty signs are as taught by "The Sage's nails are copper-colored," and so forth. If one thinks, upon seeing that the marks and signs are clear and complete on the two form bodies of a Buddha, through attachment to true existence, "Is the Buddha posited merely by these marks and signs?", that is not so, because the two form bodies of a Buddha are called the Tathāgata by way of having actualized the dharmakāya, but they are not posited merely by way of obtaining a body possessing the marks and signs. For, as taught in the Aṣṭasāhasrikā: "By finding a form body, one is not counted as being called a Tathāgata; rather, by finding omniscience of all aspects, one is counted as being called a Tathāgata." Seeing a form body adorned with the marks and signs of a body and paying homage to it and so forth with attachment to its true existence is indeed subsumed by the collection of merit of the excellent path, but it is flawed by being bound by apprehending true existence, as will be explained in the context of "Those who see me as form," and so forth; because it is also explained in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra in the context of "Attachment to the Jinas and so forth is subtle," that such a manner has the flaw of attachment to true existence. translation: "Bhagavān, that I have generated conviction having examined and known with faith the meaning of this dharma being taught is not a great wonder for me; but in future times, those sentient beings who are convinced of the meaning of emptiness and take up this dharma and so forth, they will be endowed with a supreme great wonder." This way is a great wonder, just as the Venerable Lord Nāgārjuna said: "Whoever, having known this emptiness of phenomena, relies on karma and results—this is more wonderful than the wonderful! This is more marvelous than the marvelous!" The meaning of the rest has been explained previously, and regarding "dri ba", if it appears as "da dri", it connects with asking about another meaning, and if it appears as "ba bri", it connects with writing in letters; however, according to what appears in the Madhyāntavibhāga, "Writing letters, worshipping, giving," it is the latter. These texts teach the manner of how to abide, practice, and apprehend.
