As for merely a fraction of the reasoning that they are not ultimately established: world systems accumulated from subtle particles are merely designated upon the assembly of subtle particles, but there is no separate thing called a "world system" as the individual subtle particles, their collection, or an entity distinct from them; for example, just as a vase is designated upon the collection of the vase's lip, base, belly, and so forth. Does a single subtle particle have the six directions of the four cardinal directions and above and below, or not? If it does, then because it would be larger than its own six directional parts, it would lack the meaning of being "subtle"; if it does not have those six directions, then because it lacks the capacity to occupy space, it would absurdly follow that the particle is not physical and it would also become a non-entity. Therefore, since a single subtle particle cannot exist in isolation, it must depend on collecting and assembling with others, so a subtle particle is not independently established; and because it is not established, it is said that the gross particles accumulated from it are also not independently established. In short, it is explained to meditate on emptiness by understanding that subtle particles do not truly exist as a singular nature, and world systems are not truly established as the nature of a multiple collection. Master Kamalaśīla explained that the world system in this context is intended as the world of sentient beings: the impure world system that is the basis where sentient beings dwell.

[2-67] translation already produced for this document:
As for merely a fraction of the reasoning that they are not ultimately established: world systems accumulated from subtle particles are merely designated upon the assembly of subtle particles, but there is no separate thing called a "world system" as the individual subtle particles, their collection, or an entity distinct from them; for example, just as a vase is designated upon the collection of the vase's lip, base, belly, and so forth. Does a single subtle particle have the six directions of the four cardinal directions and above and below, or not? If it does, then because it would be larger than its own six directional parts, it would lack the meaning of being "subtle"; if it does not have those six directions, then because it lacks the capacity to occupy space, it would absurdly follow that the particle is not physical and it would also become a non-entity. Therefore, since a single subtle particle cannot exist in isolation, it must depend on collecting and assembling with others, so a subtle particle is not independently established; and because it is not established, it is said that the gross particles accumulated from it are also not independently established. In short, it is explained to meditate on emptiness by understanding that subtle particles do not truly exist as a singular nature, and world systems are not truly established as the nature of a multiple collection. Master Kamalaśīla explained that the world system in this context is intended as the world of sentient beings: the impure world system that is the basis where sentient beings dwell.

Then, as for [the teaching] that not only world systems, but also the form bodies of a Buddha and their marks and signs are not ultimately established: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "Do you think that the Tathāgata should be seen—that is, apprehended—as merely a body that is the collection of those thirty-two marks of a great being of the Tathāgata?", Subhūti replied, "That is not so. The reason is that whatever thirty-two marks of a great being of the Buddha were taught by the Tathāgata to exist conventionally, those were taught as not ultimately existing as marks," which refutes the extreme of permanence of superimposition, and by the phrase, "therefore they are conventionally called 'marks of a great being'," the extreme of nihilism of deprecation is refuted; this is similar for others as well. By the force of teaching the marks, the eighty signs are also taught, because the signs are the retinue of the marks. The thirty-two marks are as taught in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "The marks of wheels on the hands and feet, and feet like a tortoise," and so forth; and the eighty signs are as taught by "The Sage's nails are copper-colored," and so forth. If one thinks, upon seeing that the marks and signs are clear and complete on the two form bodies of a Buddha, through attachment to true existence, "Is the Buddha posited merely by these marks and signs?", that is not so, because the two form bodies of a Buddha are called the Tathāgata by way of having actualized the dharmakāya, but they are not posited merely by way of obtaining a body possessing the marks and signs. For, as taught in the Aṣṭasāhasrikā: "By finding a form body, one is not counted as being called a Tathāgata; rather, by finding omniscience of all aspects, one is counted as being called a Tathāgata." Seeing a form body adorned with the marks and signs of a body and paying homage to it and so forth with attachment to its true existence is indeed subsumed by the collection of merit of the excellent path, but it is flawed by being bound by apprehending true existence, as will be explained in the context of "Those who see me as form," and so forth; because it is also explained in the Abhisamayālaṃkāra in the context of "Attachment to the Jinas and so forth is subtle," that such a manner has the flaw of attachment to true existence. In this context, apprehending true existence must be asserted as ignorance, and it is explained in many texts that if one accumulates virtuous karma motivated by ignorance, one accomplishes higher realms subsumed by saṃsāra, and if one accumulates non-virtuous karma, one accomplishes the bodies of bad migrations. translation: When he asked, "The reason is that such a perception of a self and so forth engages erroneously in the object of attachment, and therefore it is itself devoid of all right perceptions, or because those perceptions are devoid of being established as perceptions ultimately," the Bhagavān said to Subhūti, "It is so," and the reason is: "In the future, those sentient beings who, when hearing the words and meaning of this sūtra being taught, are not terrified, do not tremble, and do not become exceedingly frightened in their minds, thinking, 'If everything lacks true existence in that way, actions and agents such as karma and results would be untenable and would become non-existent,' but instead believe and generate conviction, those will be endowed with a supreme wonder." If things were established truly, they would be unsuitable to change, and thus all actions and agents such as karma and results would be unsuitable to be posited and would be untenable; whereas the way in which all actions and agents and nirvāṇa and so forth are tenable with respect to what lacks true existence or is not established by its own nature is just as it is said in the Lord's Praise of Dependent Arising: "Because nature cannot be reversed, if phenomena had some nature, nirvāṇa would be impossible, and it is taught that all elaborations would be irreversible," and, "Being empty of nature and the tenability of actions and agents do not contradict each other; when one sees the reverse of that, action is impossible in what is empty."

ངོ་མཚར་ཆེ་ཚུལ་ནི། མདོ་སྡེ་འདི་བཤད་པའི་ཚིག་དང་དོན་ལ་སེམས་ཅན་གང་དག་བདེན་ཞེན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་སྐྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ནི། ཐར་པའི་བག་ཆགས་འཇོག་ཅིང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐོབ་པའི་རྒྱུ་ཆེན་པོ་བཟུང་བས་ན་ངོ་མཚར་ཆེན་པོ་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[2-72] translation already produced for this document:
As for the manner of being a great wonder: those sentient beings who, with respect to the words and meaning of this sūtra being taught, will generate the right perception free from attachment to true existence—those sentient beings, because they place predispositions for liberation and lay hold of a great cause for obtaining Buddhahood, will be endowed with a supreme great wonder.

[2-73] source:
ཡང་དག་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཞེས་བཤད་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ནི་བདེན་པར་ཞེན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་མ་མཆིས་པའི་སླད་དུ་སྟེ། དེས་ན་བདེན་ཞེན་མེད་ཅིང་བདེན་མེད་རྟོགས་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་དེ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཞེས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་སོ། །
[2-73] translation already produced for this document:
Whatever is explained as "the right perception" is because of the absence of the perception of being attached to true existence; therefore, the Tathāgata has taught that the perception which is without attachment to true existence and realizes the lack of true existence is called "the right perception".

[2-74] source:
བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་བདག་ཆོས་འདི་བཤད་པའི་དོན་ལ་དད་པས་རྟོག་ཅིང་ཤེས་ནས་མོས་པ་སྐྱེས་པ་འདི་ནི། བདག་ལ་ངོ་མཚར་ཆེན་པོ་བྱུང་བ་མ་ལགས་ཀྱི། སླད་མའི་དུས་སུ་སེམས་ཅན་གང་དག་སྟོང་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་ལ་མོས་ཤིང་ཆོས་འདི་ལེན་པ་སོགས་བྱེད་པ་དེ་དག་ནི་ངོ་མཚར་ཆེན་པོ་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་ལགས་སོ། །ཚུལ་འདི་ངོ་མཚར་ཆེ་སྟེ། མགོན་པོ་ཀླུ་སྒྲུབ་ཞབས་ཀྱིས། ཆོས་རྣམས་སྟོང་པ་འདི་ཤེས་ནས། །ལས་དང་འབྲས་བུ་བསྟེན་པ་གང༌། །ངོ་མཚར་བས་ཀྱང་འདི་ངོ་མཚར། །རྨད་བྱུང་བས་ཀྱང་འདི་རྨད་བྱུང༌། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །གཞན་གྱི་དོན་སྔར་བཤད་ཟིན་ཅིང༌། འདྲི་བ་ལ་ནི་ད་འདྲི་འབྱུང་བ་ལྟར་ན་དོན་གཞན་ལ་འདྲི་བ་དང༌། བ་འབྲི་འབྱུང་བ་ལྟར་ན་ཡི་གེར་འབྲི་བ་དང་སྦྱོར་ཏེ། འོན་ཀྱང་དབུ་མཐའ་ལས། ཡི་གེ་འབྲི་མཆོད་སྦྱིན་པ་དང༌། །ཞེས་འབྱུང་བ་ལྟར་ན་ཕྱི་མའོ། །གཞུང་འདི་དག་གིས་ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་གནས་པ་དང་བསྒྲུབ་པ་དང་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཚུལ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[2-74] translation already produced for this document:
"Bhagavān, that I have generated conviction having examined and known with faith the meaning of this dharma being taught is not a great wonder for me; but in future times, those sentient beings who are convinced of the meaning of emptiness and take up this dharma and so forth, they will be endowed with a supreme great wonder." This way is a great wonder, just as the Venerable Lord Nāgārjuna said: "Whoever, having known this emptiness of phenomena, relies on karma and results—this is more wonderful than the wonderful! This is more marvelous than the marvelous!" The meaning of the rest has been explained previously, and regarding "dri ba", if it appears as "da dri", it connects with asking about another meaning, and if it appears as "ba bri", it connects with writing in letters; however, according to what appears in the Madhyāntavibhāga, "Writing letters, worshipping, giving," it is the latter. These texts teach the manner of how to abide, practice, and apprehend.

[2-75] source:
མ་འོངས་པའི་དུས་ན་གཞུང་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་ཐོས་བསམ་བསྒོམས་པས་འཇུག་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ལ་ནི། གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་རགས་པ་འཇུག་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཞིང༌། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་སེམས་ཅན་དང་སྲོག་དང་གང་ཟག་ཏུ་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཅི་རིགས་འཇུག་པ་སྟེ་སྐྱེ་བར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[2-75] translation already produced for this document:
In future times, for those sentient beings who engage in such a text through hearing, contemplating, and meditating, a gross perception of a self of persons will not engage; and similarly, the various perceptions of true attachment to a sentient being, a life-principle, and a person will not engage, that is, will not arise.

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: The reason for being a great wonder is: "This supreme holy prajñāpāramitā text, which teaches that all phenomena are not established by their own nature, has now been spoken by me, the Tathāgata, and because it has been spoken by measureless previous Buddha Bhagavāns." That was spoken in order to apprehend the aforementioned explanation that the phenomena of causes and results are without their own nature as a basis for belief.

Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own. Begin directly with the translation: do not write any introductory sentence such as "Here is the translation". དེ་ལྟར་གསུངས་པ་ན་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་ཆོས་ཟབ་མོ་འདི་ཐོས་ནས་ངོ་མཚར་སྐྱེས་པའི་ཤུགས་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་སྤྱན་ལས་མཆི་མ་ཕྱུང་སྟེ། རབ་འབྱོར་དེས་མཆི་མ་ཕྱིས་ནས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་ཆོས་འདི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཇི་སྙེད་བྱོན་ཅིང་བཞུགས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་གསུངས་པ་ནི་ངོ་མཚར་ཆེའོ། །

[2-71] source:
རབ་འབྱོར་བདག་གིས་ནི་རང་ལ་འཕགས་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་སྐྱེས་ཚུན་ཆད་ནས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་མ་ཐོས་ཤིང༌། དེར་མ་ཟད་སྔོན་ནམ་ཡང་འདི་མ་ཐོས་སོ་ཞེས་པ་ནི་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་སྔོན་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་མ་ཐོས་པ་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་ཆོས་ཟབ་མོ་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་གཞན་གྱིས་ཐོས་པར་དཀའ་བར་བསྟན་པའོ། །
[2-71] translation already produced for this document:
"I, Subhūti, since the time noble wisdom was born in myself, have not heard this dharma discourse; not only that, but I have never heard this before." This does not mean that Subhūti had not heard such things before, but rather it shows that such a profound dharma of the prajñāpāramitā is difficult for others to hear.

[2-72] source:
ངོ་མཚར་ཆེ་ཚུལ་ནི། མདོ་སྡེ་འདི་བཤད་པའི་ཚིག་དང་དོན་ལ་སེམས་ཅན་གང་དག་བདེན་ཞེན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་སྐྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ནི། ཐར་པའི་བག་ཆགས་འཇོག་ཅིང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐོབ་པའི་རྒྱུ་ཆེན་པོ་བཟུང་བས་ན་ངོ་མཚར་ཆེན་པོ་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[2-72] translation already produced for this document:
As for the manner of being a great wonder: those sentient beings who, with respect to the words and meaning of this sūtra being taught, will generate the right perception free from attachment to true existence—those sentient beings, because they place predispositions for liberation and lay hold of a great cause for obtaining Buddhahood, will be endowed with a supreme great wonder.

[2-73] source:
ཡང་དག་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཞེས་བཤད་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ནི་བདེན་པར་ཞེན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་མ་མཆིས་པའི་སླད་དུ་སྟེ། དེས་ན་བདེན་ཞེན་མེད་ཅིང་བདེན་མེད་རྟོགས་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་དེ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཞེས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་སོ། །

Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the sūtra, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names and technical terms in standard Sanskrit transliteration (Subhūti, Tathāgata, Dīpaṃkara, prajñāpāramitā) rather than translating them. Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own. Begin directly with the translation: do not write any introductory sentence such as "Here is the translation". Render each source line as exactly one line of continuous English prose, even where the source contains verse stanzas or lists; do not break it into several lines.

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Then, explaining specifically the perfection of patience: "Subhūti, whatever is called the perfection of patience, that perfection itself lacks ultimate existence, so it is unsuitable to be apprehended with attachment to true existence regarding the three spheres of by whom one is patient, how or what is endured, and toward whom one is patient. The reason is, Subhūti, at a previous time when the King of Kaliṅga generated an evil suspicion thinking that I was involved with his women, and severed my major limbs, minor limbs, and fingers with a sword, at that time, because I meditated on patience having known the three spheres of patience to lack true existence, focusing on the conventional 'I', perceptions ranging from the perception of attachment to a true self thinking 'I am' up to the perception of attachment to a true person did not arise, and at that time I had no such perception of attachment to true existence whatsoever; yet it was not that there were no other perceptions conventionally, because there were the perceptions of accepting suffering thinking 'I am patient', and of being unperturbed by harm, and the perception of certainty regarding phenomena realized as lacking true existence"—so he intended.

རབ་འབྱོར་བདག་གིས་ནི་རང་ལ་འཕགས་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་སྐྱེས་ཚུན་ཆད་ནས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་འདི་མ་ཐོས་ཤིང༌། དེར་མ་ཟད་སྔོན་ནམ་ཡང་འདི་མ་ཐོས་སོ་ཞེས་པ་ནི་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་སྔོན་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་མ་ཐོས་པ་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་ཆོས་ཟབ་མོ་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་གཞན་གྱིས་ཐོས་པར་དཀའ་བར་བསྟན་པའོ། །
[2-71] translation already produced for this document:
"I, Subhūti, since the time noble wisdom was born in myself, have not heard this dharma discourse; not only that, but I have never heard this before." This does not mean that Subhūti had not heard such things before, but rather it shows that such a profound dharma of the prajñāpāramitā is difficult for others to hear.

[2-72] source:
ངོ་མཚར་ཆེ་ཚུལ་ནི། མདོ་སྡེ་འདི་བཤད་པའི་ཚིག་དང་དོན་ལ་སེམས་ཅན་གང་དག་བདེན་ཞེན་མེད་པ་ཡང་དག་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་སྐྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ནི། ཐར་པའི་བག་ཆགས་འཇོག་ཅིང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐོབ་པའི་རྒྱུ་ཆེན་པོ་བཟུང་བས་ན་ངོ་མཚར་ཆེན་པོ་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[2-72] translation already produced for this document:
As for the manner of being a great wonder: those sentient beings who, with respect to the words and meaning of this sūtra being taught, will generate the right perception free from attachment to true existence—those sentient beings, because they place predispositions for liberation and lay hold of a great cause for obtaining Buddhahood, will be endowed with a supreme great wonder.

[2-73] source:
ཡང་དག་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཞེས་བཤད་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ནི་བདེན་པར་ཞེན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་མ་མཆིས་པའི་སླད་དུ་སྟེ། དེས་ན་བདེན་ཞེན་མེད་ཅིང་བདེན་མེད་རྟོགས་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་དེ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཞེས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་སོ། །
[2-73] translation already produced for this document:
Whatever is explained as "the right perception" is because of the absence of the perception of being attached to true existence; therefore, the Tathāgata has taught that the perception which is without attachment to true existence and realizes the lack of true existence is called "the right perception".

[2-74] source:
བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་བདག་ཆོས་འདི་བཤད་པའི་དོན་ལ་དད་པས་རྟོག་ཅིང་ཤེས་ནས་མོས་པ་སྐྱེས་པ་འདི་ནི། བདག་ལ་ངོ་མཚར་ཆེན་པོ་བྱུང་བ་མ་ལགས་ཀྱི། སླད་མའི་དུས་སུ་སེམས་ཅན་གང་དག་སྟོང་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་ལ་མོས་ཤིང་ཆོས་འདི་ལེན་པ་སོགས་བྱེད་པ་དེ་དག་ནི་ངོ་མཚར་ཆེན་པོ་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་ལགས་སོ། །ཚུལ་འདི་ངོ་མཚར་ཆེ་སྟེ། མགོན་པོ་ཀླུ་སྒྲུབ་ཞབས་ཀྱིས། ཆོས་རྣམས་སྟོང་པ་འདི་ཤེས་ནས། །ལས་དང་འབྲས་བུ་བསྟེན་པ་གང༌། །ངོ་མཚར་བས་ཀྱང་འདི་ངོ་མཚར། །རྨད་བྱུང་བས་ཀྱང་འདི་རྨད་བྱུང༌། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །གཞན་གྱི་དོན་སྔར་བཤད་ཟིན་ཅིང༌། འདྲི་བ་ལ་ནི་ད་འདྲི་འབྱུང་བ་ལྟར་ན་དོན་གཞན་ལ་འདྲི་བ་དང༌། བ་འབྲི་འབྱུང་བ་ལྟར་ན་ཡི་གེར་འབྲི་བ་དང་སྦྱོར་ཏེ། འོན་ཀྱང་དབུ་མཐའ་ལས། ཡི་གེ་འབྲི་མཆོད་སྦྱིན་པ་དང༌། །ཞེས་འབྱུང་བ་ལྟར་ན་ཕྱི་མའོ། །གཞུང་འདི་དག་གིས་ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་གནས་པ་དང་བསྒྲུབ་པ་དང་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཚུལ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[2-74] translation already produced for this document:
"Bhagavān, that I have generated conviction having examined and known with faith the meaning of this dharma being taught is not a great wonder for me; but in future times, those sentient beings who are convinced of the meaning of emptiness and take up this dharma and so forth, they will be endowed with a supreme great wonder." This way is a great wonder, just as the Venerable Lord Nāgārjuna said: "Whoever, having known this emptiness of phenomena, relies on karma and results—this is more wonderful than the wonderful! This is more marvelous than the marvelous!" The meaning of the rest has been explained previously, and regarding "dri ba", if it appears as "da dri", it connects with asking about another meaning, and if it appears as "ba bri", it connects with writing in letters; however, according to what appears in the Madhyāntavibhāga, "Writing letters, worshipping, giving," it is the latter. These texts teach the manner of how to abide, practice, and apprehend.

[2-75] source:
མ་འོངས་པའི་དུས་ན་གཞུང་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་ཐོས་བསམ་བསྒོམས་པས་འཇུག་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ལ་ནི། གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་རགས་པ་འཇུག་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཞིང༌། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་སེམས་ཅན་དང་སྲོག་དང་གང་ཟག་ཏུ་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཅི་རིགས་འཇུག་པ་སྟེ་སྐྱེ་བར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[2-75] translation already produced for this document:
In future times, for those sentient beings who engage in such a text through hearing, contemplating, and meditating, a gross perception of a self of persons will not engage; and similarly, the various perceptions of true attachment to a sentient being, a life-principle, and a person will not engage, that is, will not arise.

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
source: དེར་མ་ཟད། ངས་མངོན་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་མཁྱེན་ཏེ། ང་སྔོན་ཚེ་རབས་ལྔ་བརྒྱར་བཟོད་པ་སྨྲ་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་དྲང་སྲོང་དུ་གྱུར་པའི་དུས་སུ་རྐྱེན་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་གཞན་གྱིས་ངའི་ཡན་ལག་སོགས་བཅད་པ་ན་བདག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་སོགས་མ་བྱུང་ངོ༌། །གལ་ཏེ་ཡན་ལག་བཅད་པའི་དུས་ཀྱི་ང་དེ་སྟོན་པ་མིན་ཞིང༌། སྟོན་པ་ཡང་དེའི་དུས་ཀྱི་ང་དེ་མིན་པས། སྟོན་པས་ངའི་ཡན་ལག་རྣམས་གསུངས་པ་དེ་ཇི་ལྟར་འཐད་སྙམ་ན། བདེན་མོད། འདིའི་ལན་ཞིབ་ཏུ་བཤད་ན་མང་དུ་འགྱུར་བས། བསྡུས་ན་དེ་ནི་རྒྱུད་གཅིག་པ་ལ་དགོངས་ཤིང་སྐྱོན་མེད་ཚུལ་གོང་དུ་ཅུང་ཟད་བཤད་ཅིང་འཆད་པར་བྱའོ། །ངའོ་སྙམ་པའི་བདག་ཏུ་ཞེན་པ་ཡོད་ན་གནོད་སེམས་སོགས་འབྱུང་བ་ནི། རྣམ་འགྲེལ་ལས། བདག་ཡོད་ན་ནི་གཞན་དུ་ཤེས། །བདག་གཞན་ཆ་ལས་འཛིན་དང་སྡང༌། །འདི་དག་དང་ནི་ཡོངས་འབྲེལ་བས། །ཉེས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར། །ཞེས་བཤད་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །
translation: Not only that, I directly knew and cognized it: in the past, during five hundred lifetimes when I became a sage called 'Preacher of Patience', when, depending on such conditions, others severed my limbs and so forth, perceptions of a self and so forth did not arise. If one thinks, 'If the "I" at the time of the limbs being severed was not the Teacher, and the Teacher was also not the "I" of that time, how is it tenable for the Teacher to speak of "my limbs"?', it is indeed true, but if the answer to this were explained in detail it would become voluminous, so in brief, it was intended in terms of being the same continuum, and the way in which this is faultless has been somewhat explained above and will be explained. The arising of malicious intent and so forth if there is attachment to a self thinking 'I am' is just as explained in the Pramāṇavārttika: 'If there is a self, one perceives an other. From the aspects of self and other come grasping and hatred; by being fully connected with these, all faults will arise.'

Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the sūtra, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names and technical terms in standard Sanskrit transliteration (Subhūti, Tathāgata, Dīpaṃkara, prajñāpāramitā) rather than translating them. Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own. Begin directly with the translation: do not write any introductory sentence such as "Here is the translation". Render each source line as exactly one line of continuous English prose, even where the source contains verse stanzas or lists; do not break it into several lines.

མ་འོངས་པའི་དུས་ན་གཞུང་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་ཐོས་བསམ་བསྒོམས་པས་འཇུག་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ལ་ནི། གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་ཏུ་འདུ་ཤེས་རགས་པ་འཇུག་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཞིང༌། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་སེམས་ཅན་དང་སྲོག་དང་གང་ཟག་ཏུ་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཅི་རིགས་འཇུག་པ་སྟེ་སྐྱེ་བར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[2-75] translation already produced for this document:

When he asked, "The reason is that such a perception of a self and so forth engages erroneously in the object of attachment, and therefore it is itself devoid of all right perceptions, or because those perceptions are devoid of being established as perceptions ultimately," the Bhagavān said to Subhūti, "It is so," and the reason is: "In the future, those sentient beings who, when hearing the words and meaning of this sūtra being taught, are not terrified, do not tremble, and do not become exceedingly frightened in their minds, thinking, 'If everything lacks true existence in that way, actions and agents such as karma and results would be untenable and would become non-existent,' but instead believe and generate conviction, those will be endowed with a supreme wonder." heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Because I became a Buddha by the power of such patience, for that reason, bodhisattvas should completely abandon such a perception of a self, generate the mind for unsurpassed awakening, and make it increase further. Not only should they not abide through attachment to true existence in the three spheres of patience, they also should not abide in that way in forms, sounds, and so forth, and they should not abide through attachment to true existence in whatever conventional phenomena, nor should they abide through attachment to true existence in the ultimate, which is conventional phenomena's lack of true existence.

Then, explaining specifically the perfection of patience: "Subhūti, whatever is called the perfection of patience, that perfection itself lacks ultimate existence, so it is unsuitable to be apprehended with attachment to true existence regarding the three spheres of by whom one is patient, how or what is endured, and toward whom one is patient. translation: Therefore, the Tathāgata said, 'A bodhisattva should give gifts without ultimately abiding in anything'; and illustrating by that, he intended that this be applied to others such as ethical discipline as well. Bodhisattvas should completely give gifts, guard ethical discipline, and so forth in this way, without attachment to true existence.

translation: 'Subhūti, whatever phenomena of attainment the Tathāgata has awakened to or taught, among those, true ultimate phenomena are not established truly, and false conventional phenomena are also not established truly,' so it was said. Kamalaśīla seems to have explained that conventionalities, because they do not exist in the nature of the rational consciousness inquiring into the ultimate, are untrue and false; and this text also dispels the two extremes.

translation: Teaching that there is a difference in the function of giving and so forth due to realizing or not realizing the lack of true existence: 'It is like this: for example, just as a person endowed with eyes entering a great darkness would not clearly see any entities of forms as objects, similarly, those bodhisattvas who give gifts having fallen into the abyss of the view of manifest attachment, bound by apprehending true existence without directing their minds toward the lack of true existence, should be viewed as bodhisattvas similar to that example.'

translation: 'Furthermore, it is like this: just as when dawn breaks and the sun rises, a person endowed with eyes sees various aspects of good and bad objects of form, similarly, those bodhisattvas who completely give gifts without falling into entities bound by apprehending true existence should be viewed as similar to that example.' Thus, giving bound by apprehending true existence was explained as being similar to a person having entered darkness and not seeing forms, and giving with realization of the lack of true existence was explained as being similar to someone endowed with eyes seeing forms; and furthermore, the five, giving and so forth, when not embraced by the wisdom realizing the lack of true existence, are like someone blind from birth, and the perfection of wisdom realizing the lack of true existence is like someone endowed with eyes leading the blind. The Sañcaya states: "How could ten million, one hundred billion people blind from birth, without a guide, who do not even know the way, enter the city? Without wisdom, these five blind perfections, being without a guide, are unable to touch awakening." And following what was thus stated, to teach in connection with the former that if those first five perfections are not embraced by the perfection of wisdom realizing the lack of true existence, they are like being without eyes and are unable to travel to the ground of a Buddha, and if they are embraced, they are like being endowed with eyes and are able to travel there, it states: "When they are thoroughly embraced by wisdom, then they gain eyes and obtain this name." And the glorious Candrakīrti also stated in the Madhyamakāvatāra: "Just as a single person endowed with eyes easily leads an entire assembly of blind people to their desired destination, similarly here too, intelligence takes the virtues whose eyes are impaired and goes to victoriousness itself."

དེ་བས་ན་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཅི་ལ་ཡང་དོན་དམ་པར་མི་གནས་པར་སྦྱིན་པ་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། དེས་མཚོན་ནས་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་སོགས་གཞན་ལའང་སྦྱོར་བར་དགོངས་སོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་ནི་བདེན་ཞེན་མེད་པའི་ཚུལ་འདི་ལྟར་སྦྱིན་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་གཏོང་བ་དང་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་སྲུང་སོགས་བྱའོ། །

སེམས་ཅན་དུ་བདེན་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱང་དོན་དམ་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་པ་དང༌། ཐ་སྙད་དུ་སེམས་ཅན་གང་དག་ཅེས་གསུངས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ཉིད་ཀྱང་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་མེད་པའོ། །

[2-87] source:
རབ་འབྱོར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་ཐོབ་བྱའི་ཆོས་གང་ཡང་སངས་རྒྱས་པའམ་བསྟན་པ་དེ་རྣམས་ལ་བདེན་པ་དོན་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཡང་མེད་ཅིང༌། རྫུན་པ་ཀུན་རྫོབ་པའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་སོ། །ཀ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལས་ནི། ཀུན་རྫོབ་རྣམས་དོན་དམ་དཔྱོད་པའི་རིག་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོར་མེད་པས་མི་བདེན་ཅིང་རྫུན་པ་ལ་བཤད་པ་ལྟར་སྣང་སྟེ། གཞུང་འདིས་མཐའ་གཉིས་སེལ་བའང་ཡིན་ནོ། །

'Subhūti, whatever phenomena of attainment the Tathāgata has awakened to or taught, among those, true ultimate phenomena are not established truly, and false conventional phenomena are also not established truly,' so it was said. [2-88] source:

རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་རབ་འབྱོར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་དེ་ལྟར་ཆོས་རྣམས་བདེན་སྟོང་དུ་བཤད་པ་ནི་བརྫུན་དུ་གསུངས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ནི་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་ཡང་དག་པར་གསུངས་པ་དང༌། རྣམ་པ་གཞན་དུ་མི་འགྱུར་བའི་བདེན་པར་གསུངས་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་གནས་ཚུལ་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་དུ་གསུང་བ་པོ་སྟེ། ལོག་པར་གསུང་བ་པོ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །

བདེན་མེད་རྟོགས་མ་རྟོགས་པའི་དབང་གིས་སྦྱིན་སོགས་ཀྱི་བྱེད་ལས་ལ་ཁྱད་པར་ཡོད་ཅེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། འདི་ལྟ་སྟེ་དཔེར་ན། མིག་དང་ལྡན་པའི་མི་ཞིག་མུན་པ་ཆེན་པོར་ཞུགས་ནས་ཡུལ་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་དངོས་པོ་ཅི་ཡང་གསལ་བར་མི་མཐོང་བ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ། བྱང་སེམས་གང་བདེན་མེད་ལ་བློ་ཁ་མ་ཕྱོགས་ཤིང་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པའི་མངོན་ཞེན་གྱི་ལྟ་བའི་གཡང་དུ་ལྷུང་ནས་སྦྱིན་པ་གཏོང་བའི་བྱང་སེམས་རྣམས་ནི་དཔེ་དེ་དང་འདྲ་བའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །
[2-88] translation already produced for this document:
Teaching that there is a difference in the function of giving and so forth due to realizing or not realizing the lack of true existence: 'It is like this: for example, just as a person endowed with eyes entering a great darkness would not clearly see any entities of forms as objects, similarly, those bodhisattvas who give gifts having fallen into the abyss of the view of manifest attachment, bound by apprehending true existence without directing their minds toward the lack of true existence, should be viewed as bodhisattvas similar to that example.'

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Furthermore, he said, 'If compared to the benefits of giving away bodies illustrated by giving the body in the morning and afternoon times and for many eons in numbers equalling the grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, the aggregate of merit of whoever hears this text completely, is inspired by it, and does not abandon it mentally is even greater than that former one, what need is there to say that if one does things such as writing this text in letters, the merit will be greater than that?' And moreover, from taking it up through to perfectly teaching it, the latter will have greater merit, that is, benefits, than the former.

སེམས་ཅན་དུ་བདེན་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱང་དོན་དམ་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་པ་དང༌། ཐ་སྙད་དུ་སེམས་ཅན་གང་དག་ཅེས་གསུངས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ཉིད་ཀྱང་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་མེད་པའོ། །

སེམས་ཅན་དུ་བདེན་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱང་དོན་དམ་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་པ་དང༌། ཐ་སྙད་དུ་སེམས་ཅན་གང་དག་ཅེས་གསུངས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ཉིད་ཀྱང་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་མེད་པའོ། །

[2-86] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་རབ་འབྱོར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་དེ་ལྟར་ཆོས་རྣམས་བདེན་སྟོང་དུ་བཤད་པ་ནི་བརྫུན་དུ་གསུངས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ནི་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་ཡང་དག་པར་གསུངས་པ་དང༌། རྣམ་པ་གཞན་དུ་མི་འགྱུར་བའི་བདེན་པར་གསུངས་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་གནས་ཚུལ་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་དུ་གསུང་བ་པོ་སྟེ། ལོག་པར་གསུང་བ་པོ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །

[2-87] source:
རབ་འབྱོར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་ཐོབ་བྱའི་ཆོས་གང་ཡང་སངས་རྒྱས་པའམ་བསྟན་པ་དེ་རྣམས་ལ་བདེན་པ་དོན་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཡང་མེད་ཅིང༌། རྫུན་པ་ཀུན་རྫོབ་པའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་སོ། །ཀ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལས་ནི། ཀུན་རྫོབ་རྣམས་དོན་དམ་དཔྱོད་པའི་རིག་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོར་མེད་པས་མི་བདེན་ཅིང་རྫུན་པ་ལ་བཤད་པ་ལྟར་སྣང་སྟེ། གཞུང་འདིས་མཐའ་གཉིས་སེལ་བའང་ཡིན་ནོ། །

[2-88] source:
བདེན་མེད་རྟོགས་མ་རྟོགས་པའི་དབང་གིས་སྦྱིན་སོགས་ཀྱི་བྱེད་ལས་ལ་ཁྱད་པར་ཡོད་ཅེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། འདི་ལྟ་སྟེ་དཔེར་ན། མིག་དང་ལྡན་པའི་མི་ཞིག་མུན་པ་ཆེན་པོར་ཞུགས་ནས་ཡུལ་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་དངོས་པོ་ཅི་ཡང་གསལ་བར་མི་མཐོང་བ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ། བྱང་སེམས་གང་བདེན་མེད་ལ་བློ་ཁ་མ་ཕྱོགས་ཤིང་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པའི་མངོན་ཞེན་གྱི་ལྟ་བའི་གཡང་དུ་ལྷུང་ནས་སྦྱིན་པ་གཏོང་བའི་བྱང་སེམས་རྣམས་ནི་དཔེ་དེ་དང་འདྲ་བའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །

Teaching that there is a difference in the function of giving and so forth due to realizing or not realizing the lack of true existence: 'It is like this: for example, just as a person endowed with eyes entering a great darkness would not clearly see any entities of forms as objects, similarly, those bodhisattvas who give gifts having fallen into the abyss of the view of manifest attachment, bound by apprehending true existence without directing their minds toward the lack of true existence, should be viewed as bodhisattvas similar to that example.'

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: This dharma was not principally spoken for the sake of those who are inclined toward the inferior vehicle, but rather the Tathāgata spoke it for the purpose of sentient beings, bodhisattvas, who have entered the path of the great vehicle, the supreme vehicle and the most excellent vehicle. Both the supreme vehicle and the most excellent vehicle are synonyms for the great vehicle.

དེ་བས་ན་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཅི་ལ་ཡང་དོན་དམ་པར་མི་གནས་པར་སྦྱིན་པ་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། དེས་མཚོན་ནས་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་སོགས་གཞན་ལའང་སྦྱོར་བར་དགོངས་སོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་ནི་བདེན་ཞེན་མེད་པའི་ཚུལ་འདི་ལྟར་སྦྱིན་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་གཏོང་བ་དང་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་སྲུང་སོགས་བྱའོ། །

རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་རབ་འབྱོར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་དེ་ལྟར་ཆོས་རྣམས་བདེན་སྟོང་དུ་བཤད་པ་ནི་བརྫུན་དུ་གསུངས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ནི་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་ཡང་དག་པར་གསུངས་པ་དང༌། རྣམ་པ་གཞན་དུ་མི་འགྱུར་བའི་བདེན་པར་གསུངས་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་གནས་ཚུལ་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་དུ་གསུང་བ་པོ་སྟེ། ལོག་པར་གསུང་བ་པོ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །

བདེན་མེད་རྟོགས་མ་རྟོགས་པའི་དབང་གིས་སྦྱིན་སོགས་ཀྱི་བྱེད་ལས་ལ་ཁྱད་པར་ཡོད་ཅེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། འདི་ལྟ་སྟེ་དཔེར་ན། མིག་དང་ལྡན་པའི་མི་ཞིག་མུན་པ་ཆེན་པོར་ཞུགས་ནས་ཡུལ་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་དངོས་པོ་ཅི་ཡང་གསལ་བར་མི་མཐོང་བ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ། བྱང་སེམས་གང་བདེན་མེད་ལ་བློ་ཁ་མ་ཕྱོགས་ཤིང་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པའི་མངོན་ཞེན་གྱི་ལྟ་བའི་གཡང་དུ་ལྷུང་ནས་སྦྱིན་པ་གཏོང་བའི་བྱང་སེམས་རྣམས་ནི་དཔེ་དེ་དང་འདྲ་བའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །

Teaching that there is a difference in the function of giving and so forth due to realizing or not realizing the lack of true existence: 'It is like this: for example, just as a person endowed with eyes entering a great darkness would not clearly see any entities of forms as objects, similarly, those bodhisattvas who give gifts having fallen into the abyss of the view of manifest attachment, bound by apprehending true existence without directing their minds toward the lack of true existence, should be viewed as bodhisattvas similar to that example.'

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Whatever such sentient beings of the great vehicle take up and retain this dharma and so forth, the Tathāgata knows and sees them right from now, and those sentient beings will become endowed with an aggregate of merit that is immeasurable, conceptually inconceivable, unequaled, measureless, and limitless, and all those sentient beings will also swiftly obtain the state of awakening of me, the Tathāgata, as if bearing it upon their shoulders.

[2-83] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་གཟུགས་སྒྲ་སོགས་ལ་ཞེན་ཅིང་གནས་པའི་ཡུལ་གཟུགས་སོགས་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཉིད་དོན་དམ་པར་མི་གནས་པ་སྟེ་མ་གྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེས་སོ། །
[2-83] translation already produced for this document:
The reason is: 'Whatever objects such as forms are the objects of abiding with attachment to forms, sounds, and so forth, those themselves do not abide ultimately, that is, they are not established,' so it was said.

[2-84] source:
དེ་བས་ན་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཅི་ལ་ཡང་དོན་དམ་པར་མི་གནས་པར་སྦྱིན་པ་སྦྱིན་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། དེས་མཚོན་ནས་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་སོགས་གཞན་ལའང་སྦྱོར་བར་དགོངས་སོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་ནི་བདེན་ཞེན་མེད་པའི་ཚུལ་འདི་ལྟར་སྦྱིན་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་གཏོང་བ་དང་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་སྲུང་སོགས་བྱའོ། །
[2-84] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, the Tathāgata said, 'A bodhisattva should give gifts without ultimately abiding in anything'; and illustrating by that, he intended that this be applied to others such as ethical discipline as well. Bodhisattvas should completely give gifts, guard ethical discipline, and so forth in this way, without attachment to true existence.

[2-85] source:
སེམས་ཅན་དུ་བདེན་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱང་དོན་དམ་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་པ་དང༌། ཐ་སྙད་དུ་སེམས་ཅན་གང་དག་ཅེས་གསུངས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ཉིད་ཀྱང་སེམས་ཅན་དུ་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་མེད་པའོ། །
[2-85] translation already produced for this document:
That perception of true existence as a sentient being itself also lacks perception ultimately, and those very sentient beings who were spoken of conventionally as 'whatever sentient beings' also lack existence by their own nature as sentient beings.

[2-86] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་རབ་འབྱོར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་དེ་ལྟར་ཆོས་རྣམས་བདེན་སྟོང་དུ་བཤད་པ་ནི་བརྫུན་དུ་གསུངས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ནི་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་ཡང་དག་པར་གསུངས་པ་དང༌། རྣམ་པ་གཞན་དུ་མི་འགྱུར་བའི་བདེན་པར་གསུངས་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་གནས་ཚུལ་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་དུ་གསུང་བ་པོ་སྟེ། ལོག་པར་གསུང་བ་པོ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[2-86] translation already produced for this document:
The reason is: 'Subhūti, the Tathāgata thus explaining phenomena as empty of true existence did not speak falsely, because the Tathāgata speaks perfectly without error, speaks the truth that does not change into another aspect, and is a speaker of suchness exactly as the abiding mode of phenomena is, and is not a speaker of falsity.'

[2-87] source:
རབ་འབྱོར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་ཐོབ་བྱའི་ཆོས་གང་ཡང་སངས་རྒྱས་པའམ་བསྟན་པ་དེ་རྣམས་ལ་བདེན་པ་དོན་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཡང་མེད་ཅིང༌། རྫུན་པ་ཀུན་རྫོབ་པའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་སོ། །ཀ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལས་ནི། ཀུན་རྫོབ་རྣམས་དོན་དམ་དཔྱོད་པའི་རིག་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོར་མེད་པས་མི་བདེན་ཅིང་རྫུན་པ་ལ་བཤད་པ་ལྟར་སྣང་སྟེ། གཞུང་འདིས་མཐའ་གཉིས་སེལ་བའང་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[2-87] translation already produced for this document:
'Subhūti, whatever phenomena of attainment the Tathāgata has awakened to or taught, among those, true ultimate phenomena are not established truly, and false conventional phenomena are also not established truly,' so it was said. Kamalaśīla seems to have explained that conventionalities, because they do not exist in the nature of the rational consciousness inquiring into the ultimate, are untrue and false; and this text also dispels the two extremes.

[2-88] source:
བདེན་མེད་རྟོགས་མ་རྟོགས་པའི་དབང་གིས་སྦྱིན་སོགས་ཀྱི་བྱེད་ལས་ལ་ཁྱད་པར་ཡོད་ཅེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། འདི་ལྟ་སྟེ་དཔེར་ན། མིག་དང་ལྡན་པའི་མི་ཞིག་མུན་པ་ཆེན་པོར་ཞུགས་ནས་ཡུལ་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་དངོས་པོ་ཅི་ཡང་གསལ་བར་མི་མཐོང་བ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ། བྱང་སེམས་གང་བདེན་མེད་ལ་བློ་ཁ་མ་ཕྱོགས་ཤིང་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པའི་མངོན་ཞེན་གྱི་ལྟ་བའི་གཡང་དུ་ལྷུང་ནས་སྦྱིན་པ་གཏོང་བའི་བྱང་སེམས་རྣམས་ནི་དཔེ་དེ་དང་འདྲ་བའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །
[2-88] translation already produced for this document:
Teaching that there is a difference in the function of giving and so forth due to realizing or not realizing the lack of true existence: 'It is like this: for example, just as a person endowed with eyes entering a great darkness would not clearly see any entities of forms as objects, similarly, those bodhisattvas who give gifts having fallen into the abyss of the view of manifest attachment, bound by apprehending true existence without directing their minds toward the lack of true existence, should be viewed as bodhisattvas similar to that example.'

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: The reason is: those who are inclined toward the inferior dharma are unable to listen to this profound dharma discourse by way of hearing, thinking, and meditating on it, for those who view a self of persons and view a sentient being, a life force, and a person with an attachment to true existence, and individuals who assert them, like non-Buddhists, are unable to do things such as listen to and take up the words and meaning of this text, because there is no basis or opportunity to do so, because such sentient beings do not desire the meaning of selflessness.

[2-89] translation already produced for this document:
'Furthermore, it is like this: just as when dawn breaks and the sun rises, a person endowed with eyes sees various aspects of good and bad objects of form, similarly, those bodhisattvas who completely give gifts without falling into entities bound by apprehending true existence should be viewed as similar to that example.' Thus, giving bound by apprehending true existence was explained as being similar to a person having entered darkness and not seeing forms, and giving with realization of the lack of true existence was explained as being similar to someone endowed with eyes seeing forms; and furthermore, the five, giving and so forth, when not embraced by the wisdom realizing the lack of true existence, are like someone blind from birth, and the perfection of wisdom realizing the lack of true existence is like someone endowed with eyes leading the blind. The Sañcaya states: "How could ten million, one hundred billion people blind from birth, without a guide, who do not even know the way, enter the city? Without wisdom, these five blind perfections, being without a guide, are unable to touch awakening." And following what was thus stated, to teach in connection with the former that if those first five perfections are not embraced by the perfection of wisdom realizing the lack of true existence, they are like being without eyes and are unable to travel to the ground of a Buddha, and if they are embraced, they are like being endowed with eyes and are able to travel there, it states: "When they are thoroughly embraced by wisdom, then they gain eyes and obtain this name." And the glorious Candrakīrti also stated in the Madhyamakāvatāra: "Just as a single person endowed with eyes easily leads an entire assembly of blind people to their desired destination, similarly here too, intelligence takes the virtues whose eyes are impaired and goes to victoriousness itself."

Furthermore, he said, 'If compared to the benefits of giving away bodies illustrated by giving the body in the morning and afternoon times and for many eons in numbers equalling the grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, the aggregate of merit of whoever hears this text completely, is inspired by it, and does not abandon it mentally is even greater than that former one, what need is there to say that if one does things such as writing this text in letters, the merit will be greater than that?' heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Furthermore, whatever place this sūtra is taught in, that place will become worthy of being venerated, paid homage to, and circumambulated by the sentient beings of the world including gods, humans, and asuras; that place will become like a stūpa. This is similar to how the root extensive, middling, and condensed Mother sūtras and their commentaries, corresponding to the Abhisamayālaṃkāra stating, 'Awakening itself is the veneration of the support,' state that the place where a bodhisattva on the path of meditation resides is a place revered by others, like a stūpa; and principally, it refers to the place where an individual resides in whose continuum the extraordinary perfection of wisdom, the meaning expressed by this text, has arisen. Although something similar to this appeared above, it was done in terms of individual bases.

'Furthermore, it is like this: just as when dawn breaks and the sun rises, a person endowed with eyes sees various aspects of good and bad objects of form, similarly, those bodhisattvas who completely give gifts without falling into entities bound by apprehending true existence should be viewed as similar to that example.' Thus, giving bound by apprehending true existence was explained as being similar to a person having entered darkness and not seeing forms, and giving with realization of the lack of true existence was explained as being similar to someone endowed with eyes seeing forms; and furthermore, the five, giving and so forth, when not embraced by the wisdom realizing the lack of true existence, are like someone blind from birth, and the perfection of wisdom realizing the lack of true existence is like someone endowed with eyes leading the blind. The Sañcaya states: "How could ten million, one hundred billion people blind from birth, without a guide, who do not even know the way, enter the city? Without wisdom, these five blind perfections, being without a guide, are unable to touch awakening." And following what was thus stated, to teach in connection with the former that if those first five perfections are not embraced by the perfection of wisdom realizing the lack of true existence, they are like being without eyes and are unable to travel to the ground of a Buddha, and if they are embraced, they are like being endowed with eyes and are able to travel there, it states: "When they are thoroughly embraced by wisdom, then they gain eyes and obtain this name." And the glorious Candrakīrti also stated in the Madhyamakāvatāra: "Just as a single person endowed with eyes easily leads an entire assembly of blind people to their desired destination, similarly here too, intelligence takes the virtues whose eyes are impaired and goes to victoriousness itself."

source: སྔ་མ་ལས་གཞན་ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་རིགས་ཀྱི་བུའམ་བུ་མོ་གང་མདོ་སྡེ་འདི་འཛིན་འཆང་སོགས་བྱེད་ཅིང་དོན་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ནི་ནད་སྣ་ཚོགས་དང་འཐབ་རྩོད་མཚང་འདྲུ་དང་བཅིང་རྡེག་སོགས་ཀྱིས་མནར་བ་དང་ཤིན་ཏུ་མནར་བའི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་མྱོང་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ཡོད་སྲིད་ཀྱང༌། སྐྱོན་ཆེན་པོ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རྒྱུ་མཚན་དེ་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་གིས་ནི་ཚེ་རབས་འདི་དང་སྔ་མའི་དུས་སུ་མི་དགེ་བའི་ལས་ཆེན་པོ་ངན་སོང་གསུམ་དུ་སྐྱེ་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་ལས་གང་དག་བྱས་པ་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ནི་ཚེ་འདི་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཐོག་མ་སྨིན་ཏེ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱིས་མནར་བ་དེའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ཚེ་རབས་སྔ་མའི་མི་དགེ་བའི་ལས་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་འབྱང་བ་སྟེ་དག་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱང་མྱུར་དུ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལ་བརྩོན་པའི་གཉེན་པོ་ཀུན་ཏུ་སྤྱོད་པའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ནི་སྡིག་ལས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རྩ་བ་བདག་འཛིན་བཅོམ་སྟེ་ཐར་པ་དང་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཡང་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་ཞེས་བཤད་ན། ངན་འགྲོར་སྐྱེ་བའི་ལས་རྣམས་འཇོམས་པ་ལྟ་ཅི་སྨོས་སོ། །ཚུལ་དེ་ལྟར་རྟོག་གེ་འབར་བ་སོགས་ནས་བཤད་ཅིང༌། ཐར་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། ངན་འགྲོར་སྐྱེ་བའི་སྡིག་ཡོད་ཀྱང༌། །མགོ་བོ་ན་བ་ཙམ་གྱིས་འབྱང༌། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དཔེར་ན་ས་བོན་བཏབ་ཀྱང་ཆུ་ལུད་དྲོད་གཤེར་སོགས་གཏན་མེད་ན་མྱུ་གུ་མི་སྐྱེ་བ་ལྟར་བདག་འཛིན་སྤོང་ནུས་ན་ནི། བསགས་པའི་ལས་ཅི་ཡོད་ཀྱང་གྲོགས་ཉོན་མོངས་མེད་པས་རྣམ་སྨིན་འབྱིན་མི་ནུས་ཏེ། རྣམ་འགྲེལ་ལས། སྲིད་པའི་སྲེད་ལས་རྣམ་བརྒལ་བའི། །ལས་གཞན་འཕེན་ནུས་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། །ལྷན་ཅིག་བྱེད་པ་ཟད་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །
translation: Furthermore, Subhūti, other than the former, whatever sentient beings, sons or daughters of noble family, who retain, memorize, and so forth this sūtra and put its meaning into practice may experience the suffering of being tormented and extremely tormented by various illnesses, fights, having their faults exposed, being bound, beaten, and so forth, yet it is not a great fault. What is the reason for that? By the power of the fruits of all whatever great non-virtuous karmas, karmas that would lead to rebirth in the three lower realms, those sentient beings committed in this and previous lifetimes ripening upon this very life and tormenting them with suffering, all those non-virtuous karmas of previous lifetimes will be exhausted, that is, purified, and they will also swiftly obtain the awakening of a Buddha. If it is explained that by the power of thoroughly engaging in the antidotes of making effort in the perfection of wisdom, one destroys apprehending a self, which is the root of sinful karmas, and obtains freedom and omniscience, what need is there to say that it overcomes karmas of rebirth in the lower realms? Such a method is explained in texts such as the Tarkajvālā, and the Mahāmokṣa also states: 'Even though there are sins for rebirth in the lower realms, they are exhausted merely by having a headache.' For example, just as even if a seed is planted, if there is absolutely no water, fertilizer, heat, moisture, and so forth, a sprout will not grow, similarly, if one is able to abandon apprehending a self, no matter what accumulated karmas there are, since there are no afflictions as companions, they are unable to issue forth a fully ripened result, just as the Pramāṇavārttika states: 'For one who has completely transcended craving for existence, other karmas are unable to project, because the cooperative conditions are exhausted.'

Thus, giving bound by apprehending true existence was explained as being similar to a person having entered darkness and not seeing forms, and giving with realization of the lack of true existence was explained as being similar to someone endowed with eyes seeing forms; and furthermore, the five, giving and so forth, when not embraced by the wisdom realizing the lack of true existence, are like someone blind from birth, and the perfection of wisdom realizing the lack of true existence is like someone endowed with eyes leading the blind. The Sañcaya states: "How could ten million, one hundred billion people blind from birth, without a guide, who do not even know the way, enter the city? Without wisdom, these five blind perfections, being without a guide, are unable to touch awakening." And following what was thus stated, to teach in connection with the former that if those first five perfections are not embraced by the perfection of wisdom realizing the lack of true existence, they are like being without eyes and are unable to travel to the ground of a Buddha, and if they are embraced, they are like being endowed with eyes and are able to travel there, it states: "When they are thoroughly embraced by wisdom, then they gain eyes and obtain this name." And the glorious Candrakīrti also stated in the Madhyamakāvatāra: "Just as a single person endowed with eyes easily leads an entire assembly of blind people to their desired destination, similarly here too, intelligence takes the virtues whose eyes are impaired and goes to victoriousness itself."

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Subhūti, I clearly know and cognize that in the past, in time before even the measureless of measureless eons, and in time before even the earliest before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, eighty-four countless hundred thousands of ten millions of Buddhas appeared, and I venerated, served, and so forth, those, bringing them joy, without bringing them displeasure and without wearying their minds; of the two, the merit of my having done that and whatever merit there is of one who writes and so forth this sūtra in the latter time, the final five hundred years, this latter aggregate of merit is greater, such that the former aggregate of merit does not approach and does not go near even up to merely a single one out of a hundredth part, that is, when this is divided into a hundred parts, and likewise it does not bear, that is, is unable to, comparison even up to a thousandth part, a hundred thousandth part, and a number, a measure, a count, an example, a comparison, and a cause. Although all those illustrate examples, "part" means dissimilar in large or small portions and dissimilar in large or small numbers, dissimilar in example, unequal in comparison, dissimilar in reason, and "count" means unsuitable to be counted as equal.

[2-97] translation already produced for this document:
Furthermore, Subhūti, other than the former, whatever sentient beings, sons or daughters of noble family, who retain, memorize, and so forth this sūtra and put its meaning into practice may experience the suffering of being tormented and extremely tormented by various illnesses, fights, having their faults exposed, being bound, beaten, and so forth, yet it is not a great fault. What is the reason for that? By the power of the fruits of all whatever great non-virtuous karmas, karmas that would lead to rebirth in the three lower realms, those sentient beings committed in this and previous lifetimes ripening upon this very life and tormenting them with suffering, all those non-virtuous karmas of previous lifetimes will be exhausted, that is, purified, and they will also swiftly obtain the awakening of a Buddha. If it is explained that by the power of thoroughly engaging in the antidotes of making effort in the perfection of wisdom, one destroys apprehending a self, which is the root of sinful karmas, and obtains freedom and omniscience, what need is there to say that it overcomes karmas of rebirth in the lower realms? Such a method is explained in texts such as the Tarkajvālā, and the Mahāmokṣa also states: 'Even though there are sins for rebirth in the lower realms, they are exhausted merely by having a headache.' For example, just as even if a seed is planted, if there is absolutely no water, fertilizer, heat, moisture, and so forth, a sprout will not grow, similarly, if one is able to abandon apprehending a self, no matter what accumulated karmas there are, since there are no afflictions as companions, they are unable to issue forth a fully ripened result, just as the Pramāṇavārttika states: 'For one who has completely transcended craving for existence, other karmas are unable to project, because the cooperative conditions are exhausted.'

translation: If one were to perfectly analyze and express how large an aggregate of merit they fully generate and that the aggregate of merit they will retain is like this, sentient beings of inferior intellect would not believe it, and their minds becoming maddened, that is, bewildered, their minds would become completely disturbed.

[2-96] translation already produced for this document:
Furthermore, whatever place this sūtra is taught in, that place will become worthy of being venerated, paid homage to, and circumambulated by the sentient beings of the world including gods, humans, and asuras; that place will become like a stūpa. This is similar to how the root extensive, middling, and condensed Mother sūtras and their commentaries, corresponding to the Abhisamayālaṃkāra stating, 'Awakening itself is the veneration of the support,' state that the place where a bodhisattva on the path of meditation resides is a place revered by others, like a stūpa; and principally, it refers to the place where an individual resides in whose continuum the extraordinary perfection of wisdom, the meaning expressed by this text, has arisen. Although something similar to this appeared above, it was done in terms of individual bases.

སྔ་མ་ལས་གཞན་ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་རིགས་ཀྱི་བུའམ་བུ་མོ་གང་མདོ་སྡེ་འདི་འཛིན་འཆང་སོགས་བྱེད་ཅིང་དོན་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ནི་ནད་སྣ་ཚོགས་དང་འཐབ་རྩོད་མཚང་འདྲུ་དང་བཅིང་རྡེག་སོགས་ཀྱིས་མནར་བ་དང་ཤིན་ཏུ་མནར་བའི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་མྱོང་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ཡོད་སྲིད་ཀྱང༌། སྐྱོན་ཆེན་པོ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རྒྱུ་མཚན་དེ་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་གིས་ནི་ཚེ་རབས་འདི་དང་སྔ་མའི་དུས་སུ་མི་དགེ་བའི་ལས་ཆེན་པོ་ངན་སོང་གསུམ་དུ་སྐྱེ་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་ལས་གང་དག་བྱས་པ་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ནི་ཚེ་འདི་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཐོག་མ་སྨིན་ཏེ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱིས་མནར་བ་དེའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ཚེ་རབས་སྔ་མའི་མི་དགེ་བའི་ལས་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་འབྱང་བ་སྟེ་དག་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱང་མྱུར་དུ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལ་བརྩོན་པའི་གཉེན་པོ་ཀུན་ཏུ་སྤྱོད་པའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ནི་སྡིག་ལས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རྩ་བ་བདག་འཛིན་བཅོམ་སྟེ་ཐར་པ་དང་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཡང་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་ཞེས་བཤད་ན། ངན་འགྲོར་སྐྱེ་བའི་ལས་རྣམས་འཇོམས་པ་ལྟ་ཅི་སྨོས་སོ། །ཚུལ་དེ་ལྟར་རྟོག་གེ་འབར་བ་སོགས་ནས་བཤད་ཅིང༌། ཐར་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། ངན་འགྲོར་སྐྱེ་བའི་སྡིག་ཡོད་ཀྱང༌། །མགོ་བོ་ན་བ་ཙམ་གྱིས་འབྱང༌། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དཔེར་ན་ས་བོན་བཏབ་ཀྱང་ཆུ་ལུད་དྲོད་གཤེར་སོགས་གཏན་མེད་ན་མྱུ་གུ་མི་སྐྱེ་བ་ལྟར་བདག་འཛིན་སྤོང་ནུས་ན་ནི། བསགས་པའི་ལས་ཅི་ཡོད་ཀྱང་གྲོགས་ཉོན་མོངས་མེད་པས་རྣམ་སྨིན་འབྱིན་མི་ནུས་ཏེ། རྣམ་འགྲེལ་ལས། སྲིད་པའི་སྲེད་ལས་རྣམ་བརྒལ་བའི། །ལས་གཞན་འཕེན་ནུས་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། །ལྷན་ཅིག་བྱེད་པ་ཟད་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །

Furthermore, Subhūti, other than the former, whatever sentient beings, sons or daughters of noble family, who retain, memorize, and so forth this sūtra and put its meaning into practice may experience the suffering of being tormented and extremely tormented by various illnesses, fights, having their faults exposed, being bound, beaten, and so forth, yet it is not a great fault. What is the reason for that? By the power of the fruits of all whatever great non-virtuous karmas, karmas that would lead to rebirth in the three lower realms, those sentient beings committed in this and previous lifetimes ripening upon this very life and tormenting them with suffering, all those non-virtuous karmas of previous lifetimes will be exhausted, that is, purified, and they will also swiftly obtain the awakening of a Buddha. If it is explained that by the power of thoroughly engaging in the antidotes of making effort in the perfection of wisdom, one destroys apprehending a self, which is the root of sinful karmas, and obtains freedom and omniscience, what need is there to say that it overcomes karmas of rebirth in the lower realms? Such a method is explained in texts such as the Tarkajvālā, and the Mahāmokṣa also states: 'Even though there are sins for rebirth in the lower realms, they are exhausted merely by having a headache.' For example, just as even if a seed is planted, if there is absolutely no water, fertilizer, heat, moisture, and so forth, a sprout will not grow, similarly, if one is able to abandon apprehending a self, no matter what accumulated karmas there are, since there are no afflictions as companions, they are unable to issue forth a fully ripened result, just as the Pramāṇavārttika states: 'For one who has completely transcended craving for existence, other karmas are unable to project, because the cooperative conditions are exhausted.'

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Although this dharma discourse has a small text, its meaning is vast, so it is inconceivable, and the fully ripened fruition of putting its meaning into practice is also inconceivable. As for "fully ripened fruition", it does not apprehend solely the fully ripened fruition, but also includes the causally concordant fruition, the environmental fruition, the fruition of separation, and so forth. Although something like this also appeared above, it is spoken with a different contextual meaning in mind.

དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་སེམས་ཅན་གང་དག་ཆོས་འདི་ལེན་པ་དང་འཛིན་པ་སོགས་བྱེད་པ་དེ་དག་ནི། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་ད་ལྟ་ནས་མཁྱེན་ཅིང་གཟིགས་ཏེ་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ནི་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པ་དང༌། བློས་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་པ་དང༌། དེ་དང་མཚུངས་པ་མེད་པ་དང༌། མཐའ་གཞལ་དུ་མེད་པ་དང༌། ཚད་མེད་པ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ངའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་གོ་འཕང་ཕྲག་པ་ལ་ཐོགས་པ་ལྟར་མྱུར་དུ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །

Furthermore, Subhūti, other than the former, whatever sentient beings, sons or daughters of noble family, who retain, memorize, and so forth this sūtra and put its meaning into practice may experience the suffering of being tormented and extremely tormented by various illnesses, fights, having their faults exposed, being bound, beaten, and so forth, yet it is not a great fault. What is the reason for that? By the power of the fruits of all whatever great non-virtuous karmas, karmas that would lead to rebirth in the three lower realms, those sentient beings committed in this and previous lifetimes ripening upon this very life and tormenting them with suffering, all those non-virtuous karmas of previous lifetimes will be exhausted, that is, purified, and they will also swiftly obtain the awakening of a Buddha. If it is explained that by the power of thoroughly engaging in the antidotes of making effort in the perfection of wisdom, one destroys apprehending a self, which is the root of sinful karmas, and obtains freedom and omniscience, what need is there to say that it overcomes karmas of rebirth in the lower realms? Such a method is explained in texts such as the Tarkajvālā, and the Mahāmokṣa also states: 'Even though there are sins for rebirth in the lower realms, they are exhausted merely by having a headache.' For example, just as even if a seed is planted, if there is absolutely no water, fertilizer, heat, moisture, and so forth, a sprout will not grow, similarly, if one is able to abandon apprehending a self, no matter what accumulated karmas there are, since there are no afflictions as companions, they are unable to issue forth a fully ripened result, just as the Pramāṇavārttika states: 'For one who has completely transcended craving for existence, other karmas are unable to project, because the cooperative conditions are exhausted.'

translation: Furthermore, Subhūti requested of the Bhagavān, asking how one who has entered the vehicle of the bodhisattvas should abide, and so forth. Although something like this occurred previously, it was done in terms of the path of accumulation and the level of engaged interest, whereas here it is spoken with the intention of engaging in that way near the attainment of the path of seeing and upon the occasion of having attained it, so the meaning is just as explained before.

[2-97] translation already produced for this document:
Furthermore, Subhūti, other than the former, whatever sentient beings, sons or daughters of noble family, who retain, memorize, and so forth this sūtra and put its meaning into practice may experience the suffering of being tormented and extremely tormented by various illnesses, fights, having their faults exposed, being bound, beaten, and so forth, yet it is not a great fault. What is the reason for that? By the power of the fruits of all whatever great non-virtuous karmas, karmas that would lead to rebirth in the three lower realms, those sentient beings committed in this and previous lifetimes ripening upon this very life and tormenting them with suffering, all those non-virtuous karmas of previous lifetimes will be exhausted, that is, purified, and they will also swiftly obtain the awakening of a Buddha. If it is explained that by the power of thoroughly engaging in the antidotes of making effort in the perfection of wisdom, one destroys apprehending a self, which is the root of sinful karmas, and obtains freedom and omniscience, what need is there to say that it overcomes karmas of rebirth in the lower realms? Such a method is explained in texts such as the Tarkajvālā, and the Mahāmokṣa also states: 'Even though there are sins for rebirth in the lower realms, they are exhausted merely by having a headache.' For example, just as even if a seed is planted, if there is absolutely no water, fertilizer, heat, moisture, and so forth, a sprout will not grow, similarly, if one is able to abandon apprehending a self, no matter what accumulated karmas there are, since there are no afflictions as companions, they are unable to issue forth a fully ripened result, just as the Pramāṇavārttika states: 'For one who has completely transcended craving for existence, other karmas are unable to project, because the cooperative conditions are exhausted.'

[2-96] translation already produced for this document:
Furthermore, whatever place this sūtra is taught in, that place will become worthy of being venerated, paid homage to, and circumambulated by the sentient beings of the world including gods, humans, and asuras; that place will become like a stūpa. This is similar to how the root extensive, middling, and condensed Mother sūtras and their commentaries, corresponding to the Abhisamayālaṃkāra stating, 'Awakening itself is the veneration of the support,' state that the place where a bodhisattva on the path of meditation resides is a place revered by others, like a stūpa; and principally, it refers to the place where an individual resides in whose continuum the extraordinary perfection of wisdom, the meaning expressed by this text, has arisen. Although something similar to this appeared above, it was done in terms of individual bases.

སྔ་མ་ལས་གཞན་ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་རིགས་ཀྱི་བུའམ་བུ་མོ་གང་མདོ་སྡེ་འདི་འཛིན་འཆང་སོགས་བྱེད་ཅིང་དོན་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ནི་ནད་སྣ་ཚོགས་དང་འཐབ་རྩོད་མཚང་འདྲུ་དང་བཅིང་རྡེག་སོགས་ཀྱིས་མནར་བ་དང་ཤིན་ཏུ་མནར་བའི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་མྱོང་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ཡོད་སྲིད་ཀྱང༌། སྐྱོན་ཆེན་པོ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རྒྱུ་མཚན་དེ་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་གིས་ནི་ཚེ་རབས་འདི་དང་སྔ་མའི་དུས་སུ་མི་དགེ་བའི་ལས་ཆེན་པོ་ངན་སོང་གསུམ་དུ་སྐྱེ་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་ལས་གང་དག་བྱས་པ་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་ནི་ཚེ་འདི་ཉིད་ཀྱི་ཐོག་མ་སྨིན་ཏེ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱིས་མནར་བ་དེའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ཚེ་རབས་སྔ་མའི་མི་དགེ་བའི་ལས་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་འབྱང་བ་སྟེ་དག་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱང་མྱུར་དུ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལ་བརྩོན་པའི་གཉེན་པོ་ཀུན་ཏུ་སྤྱོད་པའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ནི་སྡིག་ལས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རྩ་བ་བདག་འཛིན་བཅོམ་སྟེ་ཐར་པ་དང་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཡང་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་ཞེས་བཤད་ན། ངན་འགྲོར་སྐྱེ་བའི་ལས་རྣམས་འཇོམས་པ་ལྟ་ཅི་སྨོས་སོ། །ཚུལ་དེ་ལྟར་རྟོག་གེ་འབར་བ་སོགས་ནས་བཤད་ཅིང༌། ཐར་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། ངན་འགྲོར་སྐྱེ་བའི་སྡིག་ཡོད་ཀྱང༌། །མགོ་བོ་ན་བ་ཙམ་གྱིས་འབྱང༌། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དཔེར་ན་ས་བོན་བཏབ་ཀྱང་ཆུ་ལུད་དྲོད་གཤེར་སོགས་གཏན་མེད་ན་མྱུ་གུ་མི་སྐྱེ་བ་ལྟར་བདག་འཛིན་སྤོང་ནུས་ན་ནི། བསགས་པའི་ལས་ཅི་ཡོད་ཀྱང་གྲོགས་ཉོན་མོངས་མེད་པས་རྣམ་སྨིན་འབྱིན་མི་ནུས་ཏེ། རྣམ་འགྲེལ་ལས། སྲིད་པའི་སྲེད་ལས་རྣམ་བརྒལ་བའི། །ལས་གཞན་འཕེན་ནུས་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། །ལྷན་ཅིག་བྱེད་པ་ཟད་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །

Furthermore, Subhūti, other than the former, whatever sentient beings, sons or daughters of noble family, who retain, memorize, and so forth this sūtra and put its meaning into practice may experience the suffering of being tormented and extremely tormented by various illnesses, fights, having their faults exposed, being bound, beaten, and so forth, yet it is not a great fault. What is the reason for that? By the power of the fruits of all whatever great non-virtuous karmas, karmas that would lead to rebirth in the three lower realms, those sentient beings committed in this and previous lifetimes ripening upon this very life and tormenting them with suffering, all those non-virtuous karmas of previous lifetimes will be exhausted, that is, purified, and they will also swiftly obtain the awakening of a Buddha. If it is explained that by the power of thoroughly engaging in the antidotes of making effort in the perfection of wisdom, one destroys apprehending a self, which is the root of sinful karmas, and obtains freedom and omniscience, what need is there to say that it overcomes karmas of rebirth in the lower realms? Such a method is explained in texts such as the Tarkajvālā, and the Mahāmokṣa also states: 'Even though there are sins for rebirth in the lower realms, they are exhausted merely by having a headache.' For example, just as even if a seed is planted, if there is absolutely no water, fertilizer, heat, moisture, and so forth, a sprout will not grow, similarly, if one is able to abandon apprehending a self, no matter what accumulated karmas there are, since there are no afflictions as companions, they are unable to issue forth a fully ripened result, just as the Pramāṇavārttika states: 'For one who has completely transcended craving for existence, other karmas are unable to project, because the cooperative conditions are exhausted.'

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Furthermore, when he asked, "Subhūti, do you think there are any dharmas by which I, the Tathāgata, previously took up whatever dharma from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in an ultimate sense and became a Buddha?", in reply Subhūti stated, "There are not", and the Bhagavān assented to the truth of the words by saying, "It is so," and to the truth of the meaning by saying, "It is so"; there is no such dharma at all.

དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་སེམས་ཅན་གང་དག་ཆོས་འདི་ལེན་པ་དང་འཛིན་པ་སོགས་བྱེད་པ་དེ་དག་ནི། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་ད་ལྟ་ནས་མཁྱེན་ཅིང་གཟིགས་ཏེ་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ནི་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པ་དང༌། བློས་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་པ་དང༌། དེ་དང་མཚུངས་པ་མེད་པ་དང༌། མཐའ་གཞལ་དུ་མེད་པ་དང༌། ཚད་མེད་པ་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ངའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་གོ་འཕང་ཕྲག་པ་ལ་ཐོགས་པ་ལྟར་མྱུར་དུ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །

The reason is: those who are inclined toward the inferior dharma are unable to listen to this profound dharma discourse by way of hearing, thinking, and meditating on it, for those who view a self of persons and view a sentient being, a life force, and a person with an attachment to true existence, and individuals who assert them, like non-Buddhists, are unable to do things such as listen to and take up the words and meaning of this text, because there is no basis or opportunity to do so, because such sentient beings do not desire the meaning of selflessness.

Furthermore, Subhūti, other than the former, whatever sentient beings, sons or daughters of noble family, who retain, memorize, and so forth this sūtra and put its meaning into practice may experience the suffering of being tormented and extremely tormented by various illnesses, fights, having their faults exposed, being bound, beaten, and so forth, yet it is not a great fault. What is the reason for that? By the power of the fruits of all whatever great non-virtuous karmas, karmas that would lead to rebirth in the three lower realms, those sentient beings committed in this and previous lifetimes ripening upon this very life and tormenting them with suffering, all those non-virtuous karmas of previous lifetimes will be exhausted, that is, purified, and they will also swiftly obtain the awakening of a Buddha. If it is explained that by the power of thoroughly engaging in the antidotes of making effort in the perfection of wisdom, one destroys apprehending a self, which is the root of sinful karmas, and obtains freedom and omniscience, what need is there to say that it overcomes karmas of rebirth in the lower realms? Such a method is explained in texts such as the Tarkajvālā, and the Mahāmokṣa also states: 'Even though there are sins for rebirth in the lower realms, they are exhausted merely by having a headache.' For example, just as even if a seed is planted, if there is absolutely no water, fertilizer, heat, moisture, and so forth, a sprout will not grow, similarly, if one is able to abandon apprehending a self, no matter what accumulated karmas there are, since there are no afflictions as companions, they are unable to issue forth a fully ripened result, just as the Pramāṇavārttika states: 'For one who has completely transcended craving for existence, other karmas are unable to project, because the cooperative conditions are exhausted.'

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: If there had been some such dharma, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara would not have prophesied to me, "Young brahmin, you will become a Buddha named Śākyamuni from about this time in the future," but because there is no dharma whatsoever of fully and completely awakening as a Buddha that is truly established, at that time the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara prophesied to me my awakening in that way. Furthermore, the dharmas of by what, what, and to what one is prophesied are merely nominal designations, merely bare names, but the manner of their lacking establishment in an ultimate sense has already been stated above. It is explained in a sūtra that it has been one countless and ninety-one eons since the appearance of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, and also from the annotations to the Pradīpoddyotana commentary on the Guhyasamāja Root Tantra it is stated, "Later, Dīpaṃkara appeared one countless and ninety-one great eons previously." At that time, when the Teacher became the young brahmin Dharmamegha, that very Buddha placed his feet upon his body and blessed him, so having attained great endurance in the non-arising of dharmas, he was prophesied to become a Buddha; generally, attaining endurance in the non-arising of dharmas has three: small, medium, and great; the small is the endurance of the path of preparation, the medium is the path of seeing, and the great arises from the attainment of arhatship, and in terms of the Mahāyāna, it is attained from the eighth level. To attain whichever of those three endurances, because one must realize that conditioned dharmas do not arise by their own nature, one must definitely realize emptiness, and for the medium and great one must realize emptiness directly, and for the great one must also abandon afflictions. Therefore, for a direct prophecy to become a Buddha, one definitely must have previously realized emptiness, so a direct prophecy is not given to bodhisattvas who are bound by grasping at true existence, because those who are bound by grasping at true existence, adhering to true existence in the dharmas of what is to be attained and what attains, are unsuitable as vessels to be directly prophesied, because as explained before, truly established dharmas are unable to be transformed, so it is unsuitable to posit any attainer and so forth.

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Regarding the reason for prophesying, if one asks, "Why is that?", the expression "Tathāgata" is a synonymous designation for the primordial wisdom that comprehends the authentic suchness of all dharmas being empty of true existence, so it is because he is expressed by way of that. To summarize, the meaning of "Tathāgata" is having actualized and comprehended the suchness wherein the two obscurations are abandoned, which is the meaning of his mind having gone to or cognized suchness exactly as it is.

Subhūti, I clearly know and cognize that in the past, in time before even the measureless of measureless eons, and in time before even the earliest before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, eighty-four countless hundred thousands of ten millions of Buddhas appeared, and I venerated, served, and so forth, those, bringing them joy, without bringing them displeasure and without wearying their minds; of the two, the merit of my having done that and whatever merit there is of one who writes and so forth this sūtra in the latter time, the final five hundred years, this latter aggregate of merit is greater, such that the former aggregate of merit does not approach and does not go near even up to merely a single one out of a hundredth part, that is, when this is divided into a hundred parts, and likewise it does not bear, that is, is unable to, comparison even up to a thousandth part, a hundred thousandth part, and a number, a measure, a count, an example, a comparison, and a cause. Although all those illustrate examples, "part" means dissimilar in large or small portions and dissimilar in large or small numbers, dissimilar in example, unequal in comparison, dissimilar in reason, and "count" means unsuitable to be counted as equal.

Subhūti, I clearly know and cognize that in the past, in time before even the measureless of measureless eons, and in time before even the earliest before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, eighty-four countless hundred thousands of ten millions of Buddhas appeared, and I venerated, served, and so forth, those, bringing them joy, without bringing them displeasure and without wearying their minds; of the two, the merit of my having done that and whatever merit there is of one who writes and so forth this sūtra in the latter time, the final five hundred years, this latter aggregate of merit is greater, such that the former aggregate of merit does not approach and does not go near even up to merely a single one out of a hundredth part, that is, when this is divided into a hundred parts, and likewise it does not bear, that is, is unable to, comparison even up to a thousandth part, a hundred thousandth part, and a number, a measure, a count, an example, a comparison, and a cause. heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: Although something like this occurred above, it is applied to the respective contexts, so although there is repetition in the words, there is no fault of repetition in the meaning, and knowing its meaning well comes down to knowing the root meaning of lacking own-nature. Whatever dharma the Tathāgata has awakened to or taught, within that there is no true dharma of the ultimate established by its own nature, and there is no false dharma of the conventional established in that way. There also appears to be another, different way of explaining this. Because of that reason, the Tathāgata has comprehended and actualized that all dharmas subsumed by the two truths without distinction are empty of their own nature, and in terms of that, the suchness of all dharmas being empty of true existence is like the dharmakāya of a Buddha, so all dharmas are called "the dharmas of a Buddha". This is from the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "Those have the defining characteristic of their own nature."

If there had been some such dharma, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara would not have prophesied to me, "Young brahmin, you will become a Buddha named Śākyamuni from about this time in the future," but because there is no dharma whatsoever of fully and completely awakening as a Buddha that is truly established, at that time the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara prophesied to me my awakening in that way. Furthermore, the dharmas of by what, what, and to what one is prophesied are merely nominal designations, merely bare names, but the manner of their lacking establishment in an ultimate sense has already been stated above. It is explained in a sūtra that it has been one countless and ninety-one eons since the appearance of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, and also from the annotations to the Pradīpoddyotana commentary on the Guhyasamāja Root Tantra it is stated, "Later, Dīpaṃkara appeared one countless and ninety-one great eons previously." At that time, when the Teacher became the young brahmin Dharmamegha, that very Buddha placed his feet upon his body and blessed him, so having attained great endurance in the non-arising of dharmas, he was prophesied to become a Buddha; generally, attaining endurance in the non-arising of dharmas has three: small, medium, and great; the small is the endurance of the path of preparation, the medium is the path of seeing, and the great arises from the attainment of arhatship, and in terms of the Mahāyāna, it is attained from the eighth level. To attain whichever of those three endurances, because one must realize that conditioned dharmas do not arise by their own nature, one must definitely realize emptiness, and for the medium and great one must realize emptiness directly, and for the great one must also abandon afflictions. Therefore, for a direct prophecy to become a Buddha, one definitely must have previously realized emptiness, so a direct prophecy is not given to bodhisattvas who are bound by grasping at true existence, because those who are bound by grasping at true existence, adhering to true existence in the dharmas of what is to be attained and what attains, are unsuitable as vessels to be directly prophesied, because as explained before, truly established dharmas are unable to be transformed, so it is unsuitable to posit any attainer and so forth.

Because of that reason, the Tathāgata has comprehended and actualized that all dharmas subsumed by the two truths without distinction are empty of their own nature, and in terms of that, the suchness of all dharmas being empty of true existence is like the dharmakāya of a Buddha, so all dharmas are called "the dharmas of a Buddha". This is from the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "Those have the defining characteristic of their own nature."
