[2-104] translation already produced for this document:
If there had been some such dharma, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara would not have prophesied to me, "Young brahmin, you will become a Buddha named Śākyamuni from about this time in the future," but because there is no dharma whatsoever of fully and completely awakening as a Buddha that is truly established, at that time the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara prophesied to me my awakening in that way. Furthermore, the dharmas of by what, what, and to what one is prophesied are merely nominal designations, merely bare names, but the manner of their lacking establishment in an ultimate sense has already been stated above. It is explained in a sūtra that it has been one countless and ninety-one eons since the appearance of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, and also from the annotations to the Pradīpoddyotana commentary on the Guhyasamāja Root Tantra it is stated, "Later, Dīpaṃkara appeared one countless and ninety-one great eons previously." At that time, when the Teacher became the young brahmin Dharmamegha, that very Buddha placed his feet upon his body and blessed him, so having attained great endurance in the non-arising of dharmas, he was prophesied to become a Buddha; generally, attaining endurance in the non-arising of dharmas has three: small, medium, and great; the small is the endurance of the path of preparation, the medium is the path of seeing, and the great arises from the attainment of arhatship, and in terms of the Mahāyāna, it is attained from the eighth level. To attain whichever of those three endurances, because one must realize that conditioned dharmas do not arise by their own nature, one must definitely realize emptiness, and for the medium and great one must realize emptiness directly, and for the great one must also abandon afflictions. Therefore, for a direct prophecy to become a Buddha, one definitely must have previously realized emptiness, so a direct prophecy is not given to bodhisattvas who are bound by grasping at true existence, because those who are bound by grasping at true existence, adhering to true existence in the dharmas of what is to be attained and what attains, are unsuitable as vessels to be directly prophesied, because as explained before, truly established dharmas are unable to be transformed, so it is unsuitable to posit any attainer and so forth.

Whatever dharma the Tathāgata has awakened to or taught, within that there is no true dharma of the ultimate established by its own nature, and there is no false dharma of the conventional established in that way. There also appears to be another, different way of explaining this. Because of that reason, the Tathāgata has comprehended and actualized that all dharmas subsumed by the two truths without distinction are empty of their own nature, and in terms of that, the suchness of all dharmas being empty of true existence is like the dharmakāya of a Buddha, so all dharmas are called "the dharmas of a Buddha". heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: As for teaching an example for that, he stated, "It is like a person who is endowed with a human body and has become a great body." Ācārya Kamalaśīla seems to have applied the meaning of this by applying being endowed with a body to the body of a bodhisattva and a great body to the body of a Buddha, and it should be explained like this: just as a person whose small body gradually grows and becomes large is nominally designated as a "great body" in relation to the former, I think that if one says the meaning of that example is that by gradually purifying obscurations with respect to the dharmatā of the minds of all sentient beings being empty of true existence, ultimately all obscurations are exhausted and it becomes the dharmakāya of a Buddha, it accords with his intention. Then, when Subhūti stated that although the body of such an example is not established as a body in an ultimate sense, it is posited as such conventionally, the Bhagavān assented, saying "It is so," and so forth.

[2-104] translation already produced for this document:
If there had been some such dharma, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara would not have prophesied to me, "Young brahmin, you will become a Buddha named Śākyamuni from about this time in the future," but because there is no dharma whatsoever of fully and completely awakening as a Buddha that is truly established, at that time the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara prophesied to me my awakening in that way. Furthermore, the dharmas of by what, what, and to what one is prophesied are merely nominal designations, merely bare names, but the manner of their lacking establishment in an ultimate sense has already been stated above. It is explained in a sūtra that it has been one countless and ninety-one eons since the appearance of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, and also from the annotations to the Pradīpoddyotana commentary on the Guhyasamāja Root Tantra it is stated, "Later, Dīpaṃkara appeared one countless and ninety-one great eons previously." At that time, when the Teacher became the young brahmin Dharmamegha, that very Buddha placed his feet upon his body and blessed him, so having attained great endurance in the non-arising of dharmas, he was prophesied to become a Buddha; generally, attaining endurance in the non-arising of dharmas has three: small, medium, and great; the small is the endurance of the path of preparation, the medium is the path of seeing, and the great arises from the attainment of arhatship, and in terms of the Mahāyāna, it is attained from the eighth level. To attain whichever of those three endurances, because one must realize that conditioned dharmas do not arise by their own nature, one must definitely realize emptiness, and for the medium and great one must realize emptiness directly, and for the great one must also abandon afflictions. Therefore, for a direct prophecy to become a Buddha, one definitely must have previously realized emptiness, so a direct prophecy is not given to bodhisattvas who are bound by grasping at true existence, because those who are bound by grasping at true existence, adhering to true existence in the dharmas of what is to be attained and what attains, are unsuitable as vessels to be directly prophesied, because as explained before, truly established dharmas are unable to be transformed, so it is unsuitable to posit any attainer and so forth.

Whatever dharma the Tathāgata has awakened to or taught, within that there is no true dharma of the ultimate established by its own nature, and there is no false dharma of the conventional established in that way. There also appears to be another, different way of explaining this. Because of that reason, the Tathāgata has comprehended and actualized that all dharmas subsumed by the two truths without distinction are empty of their own nature, and in terms of that, the suchness of all dharmas being empty of true existence is like the dharmakāya of a Buddha, so all dharmas are called "the dharmas of a Buddha". This is from the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "Those have the defining characteristic of their own nature."

translation: Furthermore, although a bodhisattva must generate the mind to establish immeasurable sentient beings in non-abiding nirvāṇa by way of conventional illusion, showing that in an ultimate sense no sentient being whatsoever is established in it, if any bodhisattva says with an adherence to true existence, thinking, "I will pass sentient beings completely beyond sorrow," that one is not called a bodhisattva who knows the meaning of selflessness.

If there had been some such dharma, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara would not have prophesied to me, "Young brahmin, you will become a Buddha named Śākyamuni from about this time in the future," but because there is no dharma whatsoever of fully and completely awakening as a Buddha that is truly established, at that time the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara prophesied to me my awakening in that way. Furthermore, the dharmas of by what, what, and to what one is prophesied are merely nominal designations, merely bare names, but the manner of their lacking establishment in an ultimate sense has already been stated above. It is explained in a sūtra that it has been one countless and ninety-one eons since the appearance of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, and also from the annotations to the Pradīpoddyotana commentary on the Guhyasamāja Root Tantra it is stated, "Later, Dīpaṃkara appeared one countless and ninety-one great eons previously." At that time, when the Teacher became the young brahmin Dharmamegha, that very Buddha placed his feet upon his body and blessed him, so having attained great endurance in the non-arising of dharmas, he was prophesied to become a Buddha; generally, attaining endurance in the non-arising of dharmas has three: small, medium, and great; the small is the endurance of the path of preparation, the medium is the path of seeing, and the great arises from the attainment of arhatship, and in terms of the Mahāyāna, it is attained from the eighth level. To attain whichever of those three endurances, because one must realize that conditioned dharmas do not arise by their own nature, one must definitely realize emptiness, and for the medium and great one must realize emptiness directly, and for the great one must also abandon afflictions. Therefore, for a direct prophecy to become a Buddha, one definitely must have previously realized emptiness, so a direct prophecy is not given to bodhisattvas who are bound by grasping at true existence, because those who are bound by grasping at true existence, adhering to true existence in the dharmas of what is to be attained and what attains, are unsuitable as vessels to be directly prophesied, because as explained before, truly established dharmas are unable to be transformed, so it is unsuitable to posit any attainer and so forth.

Because of that reason, the Tathāgata has comprehended and actualized that all dharmas subsumed by the two truths without distinction are empty of their own nature, and in terms of that, the suchness of all dharmas being empty of true existence is like the dharmakāya of a Buddha, so all dharmas are called "the dharmas of a Buddha". This is from the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "Those have the defining characteristic of their own nature."

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: As for the reason, when he asked, "Do you think there is any dharma at all called a bodhisattva in an ultimate sense?", in reply Subhūti stated, "There is no such thing." The Bhagavān said to Subhūti, "Because of the reason of its non-existence, the Tathāgata has said that all dharmas of thorough affliction and purification are without a sentient being established as a self of persons, without a life-force, and without a person." To summarize, if one engages with adherence to true existence, thinking, "The self is what attains," and "This is the dharma to be attained," that is explained as someone with the pride of self-conceit who arrogantly assumes that what is non-existent exists, so it is unsuitable; that is, it has been explained above that if they were truly established they would be unable to be transformed, so it is unsuitable to posit what is to be attained, what attains, and so forth for any dharma. By these, the meaning of "how should one practice?", the manner of meditating on selflessness, is taught.

[2-104] translation already produced for this document:
If there had been some such dharma, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara would not have prophesied to me, "Young brahmin, you will become a Buddha named Śākyamuni from about this time in the future," but because there is no dharma whatsoever of fully and completely awakening as a Buddha that is truly established, at that time the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara prophesied to me my awakening in that way. Furthermore, the dharmas of by what, what, and to what one is prophesied are merely nominal designations, merely bare names, but the manner of their lacking establishment in an ultimate sense has already been stated above. It is explained in a sūtra that it has been one countless and ninety-one eons since the appearance of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, and also from the annotations to the Pradīpoddyotana commentary on the Guhyasamāja Root Tantra it is stated, "Later, Dīpaṃkara appeared one countless and ninety-one great eons previously." At that time, when the Teacher became the young brahmin Dharmamegha, that very Buddha placed his feet upon his body and blessed him, so having attained great endurance in the non-arising of dharmas, he was prophesied to become a Buddha; generally, attaining endurance in the non-arising of dharmas has three: small, medium, and great; the small is the endurance of the path of preparation, the medium is the path of seeing, and the great arises from the attainment of arhatship, and in terms of the Mahāyāna, it is attained from the eighth level. To attain whichever of those three endurances, because one must realize that conditioned dharmas do not arise by their own nature, one must definitely realize emptiness, and for the medium and great one must realize emptiness directly, and for the great one must also abandon afflictions. Therefore, for a direct prophecy to become a Buddha, one definitely must have previously realized emptiness, so a direct prophecy is not given to bodhisattvas who are bound by grasping at true existence, because those who are bound by grasping at true existence, adhering to true existence in the dharmas of what is to be attained and what attains, are unsuitable as vessels to be directly prophesied, because as explained before, truly established dharmas are unable to be transformed, so it is unsuitable to posit any attainer and so forth.

[2-104] translation already produced for this document:
If there had been some such dharma, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara would not have prophesied to me, "Young brahmin, you will become a Buddha named Śākyamuni from about this time in the future," but because there is no dharma whatsoever of fully and completely awakening as a Buddha that is truly established, at that time the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara prophesied to me my awakening in that way. Furthermore, the dharmas of by what, what, and to what one is prophesied are merely nominal designations, merely bare names, but the manner of their lacking establishment in an ultimate sense has already been stated above. It is explained in a sūtra that it has been one countless and ninety-one eons since the appearance of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, and also from the annotations to the Pradīpoddyotana commentary on the Guhyasamāja Root Tantra it is stated, "Later, Dīpaṃkara appeared one countless and ninety-one great eons previously." At that time, when the Teacher became the young brahmin Dharmamegha, that very Buddha placed his feet upon his body and blessed him, so having attained great endurance in the non-arising of dharmas, he was prophesied to become a Buddha; generally, attaining endurance in the non-arising of dharmas has three: small, medium, and great; the small is the endurance of the path of preparation, the medium is the path of seeing, and the great arises from the attainment of arhatship, and in terms of the Mahāyāna, it is attained from the eighth level. To attain whichever of those three endurances, because one must realize that conditioned dharmas do not arise by their own nature, one must definitely realize emptiness, and for the medium and great one must realize emptiness directly, and for the great one must also abandon afflictions. Therefore, for a direct prophecy to become a Buddha, one definitely must have previously realized emptiness, so a direct prophecy is not given to bodhisattvas who are bound by grasping at true existence, because those who are bound by grasping at true existence, adhering to true existence in the dharmas of what is to be attained and what attains, are unsuitable as vessels to be directly prophesied, because as explained before, truly established dharmas are unable to be transformed, so it is unsuitable to posit any attainer and so forth.

Whatever dharma the Tathāgata has awakened to or taught, within that there is no true dharma of the ultimate established by its own nature, and there is no false dharma of the conventional established in that way. There also appears to be another, different way of explaining this. Because of that reason, the Tathāgata has comprehended and actualized that all dharmas subsumed by the two truths without distinction are empty of their own nature, and in terms of that, the suchness of all dharmas being empty of true existence is like the dharmakāya of a Buddha, so all dharmas are called "the dharmas of a Buddha". This is from the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "Those have the defining characteristic of their own nature."

If there had been some such dharma, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara would not have prophesied to me, "Young brahmin, you will become a Buddha named Śākyamuni from about this time in the future," but because there is no dharma whatsoever of fully and completely awakening as a Buddha that is truly established, at that time the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara prophesied to me my awakening in that way. Furthermore, the dharmas of by what, what, and to what one is prophesied are merely nominal designations, merely bare names, but the manner of their lacking establishment in an ultimate sense has already been stated above. It is explained in a sūtra that it has been one countless and ninety-one eons since the appearance of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, and also from the annotations to the Pradīpoddyotana commentary on the Guhyasamāja Root Tantra it is stated, "Later, Dīpaṃkara appeared one countless and ninety-one great eons previously." At that time, when the Teacher became the young brahmin Dharmamegha, that very Buddha placed his feet upon his body and blessed him, so having attained great endurance in the non-arising of dharmas, he was prophesied to become a Buddha; generally, attaining endurance in the non-arising of dharmas has three: small, medium, and great; the small is the endurance of the path of preparation, the medium is the path of seeing, and the great arises from the attainment of arhatship, and in terms of the Mahāyāna, it is attained from the eighth level. To attain whichever of those three endurances, because one must realize that conditioned dharmas do not arise by their own nature, one must definitely realize emptiness, and for the medium and great one must realize emptiness directly, and for the great one must also abandon afflictions. Therefore, for a direct prophecy to become a Buddha, one definitely must have previously realized emptiness, so a direct prophecy is not given to bodhisattvas who are bound by grasping at true existence, because those who are bound by grasping at true existence, adhering to true existence in the dharmas of what is to be attained and what attains, are unsuitable as vessels to be directly prophesied, because as explained before, truly established dharmas are unable to be transformed, so it is unsuitable to posit any attainer and so forth.

Because of that reason, the Tathāgata has comprehended and actualized that all dharmas subsumed by the two truths without distinction are empty of their own nature, and in terms of that, the suchness of all dharmas being empty of true existence is like the dharmakāya of a Buddha, so all dharmas are called "the dharmas of a Buddha". This is from the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "Those have the defining characteristic of their own nature."

heading: ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པར་ཤེས་ཤིང་བསྒོམས་ན་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེ་བ།
translation: If any bodhisattva is inclined to and realizes thus, thinking, "Forms and so forth are without a self of persons and without a self of dharmas", the Tathāgata expresses that one as a "great bodhisattva who has realized selflessness". By this as well, it is explained that one must meditate on the two selflessnesses.

[2-104] translation already produced for this document:
If there had been some such dharma, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara would not have prophesied to me, "Young brahmin, you will become a Buddha named Śākyamuni from about this time in the future," but because there is no dharma whatsoever of fully and completely awakening as a Buddha that is truly established, at that time the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara prophesied to me my awakening in that way. Furthermore, the dharmas of by what, what, and to what one is prophesied are merely nominal designations, merely bare names, but the manner of their lacking establishment in an ultimate sense has already been stated above. It is explained in a sūtra that it has been one countless and ninety-one eons since the appearance of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, and also from the annotations to the Pradīpoddyotana commentary on the Guhyasamāja Root Tantra it is stated, "Later, Dīpaṃkara appeared one countless and ninety-one great eons previously." At that time, when the Teacher became the young brahmin Dharmamegha, that very Buddha placed his feet upon his body and blessed him, so having attained great endurance in the non-arising of dharmas, he was prophesied to become a Buddha; generally, attaining endurance in the non-arising of dharmas has three: small, medium, and great; the small is the endurance of the path of preparation, the medium is the path of seeing, and the great arises from the attainment of arhatship, and in terms of the Mahāyāna, it is attained from the eighth level. To attain whichever of those three endurances, because one must realize that conditioned dharmas do not arise by their own nature, one must definitely realize emptiness, and for the medium and great one must realize emptiness directly, and for the great one must also abandon afflictions. Therefore, for a direct prophecy to become a Buddha, one definitely must have previously realized emptiness, so a direct prophecy is not given to bodhisattvas who are bound by grasping at true existence, because those who are bound by grasping at true existence, adhering to true existence in the dharmas of what is to be attained and what attains, are unsuitable as vessels to be directly prophesied, because as explained before, truly established dharmas are unable to be transformed, so it is unsuitable to posit any attainer and so forth.

Although something like this occurred above, it is applied to the respective contexts, so although there is repetition in the words, there is no fault of repetition in the meaning, and knowing its meaning well comes down to knowing the root meaning of lacking own-nature. Whatever dharma the Tathāgata has awakened to or taught, within that there is no true dharma of the ultimate established by its own nature, and there is no false dharma of the conventional established in that way. There also appears to be another, different way of explaining this. Because of that reason, the Tathāgata has comprehended and actualized that all dharmas subsumed by the two truths without distinction are empty of their own nature, and in terms of that, the suchness of all dharmas being empty of true existence is like the dharmakāya of a Buddha, so all dharmas are called "the dharmas of a Buddha". This is from the Abhisamayālaṃkāra: "Those have the defining characteristic of their own nature."

heading: དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་སྤྱན་ལྔ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་ཡོད་པར་སྟོན་པ།
source: འོ་ན་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་བདག་མེད་ཀྱི་དོན་གཟིགས་པའི་མཁྱེན་པ་ཇི་ལྟར་ ཡོད་སྙམ་ན། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་སྤྱན་ལྔ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་ཡོད་དོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་ཤའི་སྤྱན་དང༌། ལྷ་དང༌། ཤེས་རབ་དང༌། ཆོས་དང༌། སངས་རྒྱས་སྤྱན་མངའ་མ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། ལན་དུ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་དེ་དག་མངའོ་ཞེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །སྤྱིར་སྤྱན་ལྔས་ཡུལ་མཐོང་ཚུལ་ལ་རྒྱ་ཆེ་ཆུང་ཡོད་ཀྱང་འདིར་སངས་རྒྱས་དང་སྦྱར་ན། ཤའི་སྤྱན་གྱིས་ནི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཁམས་ཀྱི་གཟུགས་ཕྲ་རགས་ཐམས་ཅད་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གཟིགས་ཤིང༌། ལྷའི་སྤྱན་གྱིས་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སྐྱེ་འཆིའི་རིམས་སོགས་དང༌། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་གྱིས་བདག་མེད་ཕྲ་རགས་ཐམས་ཅད་དང༌། ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་གྱིས་ཀུན་རྫོབ་པའི་རབ་དབྱེ་ཐམས་ཅད་དང༌། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་གྱིས་ནི་བདེན་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་བསྡུས་པའི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་དུ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གཟིགས་པའོ། །དེ་ལ་ཤའི་སྤྱན་དང་ལྷའི་སྤྱན་ནི་མིག་གི་དབང་པོའམ་དེ་ལ་བརྟེན་པའི་དབང་ཤེས་ཡིན་ལ། གཞན་གསུམ་ནི་ཡིད་ཤེས་སོ། །འོན་ཀྱང་དེ་དག་ནི་རང་གི་ཡུལ་སོ་སོ་བའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པ་སྟེ། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་མིག་ཤེས་སོགས་དབང་ཤེས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་གཟིགས་པས་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་དངོས་དང་ཁྱད་པར་མེད་པར་བཤད་ཅིང༌། མདོ་ལས། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གཙུག་ཏོར་གྱིས་ཀྱང་གཟིགས་སོ་ཞེས་སོགས་དང༌། མཚན་བརྗོད་དུ། སྐྲ་ཡང་རྡོ་རྗེ་འབར་བ་སྟེ། །ཞེས་པའི་སྐབས་སུ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སྐུའི་ཆ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་ཤེས་བྱ་མཁྱེན་པར་།བཤད་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །དེ་ཡང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་དང་དབང་ཤེས་ནི་ཡིད་ཤེས་དང་ངོ་བོ་གཅིག་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་འཇུག་པ་ལ་དགོངས་པར་སེམས་ལ། བདེ་མཆོག་རྩ་རྒྱུད་ལེའུ་ལྔ་བཅུ་པ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། ཀུན་ཏུ་ཕྱག་དང་ཞབས་ལྡན་ཞིང༌། །ཀུན་ཏུ་སྤྱན་དང་དབུ་དང་ཞལ། །ཞེས་པའི་སྐབས་སུ་ཡང་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འབྱུང་ངོ༌། །
translation: If one wonders, "How does the Tathāgata possess the knowledge that sees the meaning of selflessness?", showing that the Tathāgata possesses the five excellent eyes: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "Does the Tathāgata possess the eye of flesh, the divine, the wisdom, the dharma, and the Buddha eye?", in reply Subhūti stated, "The Tathāgata possesses them." In general, although there are large and small scopes in the manner in which the five eyes see objects, if they are applied here to a Buddha: with the eye of flesh he directly sees all subtle and gross forms in the world realms, with the divine eye the series of births and deaths of sentient beings and so forth, with the wisdom eye all subtle and gross selflessness, with the dharma eye all the divisions of the conventional, and with the Buddha eye he directly sees all dharmas subsumed by the two truths exactly as they are. Herein, the eye of flesh and the divine eye are the sense faculty of the eye or the sense consciousness depending upon it, while the other three are mental consciousness. However, these are posited in terms of their respective individual objects, for it is explained that since the Buddha sees all dharmas even with sense consciousnesses such as eye consciousness, there is no difference from actual omniscience; and it is just as it is explained in the sūtra, "He sees even with the uṣṇīṣa of a Buddha" and so forth, and in the Nāmasaṃgīti, at the occasion of "Even his hair is a blazing vajra", that all parts of the Buddha's body know the objects of knowledge. Furthermore, I think this intends that the body and sense consciousnesses of a Buddha engage in the manner of being of one nature with mental consciousness, and similarly it also occurs in the fiftieth chapter of the Cakrasaṃvara Root Tantra at the occasion of, "Possessing hands and feet everywhere, possessing eyes, heads, and faces everywhere."

As for teaching an example for that, he stated, "It is like a person who is endowed with a human body and has become a great body." Ācārya Kamalaśīla seems to have applied the meaning of this by applying being endowed with a body to the body of a bodhisattva and a great body to the body of a Buddha, and it should be explained like this: just as a person whose small body gradually grows and becomes large is nominally designated as a "great body" in relation to the former, I think that if one says the meaning of that example is that by gradually purifying obscurations with respect to the dharmatā of the minds of all sentient beings being empty of true existence, ultimately all obscurations are exhausted and it becomes the dharmakāya of a Buddha, it accords with his intention. Then, when Subhūti stated that although the body of such an example is not established as a body in an ultimate sense, it is posited as such conventionally, the Bhagavān assented, saying "It is so," and so forth.

[2-112] source:
ཡང༌། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་ཐ་སྙད་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་སེམས་ཅན་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པ་མི་གནས་པའི་མྱང་འདས་ལ་འགོད་པར་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་དགོས་ཀྱང༌། དོན་དམ་པར་སེམས་ཅན་གང་ཡང་དེ་ལ་འགོད་པ་མེད་ཅེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ། བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་བདག་གིས་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་བཟླའོ་ཟེར་ན། དེ་བདག་མེད་ཀྱི་དོན་ཤེས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་མི་བྱའོ། །
[2-112] translation already produced for this document:
Furthermore, although a bodhisattva must generate the mind to establish immeasurable sentient beings in non-abiding nirvāṇa by way of conventional illusion, showing that in an ultimate sense no sentient being whatsoever is established in it, if any bodhisattva says with an adherence to true existence, thinking, "I will pass sentient beings completely beyond sorrow," that one is not called a bodhisattva who knows the meaning of selflessness.

[2-113] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་དེ་གང་ཡང་ཡོད་སྙམ་མམ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། ལན་དུ་རབ་འབྱོར་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ཡོད་པ་མ་ལགས་ཞེས་གསོལ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་དེ་མེད་པའི་རྒྱུ་མཚན་དེ་བས་ན་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཀུན་བྱང་གི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་ཏུ་གྲུབ་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་མེད་པ། སྲོག་མེད་པ། གང་ཟག་མེད་པའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །བསྡུ་ན་བདག་ནི་ཐོབ་པར་བྱེད་པའོ། །འདི་ནི་ཐོབ་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་སོ་སྙམ་དུ་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་འཇུག་ན་མེད་པ་ལ་ཡོད་པར་རློམ་པ་མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་ཅན་དུ་བཤད་པས་མི་རུང་ཞེས་པ་སྟེ་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་ན་བསྒྱུར་དུ་མི་རུང་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཆོས་གང་ལའང་ཐོབ་བྱ་ཐོབ་བྱེད་སོགས་བཞག་ཏུ་མི་རུང་ངོ་ཞེས་གོང་དུ་བཤད་ཟིན་ཏོ། །འདི་དག་གིས་ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་བདག་མེད་བསྒོམ་ཚུལ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[2-113] translation already produced for this document:
As for the reason, when he asked, "Do you think there is any dharma at all called a bodhisattva in an ultimate sense?", in reply Subhūti stated, "There is no such thing." The Bhagavān said to Subhūti, "Because of the reason of its non-existence, the Tathāgata has said that all dharmas of thorough affliction and purification are without a sentient being established as a self of persons, without a life-force, and without a person." To summarize, if one engages with adherence to true existence, thinking, "The self is what attains," and "This is the dharma to be attained," that is explained as someone with the pride of self-conceit who arrogantly assumes that what is non-existent exists, so it is unsuitable; that is, it has been explained above that if they were truly established they would be unable to be transformed, so it is unsuitable to posit what is to be attained, what attains, and so forth for any dharma. By these, the meaning of "how should one practice?", the manner of meditating on selflessness, is taught.

heading: དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་སྤྱན་ལྔ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་ཡོད་པར་སྟོན་པ།
translation: Showing that because the Tathāgata possesses such eyes he sees all dharmas and also sees the mind streams of sentient beings: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "For example, however many numerous grains of sand there are in the Gaṅgā river, if there were exactly that many Gaṅgā rivers, would those world realms be many?", in reply Subhūti stated, "Many," and so the Bhagavān said, "I thoroughly know the streams and aspects of the various, dissimilar, and diverse minds of those sentient beings existing in all those world realms."

As for teaching an example for that, he stated, "It is like a person who is endowed with a human body and has become a great body." Ācārya Kamalaśīla seems to have applied the meaning of this by applying being endowed with a body to the body of a bodhisattva and a great body to the body of a Buddha, and it should be explained like this: just as a person whose small body gradually grows and becomes large is nominally designated as a "great body" in relation to the former, I think that if one says the meaning of that example is that by gradually purifying obscurations with respect to the dharmatā of the minds of all sentient beings being empty of true existence, ultimately all obscurations are exhausted and it becomes the dharmakāya of a Buddha, it accords with his intention. Then, when Subhūti stated that although the body of such an example is not established as a body in an ultimate sense, it is posited as such conventionally, the Bhagavān assented, saying "It is so," and so forth.

[2-112] source:

heading: དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་སྤྱན་ལྔ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་ཡོད་པར་སྟོན་པ།
translation: "Even so, I have explained that the mind streams of sentient beings are not established as what is called a stream in an ultimate sense; therefore, because they are non-existent in an ultimate sense, conventionally they are expressed as what is called a 'mind stream'." By this, it is taught that the five eyes and the objects of the five eyes are also merely posited conventionally, but are not established in an ultimate sense.

As for teaching an example for that, he stated, "It is like a person who is endowed with a human body and has become a great body." Ācārya Kamalaśīla seems to have applied the meaning of this by applying being endowed with a body to the body of a bodhisattva and a great body to the body of a Buddha, and it should be explained like this: just as a person whose small body gradually grows and becomes large is nominally designated as a "great body" in relation to the former, I think that if one says the meaning of that example is that by gradually purifying obscurations with respect to the dharmatā of the minds of all sentient beings being empty of true existence, ultimately all obscurations are exhausted and it becomes the dharmakāya of a Buddha, it accords with his intention. Then, when Subhūti stated that although the body of such an example is not established as a body in an ultimate sense, it is posited as such conventionally, the Bhagavān assented, saying "It is so," and so forth.

[2-112] source:
ཡང༌། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་ཐ་སྙད་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་སེམས་ཅན་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པ་མི་གནས་པའི་མྱང་འདས་ལ་འགོད་པར་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་དགོས་ཀྱང༌། དོན་དམ་པར་སེམས་ཅན་གང་ཡང་དེ་ལ་འགོད་པ་མེད་ཅེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ། བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་བདག་གིས་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཡོངས་སུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་བཟླའོ་ཟེར་ན། དེ་བདག་མེད་ཀྱི་དོན་ཤེས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་མི་བྱའོ། །
[2-112] translation already produced for this document:
Furthermore, although a bodhisattva must generate the mind to establish immeasurable sentient beings in non-abiding nirvāṇa by way of conventional illusion, showing that in an ultimate sense no sentient being whatsoever is established in it, if any bodhisattva says with an adherence to true existence, thinking, "I will pass sentient beings completely beyond sorrow," that one is not called a bodhisattva who knows the meaning of selflessness.

[2-113] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་དེ་གང་ཡང་ཡོད་སྙམ་མམ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། ལན་དུ་རབ་འབྱོར་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ཡོད་པ་མ་ལགས་ཞེས་གསོལ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་དེ་མེད་པའི་རྒྱུ་མཚན་དེ་བས་ན་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཀུན་བྱང་གི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་ཏུ་གྲུབ་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་མེད་པ། སྲོག་མེད་པ། གང་ཟག་མེད་པའོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །བསྡུ་ན་བདག་ནི་ཐོབ་པར་བྱེད་པའོ། །འདི་ནི་ཐོབ་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་སོ་སྙམ་དུ་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་འཇུག་ན་མེད་པ་ལ་ཡོད་པར་རློམ་པ་མངོན་པའི་ང་རྒྱལ་ཅན་དུ་བཤད་པས་མི་རུང་ཞེས་པ་སྟེ་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་ན་བསྒྱུར་དུ་མི་རུང་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཆོས་གང་ལའང་ཐོབ་བྱ་ཐོབ་བྱེད་སོགས་བཞག་ཏུ་མི་རུང་ངོ་ཞེས་གོང་དུ་བཤད་ཟིན་ཏོ། །འདི་དག་གིས་ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་བདག་མེད་བསྒོམ་ཚུལ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[2-113] translation already produced for this document:
As for the reason, when he asked, "Do you think there is any dharma at all called a bodhisattva in an ultimate sense?", in reply Subhūti stated, "There is no such thing." The Bhagavān said to Subhūti, "Because of the reason of its non-existence, the Tathāgata has said that all dharmas of thorough affliction and purification are without a sentient being established as a self of persons, without a life-force, and without a person." To summarize, if one engages with adherence to true existence, thinking, "The self is what attains," and "This is the dharma to be attained," that is explained as someone with the pride of self-conceit who arrogantly assumes that what is non-existent exists, so it is unsuitable; that is, it has been explained above that if they were truly established they would be unable to be transformed, so it is unsuitable to posit what is to be attained, what attains, and so forth for any dharma. By these, the meaning of "how should one practice?", the manner of meditating on selflessness, is taught.

[2-114] source:
དེ་ནས་སེམས་ཅན་མྱང་འདས་ལ་འགོད་པ་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་མི་བྱེད་པར་མ་ཟད། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་གཟུང་བ་ཡང་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་བྱེད་ཀྱང་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་མི་བྱའོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ། བདག་གིས་གང་དུ་འཚང་རྒྱ་བའི་གནས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་གི་བཀོད་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་རྣམ་པར་དོན་དམ་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་ཞེན་ཅིང་ཚིག་གིས་ཟེར་ན། དེ་ཡང་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་བརྗོད་ཅིང་ཞེན་པར་བྱར་མི་རུང་ངོ༌། །
[2-114] translation already produced for this document:
Then, showing that not only does one not adhere to true existence regarding establishing sentient beings in nirvāṇa, but also although one adopts a Buddha field conventionally, one should not do so with adherence to true existence: "Subhūti, if any bodhisattva says with words, adhering thus, thinking, 'I will thoroughly establish in an ultimate sense the excellent arrangements of the field of the place where I will awaken as a Buddha', it is also unsuitable to express and adhere to it in that way."

[2-115] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་ལ་ཞིང་གི་བཀོད་པ་དེ་དག་ནི། ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ཚོགས་ཤིང་འདུས་པ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟར་ཡོད་པ་ལས་གཞན་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པའི་བཀོད་པ་མེད་པར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། དེས་ན་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཞིང་བཀོད་པ་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །
[2-115] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the reason, it is because the Tathāgata has said that other than those arrangements of the field existing conventionally as accumulated and assembled like an illusion, there are no truly established arrangements; therefore, they are nominally called "arrangements of the field".

[2-116] source:
བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་གཟུགས་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ནི། གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདག་མེད་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་མོས་ཤིང་རྟོགས་པ་དེ་ནི། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དོ། །འདིས་ཀྱང་བདག་མེད་གཉིས་བསྒོམ་དགོས་པར་བཤད་དོ། །
[2-116] translation already produced for this document:
If any bodhisattva is inclined to and realizes thus, thinking, "Forms and so forth are without a self of persons and without a self of dharmas", the Tathāgata expresses that one as a "great bodhisattva who has realized selflessness". By this as well, it is explained that one must meditate on the two selflessnesses.

heading: སེམས་སེམས་བྱུང་།
source: འདས་པའི་སེམས་རྣམས་ནི་འདས་ཟིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་དོན་དམ་པར་དམིགས་སུ་མེད། མ་འོངས་པའི་སེམས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ད་ལྟ་མ་སྐྱེས་ཤིང་མ་བྱུང་བའི་ཕྱིར་དོན་དམ་པར་མེད། ད་ལྟར་བྱུང་བའི་སེམས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་རང་དབང་གིས་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དོན་དམ་པར་མེད་དོ། །སེམས་ཞེས་པ་ནི་གཙོ་སེམས་ཙམ་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། སེམས་དང་སེམས་བྱུང་ཐམས་ཅད་སྡུད་པའོ། །སེམས་བྱུང་རྣམས་ལས་ཚོར་བ་རྣམས་ནི་བདེན་པར་འཛིན་པའི་གཞི་ཆེ་སྟེ། ཚོར་བ་བདེ་སྡུག་དྲག་པོ་བྱུང་བ་ན་བདག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པའི་བློ་ཡང་ཤུགས་དྲག་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེས་ན་ཚོར་བ་བདེན་པར་མ་གྲུབ་པར་སྟོན་པའི་རིགས་པ་མང་ཡང་རྩ་བ་ནི། ཞི་བ་ལྷས། གང་ཚེ་ཚོར་བོ་འགའ་མེད་ན། །ཚོར་བ་འགའ་ཡང་ཡོད་མིན་ཏེ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ཡིན་ལ། དེ་ནི་ཚོར་བ་མྱོང་བ་པོའི་བདག་ནི་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་མེད་ན་དེ་ལ་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཚོར་བ་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་ག་ལ་ཡོད་དེ། ཁྱད་གཞི་མེད་པའི་ཁྱད་ཆོས་མི་སྲིད་པའི་ཕྱིར། ཚོར་བ་བདེ་སྡུག་ནི་ལུས་ཡིད་དང་འཕྲོད་མི་འཕྲོད་པའི་ངོ་བོར་སྐྱེས་ནས་མྱོང་བ་ཡིན་གྱི། ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ནི་མིན་ཏེ། ལུས་ཡིད་གང་རུང་མེད་ན་ཚོར་བ་ཡང་མེད་ཅིང༌། ལུས་ཡོད་ཀྱང་ཡིད་མེད་ནའང་ཚོར་བ་མི་མྱོང་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། རོ་དང་ས་རྡོ་སོགས་བཤིག་ཀྱང་ཚོར་བ་བདེ་སྡུག་མི་འབྱུང་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །མདོར་ན་ཚོར་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཤེས་པ་ཀུན་ཀྱང་དམིགས་པ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་མར་མེའི་འོད་བཞིན་དུ་ཐ་སྙད་ཙམ་དུ་སྐྱེའི། དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་མ་བརྟེན་པར་རང་དབང་གིས་མི་སྐྱེ་བས་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་མ་གྲུབ་བོ། །རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་གྲུབ་པ། བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ། དོན་དམ་པར་གྲུབ་པ། རང་གི་ངོ་བོས་གྲུབ་པ། རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་གྲུབ་པ། རང་དབང་གིས་གྲུབ་པ། ཡང་དག་པར་གྲུབ་པ། བལྟོས་མེད་དུ་གྲུབ་པ་རྣམས་ནི་དོན་གཅིག་མིང་གི་རྣམ་གྲངས་ཙམ་མོ། །འདིས་སེམས་ཇི་ལྟར་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཚུལ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
translation: Past minds are unapprehendable in an ultimate sense because they have passed away. Future minds are also non-existent in an ultimate sense because they are presently unproduced and have not arisen. Presently arisen minds are also non-existent in an ultimate sense because they do not exist independently. "Mind" does not mean merely the main mind, but subsumes all minds and mental factors. Among mental factors, feelings are a great basis for grasping at true existence, because when intense feelings of pleasure and pain arise, the mind grasping at a self also arises with intense force. Therefore, although there are many reasonings showing that feelings are not truly established, the root is like this statement by Śāntideva: "When there is no feeler at all, there is not any feeling either." As for that, if the self who experiences feelings does not exist by its own nature, how could the feelings arising for it exist by their own nature, since characteristics are impossible without a basis of characteristics? Feelings of pleasure and pain are experienced having arisen in the nature of meeting or not meeting with body and mind, but not by their very essence, because if either body or mind is absent, feelings are also absent, and even if the body is present, if the mind is absent, feelings are not experienced: just as feelings of pleasure and pain do not arise even if corpses, earth, stones, and so forth are destroyed. In short, all consciousnesses such as feelings also arise merely conventionally like the light of a butter lamp in dependence upon an object, but because they do not arise independently without depending on such things, they are not established by their own nature. Established by its own nature, truly established, established in an ultimate sense, established by its own essence, established by its own characteristics, independently established, genuinely established, and established without dependence are equivalent in meaning and merely synonyms. By this, the manner of how the mind is to be held is taught.

དེ་ནས་སེམས་ཅན་མྱང་འདས་ལ་འགོད་པ་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་མི་བྱེད་པར་མ་ཟད། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་གཟུང་བ་ཡང་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་བྱེད་ཀྱང་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་མི་བྱའོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ། བདག་གིས་གང་དུ་འཚང་རྒྱ་བའི་གནས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་གི་བཀོད་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་རྣམ་པར་དོན་དམ་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་ཞེན་ཅིང་ཚིག་གིས་ཟེར་ན། དེ་ཡང་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་བརྗོད་ཅིང་ཞེན་པར་བྱར་མི་རུང་ངོ༌། །
[2-114] translation already produced for this document:
Then, showing that not only does one not adhere to true existence regarding establishing sentient beings in nirvāṇa, but also although one adopts a Buddha field conventionally, one should not do so with adherence to true existence: "Subhūti, if any bodhisattva says with words, adhering thus, thinking, 'I will thoroughly establish in an ultimate sense the excellent arrangements of the field of the place where I will awaken as a Buddha', it is also unsuitable to express and adhere to it in that way."

[2-115] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་ལ་ཞིང་གི་བཀོད་པ་དེ་དག་ནི། ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་ཚོགས་ཤིང་འདུས་པ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟར་ཡོད་པ་ལས་གཞན་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པའི་བཀོད་པ་མེད་པར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། དེས་ན་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཞིང་བཀོད་པ་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །
[2-115] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the reason, it is because the Tathāgata has said that other than those arrangements of the field existing conventionally as accumulated and assembled like an illusion, there are no truly established arrangements; therefore, they are nominally called "arrangements of the field".

[2-116] source:
བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་གཟུགས་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ནི། གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདག་མེད་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་མོས་ཤིང་རྟོགས་པ་དེ་ནི། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དོ། །འདིས་ཀྱང་བདག་མེད་གཉིས་བསྒོམ་དགོས་པར་བཤད་དོ། །
[2-116] translation already produced for this document:
If any bodhisattva is inclined to and realizes thus, thinking, "Forms and so forth are without a self of persons and without a self of dharmas", the Tathāgata expresses that one as a "great bodhisattva who has realized selflessness". If one wonders, "How does the Tathāgata possess the knowledge that sees the meaning of selflessness?", showing that the Tathāgata possesses the five excellent eyes: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "Does the Tathāgata possess the eye of flesh, the divine, the wisdom, the dharma, and the Buddha eye?", in reply Subhūti stated, "The Tathāgata possesses them." In general, although there are large and small scopes in the manner in which the five eyes see objects, if they are applied here to a Buddha: with the eye of flesh he directly sees all subtle and gross forms in the world realms, with the divine eye the series of births and deaths of sentient beings and so forth, with the wisdom eye all subtle and gross selflessness, with the dharma eye all the divisions of the conventional, and with the Buddha eye he directly sees all dharmas subsumed by the two truths exactly as they are. Herein, the eye of flesh and the divine eye are the sense faculty of the eye or the sense consciousness depending upon it, while the other three are mental consciousness. However, these are posited in terms of their respective individual objects, for it is explained that since the Buddha sees all dharmas even with sense consciousnesses such as eye consciousness, there is no difference from actual omniscience; and it is just as it is explained in the sūtra, "He sees even with the uṣṇīṣa of a Buddha" and so forth, and in the Nāmasaṃgīti, at the occasion of "Even his hair is a blazing vajra", that all parts of the Buddha's body know the objects of knowledge. Furthermore, I think this intends that the body and sense consciousnesses of a Buddha engage in the manner of being of one nature with mental consciousness, and similarly it also occurs in the fiftieth chapter of the Cakrasaṃvara Root Tantra at the occasion of, "Possessing hands and feet everywhere, possessing eyes, heads, and faces everywhere."

translation: If one wonders, 'If the mind stream does not exist by its own nature, won't results fail to arise from actions such as giving generosity in dependence upon the mind?', showing that although the mind stream and so forth do not exist by their own nature, conventionally results are produced in dependence upon the mind: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, 'If someone filled this three-thousandfold great thousandfold world realm with the previously explained seven precious things such as gold and silver and gave it as generosity to others, would they generate much merit from that?', in reply he stated, 'It would be much,' and then he validated it to Subhūti, saying, 'That is exactly so' and so forth.

If one wonders, "How does the Tathāgata possess the knowledge that sees the meaning of selflessness?", showing that the Tathāgata possesses the five excellent eyes: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "Does the Tathāgata possess the eye of flesh, the divine, the wisdom, the dharma, and the Buddha eye?", in reply Subhūti stated, "The Tathāgata possesses them." In general, although there are large and small scopes in the manner in which the five eyes see objects, if they are applied here to a Buddha: with the eye of flesh he directly sees all subtle and gross forms in the world realms, with the divine eye the series of births and deaths of sentient beings and so forth, with the wisdom eye all subtle and gross selflessness, with the dharma eye all the divisions of the conventional, and with the Buddha eye he directly sees all dharmas subsumed by the two truths exactly as they are. Herein, the eye of flesh and the divine eye are the sense faculty of the eye or the sense consciousness depending upon it, while the other three are mental consciousness. However, these are posited in terms of their respective individual objects, for it is explained that since the Buddha sees all dharmas even with sense consciousnesses such as eye consciousness, there is no difference from actual omniscience; and it is just as it is explained in the sūtra, "He sees even with the uṣṇīṣa of a Buddha" and so forth, and in the Nāmasaṃgīti, at the occasion of "Even his hair is a blazing vajra", that all parts of the Buddha's body know the objects of knowledge. Furthermore, I think this intends that the body and sense consciousnesses of a Buddha engage in the manner of being of one nature with mental consciousness, and similarly it also occurs in the fiftieth chapter of the Cakrasaṃvara Root Tantra at the occasion of, "Possessing hands and feet everywhere, possessing eyes, heads, and faces everywhere."

Showing that because the Tathāgata possesses such eyes he sees all dharmas and also sees the mind streams of sentient beings: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "For example, however many numerous grains of sand there are in the Gaṅgā river, if there were exactly that many Gaṅgā rivers, would those world realms be many?", in reply Subhūti stated, "Many," and so the Bhagavān said, "I thoroughly know the streams and aspects of the various, dissimilar, and diverse minds of those sentient beings existing in all those world realms."

heading: སེམས་སེམས་བྱུང་།
translation: Those heaps of merit have arisen conventionally from a collection like an illusion, but if they were established by their own very essence without depending on such things, the Tathāgata would not have spoken of a 'heap of merit'. The reason is that he intended that the meaning of 'heap' in 'heap of merit' is the meaning of a collection, and if it were established independently, it would be established without depending upon a collection.

[2-117] translation already produced for this document:
If one wonders, "How does the Tathāgata possess the knowledge that sees the meaning of selflessness?", showing that the Tathāgata possesses the five excellent eyes: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "Does the Tathāgata possess the eye of flesh, the divine, the wisdom, the dharma, and the Buddha eye?", in reply Subhūti stated, "The Tathāgata possesses them." In general, although there are large and small scopes in the manner in which the five eyes see objects, if they are applied here to a Buddha: with the eye of flesh he directly sees all subtle and gross forms in the world realms, with the divine eye the series of births and deaths of sentient beings and so forth, with the wisdom eye all subtle and gross selflessness, with the dharma eye all the divisions of the conventional, and with the Buddha eye he directly sees all dharmas subsumed by the two truths exactly as they are. Herein, the eye of flesh and the divine eye are the sense faculty of the eye or the sense consciousness depending upon it, while the other three are mental consciousness. However, these are posited in terms of their respective individual objects, for it is explained that since the Buddha sees all dharmas even with sense consciousnesses such as eye consciousness, there is no difference from actual omniscience; and it is just as it is explained in the sūtra, "He sees even with the uṣṇīṣa of a Buddha" and so forth, and in the Nāmasaṃgīti, at the occasion of "Even his hair is a blazing vajra", that all parts of the Buddha's body know the objects of knowledge. Furthermore, I think this intends that the body and sense consciousnesses of a Buddha engage in the manner of being of one nature with mental consciousness, and similarly it also occurs in the fiftieth chapter of the Cakrasaṃvara Root Tantra at the occasion of, "Possessing hands and feet everywhere, possessing eyes, heads, and faces everywhere."

Showing that because the Tathāgata possesses such eyes he sees all dharmas and also sees the mind streams of sentient beings: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "For example, however many numerous grains of sand there are in the Gaṅgā river, if there were exactly that many Gaṅgā rivers, would those world realms be many?", in reply Subhūti stated, "Many," and so the Bhagavān said, "I thoroughly know the streams and aspects of the various, dissimilar, and diverse minds of those sentient beings existing in all those world realms."

heading: སེམས་སེམས་བྱུང་།
translation: If one wonders, 'If the heap of merit is not truly existent, then the form body of a Buddha that is born from it would also be non-existent', showing that this does not follow: when he asked, 'Do you think one should view, that is, apprehend and assert, this perfectly established form body as the Tathāgata in an ultimate sense?', in reply he stated, 'It is not so; one should not view it in that way.' The reason is that the form body is also established from a collection of causes and conditions, but is not established in an ultimate sense, which is similar to the heap of merit; conventionally it is expressed as 'established as the form body'.

དེ་ནས་སེམས་ཅན་མྱང་འདས་ལ་འགོད་པ་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་མི་བྱེད་པར་མ་ཟད། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་གཟུང་བ་ཡང་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་བྱེད་ཀྱང་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་མི་བྱའོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ། བདག་གིས་གང་དུ་འཚང་རྒྱ་བའི་གནས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་གི་བཀོད་པ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་རྣམ་པར་དོན་དམ་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་ཞེན་ཅིང་ཚིག་གིས་ཟེར་ན། དེ་ཡང་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་བརྗོད་ཅིང་ཞེན་པར་བྱར་མི་རུང་ངོ༌། །
[2-114] translation already produced for this document:
Then, showing that not only does one not adhere to true existence regarding establishing sentient beings in nirvāṇa, but also although one adopts a Buddha field conventionally, one should not do so with adherence to true existence: "Subhūti, if any bodhisattva says with words, adhering thus, thinking, 'I will thoroughly establish in an ultimate sense the excellent arrangements of the field of the place where I will awaken as a Buddha', it is also unsuitable to express and adhere to it in that way."

བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་གཟུགས་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ནི། གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདག་མེད་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་མོས་ཤིང་རྟོགས་པ་དེ་ནི། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དོ། །འདིས་ཀྱང་བདག་མེད་གཉིས་བསྒོམ་དགོས་པར་བཤད་དོ། །

[2-117] source:
འོ་ན་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་བདག་མེད་ཀྱི་དོན་གཟིགས་པའི་མཁྱེན་པ་ཇི་ལྟར་ ཡོད་སྙམ་ན། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་སྤྱན་ལྔ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་ཡོད་དོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་ཤའི་སྤྱན་དང༌། ལྷ་དང༌། ཤེས་རབ་དང༌། ཆོས་དང༌། སངས་རྒྱས་སྤྱན་མངའ་མ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། ལན་དུ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་དེ་དག་མངའོ་ཞེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །སྤྱིར་སྤྱན་ལྔས་ཡུལ་མཐོང་ཚུལ་ལ་རྒྱ་ཆེ་ཆུང་ཡོད་ཀྱང་འདིར་སངས་རྒྱས་དང་སྦྱར་ན། ཤའི་སྤྱན་གྱིས་ནི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཁམས་ཀྱི་གཟུགས་ཕྲ་རགས་ཐམས་ཅད་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གཟིགས་ཤིང༌། ལྷའི་སྤྱན་གྱིས་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སྐྱེ་འཆིའི་རིམས་སོགས་དང༌། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་གྱིས་བདག་མེད་ཕྲ་རགས་ཐམས་ཅད་དང༌། ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་གྱིས་ཀུན་རྫོབ་པའི་རབ་དབྱེ་ཐམས་ཅད་དང༌། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སྤྱན་གྱིས་ནི་བདེན་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་བསྡུས་པའི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་དུ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གཟིགས་པའོ། །དེ་ལ་ཤའི་སྤྱན་དང་ལྷའི་སྤྱན་ནི་མིག་གི་དབང་པོའམ་དེ་ལ་བརྟེན་པའི་དབང་ཤེས་ཡིན་ལ། གཞན་གསུམ་ནི་ཡིད་ཤེས་སོ། །འོན་ཀྱང་དེ་དག་ནི་རང་གི་ཡུལ་སོ་སོ་བའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པ་སྟེ། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་མིག་ཤེས་སོགས་དབང་ཤེས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་གཟིགས་པས་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་དངོས་དང་ཁྱད་པར་མེད་པར་བཤད་ཅིང༌། མདོ་ལས། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གཙུག་ཏོར་གྱིས་ཀྱང་གཟིགས་སོ་ཞེས་སོགས་དང༌། མཚན་བརྗོད་དུ། སྐྲ་ཡང་རྡོ་རྗེ་འབར་བ་སྟེ། །ཞེས་པའི་སྐབས་སུ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སྐུའི་ཆ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་ཤེས་བྱ་མཁྱེན་པར་།བཤད་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །དེ་ཡང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་དང་དབང་ཤེས་ནི་ཡིད་ཤེས་དང་ངོ་བོ་གཅིག་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་འཇུག་པ་ལ་དགོངས་པར་སེམས་ལ། བདེ་མཆོག་རྩ་རྒྱུད་ལེའུ་ལྔ་བཅུ་པ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། ཀུན་ཏུ་ཕྱག་དང་ཞབས་ལྡན་ཞིང༌། །ཀུན་ཏུ་སྤྱན་དང་དབུ་དང་ཞལ། །ཞེས་པའི་སྐབས་སུ་ཡང་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འབྱུང་ངོ༌། །
[2-117] translation already produced for this document:
If one wonders, "How does the Tathāgata possess the knowledge that sees the meaning of selflessness?", showing that the Tathāgata possesses the five excellent eyes: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "Does the Tathāgata possess the eye of flesh, the divine, the wisdom, the dharma, and the Buddha eye?", in reply Subhūti stated, "The Tathāgata possesses them." In general, although there are large and small scopes in the manner in which the five eyes see objects, if they are applied here to a Buddha: with the eye of flesh he directly sees all subtle and gross forms in the world realms, with the divine eye the series of births and deaths of sentient beings and so forth, with the wisdom eye all subtle and gross selflessness, with the dharma eye all the divisions of the conventional, and with the Buddha eye he directly sees all dharmas subsumed by the two truths exactly as they are. Herein, the eye of flesh and the divine eye are the sense faculty of the eye or the sense consciousness depending upon it, while the other three are mental consciousness. However, these are posited in terms of their respective individual objects, for it is explained that since the Buddha sees all dharmas even with sense consciousnesses such as eye consciousness, there is no difference from actual omniscience; and it is just as it is explained in the sūtra, "He sees even with the uṣṇīṣa of a Buddha" and so forth, and in the Nāmasaṃgīti, at the occasion of "Even his hair is a blazing vajra", that all parts of the Buddha's body know the objects of knowledge. Furthermore, I think this intends that the body and sense consciousnesses of a Buddha engage in the manner of being of one nature with mental consciousness, and similarly it also occurs in the fiftieth chapter of the Cakrasaṃvara Root Tantra at the occasion of, "Possessing hands and feet everywhere, possessing eyes, heads, and faces everywhere."

[2-118] source:
དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་སྤྱན་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་མངའ་བས་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་གཟིགས་ཤིང༌། སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སེམས་རྒྱུད་ཀྱང་གཟིགས་སོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་དཔེར་ན་གངྒཱའི་ཀླུང་གི་བྱེ་མའི་གྲངས་མང་པོ་ཇི་སྙེད་ཡོད་པ་དེ་ཙམ་དུ། གངྒཱའི་ཀླུང་ཡང་གྲངས་དེ་སྙེད་ཁོ་ནར་གྱུར་ན་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་དེ་དག་མང་ངམ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། ལན་དུ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་མང་ཞེས་ཞུས་པས། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་ན་ཡོད་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་གི་བསམ་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་པ་མི་འདྲ་བ་ཐ་དད་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་དང་རྣམ་པ་ངས་རབ་ཏུ་ཤེས་སོ། །
[2-118] translation already produced for this document:
Showing that because the Tathāgata possesses such eyes he sees all dharmas and also sees the mind streams of sentient beings: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, "For example, however many numerous grains of sand there are in the Gaṅgā river, if there were exactly that many Gaṅgā rivers, would those world realms be many?", in reply Subhūti stated, "Many," and so the Bhagavān said, "I thoroughly know the streams and aspects of the various, dissimilar, and diverse minds of those sentient beings existing in all those world realms."

[2-119] source:
དེ་ལྟར་ཡིན་ཀྱང་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་ནི་དོན་དམ་པར་རྒྱུན་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་པར་ངས་བཤད་དེ། དོན་དམ་པར་མེད་པ་དེས་ན་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་བརྗོད་དོ། །འདིས་སྤྱན་ལྔ་དང་སྤྱན་ལྔའི་ཡུལ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཐ་སྙད་ཙམ་དུ་འཇོག་གི །དོན་དམ་པར་མ་གྲུབ་ཅེས་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[2-119] translation already produced for this document:
"Even so, I have explained that the mind streams of sentient beings are not established as what is called a stream in an ultimate sense; therefore, because they are non-existent in an ultimate sense, conventionally they are expressed as what is called a 'mind stream'." By this, it is taught that the five eyes and the objects of the five eyes are also merely posited conventionally, but are not established in an ultimate sense.

heading: སེམས་སེམས་བྱུང་།
translation: If one wonders, 'If a form body exists, are its marks and signs truly established?', showing that they are not: in reply to the question, 'Do you think one should view the Tathāgata by the perfection of marks and signs?', he stated, 'One should not view him in that way.' One does not view the Tathāgata with grasping at true existence by way of a perfection of marks and signs existing as truly established on the body of the Tathāgata, because those perfections of marks and signs are things that are gathered and assembled, established like an illusion; therefore, although the perfection of marks and signs is not established in an ultimate sense, conventionally it is expressed as such. Although something similar to this occurred earlier, that was from the perspective of taking it into practice from the stage of engagement by conviction, while here it is from the perspective of taking it into practice from the noble stage of pure superior resolve, as Kamalaśīla states. Likewise, the meaning of the statement that there is no Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is also as explained above. If someone asserts and says with grasping at true existence that 'The Tathāgata has taught the Dharma in an ultimate sense', that is a bondage seized by grasping at true existence that grasps at what is non-existent as existent and conceives falsely, and thus they would be deprecating me, the Tathāgata.
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Diamond Sūtra (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the sūtra, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names and technical terms in standard Sanskrit transliteration (Subhūti, Tathāgata, Dīpaṃkara, prajñāpāramitā) rather than translating them. Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own. Begin directly with the translation: do not write any introductory sentence such as "Here is the translation". Render each source line as exactly one line of continuous English prose, even where the source contains verse stanzas or lists; do not break it into several lines.

Work: རྡོར་གཅོད་ཀྱི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཐར་པར་བགྲོད་པའི་ལམ་བཟང་ཟབ་དོན་གསལ་བའི་ཉི་མ། (The Sun that Illuminates the Profound Meaning of the Excellent Path for Travelling to Freedom), author: ཅོ་ནེ་གྲགས་པ་བཤད་སྒྲུབ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

[2-119] translation already produced for this document:
"Even so, I have explained that the mind streams of sentient beings are not established as what is called a stream in an ultimate sense; therefore, because they are non-existent in an ultimate sense, conventionally they are expressed as what is called a 'mind stream'." By this, it is taught that the five eyes and the objects of the five eyes are also merely posited conventionally, but are not established in an ultimate sense.

[2-120] source:
འདས་པའི་སེམས་རྣམས་ནི་འདས་ཟིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་དོན་དམ་པར་དམིགས་སུ་མེད། མ་འོངས་པའི་སེམས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ད་ལྟ་མ་སྐྱེས་ཤིང་མ་བྱུང་བའི་ཕྱིར་དོན་དམ་པར་མེད། ད་ལྟར་བྱུང་བའི་སེམས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་རང་དབང་གིས་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དོན་དམ་པར་མེད་དོ། །སེམས་ཞེས་པ་ནི་གཙོ་སེམས་ཙམ་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། སེམས་དང་སེམས་བྱུང་ཐམས་ཅད་སྡུད་པའོ། །སེམས་བྱུང་རྣམས་ལས་ཚོར་བ་རྣམས་ནི་བདེན་པར་འཛིན་པའི་གཞི་ཆེ་སྟེ། ཚོར་བ་བདེ་སྡུག་དྲག་པོ་བྱུང་བ་ན་བདག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པའི་བློ་ཡང་ཤུགས་དྲག་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེས་ན་ཚོར་བ་བདེན་པར་མ་གྲུབ་པར་སྟོན་པའི་རིགས་པ་མང་ཡང་རྩ་བ་ནི། ཞི་བ་ལྷས། གང་ཚེ་ཚོར་བོ་འགའ་མེད་ན། །ཚོར་བ་འགའ་ཡང་ཡོད་མིན་ཏེ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ཡིན་ལ། དེ་ནི་ཚོར་བ་མྱོང་བ་པོའི་བདག་ནི་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་མེད་ན་དེ་ལ་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཚོར་བ་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་ག་ལ་ཡོད་དེ། ཁྱད་གཞི་མེད་པའི་ཁྱད་ཆོས་མི་སྲིད་པའི་ཕྱིར། ཚོར་བ་བདེ་སྡུག་ནི་ལུས་ཡིད་དང་འཕྲོད་མི་འཕྲོད་པའི་ངོ་བོར་སྐྱེས་ནས་མྱོང་བ་ཡིན་གྱི། ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ནི་མིན་ཏེ། ལུས་ཡིད་གང་རུང་མེད་ན་ཚོར་བ་ཡང་མེད་ཅིང༌། ལུས་ཡོད་ཀྱང་ཡིད་མེད་ནའང་ཚོར་བ་མི་མྱོང་བའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། རོ་དང་ས་རྡོ་སོགས་བཤིག་ཀྱང་ཚོར་བ་བདེ་སྡུག་མི་འབྱུང་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །མདོར་ན་ཚོར་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཤེས་པ་ཀུན་ཀྱང་དམིགས་པ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་མར་མེའི་འོད་བཞིན་དུ་ཐ་སྙད་ཙམ་དུ་སྐྱེའི། དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་མ་བརྟེན་པར་རང་དབང་གིས་མི་སྐྱེ་བས་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་མ་གྲུབ་བོ། །རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་གྲུབ་པ། བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ། དོན་དམ་པར་གྲུབ་པ། རང་གི་ངོ་བོས་གྲུབ་པ། རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་གྲུབ་པ། རང་དབང་གིས་གྲུབ་པ། ཡང་དག་པར་གྲུབ་པ། བལྟོས་མེད་དུ་གྲུབ་པ་རྣམས་ནི་དོན་གཅིག་མིང་གི་རྣམ་གྲངས་ཙམ་མོ། །འདིས་སེམས་ཇི་ལྟར་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཚུལ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[2-120] translation already produced for this document:
Past minds are unapprehendable in an ultimate sense because they have passed away. Future minds are also non-existent in an ultimate sense because they are presently unproduced and have not arisen. Presently arisen minds are also non-existent in an ultimate sense because they do not exist independently. "Mind" does not mean merely the main mind, but subsumes all minds and mental factors. Among mental factors, feelings are a great basis for grasping at true existence, because when intense feelings of pleasure and pain arise, the mind grasping at a self also arises with intense force. Therefore, although there are many reasonings showing that feelings are not truly established, the root is like this statement by Śāntideva: "When there is no feeler at all, there is not any feeling either." As for that, if the self who experiences feelings does not exist by its own nature, how could the feelings arising for it exist by their own nature, since characteristics are impossible without a basis of characteristics? Feelings of pleasure and pain are experienced having arisen in the nature of meeting or not meeting with body and mind, but not by their very essence, because if either body or mind is absent, feelings are also absent, and even if the body is present, if the mind is absent, feelings are not experienced: just as feelings of pleasure and pain do not arise even if corpses, earth, stones, and so forth are destroyed. In short, all consciousnesses such as feelings also arise merely conventionally like the light of a butter lamp in dependence upon an object, but because they do not arise independently without depending on such things, they are not established by their own nature. Established by its own nature, truly established, established in an ultimate sense, established by its own essence, established by its own characteristics, independently established, genuinely established, and established without dependence are equivalent in meaning and merely synonyms. By this, the manner of how the mind is to be held is taught.

[2-121] source:
གལ་ཏེ་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་མེད་ན། སེམས་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་སྦྱིན་པ་བཏང་བ་སོགས་ལས་འབྲས་བུ་མི་འབྱུང་ངམ་སྙམ་པ་ལ་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུན་སོགས་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་མེད་ཀྱང་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་སེམས་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་འབྲས་བུ་འབྱིན་ནོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་གང་གིས་སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སྟོང་ཆེན་པོའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་འདི་གསེར་དང་དངུལ་སོགས་སྔར་བཤད་པའི་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྣ་བདུན་གྱིས་གང་བར་བྱས་ཏེ་གཞན་ལ་སྦྱིན་པ་བྱིན་ན། དེ་ལས་བསོད་ནམས་མང་དུ་བསྐྱེད་དམ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། ལན་དུ་དེ་མང་ངོ་ཞེས་གསོལ་ནས། རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་དེ་དེ་བཞིན་ནོ་ཞེས་སོགས་བདེན་ཁ་བྱིན་ནོ། །
[2-121] translation already produced for this document:
If one wonders, 'If the mind stream does not exist by its own nature, won't results fail to arise from actions such as giving generosity in dependence upon the mind?', showing that although the mind stream and so forth do not exist by their own nature, conventionally results are produced in dependence upon the mind: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, 'If someone filled this three-thousandfold great thousandfold world realm with the previously explained seven precious things such as gold and silver and gave it as generosity to others, would they generate much merit from that?', in reply he stated, 'It would be much,' and then he validated it to Subhūti, saying, 'That is exactly so' and so forth.

[2-122] source:
བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་དེ་དག་ནི་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟར་ཚོགས་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བ་ཡིན་གྱི། དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་མ་བལྟོས་པར་གལ་ཏེ་རང་གི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་གྲུབ་ན་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ཞེས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་མི་གསུང་ངོ༌། །རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ཞེས་པའི་ཕུང་པོའི་དོན་ནི་ཚོགས་པའི་དོན་ཡིན་ལ། རང་དབང་གིས་གྲུབ་ན་ཚོགས་པ་ལ་མ་བལྟོས་པར་གྲུབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ་ཞེས་དགོངས་སོ། །
[2-122] translation already produced for this document:
Those heaps of merit have arisen conventionally from a collection like an illusion, but if they were established by their own very essence without depending on such things, the Tathāgata would not have spoken of a 'heap of merit'. The reason is that he intended that the meaning of 'heap' in 'heap of merit' is the meaning of a collection, and if it were established independently, it would be established without depending upon a collection.

[2-123] source:
གལ་ཏེ་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་བདེན་པར་མེད་ན་དེ་ལས་འཁྲུངས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡང་མེད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ་སྙམ་ན་དེ་མི་འགྱུར་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡོངས་སུ་གྲུབ་པ་འདི་ལ་དོན་དམ་པར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་བལྟ་བ་སྟེ་བཟུང་ཞིང་འདོད་པར་བྱ་སྙམ་འམ་ཞེས་དྲིས་བ་ན། ལན་དུ་དེ་ནི་མ་ལགས་ཏེ། དེ་ལ་དེ་ལྟར་བལྟ་བར་མི་བགྱི་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་གསོལ། རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཡང་རྒྱུ་རྐྱེན་ཚོགས་པ་ལས་གྲུབ་ཀྱི། དོན་དམ་པར་གྲུབ་པ་མ་མཆིས་པ་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་དང་འདྲ་སྟེ། ཐ་སྙད་དུ་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུར་གྲུབ་པ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དོ། །

If one wonders, 'If the heap of merit is not truly existent, then the form body of a Buddha that is born from it would also be non-existent', showing that this does not follow: when he asked, 'Do you think one should view, that is, apprehend and assert, this perfectly established form body as the Tathāgata in an ultimate sense?', in reply he stated, 'It is not so; one should not view it in that way.' The reason is that the form body is also established from a collection of causes and conditions, but is not established in an ultimate sense, which is similar to the heap of merit; conventionally it is expressed as 'established as the form body'.

heading: སེམས་སེམས་བྱུང་།
source: རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་ཆོས་དང་ཆོས་བསྟན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཐ་སྙད་ཙམ་མ་གཏོགས་གང་ཡང་དོན་དམ་པར་མ་གྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་ནི་སྔར་བཤད་ཟིན་ཅིང༌། འདིར་ལུང་གིས་བརྗོད་ན། མདོ་ལས། མིང་ནི་གང་དང་གང་གིས་ནི། །ཆོས་རྣམས་གང་དང་གང་བརྗོད་པ། །དེ་དང་དེ་ནི་ཡོད་མ་ཡིན། །དེ་ནི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཆོས་ཉིད་དོ། །ཞེས་དང༌། རིན་པོ་ཆེ་མཐའི་མདོ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། འཇམ་དཔལ་གྱིས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་འདི་ན་གང་དང་གང་གིས་གང་དང་གང་བརྗོད་པའི་ཆོས་དེ་དང་དེ་ལ། ཆོས་དེ་དང་དེ་མ་མཆིས་ལགས་སོ། །གང་མ་མཆིས་པ་དེ་ནི་སྟོང་པ་ལགས་སོ། །ཞེས་དང༌། རྣམ་འགྲེལ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། སྒྲ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ནི་བརྡར་བཏགས་སྟོན། །དེ་ནི་ཐ་སྙད་ཆེད་དུ་བྱས། །དེ་ཚེ་རང་གི་མཚན་ཉིད་མེད། །ཅེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །འདི་དག་གི་དོན་རྒྱ་ཆེ་ཡང་མཚོན་ཙམ་ནི། བུམ་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ལ་ནི་དེ་དང་དེའོ་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པའི་ཚེ་སྒྲས་ནི་དངོས་སུ་དོན་སྤྱི་བརྗོད་ཀྱི། བུམ་སོགས་རང་མཚན་རྣམས་ནི་སྒྲའི་དངོས་ཀྱི་བརྗོད་བྱར་རང་དབང་དུ་མེད་པས། དེ་དག་ནི་རང་རང་གི་མིང་གི་ཐ་སྙད་འཇུག་པའི་གཞིར་རང་དབང་གིས་མ་གྲུབ་ཅིང༌། སྒྲ་དེ་དང་དེའི་བརྗོད་བྱའི་རང་ལྡོག་རྣམས་ནི་བདེན་པར་མ་གྲུབ་ཅེས་སྟོན་པའོ། །དེར་གྲུབ་ན་ནི་གནོད་བྱེད་ཅི་ཡོད་ཞེ་ན། ཡོད་དེ། འཕགས་པ་ཐོགས་མེད་ཀྱིས་ཐེག་བསྡུས་ལས། མིང་གི་སྔ་རོལ་བློ་མེད་ཕྱིར། །མེད་ པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་མ་འདྲེས་ཕྱིར། །དེ་ཡི་བདག་ཉིད་བདག་མེད་དང༌། །བདག་འདྲེས་འགལ་བས་འགྲུབ་པར་འགྱུར། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་བསྡུས་ཏེ་བརྗོད་ན། སྒྲ་རྣམས་ནི་དོན་དེ་དང་དེ་ལ་ཐ་སྙད་ཀྱི་དབང་གིས་འཇུག་གི །དངོས་པོའི་དབང་གིས་མི་འཇུག་སྟེ། བུམ་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་གང་ལ་ཡང་དེའི་མིང་མ་བཏགས་པའི་སྔ་རོལ་དུ་བུམ་སོགས་ཀྱི་འདུ་ཤེས་མི་སྐྱེ་བ་དང༌། དོན་གཅིག་ལ་ཡང་མིང་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་བརྗོད་ཆོག་པ་དང༌། དོན་དུ་མ་ལ་ཡང་མིང་གཅིག་གིས་བརྗོད་ཆོག་པའི་ཕྱིར། དངོས་པོའི་དབང་གིས་འཇུག་ན་ནི། མིང་མ་བཏགས་པའི་སྔོན་དུ་ཡང་དེའོ་སྙམ་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་འབྱུང་བར་ཐལ་བ་དང༌། དོན་གཅིག་ཏུ་མར་ཐལ་ཞིང་དོན་དུ་མ་ཡང་གཅིག་ཏུ་འགྱུར་ལ། བུམ་སོགས་མེད་པའི་གཞིར་ཡང་དེ་དག་གི་མིང་ནས་བརྗོད་པ་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་དེ་ན་བུམ་སོགས་ཀྱང་ཡོད་པར་འགྱུར་བས་སེམས་ཅན་འགའ་ཡང་བུམ་སོགས་ཀུན་གྱིས་མི་ཕོངས་པར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་སོགས་མང་ངོ༌། །
translation: "The reason is that what is called 'Dharma' and 'teaching the Dharma' is nothing but merely conventional, and nothing is established in an ultimate sense" – the meaning of this has already been explained, and if expressed here by way of scripture, it is as stated in a sūtra: "Whatever things are expressed by whatever names, they do not exist; that is the dharmatā of things." And also from the Ratnakoṭi-sūtra: Mañjuśrī said to the Bhagavān, "Here, whatever thing is expressed by whatever expression, as for that thing, that thing is non-existent. What is non-existent is empty." And also from the Pramāṇavārttika: "Words show what is imputed by convention; that is done for the sake of convention; at that time, there are no own characteristics." Although the meaning of these is extensive, merely to illustrate it: when things such as a vase are expressed as 'this and that', the word directly expresses the meaning generality, but the specifically characterized phenomena such as a vase do not exist independently as the direct objects of expression of the word, so they are not independently established as the basis for the engagement of the conventions of their respective names, and it is taught that the self-isolates of the objects of expression of those various words are not truly established. If one wonders, 'What invalidates them being established in that way?', there is: noble Asaṅga states in the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, "Because there is no awareness prior to the name, because of non-existence, and because of being unmixed, their nature is established as selflessness and contradicted by mixing with the self." If the meaning of this is stated in brief: words engage with various meanings by the power of convention, but not by the power of the things themselves, because for any thing such as a vase, the perception of a vase does not arise prior to its name being imputed, and a single meaning can also be expressed by various names, and multiple meanings can also be expressed by a single name. If they were to engage by the power of the things themselves, it would follow that even prior to the name being imputed, the perception thinking 'it is that' would arise, and a single meaning would follow as being multiple, and multiple meanings would also become single, and because there is the expression of their names even on a basis where a vase and so forth are non-existent, a vase and so forth would also exist there, so it would follow that no sentient being would be destitute of all things such as a vase, and so forth—there are many.

"Even so, I have explained that the mind streams of sentient beings are not established as what is called a stream in an ultimate sense; therefore, because they are non-existent in an ultimate sense, conventionally they are expressed as what is called a 'mind stream'." [2-120] translation already produced for this document:
Past minds are unapprehendable in an ultimate sense because they have passed away. Future minds are also non-existent in an ultimate sense because they are presently unproduced and have not arisen. Presently arisen minds are also non-existent in an ultimate sense because they do not exist independently. "Mind" does not mean merely the main mind, but subsumes all minds and mental factors. Among mental factors, feelings are a great basis for grasping at true existence, because when intense feelings of pleasure and pain arise, the mind grasping at a self also arises with intense force. Therefore, although there are many reasonings showing that feelings are not truly established, the root is like this statement by Śāntideva: "When there is no feeler at all, there is not any feeling either." As for that, if the self who experiences feelings does not exist by its own nature, how could the feelings arising for it exist by their own nature, since characteristics are impossible without a basis of characteristics? Feelings of pleasure and pain are experienced having arisen in the nature of meeting or not meeting with body and mind, but not by their very essence, because if either body or mind is absent, feelings are also absent, and even if the body is present, if the mind is absent, feelings are not experienced: just as feelings of pleasure and pain do not arise even if corpses, earth, stones, and so forth are destroyed. In short, all consciousnesses such as feelings also arise merely conventionally like the light of a butter lamp in dependence upon an object, but because they do not arise independently without depending on such things, they are not established by their own nature. Established by its own nature, truly established, established in an ultimate sense, established by its own essence, established by its own characteristics, independently established, genuinely established, and established without dependence are equivalent in meaning and merely synonyms. By this, the manner of how the mind is to be held is taught.

[2-120] translation already produced for this document:
Past minds are unapprehendable in an ultimate sense because they have passed away. Future minds are also non-existent in an ultimate sense because they are presently unproduced and have not arisen. Presently arisen minds are also non-existent in an ultimate sense because they do not exist independently. "Mind" does not mean merely the main mind, but subsumes all minds and mental factors. Among mental factors, feelings are a great basis for grasping at true existence, because when intense feelings of pleasure and pain arise, the mind grasping at a self also arises with intense force. Therefore, although there are many reasonings showing that feelings are not truly established, the root is like this statement by Śāntideva: "When there is no feeler at all, there is not any feeling either." As for that, if the self who experiences feelings does not exist by its own nature, how could the feelings arising for it exist by their own nature, since characteristics are impossible without a basis of characteristics? Feelings of pleasure and pain are experienced having arisen in the nature of meeting or not meeting with body and mind, but not by their very essence, because if either body or mind is absent, feelings are also absent, and even if the body is present, if the mind is absent, feelings are not experienced: just as feelings of pleasure and pain do not arise even if corpses, earth, stones, and so forth are destroyed. In short, all consciousnesses such as feelings also arise merely conventionally like the light of a butter lamp in dependence upon an object, but because they do not arise independently without depending on such things, they are not established by their own nature. Established by its own nature, truly established, established in an ultimate sense, established by its own essence, established by its own characteristics, independently established, genuinely established, and established without dependence are equivalent in meaning and merely synonyms. By this, the manner of how the mind is to be held is taught.

If one wonders, 'If the mind stream does not exist by its own nature, won't results fail to arise from actions such as giving generosity in dependence upon the mind?', showing that although the mind stream and so forth do not exist by their own nature, conventionally results are produced in dependence upon the mind: when the Bhagavān asked Subhūti, 'If someone filled this three-thousandfold great thousandfold world realm with the previously explained seven precious things such as gold and silver and gave it as generosity to others, would they generate much merit from that?', in reply he stated, 'It would be much,' and then he validated it to Subhūti, saying, 'That is exactly so' and so forth.

Those heaps of merit have arisen conventionally from a collection like an illusion, but if they were established by their own very essence without depending on such things, the Tathāgata would not have spoken of a 'heap of merit'. The reason is that he intended that the meaning of 'heap' in 'heap of merit' is the meaning of a collection, and if it were established independently, it would be established without depending upon a collection.

[2-123] translation already produced for this document:
If one wonders, 'If the heap of merit is not truly existent, then the form body of a Buddha that is born from it would also be non-existent', showing that this does not follow: when he asked, 'Do you think one should view, that is, apprehend and assert, this perfectly established form body as the Tathāgata in an ultimate sense?', in reply he stated, 'It is not so; one should not view it in that way.' The reason is that the form body is also established from a collection of causes and conditions, but is not established in an ultimate sense, which is similar to the heap of merit; conventionally it is expressed as 'established as the form body'.

heading: སེམས་སེམས་བྱུང་།
translation: The Bhagavān too, considering that the answer to this had already been given, stated: 'Those sentient beings are neither established as sentient beings in an ultimate sense, nor are they non-existent as sentient beings conventionally.'
