[2-132] translation already produced for this document:
The reason is because in an ultimate sense there are no sentient beings whatsoever whom the Tathāgata has released from the bondage of grasping at true existence and caused to be liberated. If the Tathāgata were to have such an idea, that itself would become the fault of the Tathāgata grasping at a self, a sentient being, a person, and a life-principle as truly existent; but that is inappropriate, because the Tathāgata has no grasping at or clinging to a self, and so forth, because he has abandoned all clinging that grasps at a self. Although conventionally the Tathāgata releases sentient beings who are bound by grasping at true existence, in an ultimate sense there is no releasing them from that bondage, because if they were to exist in an ultimate sense, they would be immutable, so they would be unfit and unable to be released.

རབ་འབྱོར་བདག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པའི་བདག་འཛིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་དེ་སྤངས་ཤིང་རང་ལ་དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་བདེན་ཞེན་མེད་པར་གསུངས་ཏེ། དེ་ལྟ་ནའང་བདེན་མེད་མི་ཤེས་པའི་བྱིས་པ་སོ་སོའི་སྐྱེ་བོ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཀུན་ལ་བདག་ཏུ་ཞེན་ཅིང་བཟུང་ངོ༌། །འདིར་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་མི་ཤེས་པའི་སོ་སྐྱེ་ལ་བྱིས་པའི་མིང་གིས་བཏགས་པ་སྟེ།།འཕགས་པས་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གཟིགས་པས་བྱིས་པ་ཞེས་མི་བྱ་བར་མཁས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་ལ། དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་སོ་སྐྱེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་དེ་ལྟར་མི་ཤེས་པའི་ཕྱིར་བྱིས་པ་དང་འདྲ་བས་དེའི་མིང་གིས་བརྗོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་འཛིན་པ་མེད་ཅེས་པའི་དོན་ནི་བདག་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཟུང་བའི་དོན་ལྟར་མེད་ཅེས་བཤད་ཀྱང་རུང་བར་སེམས། བྱིས་པ་ཞེས་དམིགས་བསལ་མཛད་པ་ནི། བདག་མེད་ཀྱི་དོན་ལ་མཁས་ཤིང་ཤེས་པའི་སོ་སྐྱེ་རྣམས་ལ་བྱིས་པ་ཞེས་མི་བྱ་བའི་ཆེད་དོ། །
[2-133] translation already produced for this document:
'Subhūti, as for what is called grasping at a self', the Tathāgata stated that he has abandoned it and that he himself possesses no such clinging to true existence; nevertheless, childish ordinary beings who do not know the lack of true existence cling to and grasp at all dharmas as a self. Here, ordinary beings who do not know the meaning of reality are designated by the name 'childish'; since noble ones directly see the reality of dharmas, they are not called 'childish' but are called 'wise', and because such ordinary beings do not know it in that way, they are like children, so they are referred to by that name. I think it is also suitable to explain the meaning of 'that grasping is non-existent' as meaning that it does not exist in the manner of the object grasped by grasping at a self. Making the specific distinction of 'childish' is for the sake of not calling 'childish' those ordinary beings who are wise and know the meaning of selflessness.

རབ་འབྱོར་བྱིས་པ་སོ་སོའི་སྐྱེ་བོ་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དེ་དག་དོན་དམ་པར་སྐྱེ་བོ་ཉིད་དུ་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་པར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་ཏེ། །ཐ་སྙད་དུ་མིང་གིས་དེ་སྐད་ཅེས་བརྗོད་དོ། །སོ་སོའི་སྐྱེ་བོའི་སྒྲ་དོན་ནི། ལས་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་འགྲོ་བ་སོ་སོ་ཐ་དད་པ་རྣམས་སུ་སྐྱེ་བས་ན་དེ་ལྟར་དུ་བཤད་དོ། །ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་བལྟ་ཞིང་འདོད་པར་བྱ་སྙམ་མམ་ཞེས་དྲིས། འམ་དང་མམ་གཉིས་ནི་འགྱུར་ཁྱད་ཙམ་ཡིན་ཅིང་དོན་ལ་ཁྱད་མེད་དོ། །

'Subhūti, regarding what are called childish ordinary beings, the Tathāgata has taught that they are not established as ordinary beings in an ultimate sense; conventionally they are expressed like that by name.' The meaning of the term 'ordinary beings' is that they are explained as such because by the power of karma they are born in various different migrations. Furthermore, he asked, 'Subhūti, do you think that one should view and consider him as the Tathāgata merely by his possessing the perfect major and minor marks?' The two 'am and mam are merely a difference in translation, but there is no difference in meaning.

The Bhagavān gave his approval, saying 'It is exactly so,' and so forth; one should not view a body merely possessing the major and minor marks as the Tathāgata. He stated, 'Subhūti, if one were to view him in that way, since a wheel-turning king also has the major and minor marks, it would absurdly follow that he himself must be considered the Tathāgata, but since that is not accepted, one should not view and consider him as the Tathāgata merely by his possessing the perfect marks.'

Then Subhūti stated, 'According to how I understand the meaning of what the Bhagavān has said, I do not view him in that way.' Although a wheel-turning king has the thirty-two marks, they are not as clear and are not complete, whereas a Buddha's major and minor marks are clear and complete; as it is stated, 'Although it is accepted that all wheel-turning kings have these,' and, 'The marks of the Sage are superior because they are situated in their proper places, and are clear and complete.'

translation: The Bhagavān spoke in verse, stating, 'Those who see me as form,' and so forth; as for the meaning of this, the Lord himself quoted that scripture in his commentary on the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā and explained the meaning as follows: "These words indicate that because grasping at conceptualized dharmas such as form and sound as truly existent is engaging wrongly with the reality of the Buddha and abandoning it, by that one does not see the reality of the Buddha, and therefore the reality of the Buddha is to be viewed as dharmatā and the dharmakāya. That dharmakāya is not to be known by way of grasping as before, because it is impossible to know it in that way"—having taught that, as he stated, "Because the eye of the mind is impaired by conceptual proliferation, it acts as the proof for not seeing the reality of the Tathāgata." As for the meaning of the words: "Whatever sentient beings, seeing the major and minor marks and so forth of me the Tathāgata, view and see, that is, grasp at, me as form through clinging to true existence, and whatever sentient beings know me as truly existent, that is, cling to and grasp at me, through hearing my name and so forth and expressing me as sound—in short, those who are bound by grasping at true existence that clings to the Tathāgata as truly existent as a body of name and form, have engaged wrongly in viewing the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata; those beings do not see my dharmakāya, emptiness, as the Tathāgata." Work: རྡོར་གཅོད་ཀྱི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཐར་པར་བགྲོད་པའི་ལམ་བཟང་ཟབ་དོན་གསལ་བའི་ཉི་མ། (The Sun that Illuminates the Profound Meaning of the Excellent Path for Travelling to Freedom), author: ཅོ་ནེ་གྲགས་པ་བཤད་སྒྲུབ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[2-132] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་དོན་དམ་པར་སེམས་ཅན་གང་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པ་ལས་བཀྲོལ་ཏེ་ཐར་བར་བྱས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་གང་ཡང་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གལ་ཏེ་དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་བློ་ཞིག་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་ཡོད་ན་ནི། དེ་ཉིད་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་བདག་དང་སེམས་ཅན་དང་གང་ཟག་དང་སྲོག་ཏུ་བདེན་པར་འཛིན་པའི་སྐྱོན་དུ་འགྱུར་ན། དེ་ནི་མི་རིགས་ཏེ། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་བདག་ཏུ་འཛིན་ཅིང་ཞེན་པ་སོགས་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། དེས་བདག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པའི་མངོན་ཞེན་ཐམས་ཅད་སྤངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་བཀྲོལ་བ་ཡོད་ཀྱང༌། དོན་དམ་པར་བཅིངས་པ་དེ་ལས་བཀྲོལ་བ་མེད་དེ། དོན་དམ་པར་ཡོད་ན་བསྒྱུར་དུ་མེད་པས་བཀྲོལ་དུ་ཡང་མི་རུང་ཞིང་མི་ནུས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[2-132] translation already produced for this document:
The reason is because in an ultimate sense there are no sentient beings whatsoever whom the Tathāgata has released from the bondage of grasping at true existence and caused to be liberated. If the Tathāgata were to have such an idea, that itself would become the fault of the Tathāgata grasping at a self, a sentient being, a person, and a life-principle as truly existent; but that is inappropriate, because the Tathāgata has no grasping at or clinging to a self, and so forth, because he has abandoned all clinging that grasps at a self. Although conventionally the Tathāgata releases sentient beings who are bound by grasping at true existence, in an ultimate sense there is no releasing them from that bondage, because if they were to exist in an ultimate sense, they would be immutable, so they would be unfit and unable to be released.

[2-133] source:
རབ་འབྱོར་བདག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པའི་བདག་འཛིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་དེ་སྤངས་ཤིང་རང་ལ་དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་བདེན་ཞེན་མེད་པར་གསུངས་ཏེ། དེ་ལྟ་ནའང་བདེན་མེད་མི་ཤེས་པའི་བྱིས་པ་སོ་སོའི་སྐྱེ་བོ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཀུན་ལ་བདག་ཏུ་ཞེན་ཅིང་བཟུང་ངོ༌། །འདིར་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་མི་ཤེས་པའི་སོ་སྐྱེ་ལ་བྱིས་པའི་མིང་གིས་བཏགས་པ་སྟེ།།འཕགས་པས་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གཟིགས་པས་བྱིས་པ་ཞེས་མི་བྱ་བར་མཁས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་ལ། དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་སོ་སྐྱེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་དེ་ལྟར་མི་ཤེས་པའི་ཕྱིར་བྱིས་པ་དང་འདྲ་བས་དེའི་མིང་གིས་བརྗོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་འཛིན་པ་མེད་ཅེས་པའི་དོན་ནི་བདག་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཟུང་བའི་དོན་ལྟར་མེད་ཅེས་བཤད་ཀྱང་རུང་བར་སེམས། བྱིས་པ་ཞེས་དམིགས་བསལ་མཛད་པ་ནི། བདག་མེད་ཀྱི་དོན་ལ་མཁས་ཤིང་ཤེས་པའི་སོ་སྐྱེ་རྣམས་ལ་བྱིས་པ་ཞེས་མི་བྱ་བའི་ཆེད་དོ། །
[2-133] translation already produced for this document:
'Subhūti, as for what is called grasping at a self', the Tathāgata stated that he has abandoned it and that he himself possesses no such clinging to true existence; nevertheless, childish ordinary beings who do not know the lack of true existence cling to and grasp at all dharmas as a self. Here, ordinary beings who do not know the meaning of reality are designated by the name 'childish'; since noble ones directly see the reality of dharmas, they are not called 'childish' but are called 'wise', and because such ordinary beings do not know it in that way, they are like children, so they are referred to by that name. I think it is also suitable to explain the meaning of 'that grasping is non-existent' as meaning that it does not exist in the manner of the object grasped by grasping at a self. Making the specific distinction of 'childish' is for the sake of not calling 'childish' those ordinary beings who are wise and know the meaning of selflessness.

[2-134] source:
རབ་འབྱོར་བྱིས་པ་སོ་སོའི་སྐྱེ་བོ་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དེ་དག་དོན་དམ་པར་སྐྱེ་བོ་ཉིད་དུ་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་པར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་ཏེ། །ཐ་སྙད་དུ་མིང་གིས་དེ་སྐད་ཅེས་བརྗོད་དོ། །སོ་སོའི་སྐྱེ་བོའི་སྒྲ་དོན་ནི། ལས་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་འགྲོ་བ་སོ་སོ་ཐ་དད་པ་རྣམས་སུ་སྐྱེ་བས་ན་དེ་ལྟར་དུ་བཤད་དོ། །ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་བལྟ་ཞིང་འདོད་པར་བྱ་སྙམ་མམ་ཞེས་དྲིས། འམ་དང་མམ་གཉིས་ནི་འགྱུར་ཁྱད་ཙམ་ཡིན་ཅིང་དོན་ལ་ཁྱད་མེད་དོ། །
[2-134] translation already produced for this document:
'Subhūti, regarding what are called childish ordinary beings, the Tathāgata has taught that they are not established as ordinary beings in an ultimate sense; conventionally they are expressed like that by name.' The meaning of the term 'ordinary beings' is that they are explained as such because by the power of karma they are born in various different migrations. Furthermore, he asked, 'Subhūti, do you think that one should view and consider him as the Tathāgata merely by his possessing the perfect major and minor marks?' The two 'am and mam are merely a difference in translation, but there is no difference in meaning.

[2-135] source:
ལན་དུ་དེ་ནི་མ་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཞུས། གོང་དུ་ཡང་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞིག་བྱུང་ཀྱང་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་གཙོ་བོར་སྟོན་པའི་ཆེད་དུ་མིན་ལ། །འདིར་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་སྟོན་པའི་ཆེད་དུ་སླར་དྲིས་སོ། །
[2-135] translation already produced for this document:
In reply, he stated, 'It is not so,' and so forth. Although something similar to this occurred earlier as well, it was not for the sake of primarily teaching the dharmakāya, whereas here it is asked again for the sake of teaching the dharmakāya.

[2-136] source:
བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་དེ་དེ་བཞིན་ནོ་ཞེས་སོགས་གནང་སྟེ། མཚན་དཔེ་ཡོད་ཙམ་གྱི་སྐུ་ལ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་བལྟ་བར་མི་བྱའོ། །རབ་འབྱོར་གལ་ཏེ་དེ་ལྟར་བལྟ་བར་བྱེད་ན་ནི་འཁོར་ལོ་སྒྱུར་བའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་ལའང་མཚན་དཔེ་ཡོད་པས་དེ་ཉིད་།དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་འདོད་དགོས་པར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་ན། དེ་མི་འདོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ན་མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་མངའ་བ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་བལྟ་ཞིང་འདོད་པར་མི་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་དང༌། །
[2-136] translation already produced for this document:
The Bhagavān gave his approval, saying 'It is exactly so,' and so forth; one should not view a body merely possessing the major and minor marks as the Tathāgata. He stated, 'Subhūti, if one were to view him in that way, since a wheel-turning king also has the major and minor marks, it would absurdly follow that he himself must be considered the Tathāgata, but since that is not accepted, one should not view and consider him as the Tathāgata merely by his possessing the perfect marks.'

[2-137] source:
དེ་ནས་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་བདག་གིས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ཤེས་པ་ལྟར་ན་དེ་ལྟར་མི་བལྟའོ་ཞེས་ཞུས་སོ། །འཁོར་ལོས་སྒྱུར་བའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་ལ་མཚན་སོ་གཉིས་ཡོད་ཀྱང་དེ་ཙམ་མི་གསལ་ཞིང་མ་རྫོགས་ལ།སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཚན་དཔེ་རྣམས་ནི་གསལ་ཞིང་རྫོགས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། །ཇི་སྐད་དུ། །འཁོར་ལོས་སྒྱུར་བ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ། །འདི་དག་ཡོད་པར་འདོད་མོད་ཀྱི། །ཞེས་དང༌། ཐུབ་མཚན་ཡུལ་ན་གནས་པ་དང༌། །གསལ་ལ་རྫོགས་པས་འཕགས་པ་ཡིན། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །
[2-137] translation already produced for this document:
Then Subhūti stated, 'According to how I understand the meaning of what the Bhagavān has said, I do not view him in that way.' Although a wheel-turning king has the thirty-two marks, they are not as clear and are not complete, whereas a Buddha's major and minor marks are clear and complete; as it is stated, 'Although it is accepted that all wheel-turning kings have these,' and, 'The marks of the Sage are superior because they are situated in their proper places, and are clear and complete.'

heading: ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: the dharmakāya of the guiding Buddhas, the dharmatā which is ultimate truth, is not to be known by a mind bound by grasping at true existence, because that dharmakāya cannot be completely known by such a mind, because knowing the emptiness which is the dharmakāya of the Buddha requires realizing emptiness. Illustrated by this, it is similar that if there is clinging to true existence regarding any dharma, one does not see the dharmatā of that dharma. Whenever any conventional dharma such as form is directly realized, it must be realized in a manner where it appears together with conceptual proliferation, whereas whenever the ultimate dharma, which is the dharmatā of those, is directly realized, it must be realized in a manner where conceptual proliferation is eliminated; this distinction between the respective ways of seeing the two truths is a point that is difficult to realize. Not only that, but even if whatever dharma it is, is not directly realized as lacking true existence, although conceptual proliferation appears to the appearing aspect of the mind that realizes it by way of a meaning-generality, conceptual proliferation must be eliminated in its ascertained aspect. As for summarizing the meaning of that:
style_instruction: Translate this passage of a Tibetan Buddhist commentary on the Diamond Sūtra (Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā) into clear, accurate English prose. Translate the whole passage completely and in the same order: do not summarise, shorten or omit anything, and keep the same number of lines as the source. Where the commentary quotes or glosses words of the sūtra, keep those quoted words recognisable in the translation. Keep proper names and technical terms in standard Sanskrit transliteration (Subhūti, Tathāgata, Dīpaṃkara, prajñāpāramitā) rather than translating them. Do not add commentary, notes, or explanation of your own. Begin directly with the translation: do not write any introductory sentence such as "Here is the translation". Render each source line as exactly one line of continuous English prose, even where the source contains verse stanzas or lists; do not break it into several lines.

Work: རྡོར་གཅོད་ཀྱི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཐར་པར་བགྲོད་པའི་ལམ་བཟང་ཟབ་དོན་གསལ་བའི་ཉི་མ། (The Sun that Illuminates the Profound Meaning of the Excellent Path for Travelling to Freedom), author: ཅོ་ནེ་གྲགས་པ་བཤད་སྒྲུབ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

[2-132] source:
རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་དོན་དམ་པར་སེམས་ཅན་གང་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པ་ལས་བཀྲོལ་ཏེ་ཐར་བར་བྱས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་དེ་དག་གང་ཡང་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གལ་ཏེ་དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་བློ་ཞིག་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་ཡོད་ན་ནི། དེ་ཉིད་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་བདག་དང་སེམས་ཅན་དང་གང་ཟག་དང་སྲོག་ཏུ་བདེན་པར་འཛིན་པའི་སྐྱོན་དུ་འགྱུར་ན། དེ་ནི་མི་རིགས་ཏེ། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་བདག་ཏུ་འཛིན་ཅིང་ཞེན་པ་སོགས་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། དེས་བདག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པའི་མངོན་ཞེན་ཐམས་ཅད་སྤངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་བཀྲོལ་བ་ཡོད་ཀྱང༌། དོན་དམ་པར་བཅིངས་པ་དེ་ལས་བཀྲོལ་བ་མེད་དེ། དོན་དམ་པར་ཡོད་ན་བསྒྱུར་དུ་མེད་པས་བཀྲོལ་དུ་ཡང་མི་རུང་ཞིང་མི་ནུས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །
[2-132] translation already produced for this document:
The reason is because in an ultimate sense there are no sentient beings whatsoever whom the Tathāgata has released from the bondage of grasping at true existence and caused to be liberated. If the Tathāgata were to have such an idea, that itself would become the fault of the Tathāgata grasping at a self, a sentient being, a person, and a life-principle as truly existent; but that is inappropriate, because the Tathāgata has no grasping at or clinging to a self, and so forth, because he has abandoned all clinging that grasps at a self. Although conventionally the Tathāgata releases sentient beings who are bound by grasping at true existence, in an ultimate sense there is no releasing them from that bondage, because if they were to exist in an ultimate sense, they would be immutable, so they would be unfit and unable to be released.

[2-133] source:
རབ་འབྱོར་བདག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པའི་བདག་འཛིན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་དེ་སྤངས་ཤིང་རང་ལ་དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་བདེན་ཞེན་མེད་པར་གསུངས་ཏེ། དེ་ལྟ་ནའང་བདེན་མེད་མི་ཤེས་པའི་བྱིས་པ་སོ་སོའི་སྐྱེ་བོ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཀུན་ལ་བདག་ཏུ་ཞེན་ཅིང་བཟུང་ངོ༌། །འདིར་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་མི་ཤེས་པའི་སོ་སྐྱེ་ལ་བྱིས་པའི་མིང་གིས་བཏགས་པ་སྟེ།།འཕགས་པས་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གཟིགས་པས་བྱིས་པ་ཞེས་མི་བྱ་བར་མཁས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་ལ། དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་སོ་སྐྱེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་དེ་ལྟར་མི་ཤེས་པའི་ཕྱིར་བྱིས་པ་དང་འདྲ་བས་དེའི་མིང་གིས་བརྗོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེ་འཛིན་པ་མེད་ཅེས་པའི་དོན་ནི་བདག་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཟུང་བའི་དོན་ལྟར་མེད་ཅེས་བཤད་ཀྱང་རུང་བར་སེམས། བྱིས་པ་ཞེས་དམིགས་བསལ་མཛད་པ་ནི། བདག་མེད་ཀྱི་དོན་ལ་མཁས་ཤིང་ཤེས་པའི་སོ་སྐྱེ་རྣམས་ལ་བྱིས་པ་ཞེས་མི་བྱ་བའི་ཆེད་དོ། །
[2-133] translation already produced for this document:
'Subhūti, as for what is called grasping at a self', the Tathāgata stated that he has abandoned it and that he himself possesses no such clinging to true existence; nevertheless, childish ordinary beings who do not know the lack of true existence cling to and grasp at all dharmas as a self. Here, ordinary beings who do not know the meaning of reality are designated by the name 'childish'; since noble ones directly see the reality of dharmas, they are not called 'childish' but are called 'wise', and because such ordinary beings do not know it in that way, they are like children, so they are referred to by that name. I think it is also suitable to explain the meaning of 'that grasping is non-existent' as meaning that it does not exist in the manner of the object grasped by grasping at a self. Making the specific distinction of 'childish' is for the sake of not calling 'childish' those ordinary beings who are wise and know the meaning of selflessness.

[2-134] source:
རབ་འབྱོར་བྱིས་པ་སོ་སོའི་སྐྱེ་བོ་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་དེ་དག་དོན་དམ་པར་སྐྱེ་བོ་ཉིད་དུ་གྲུབ་པ་མེད་པར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་ཏེ། །ཐ་སྙད་དུ་མིང་གིས་དེ་སྐད་ཅེས་བརྗོད་དོ། །སོ་སོའི་སྐྱེ་བོའི་སྒྲ་དོན་ནི། ལས་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་འགྲོ་བ་སོ་སོ་ཐ་དད་པ་རྣམས་སུ་སྐྱེ་བས་ན་དེ་ལྟར་དུ་བཤད་དོ། །ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་བལྟ་ཞིང་འདོད་པར་བྱ་སྙམ་མམ་ཞེས་དྲིས། འམ་དང་མམ་གཉིས་ནི་འགྱུར་ཁྱད་ཙམ་ཡིན་ཅིང་དོན་ལ་ཁྱད་མེད་དོ། །
[2-134] translation already produced for this document:
'Subhūti, regarding what are called childish ordinary beings, the Tathāgata has taught that they are not established as ordinary beings in an ultimate sense; conventionally they are expressed like that by name.' The meaning of the term 'ordinary beings' is that they are explained as such because by the power of karma they are born in various different migrations. Furthermore, he asked, 'Subhūti, do you think that one should view and consider him as the Tathāgata merely by his possessing the perfect major and minor marks?' The two 'am and mam are merely a difference in translation, but there is no difference in meaning.

[2-135] source:
ལན་དུ་དེ་ནི་མ་ལགས་སོ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཞུས། གོང་དུ་ཡང་འདི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞིག་བྱུང་ཀྱང་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་གཙོ་བོར་སྟོན་པའི་ཆེད་དུ་མིན་ལ། །འདིར་ནི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་སྟོན་པའི་ཆེད་དུ་སླར་དྲིས་སོ། །
[2-135] translation already produced for this document:
In reply, he stated, 'It is not so,' and so forth. Although something similar to this occurred earlier as well, it was not for the sake of primarily teaching the dharmakāya, whereas here it is asked again for the sake of teaching the dharmakāya.

[2-136] source:
བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་དེ་དེ་བཞིན་ནོ་ཞེས་སོགས་གནང་སྟེ། མཚན་དཔེ་ཡོད་ཙམ་གྱི་སྐུ་ལ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་བལྟ་བར་མི་བྱའོ། །རབ་འབྱོར་གལ་ཏེ་དེ་ལྟར་བལྟ་བར་བྱེད་ན་ནི་འཁོར་ལོ་སྒྱུར་བའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་ལའང་མཚན་དཔེ་ཡོད་པས་དེ་ཉིད་།དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་འདོད་དགོས་པར་ཐལ་བར་འགྱུར་ན། དེ་མི་འདོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ན་མཚན་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་མངའ་བ་ཙམ་གྱིས་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པར་བལྟ་ཞིང་འདོད་པར་མི་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་དང༌། །
[2-136] translation already produced for this document:
The Bhagavān gave his approval, saying 'It is exactly so,' and so forth; one should not view a body merely possessing the major and minor marks as the Tathāgata. He stated, 'Subhūti, if one were to view him in that way, since a wheel-turning king also has the major and minor marks, it would absurdly follow that he himself must be considered the Tathāgata, but since that is not accepted, one should not view and consider him as the Tathāgata merely by his possessing the perfect marks.'

[2-137] source:
དེ་ནས་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་བདག་གིས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ཤེས་པ་ལྟར་ན་དེ་ལྟར་མི་བལྟའོ་ཞེས་ཞུས་སོ། །འཁོར་ལོས་སྒྱུར་བའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་ལ་མཚན་སོ་གཉིས་ཡོད་ཀྱང་དེ་ཙམ་མི་གསལ་ཞིང་མ་རྫོགས་ལ།སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཚན་དཔེ་རྣམས་ནི་གསལ་ཞིང་རྫོགས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། །ཇི་སྐད་དུ། །འཁོར་ལོས་སྒྱུར་བ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ། །འདི་དག་ཡོད་པར་འདོད་མོད་ཀྱི། །ཞེས་དང༌། ཐུབ་མཚན་ཡུལ་ན་གནས་པ་དང༌། །གསལ་ལ་རྫོགས་པས་འཕགས་པ་ཡིན། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །
[2-137] translation already produced for this document:
Then Subhūti stated, 'According to how I understand the meaning of what the Bhagavān has said, I do not view him in that way.' Although a wheel-turning king has the thirty-two marks, they are not as clear and are not complete, whereas a Buddha's major and minor marks are clear and complete; as it is stated, 'Although it is accepted that all wheel-turning kings have these,' and, 'The marks of the Sage are superior because they are situated in their proper places, and are clear and complete.'

heading: ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: In that way, from the perspective of the dharmakāya, the Tathāgata has not awakened to unsurpassed enlightenment merely by possessing the perfect major and minor marks. As for refuting the view of nihilism regarding that:

The reason is because in an ultimate sense there are no sentient beings whatsoever whom the Tathāgata has released from the bondage of grasping at true existence and caused to be liberated. If the Tathāgata were to have such an idea, that itself would become the fault of the Tathāgata grasping at a self, a sentient being, a person, and a life-principle as truly existent; but that is inappropriate, because the Tathāgata has no grasping at or clinging to a self, and so forth, because he has abandoned all clinging that grasps at a self. Although conventionally the Tathāgata releases sentient beings who are bound by grasping at true existence, in an ultimate sense there is no releasing them from that bondage, because if they were to exist in an ultimate sense, they would be immutable, so they would be unfit and unable to be released.

'Subhūti, as for what is called grasping at a self', the Tathāgata stated that he has abandoned it and that he himself possesses no such clinging to true existence; nevertheless, childish ordinary beings who do not know the lack of true existence cling to and grasp at all dharmas as a self. Here, ordinary beings who do not know the meaning of reality are designated by the name 'childish'; since noble ones directly see the reality of dharmas, they are not called 'childish' but are called 'wise', and because such ordinary beings do not know it in that way, they are like children, so they are referred to by that name. I think it is also suitable to explain the meaning of 'that grasping is non-existent' as meaning that it does not exist in the manner of the object grasped by grasping at a self. Making the specific distinction of 'childish' is for the sake of not calling 'childish' those ordinary beings who are wise and know the meaning of selflessness.

The reason is because in an ultimate sense there are no sentient beings whatsoever whom the Tathāgata has released from the bondage of grasping at true existence and caused to be liberated. If the Tathāgata were to have such an idea, that itself would become the fault of the Tathāgata grasping at a self, a sentient being, a person, and a life-principle as truly existent; but that is inappropriate, because the Tathāgata has no grasping at or clinging to a self, and so forth, because he has abandoned all clinging that grasps at a self. Although conventionally the Tathāgata releases sentient beings who are bound by grasping at true existence, in an ultimate sense there is no releasing them from that bondage, because if they were to exist in an ultimate sense, they would be immutable, so they would be unfit and unable to be released.

'Subhūti, as for what is called grasping at a self', the Tathāgata stated that he has abandoned it and that he himself possesses no such clinging to true existence; nevertheless, childish ordinary beings who do not know the lack of true existence cling to and grasp at all dharmas as a self. Here, ordinary beings who do not know the meaning of reality are designated by the name 'childish'; since noble ones directly see the reality of dharmas, they are not called 'childish' but are called 'wise', and because such ordinary beings do not know it in that way, they are like children, so they are referred to by that name. I think it is also suitable to explain the meaning of 'that grasping is non-existent' as meaning that it does not exist in the manner of the object grasped by grasping at a self. Making the specific distinction of 'childish' is for the sake of not calling 'childish' those ordinary beings who are wise and know the meaning of selflessness.

heading: ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Those bodhisattvas have not destroyed or designated as annihilated any dharma whatsoever, because when it is realized in that way, that dharma is realized as lacking true existence, but that dharma is not realized as non-existent. Although those conventional dharmas do not exist for the ascertained aspect of the mind that realizes it in that way, that mind does not realize them as non-existent, because although they do not exist for the aspect of that mind, they generally exist; for example, although a vase and so forth that appears as empty of true existence does not exist for the aspect of a mind bound by grasping at true existence, it generally exists.

The reason is because in an ultimate sense there are no sentient beings whatsoever whom the Tathāgata has released from the bondage of grasping at true existence and caused to be liberated. If the Tathāgata were to have such an idea, that itself would become the fault of the Tathāgata grasping at a self, a sentient being, a person, and a life-principle as truly existent; but that is inappropriate, because the Tathāgata has no grasping at or clinging to a self, and so forth, because he has abandoned all clinging that grasps at a self. Although conventionally the Tathāgata releases sentient beings who are bound by grasping at true existence, in an ultimate sense there is no releasing them from that bondage, because if they were to exist in an ultimate sense, they would be immutable, so they would be unfit and unable to be released.

'Subhūti, as for what is called grasping at a self', the Tathāgata stated that he has abandoned it and that he himself possesses no such clinging to true existence; nevertheless, childish ordinary beings who do not know the lack of true existence cling to and grasp at all dharmas as a self. Here, ordinary beings who do not know the meaning of reality are designated by the name 'childish'; since noble ones directly see the reality of dharmas, they are not called 'childish' but are called 'wise', and because such ordinary beings do not know it in that way, they are like children, so they are referred to by that name. I think it is also suitable to explain the meaning of 'that grasping is non-existent' as meaning that it does not exist in the manner of the object grasped by grasping at a self. Making the specific distinction of 'childish' is for the sake of not calling 'childish' those ordinary beings who are wise and know the meaning of selflessness.

translation: Furthermore, than the merit of whatever person filling world systems equal in number to the sand of the river Gaṅgā with the seven kinds of precious jewels and giving them as a gift, if whatever bodhisattva directly realizes the meaning of non-self relying on this dharma-discourse, the text of the prajñāpāramitā, and obtains great forbearance towards the ultimate non-arising, that is, the dharma of non-arising, that very person will generate a much more incalculable and immeasurable heap of merit from that basis of obtaining forbearance; the meaning of 'obtaining forbearance towards the dharma of non-arising' has already been explained earlier.

The Bhagavān spoke in verse, stating, 'Those who see me as form,' and so forth; as for the meaning of this, the Lord himself quoted that scripture in his commentary on the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā and explained the meaning as follows: "These words indicate that because grasping at conceptualized dharmas such as form and sound as truly existent is engaging wrongly with the reality of the Buddha and abandoning it, by that one does not see the reality of the Buddha, and therefore the reality of the Buddha is to be viewed as dharmatā and the dharmakāya. That dharmakāya is not to be known by way of grasping as before, because it is impossible to know it in that way"—having taught that, as he stated, "Because the eye of the mind is impaired by conceptual proliferation, it acts as the proof for not seeing the reality of the Tathāgata." As for the meaning of the words: "Whatever sentient beings, seeing the major and minor marks and so forth of me the Tathāgata, view and see, that is, grasp at, me as form through clinging to true existence, and whatever sentient beings know me as truly existent, that is, cling to and grasp at me, through hearing my name and so forth and expressing me as sound—in short, those who are bound by grasping at true existence that clings to the Tathāgata as truly existent as a body of name and form, have engaged wrongly in viewing the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata; those beings do not see my dharmakāya, emptiness, as the Tathāgata." the dharmakāya of the guiding Buddhas, the dharmatā which is ultimate truth, is not to be known by a mind bound by grasping at true existence, because that dharmakāya cannot be completely known by such a mind, because knowing the emptiness which is the dharmakāya of the Buddha requires realizing emptiness. Illustrated by this, it is similar that if there is clinging to true existence regarding any dharma, one does not see the dharmatā of that dharma. Whenever any conventional dharma such as form is directly realized, it must be realized in a manner where it appears together with conceptual proliferation, whereas whenever the ultimate dharma, which is the dharmatā of those, is directly realized, it must be realized in a manner where conceptual proliferation is eliminated; this distinction between the respective ways of seeing the two truths is a point that is difficult to realize. Not only that, but even if whatever dharma it is, is not directly realized as lacking true existence, although conceptual proliferation appears to the appearing aspect of the mind that realizes it by way of a meaning-generality, conceptual proliferation must be eliminated in its ascertained aspect. Those bodhisattvas have not destroyed or designated as annihilated any dharma whatsoever, because when it is realized in that way, that dharma is realized as lacking true existence, but that dharma is not realized as non-existent. Work: རྡོར་གཅོད་ཀྱི་འགྲེལ་པ་ཐར་པར་བགྲོད་པའི་ལམ་བཟང་ཟབ་དོན་གསལ་བའི་ཉི་མ། (The Sun that Illuminates the Profound Meaning of the Excellent Path for Travelling to Freedom), author: ཅོ་ནེ་གྲགས་པ་བཤད་སྒྲུབ།. A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[2-138] source:
དེས་ནི་གཟུགས་སྐུ་བསྟན་ནས་ཆོས་སྐུ་སྟོན་པ་ནི། །
[2-138] translation already produced for this document:
Through that, having indicated the form body, as for teaching the dharmakāya:

[2-139] source:
བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་དེ་བཀའ་སྩལ་བ་ནི། གང་དག་ང་ལ་གཟུགས་སུ་མཐོང༌། །ཞེས་སོགས་གསུངས་ཏེ། །འདིའི་དོན་དབུ་མ་རྩ་བ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་འགྲེལ་བར་རྗེ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ལུང་དེ་དྲངས་ནས། དོན་འདི་ལྟར་བཤད་དེ། ཚིག་དེ་དག་གིས་ནི་གཟུགས་སྒྲ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་སྤྲོས་པའི་ཆོས་སུ་བདེན་པར་འཛིན་པས་ནི། །སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་ལ་ལོག་པར་ཞུགས་ཤིང་སྤོང་བ་ཡིན་པས། དེས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་མི་མཐོང་བས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་ནི་ཆོས་ཉིད་དུ་བལྟ་བར་བྱ་བ་དང་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུའོ། །ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་དེ་ནི་སྔར་ལྟར་བཟུང་བའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་བ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཚུལ་དེས་ཤེས་པར་མི་ནུས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ་ཞེས་བསྟན་ཏེ་སྤྲོས་པས་བློ་མིག་ཉམས་པས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་དེ་ཉིད་མི་མཐོང་བའི་ཤེས་བྱེད་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །ཚིག་དོན་ནི། །སེམས་ཅན་གང་དག་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ངའི་མཚན་དཔེ་སོགས་མཐོང་ན་ང་ལ་གཟུགས་སུ་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་ལྟ་ཞིང་མཐོང་བ་སྟེ་འཛིན་པ་དང༌། སེམས་ཅན་གང་དག་ང་ལ་ངའི་མིང་སོགས་ཐོས་ཤིང་སྒྲར་བརྗོད་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བདེན་པར་ཤེས་པ་སྟེ་ཞེན་ནས་འཛིན་པ་སོགས་མདོར་ན། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ལ་མིང་དང་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་སྐུར་བདེན་པར་ཞེན་པའི་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པ་དེ་དག་ནི། །དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ལྟ་བ་ལ་ལོག་པར་ཞུགས་པ་སྟེ། །སྐྱེ་བོ་དེ་དག་གིས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ངའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་མི་མཐོང་ངོ༌། །མི་མཐོང་བའི་རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྐུ་དེ་ནི་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྐུར་ལྟ་དགོས་ཤིང༌། །
[2-139] translation already produced for this document:
The Bhagavān spoke in verse, stating, 'Those who see me as form,' and so forth; as for the meaning of this, the Lord himself quoted that scripture in his commentary on the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā and explained the meaning as follows: "These words indicate that because grasping at conceptualized dharmas such as form and sound as truly existent is engaging wrongly with the reality of the Buddha and abandoning it, by that one does not see the reality of the Buddha, and therefore the reality of the Buddha is to be viewed as dharmatā and the dharmakāya. That dharmakāya is not to be known by way of grasping as before, because it is impossible to know it in that way"—having taught that, as he stated, "Because the eye of the mind is impaired by conceptual proliferation, it acts as the proof for not seeing the reality of the Tathāgata." As for the meaning of the words: "Whatever sentient beings, seeing the major and minor marks and so forth of me the Tathāgata, view and see, that is, grasp at, me as form through clinging to true existence, and whatever sentient beings know me as truly existent, that is, cling to and grasp at me, through hearing my name and so forth and expressing me as sound—in short, those who are bound by grasping at true existence that clings to the Tathāgata as truly existent as a body of name and form, have engaged wrongly in viewing the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata; those beings do not see my dharmakāya, emptiness, as the Tathāgata." The reason they do not see it is that the dharmakāya of the Buddhas, the svabhāvikakāya, must be viewed as the body of dharmatā, and

[2-140] source:
འདྲེན་པ་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ཆོས་ཉིད་དོན་དམ་བདེན་པ་དེ་ནི། བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པའི་བློ་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་བ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་དེ་ནི་བློ་དེས་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་མི་ནུས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་སྐུ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཤེས་པ་ལ་སྟོང་ཉིད་རྟོགས་དགོས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །དེས་མཚོན་ཏེ་ཆོས་གང་ལ་ཡང་བདེན་ཞེན་ཡོད་ན་ཆོས་དེའི་ཆོས་ཉིད་མི་མཐོང་བ་ནི་འདྲའོ། །གཟུགས་སོགས་ཀུན་རྫོབ་པའི་ཆོས་གང་ཡིན་ཡང་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་རྟོགས་པ་དེའི་ཚེ་སྤྲོས་བཅས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པར་ཤར་བའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་རྟོགས་དགོས་ལ། །དེ་དག་གི་ཆོས་ཉིད་དོན་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་གང་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་རྟོགས་པ་དེའི་ཚེ་སྤྲོས་པ་རྣམ་པར་བཅད་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་རྟོགས་དགོས་ཏེ། །བདེན་གཉིས་སོ་སོའི་མཐོང་ཚུལ་གྱི་ཁྱད་པར་འདི་ནི་རྟོགས་པར་དཀའ་བའི་གནས་སོ། །དེར་མ་ཟད། །ཆོས་གང་ཡིན་ཡང་དེ་བདེན་མེད་དུ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་མ་རྟོགས་ཀྱང༌། །དོན་སྤྱིའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་རྟོགས་པའི་བློ་དེའི་སྣང་ངོར་སྤྲོས་པ་འཆར་ཡང་ངེས་ངོར་སྤྲོས་པ་གཅོད་དགོས་སོ། །དེའི་དོན་བསྡུ་བ་ནི། །
[2-140] translation already produced for this document:
the dharmakāya of the guiding Buddhas, the dharmatā which is ultimate truth, is not to be known by a mind bound by grasping at true existence, because that dharmakāya cannot be completely known by such a mind, because knowing the emptiness which is the dharmakāya of the Buddha requires realizing emptiness. Illustrated by this, it is similar that if there is clinging to true existence regarding any dharma, one does not see the dharmatā of that dharma. Whenever any conventional dharma such as form is directly realized, it must be realized in a manner where it appears together with conceptual proliferation, whereas whenever the ultimate dharma, which is the dharmatā of those, is directly realized, it must be realized in a manner where conceptual proliferation is eliminated; this distinction between the respective ways of seeing the two truths is a point that is difficult to realize. Not only that, but even if whatever dharma it is, is not directly realized as lacking true existence, although conceptual proliferation appears to the appearing aspect of the mind that realizes it by way of a meaning-generality, conceptual proliferation must be eliminated in its ascertained aspect. As for summarizing the meaning of that:

[2-141] source:
དེ་ལྟར་ཆོས་སྐུའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ན་མཚན་དཔེ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་སངས་རྒྱས་པ་མེད་དོ། །དེ་ལ་ཆད་ལྟ་འགོག་པ་ནི། །
[2-141] translation already produced for this document:
In that way, from the perspective of the dharmakāya, the Tathāgata has not awakened to unsurpassed enlightenment merely by possessing the perfect major and minor marks. As for refuting the view of nihilism regarding that:

[2-142] source:
རབ་འབྱོར་ཁྱོད་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཐེག་པ་ལ་ཡང་དག་པར་ཞུགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་གཟུགས་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་གང་ལ་ལ་ཞིག་དོན་དམ་པར་མ་གྲུབ་པར་རྟོགས་པ་ན། །ཆོས་དེ་རིགས་པས་རྣམ་པར་བཤིག་པའམ། །མེད་པར་བྱས་ཏེ་ཆད་པར་བཏགས་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཤིང་འཛིན་ན། །དེ་ལྟར་བལྟ་ཞིང་འདོད་པར་མི་བྱ་སྟེ། །
[2-142] translation already produced for this document:
'Subhūti, if you think and grasp that when those who have correctly entered the vehicle of bodhisattvas realize that some dharma such as form is not established in an ultimate sense, that dharma has been destroyed by reasoning or made non-existent and designated as annihilated, you should not view and consider it in that way.'

[2-143] source:
བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་གང་ཡང་རྣམ་པར་བཤིག་པའམ་ཆད་པར་བཏགས་པ་མེད་དེ། །དེ་ལྟར་རྟོགས་པ་དེའི་ཚེ་ཆོས་དེ་བདེན་མེད་དུ་རྟོགས་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། །ཆོས་དེ་མེད་པར་རྟོགས་པ་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། དེ་ལྟར་རྟོགས་པའི་བློའི་ངེས་ངོ་ན་ཀུན་རྫོབ་པའི་ཆོས་དེ་དག་མེད་ཀྱང་བློ་དེས་དེ་དག་མེད་པར་རྟོགས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། །བློ་དེའི་ངོ་ན་མེད་ཀྱང་སྤྱིར་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། །དཔེར་ན་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པའི་བློ་ངོ་ན་བདེན་སྟོང་དུ་སྣང་བའི་བུམ་སོགས་མེད་ཀྱང་སྤྱིར་དེ་ཡོད་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །
[2-143] translation already produced for this document:
Those bodhisattvas have not destroyed or designated as annihilated any dharma whatsoever, because when it is realized in that way, that dharma is realized as lacking true existence, but that dharma is not realized as non-existent. Although those conventional dharmas do not exist for the ascertained aspect of the mind that realizes it in that way, that mind does not realize them as non-existent, because although they do not exist for the aspect of that mind, they generally exist; for example, although a vase and so forth that appears as empty of true existence does not exist for the aspect of a mind bound by grasping at true existence, it generally exists.

The Bhagavān spoke in verse, stating, 'Those who see me as form,' and so forth; as for the meaning of this, the Lord himself quoted that scripture in his commentary on the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā and explained the meaning as follows: "These words indicate that because grasping at conceptualized dharmas such as form and sound as truly existent is engaging wrongly with the reality of the Buddha and abandoning it, by that one does not see the reality of the Buddha, and therefore the reality of the Buddha is to be viewed as dharmatā and the dharmakāya. That dharmakāya is not to be known by way of grasping as before, because it is impossible to know it in that way"—having taught that, as he stated, "Because the eye of the mind is impaired by conceptual proliferation, it acts as the proof for not seeing the reality of the Tathāgata." As for the meaning of the words: "Whatever sentient beings, seeing the major and minor marks and so forth of me the Tathāgata, view and see, that is, grasp at, me as form through clinging to true existence, and whatever sentient beings know me as truly existent, that is, cling to and grasp at me, through hearing my name and so forth and expressing me as sound—in short, those who are bound by grasping at true existence that clings to the Tathāgata as truly existent as a body of name and form, have engaged wrongly in viewing the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata; those beings do not see my dharmakāya, emptiness, as the Tathāgata." the dharmakāya of the guiding Buddhas, the dharmatā which is ultimate truth, is not to be known by a mind bound by grasping at true existence, because that dharmakāya cannot be completely known by such a mind, because knowing the emptiness which is the dharmakāya of the Buddha requires realizing emptiness. Illustrated by this, it is similar that if there is clinging to true existence regarding any dharma, one does not see the dharmatā of that dharma. Whenever any conventional dharma such as form is directly realized, it must be realized in a manner where it appears together with conceptual proliferation, whereas whenever the ultimate dharma, which is the dharmatā of those, is directly realized, it must be realized in a manner where conceptual proliferation is eliminated; this distinction between the respective ways of seeing the two truths is a point that is difficult to realize. Not only that, but even if whatever dharma it is, is not directly realized as lacking true existence, although conceptual proliferation appears to the appearing aspect of the mind that realizes it by way of a meaning-generality, conceptual proliferation must be eliminated in its ascertained aspect. Those bodhisattvas have not destroyed or designated as annihilated any dharma whatsoever, because when it is realized in that way, that dharma is realized as lacking true existence, but that dharma is not realized as non-existent. Although those conventional dharmas do not exist for the ascertained aspect of the mind that realizes it in that way, that mind does not realize them as non-existent, because although they do not exist for the aspect of that mind, they generally exist; for example, although a vase and so forth that appears as empty of true existence does not exist for the aspect of a mind bound by grasping at true existence, it generally exists.

heading: ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: 'Subhūti, the Tathāgata ultimately has not departed to anywhere in any direction, and has not come here from any direction; for that reason, he is called a perfectly complete Buddha conventionally.' As for the meaning of the word 'Tathāgata,' as it was stated in a sūtra: 'The Tathāgata perfectly saw emptiness, perfectly knew it, and excellently realized it; therefore he is called omniscient'—it is by way of having directly seen emptiness, and although conventionally there is coming and departing and so forth, from the perspective of the dharmakāya, emptiness, coming and departing and so forth are ultimately non-existent; regarding how the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata are in the noble Aṣṭasāhasrikā from the section on Sadāprarudita relying on Dharmodgata, the manners of Sadāprarudita asking Dharmodgata, which are explained extensively later in the avadāna of Sadāprarudita, if set out here would be feared to be too much, so to express a brief summary: in the time of summer, at the boundary of mountain and plain, near sand or pale cliffs and so forth, a mirage is indeed seen moving with a shimmering blue appearance, but that mirage water initially did not come here from anywhere, and finally will not actually go anywhere in any direction—similarly, the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata is also like that; and similarly, pebbles and twigs and so forth emanated by a magician into individuals such as humans and animals, and furthermore various forms of buddhas or sentient beings appearing in a dream, and sounds arising from a lute—these initially did not arise from anywhere by their own essence.

The Bhagavān spoke in verse, stating, 'Those who see me as form,' and so forth; as for the meaning of this, the Lord himself quoted that scripture in his commentary on the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā and explained the meaning as follows: "These words indicate that because grasping at conceptualized dharmas such as form and sound as truly existent is engaging wrongly with the reality of the Buddha and abandoning it, by that one does not see the reality of the Buddha, and therefore the reality of the Buddha is to be viewed as dharmatā and the dharmakāya. That dharmakāya is not to be known by way of grasping as before, because it is impossible to know it in that way"—having taught that, as he stated, "Because the eye of the mind is impaired by conceptual proliferation, it acts as the proof for not seeing the reality of the Tathāgata." As for the meaning of the words: "Whatever sentient beings, seeing the major and minor marks and so forth of me the Tathāgata, view and see, that is, grasp at, me as form through clinging to true existence, and whatever sentient beings know me as truly existent, that is, cling to and grasp at me, through hearing my name and so forth and expressing me as sound—in short, those who are bound by grasping at true existence that clings to the Tathāgata as truly existent as a body of name and form, have engaged wrongly in viewing the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata; those beings do not see my dharmakāya, emptiness, as the Tathāgata." heading: ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Finally, like the example of not going anywhere by their own essence, similarly, the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata are also explained as being similar to that. Furthermore, in the Questions of the Old Woman, it is said: 'Not only the Tathāgata, but arising has not come from anywhere and does not go anywhere,' and so forth; at the end of stating this applied to other dharmas as well, the application with an example is: Indeed, sound arises from beating a drum; although that sound initially does not abide and does not arise by its own essence in the drum's wood, the leather, the beater's hand, the stick, and so forth, and finally does not go anywhere, when conditions gather, it must be accepted just as it is explained to arise and cease conventionally; from that very text it is also said: 'Whoever perfectly knows the manner of the drum's sound, that one perfectly knows emptiness.' Furthermore, just as it is said: 'Mañjuśrī, the nature, the entity of all dharmas, is without abiding, free from going and coming, like space'; since this is said, the dharmakāya, emptiness, is like space, meaning it cannot be pointed out as ultimately abiding here, and just as space does not go or come elsewhere, the dharmakāya, emptiness, also does not go away from here or come here from there; this is merely an illustration.

As for the meaning of the word 'Tathāgata,' as it was stated in a sūtra: 'The Tathāgata perfectly saw emptiness, perfectly knew it, and excellently realized it; therefore he is called omniscient'—it is by way of having directly seen emptiness, and although conventionally there is coming and departing and so forth, from the perspective of the dharmakāya, emptiness, coming and departing and so forth are ultimately non-existent; regarding how the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata are in the noble Aṣṭasāhasrikā from the section on Sadāprarudita relying on Dharmodgata, the manners of Sadāprarudita asking Dharmodgata, which are explained extensively later in the avadāna of Sadāprarudita, if set out here would be feared to be too much, so to express a brief summary: in the time of summer, at the boundary of mountain and plain, near sand or pale cliffs and so forth, a mirage is indeed seen moving with a shimmering blue appearance, but that mirage water initially did not come here from anywhere, and finally will not actually go anywhere in any direction—similarly, the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata is also like that; and similarly, pebbles and twigs and so forth emanated by a magician into individuals such as humans and animals, and furthermore various forms of buddhas or sentient beings appearing in a dream, and sounds arising from a lute—these initially did not arise from anywhere by their own essence.

translation: Furthermore, upon asking Subhūti, 'If some sentient being were to grind however many earth particles there are in the great three-thousandfold world system into powder in an extremely small form, for example, like a collection of extremely subtle particles, would those powdered collections be many?', in reply he stated, 'That would be many,' and: 'If a collection of particles were to ultimately exist, the Bhagavān would not have spoken conventionally of "a collection of extremely subtle particles", because if they ultimately existed, he would have had to state that they exist in that way.'

Finally, like the example of not going anywhere by their own essence, similarly, the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata are also explained as being similar to that. Furthermore, in the Questions of the Old Woman, it is said: 'Not only the Tathāgata, but arising has not come from anywhere and does not go anywhere,' and so forth; at the end of stating this applied to other dharmas as well, the application with an example is: Indeed, sound arises from beating a drum; although that sound initially does not abide and does not arise by its own essence in the drum's wood, the leather, the beater's hand, the stick, and so forth, and finally does not go anywhere, when conditions gather, it must be accepted just as it is explained to arise and cease conventionally; from that very text it is also said: 'Whoever perfectly knows the manner of the drum's sound, that one perfectly knows emptiness.' Furthermore, just as it is said: 'Mañjuśrī, the nature, the entity of all dharmas, is without abiding, free from going and coming, like space'; since this is said, the dharmakāya, emptiness, is like space, meaning it cannot be pointed out as ultimately abiding here, and just as space does not go or come elsewhere, the dharmakāya, emptiness, also does not go away from here or come here from there; this is merely an illustration.

translation: As for whatever was spoken as 'a collection of extremely subtle particles' whose nature is to be ultimately non-existent, it is because the Tathāgata spoke having known that they are not ultimately established as a collection; therefore, it is called 'a collection of extremely subtle particles' conventionally. The smallest limit of all forms is the extremely subtle particle, and there is no particle smaller than that, and although there is the assertion that it is partless, since that is harmed by reasoning, it must be accepted as having parts; and having parts is established because it exists surrounded by six particles in the four directions and above and below, and if it did not exist, the manner of demonstrating the reasoning that harms that has already been merely illustrated earlier.

'Subhūti, the Tathāgata ultimately has not departed to anywhere in any direction, and has not come here from any direction; for that reason, he is called a perfectly complete Buddha conventionally.' As for the meaning of the word 'Tathāgata,' as it was stated in a sūtra: 'The Tathāgata perfectly saw emptiness, perfectly knew it, and excellently realized it; therefore he is called omniscient'—it is by way of having directly seen emptiness, and although conventionally there is coming and departing and so forth, from the perspective of the dharmakāya, emptiness, coming and departing and so forth are ultimately non-existent; regarding how the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata are in the noble Aṣṭasāhasrikā from the section on Sadāprarudita relying on Dharmodgata, the manners of Sadāprarudita asking Dharmodgata, which are explained extensively later in the avadāna of Sadāprarudita, if set out here would be feared to be too much, so to express a brief summary: in the time of summer, at the boundary of mountain and plain, near sand or pale cliffs and so forth, a mirage is indeed seen moving with a shimmering blue appearance, but that mirage water initially did not come here from anywhere, and finally will not actually go anywhere in any direction—similarly, the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata is also like that; and similarly, pebbles and twigs and so forth emanated by a magician into individuals such as humans and animals, and furthermore various forms of buddhas or sentient beings appearing in a dream, and sounds arising from a lute—these initially did not arise from anywhere by their own essence.

Finally, like the example of not going anywhere by their own essence, similarly, the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata are also explained as being similar to that. Furthermore, in the Questions of the Old Woman, it is said: 'Not only the Tathāgata, but arising has not come from anywhere and does not go anywhere,' and so forth; at the end of stating this applied to other dharmas as well, the application with an example is: Indeed, sound arises from beating a drum; although that sound initially does not abide and does not arise by its own essence in the drum's wood, the leather, the beater's hand, the stick, and so forth, and finally does not go anywhere, when conditions gather, it must be accepted just as it is explained to arise and cease conventionally; from that very text it is also said: 'Whoever perfectly knows the manner of the drum's sound, that one perfectly knows emptiness.' Furthermore, just as it is said: 'Mañjuśrī, the nature, the entity of all dharmas, is without abiding, free from going and coming, like space'; since this is said, the dharmakāya, emptiness, is like space, meaning it cannot be pointed out as ultimately abiding here, and just as space does not go or come elsewhere, the dharmakāya, emptiness, also does not go away from here or come here from there; this is merely an illustration.

Furthermore, upon asking Subhūti, 'If some sentient being were to grind however many earth particles there are in the great three-thousandfold world system into powder in an extremely small form, for example, like a collection of extremely subtle particles, would those powdered collections be many?', in reply he stated, 'That would be many,' and: 'If a collection of particles were to ultimately exist, the Bhagavān would not have spoken conventionally of "a collection of extremely subtle particles", because if they ultimately existed, he would have had to state that they exist in that way.'

heading: རྡུལ་རགས་པ་བརྩམ་ཚུལ།
translation: Having explained that the extremely subtle particle is not established by its own nature, demonstrating that the coarse forms accumulated from them are also not established by their own nature is as follows: The Tathāgata has spoken of even that great three-thousandfold world system as not being ultimately established as a world system; therefore, it is called 'the great three-thousandfold world system' merely conventionally by name. By this, both the environment and its inhabitants are illustrated. If such a world system of environment and inhabitants were to ultimately exist, it would have to be established and apprehended as a single coarse whole without depending on being collected and gathered; and if it were established in that way, the Tathāgata would also have had to see it. Because the Tathāgata did not see such world systems of environment and inhabitants as being established as a single partless coarse whole that is not collected and gathered, regarding the statement 'whatever grasping as being established as a single partless solid coarse whole in the world was spoken of, that grasping is also not ultimately established as grasping'—the former is the apprehended object, and this is explained as demonstrating that the apprehending subject is also ultimately established. If this latter one is treated from the perspective of demonstrating the world of the inhabitants, the bodies of the sentient beings who are the inhabitants are coarse forms arising from the accumulation of extremely subtle particles; that refutes apprehending them as a single partless coarse whole by their own essence, without depending on the collecting and gathering of minute particles. Although it is easy to ascertain that the coarse forms accumulated from the extremely subtle are false things that are collected and gathered, due to it being somewhat difficult to ascertain the extremely subtle particle as false, there have also occurred assertions of it as partless, permanent, and ultimately true.

'Subhūti, the Tathāgata ultimately has not departed to anywhere in any direction, and has not come here from any direction; for that reason, he is called a perfectly complete Buddha conventionally.' As for the meaning of the word 'Tathāgata,' as it was stated in a sūtra: 'The Tathāgata perfectly saw emptiness, perfectly knew it, and excellently realized it; therefore he is called omniscient'—it is by way of having directly seen emptiness, and although conventionally there is coming and departing and so forth, from the perspective of the dharmakāya, emptiness, coming and departing and so forth are ultimately non-existent; regarding how the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata are in the noble Aṣṭasāhasrikā from the section on Sadāprarudita relying on Dharmodgata, the manners of Sadāprarudita asking Dharmodgata, which are explained extensively later in the avadāna of Sadāprarudita, if set out here would be feared to be too much, so to express a brief summary: in the time of summer, at the boundary of mountain and plain, near sand or pale cliffs and so forth, a mirage is indeed seen moving with a shimmering blue appearance, but that mirage water initially did not come here from anywhere, and finally will not actually go anywhere in any direction—similarly, the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata is also like that; and similarly, pebbles and twigs and so forth emanated by a magician into individuals such as humans and animals, and furthermore various forms of buddhas or sentient beings appearing in a dream, and sounds arising from a lute—these initially did not arise from anywhere by their own essence.

Finally, like the example of not going anywhere by their own essence, similarly, the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata are also explained as being similar to that. Furthermore, in the Questions of the Old Woman, it is said: 'Not only the Tathāgata, but arising has not come from anywhere and does not go anywhere,' and so forth; at the end of stating this applied to other dharmas as well, the application with an example is: Indeed, sound arises from beating a drum; although that sound initially does not abide and does not arise by its own essence in the drum's wood, the leather, the beater's hand, the stick, and so forth, and finally does not go anywhere, when conditions gather, it must be accepted just as it is explained to arise and cease conventionally; from that very text it is also said: 'Whoever perfectly knows the manner of the drum's sound, that one perfectly knows emptiness.' Furthermore, just as it is said: 'Mañjuśrī, the nature, the entity of all dharmas, is without abiding, free from going and coming, like space'; since this is said, the dharmakāya, emptiness, is like space, meaning it cannot be pointed out as ultimately abiding here, and just as space does not go or come elsewhere, the dharmakāya, emptiness, also does not go away from here or come here from there; this is merely an illustration.

As for whatever was spoken as 'a collection of extremely subtle particles' whose nature is to be ultimately non-existent, it is because the Tathāgata spoke having known that they are not ultimately established as a collection; therefore, it is called 'a collection of extremely subtle particles' conventionally. The smallest limit of all forms is the extremely subtle particle, and there is no particle smaller than that, and although there is the assertion that it is partless, since that is harmed by reasoning, it must be accepted as having parts; and having parts is established because it exists surrounded by six particles in the four directions and above and below, and if it did not exist, the manner of demonstrating the reasoning that harms that has already been merely illustrated earlier.

heading: རྡུལ་རགས་པ་བརྩམ་ཚུལ།
translation: Then the Bhagavān said to Subhūti: 'That very grasping as a whole exists in worldly convention and does not ultimately exist; and although that dharma which is the apprehended object is ultimately inexpressible, ordinary childish beings have grasped it by adhering to it as being ultimately expressible.' By these, both the profound and the extensive aspects have been explained. However, in order to excellently know the manner in which it is ultimately inexpressible, one appears to need to excellently know this manner in which expressing sounds do not engage with their own objects by the power of real entities, but engage by the power of intention and the power of convention.

'Subhūti, the Tathāgata ultimately has not departed to anywhere in any direction, and has not come here from any direction; for that reason, he is called a perfectly complete Buddha conventionally.' As for the meaning of the word 'Tathāgata,' as it was stated in a sūtra: 'The Tathāgata perfectly saw emptiness, perfectly knew it, and excellently realized it; therefore he is called omniscient'—it is by way of having directly seen emptiness, and although conventionally there is coming and departing and so forth, from the perspective of the dharmakāya, emptiness, coming and departing and so forth are ultimately non-existent; regarding how the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata are in the noble Aṣṭasāhasrikā from the section on Sadāprarudita relying on Dharmodgata, the manners of Sadāprarudita asking Dharmodgata, which are explained extensively later in the avadāna of Sadāprarudita, if set out here would be feared to be too much, so to express a brief summary: in the time of summer, at the boundary of mountain and plain, near sand or pale cliffs and so forth, a mirage is indeed seen moving with a shimmering blue appearance, but that mirage water initially did not come here from anywhere, and finally will not actually go anywhere in any direction—similarly, the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata is also like that; and similarly, pebbles and twigs and so forth emanated by a magician into individuals such as humans and animals, and furthermore various forms of buddhas or sentient beings appearing in a dream, and sounds arising from a lute—these initially did not arise from anywhere by their own essence.

Finally, like the example of not going anywhere by their own essence, similarly, the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata are also explained as being similar to that. Furthermore, in the Questions of the Old Woman, it is said: 'Not only the Tathāgata, but arising has not come from anywhere and does not go anywhere,' and so forth; at the end of stating this applied to other dharmas as well, the application with an example is: Indeed, sound arises from beating a drum; although that sound initially does not abide and does not arise by its own essence in the drum's wood, the leather, the beater's hand, the stick, and so forth, and finally does not go anywhere, when conditions gather, it must be accepted just as it is explained to arise and cease conventionally; from that very text it is also said: 'Whoever perfectly knows the manner of the drum's sound, that one perfectly knows emptiness.' Furthermore, just as it is said: 'Mañjuśrī, the nature, the entity of all dharmas, is without abiding, free from going and coming, like space'; since this is said, the dharmakāya, emptiness, is like space, meaning it cannot be pointed out as ultimately abiding here, and just as space does not go or come elsewhere, the dharmakāya, emptiness, also does not go away from here or come here from there; this is merely an illustration.

translation: 'Then, Subhūti, if some sentient being were to say this: "The Tathāgata has spoken of the view of a personal self, and the view of a sentient being, a life-principle, and a person in his own system," would that be speaking by speaking correctly, that is, excellently?'—upon asking this, in reply Subhūti said, 'That is not so.'

'Subhūti, the Tathāgata ultimately has not departed to anywhere in any direction, and has not come here from any direction; for that reason, he is called a perfectly complete Buddha conventionally.' As for the meaning of the word 'Tathāgata,' as it was stated in a sūtra: 'The Tathāgata perfectly saw emptiness, perfectly knew it, and excellently realized it; therefore he is called omniscient'—it is by way of having directly seen emptiness, and although conventionally there is coming and departing and so forth, from the perspective of the dharmakāya, emptiness, coming and departing and so forth are ultimately non-existent; regarding how the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata are in the noble Aṣṭasāhasrikā from the section on Sadāprarudita relying on Dharmodgata, the manners of Sadāprarudita asking Dharmodgata, which are explained extensively later in the avadāna of Sadāprarudita, if set out here would be feared to be too much, so to express a brief summary: in the time of summer, at the boundary of mountain and plain, near sand or pale cliffs and so forth, a mirage is indeed seen moving with a shimmering blue appearance, but that mirage water initially did not come here from anywhere, and finally will not actually go anywhere in any direction—similarly, the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata is also like that; and similarly, pebbles and twigs and so forth emanated by a magician into individuals such as humans and animals, and furthermore various forms of buddhas or sentient beings appearing in a dream, and sounds arising from a lute—these initially did not arise from anywhere by their own essence.

Finally, like the example of not going anywhere by their own essence, similarly, the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata are also explained as being similar to that. Furthermore, in the Questions of the Old Woman, it is said: 'Not only the Tathāgata, but arising has not come from anywhere and does not go anywhere,' and so forth; at the end of stating this applied to other dharmas as well, the application with an example is: Indeed, sound arises from beating a drum; although that sound initially does not abide and does not arise by its own essence in the drum's wood, the leather, the beater's hand, the stick, and so forth, and finally does not go anywhere, when conditions gather, it must be accepted just as it is explained to arise and cease conventionally; from that very text it is also said: 'Whoever perfectly knows the manner of the drum's sound, that one perfectly knows emptiness.' Furthermore, just as it is said: 'Mañjuśrī, the nature, the entity of all dharmas, is without abiding, free from going and coming, like space'; since this is said, the dharmakāya, emptiness, is like space, meaning it cannot be pointed out as ultimately abiding here, and just as space does not go or come elsewhere, the dharmakāya, emptiness, also does not go away from here or come here from there; this is merely an illustration.

translation: 'For what reason is that? Whatever the Tathāgata has spoken of as the view of a self by others and so forth, is the complete dismantling of the view of a self and so forth, and it is because the Tathāgata has spoken of the adhered objects of those views being non-existent and that view also being ultimately non-existent; therefore, it is called the view of a self and so forth conventionally.'

'Subhūti, the Tathāgata ultimately has not departed to anywhere in any direction, and has not come here from any direction; for that reason, he is called a perfectly complete Buddha conventionally.' As for the meaning of the word 'Tathāgata,' as it was stated in a sūtra: 'The Tathāgata perfectly saw emptiness, perfectly knew it, and excellently realized it; therefore he is called omniscient'—it is by way of having directly seen emptiness, and although conventionally there is coming and departing and so forth, from the perspective of the dharmakāya, emptiness, coming and departing and so forth are ultimately non-existent; regarding how the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata are in the noble Aṣṭasāhasrikā from the section on Sadāprarudita relying on Dharmodgata, the manners of Sadāprarudita asking Dharmodgata, which are explained extensively later in the avadāna of Sadāprarudita, if set out here would be feared to be too much, so to express a brief summary: in the time of summer, at the boundary of mountain and plain, near sand or pale cliffs and so forth, a mirage is indeed seen moving with a shimmering blue appearance, but that mirage water initially did not come here from anywhere, and finally will not actually go anywhere in any direction—similarly, the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata is also like that; and similarly, pebbles and twigs and so forth emanated by a magician into individuals such as humans and animals, and furthermore various forms of buddhas or sentient beings appearing in a dream, and sounds arising from a lute—these initially did not arise from anywhere by their own essence.

མཐར་གང་དུ་ཡང་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་འགྲོ་བ་མེད་པའི་དཔེ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་འབྱོན་བཞུད་སོགས་ཀྱང་དེ་དང་མཚུངས་པར་བཤད་དོ། །གཞན་ཡང༌། བགྲེས་མོས་ཞུས་པ་ལས། དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཙམ་དུ་མ་ཟད། སྐྱེ་བ་གང་ནས་ཀྱང་མ་འོངས། གང་དུ་ཡང་མི་འགྲོ །ཞེས་སོགས་ཆོས་གཞན་ལའང་སྦྱར་ནས་གསུངས་པའི་མཇུག་ཏུ་དཔེ་དང་སྦྱོར་བ་ནི། །རྔ་བརྡུང་བ་ལས་སྒྲ་འབྱུང་མོད། །སྒྲ་དེ་དང་པོར་རྔའི་ཤིང་དང་ལྤགས་པ་དང་བརྡུང་མཁན་གྱི་ལག་པ་དང་དབྱུག་གུ་སོགས་ལ་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་མི་གནས་ཤིང་མི་འབྱུང་ལ་མཐར་གང་དུ་ཡང་མི་འགྲོ་མོད། །རྐྱེན་ཚོགས་ན་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་སྐྱེ་འགག་བྱེད་པར་བཤད་པ་བཞིན་འདོད་དགོས་ཏེ། །དེ་ཉིད་ལས། །སུས་རྔ་སྒྲའི་ཚུལ་རབ་ཏུ་ཤེས་པ་དེས་ནི་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་རབ་ཏུ་ཤེས་སོ། །ཞེས་ཀྱང་གསུངས་སོ། །གཞན་ཡང་ཇི་སྐད་དུ། །འཇམ་དཔལ་རང་།བཞིན་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀུན་གྱི་དངོས། །གནས་མེད་འགྲོ་འོང་བྲལ་བ་ནམ་མཁའ་བཞིན། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པས། ཆོས་སྐུ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་དེ་ནི་ནམ་མཁའ་ལྟ་བུ་སྟེ་དོན་དམ་པར་འདི་ན་གནས་ཞེས་བསྟན་དུ་མེད་ཅིང་། ནམ་མཁའ་ནི་གཞན་དུ་འགྲོ་འོང་མི་བྱེད་པ་ལྟར་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་དེ་ཡང་འདི་ནས་ཕར་འགྲོ་ཞིང་དེ་ནས་ཚུར་འོང་བ་ཡང་མེད་དོ་ཞེས་པ་སྟེ་མཚོན་ཙམ་མོ། །

Finally, like the example of not going anywhere by their own essence, similarly, the coming and departing and so forth of the Tathāgata are also explained as being similar to that. Furthermore, in the Questions of the Old Woman, it is said: 'Not only the Tathāgata, but arising has not come from anywhere and does not go anywhere,' and so forth; at the end of stating this applied to other dharmas as well, the application with an example is: Indeed, sound arises from beating a drum; although that sound initially does not abide and does not arise by its own essence in the drum's wood, the leather, the beater's hand, the stick, and so forth, and finally does not go anywhere, when conditions gather, it must be accepted just as it is explained to arise and cease conventionally; from that very text it is also said: 'Whoever perfectly knows the manner of the drum's sound, that one perfectly knows emptiness.' Furthermore, just as it is said: 'Mañjuśrī, the nature, the entity of all dharmas, is without abiding, free from going and coming, like space'; since this is said, the dharmakāya, emptiness, is like space, meaning it cannot be pointed out as ultimately abiding here, and just as space does not go or come elsewhere, the dharmakāya, emptiness, also does not go away from here or come here from there; this is merely an illustration.

ཡང་རབ་འབྱོར་ལ་སེམས་ཅན་གང་ལ་ལ་ཞིག་གིས་སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སྟོང་ཆེན་པོའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་ན་སའི་རྡུལ་ཇི་སྙེད་ཡོད་པ་དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་དཔེར་ན། རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་བཞིན་དུ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཆུང་བའི་གཟུགས་སུ་ཕྱེ་མར་བྱས་ན། ཕྱེ་མར་བྱས་པའི་ཚོགས་དེ་དག་མང་ངམ་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ན། ལན་དུ་དེ་མང་ངོ་ཞེས་ཞུས་ཤིང་། གལ་ཏེ་རྡུལ་གྱི་ཚོགས་ཤིག་དོན་དམ་པར་མཆིས་པར་གྱུར་ན་ནི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཞེས་བཀའ་མི་སྩོལ་ཏེ། དེ་རྣམས་དོན་དམ་པར་ཡོད་ན་དེར་ཡོད་ཅེས་གསུངས་དགོས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །

Furthermore, upon asking Subhūti, 'If some sentient being were to grind however many earth particles there are in the great three-thousandfold world system into powder in an extremely small form, for example, like a collection of extremely subtle particles, would those powdered collections be many?', in reply he stated, 'That would be many,' and: 'If a collection of particles were to ultimately exist, the Bhagavān would not have spoken conventionally of "a collection of extremely subtle particles", because if they ultimately existed, he would have had to state that they exist in that way.'

དེ་རྣམས་དོན་དམ་པར་མེད་པའི་རང་བཞིན་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཞེས་གང་གསུངས་པ་དེ་ནི། དེ་རྣམས་དོན་དམ་པར་ཚོགས་སུ་གྲུབ་པ་མ་མཆིས་པར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་མཁྱེན་ནས་གསུངས་པའི་སླད་དུ་སྟེ། དེས་ན་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཞེས་བགྱིའོ། །གཟུགས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་ཆུང་མཐའ་ནི་རྡུལ་ཕྲ་རབ་ཡིན་ཞིང་དེ་ལས་ཆུང་བའི་རྡུལ་མེད་ལ། དེ་ནི་ཆ་མེད་དུ་འདོད་པ་ཡོད་ཀྱང་དེ་ལ་རིགས་པས་གནོད་པས་ཆ་བཅས་སུ་ཁས་ལེན་དགོས་ཤིང་། ཆ་བཅས་ཀྱང་འདི་ལ་ཕྱོགས་བཞི་དང་སྟེང་འོག་ཏུ་རྡུལ་དྲུག་གིས་བསྐོར་ནས་གནས་པས་འགྲུབ་ལ། མེད་ན་དེ་ལ་རིགས་པའི་གནོད་བྱེད་སྟོན་ཚུལ་མཚོན་ཙམ་སྔར་བཤད་ཟིན་ཏོ། །

As for whatever was spoken as 'a collection of extremely subtle particles' whose nature is to be ultimately non-existent, it is because the Tathāgata spoke having known that they are not ultimately established as a collection; therefore, it is called 'a collection of extremely subtle particles' conventionally. The smallest limit of all forms is the extremely subtle particle, and there is no particle smaller than that, and although there is the assertion that it is partless, since that is harmed by reasoning, it must be accepted as having parts; and having parts is established because it exists surrounded by six particles in the four directions and above and below, and if it did not exist, the manner of demonstrating the reasoning that harms that has already been merely illustrated earlier.

heading: རྡུལ་རགས་པ་བརྩམ་ཚུལ།
translation: Then, wishing to conclude, the Bhagavān said: 'Subhūti, here, those who have correctly entered the bodhisattva vehicle should know, view, and resolve upon all dharmas by applying them just as they were explained'; regarding this, 'knowing' is the prajñā of hearing, 'viewing' is the prajñā of reflection, and 'resolving' means one should generate the prajñā of meditation. As for 'by all means the perception of a dharma', one should not generate the perception of grasping at true existence, thinking that any dharma whatsoever is truly established, and one should not abide in the perception of truth.

Having explained that the extremely subtle particle is not established by its own nature, demonstrating that the coarse forms accumulated from them are also not established by their own nature is as follows: The Tathāgata has spoken of even that great three-thousandfold world system as not being ultimately established as a world system; therefore, it is called 'the great three-thousandfold world system' merely conventionally by name. By this, both the environment and its inhabitants are illustrated. If such a world system of environment and inhabitants were to ultimately exist, it would have to be established and apprehended as a single coarse whole without depending on being collected and gathered; and if it were established in that way, the Tathāgata would also have had to see it. Because the Tathāgata did not see such world systems of environment and inhabitants as being established as a single partless coarse whole that is not collected and gathered, regarding the statement 'whatever grasping as being established as a single partless solid coarse whole in the world was spoken of, that grasping is also not ultimately established as grasping'—the former is the apprehended object, and this is explained as demonstrating that the apprehending subject is also ultimately established. If this latter one is treated from the perspective of demonstrating the world of the inhabitants, the bodies of the sentient beings who are the inhabitants are coarse forms arising from the accumulation of extremely subtle particles; that refutes apprehending them as a single partless coarse whole by their own essence, without depending on the collecting and gathering of minute particles. Although it is easy to ascertain that the coarse forms accumulated from the extremely subtle are false things that are collected and gathered, due to it being somewhat difficult to ascertain the extremely subtle particle as false, there have also occurred assertions of it as partless, permanent, and ultimately true.

Then the Bhagavān said to Subhūti: 'That very grasping as a whole exists in worldly convention and does not ultimately exist; and although that dharma which is the apprehended object is ultimately inexpressible, ordinary childish beings have grasped it by adhering to it as being ultimately expressible.'
