source: རྒྱུ་མཚན་དེ་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། རབ་འབྱོར་ཆོས་སུ་འདུ་ཤེས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། འདུ་ཤེས་པའི་ཡུལ་དང་འདུ་ཤེས་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱང་དོན་དམ་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་པར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། དེས་ན་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་ཆོས་སུ་འདུ་ཤེས་ཞེས་བགྱིའོ། །དེ་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན་དང་། དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེ་ན་གཉིས་ཀྱི་ཕྱིར་དང་སླད་དུ་ནི་གཏན་ཚིགས་སམ། རྒྱུ་མཚན་ཡིན་ཞིང་སྐད་དོད་ཨ་ཐ་ཞེས་པར་འདྲ་ཡང་། སྔ་མ་ནི་སྟོན་པའི་གསུངས་ཏེ་ཞེ་ས་མེད་ལ། ཕྱི་མ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱི་གསུང་ནི་ཞེ་སར་བསྒྱུར་བའོ། དེ་ལྟར་བདེན་མེད་ཡང་དང་ཡང་དུ་བཤད་ནས་བདེན་འཛིན་ནན་ཏན་དུ་མཛད་ནས་བཀག་གོ །འགོག་ཚུལ་ནི། བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཟུང་བ་ལྟར་དེའི་ཞེན་ཡུལ་ལ་རིགས་པའི་གནོད་བྱེད་བསྟན་ནས་འགོག་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། ཚེར་མ་འདོན་པ་ལྟར་མིན་ཏེ། འཕགས་པ་ལྷས། ཡུལ་ལ་བདག་མེད་མཐོང་ན་ནི། །སྲིད་པའི་ས་བོན་འགག་པར་འགྱུར། །ཞེས་དང་། རྣམ་འགྲེལ་ལས། འདི་ཡུལ་སུན་དབྱུང་མེད་པར་ནི། །དེ་སྤོང་བ་ནི་ནུས་མ་ཡིན། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །འགོག་པའི་རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི། བདེན་འཛིན་མ་རིག་པ་ཡིན་པས་དེའི་དབང་གིས་འཁོར་བར་འཁོར་བ་དང་། བདེན་འཛིན་སྤོང་བ་ལ་བདེན་མེད་རྟོགས་དགོས་ཤིང་དེ་རྟོགས་ནས་བསྒོམས་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་འཁོར་བ་ལས་གྲོལ་ནས་ཐར་པ་དང་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པའི་གོ་འཕང་ཡང་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་སྙམ་དུ་དགོངས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། མདོ་སྡུད་པ་ལས། འཁོར་བར་ཆགས་པའི་ཡིད་དང་ལྡན་རྣམས་རྟག་ཏུ་འཁོར། །
translation: 'For what reason is that? Subhūti, what is called the perception of a dharma, is because the Tathāgata has spoken of the object of perception and the perception itself as ultimately not existing as perception; therefore, it is called the perception of a dharma conventionally.' Regarding both 'de ci'i phyir zhe na' and 'de ci'i slad du zhe na', 'phyir' and 'slad du' indicate the logic or reason, and although their original term is identical as 'atha', the former is the Teacher's speech and has no honorific, while the latter is Subhūti's speech and is translated with an honorific. Thus, having repeatedly explained the absence of true existence, grasping at true existence is emphatically refuted. As for the manner of refuting it, it is refuted by demonstrating logical invalidation to its adhered object, just as it is apprehended by grasping at true existence, but it is not like extracting a thorn; for Āryadeva said, 'If one sees the lack of self in objects, the seed of existence will be stopped,' and the Pramāṇavārttika says, 'Without invalidating its object, one is unable to abandon it.' As for the reason for refuting it, it is because grasping at true existence is ignorance, and by its power one cycles in saṃsāra, and to abandon grasping at true existence one must realize the lack of true existence, and having realized it, through the power of meditation one will be liberated from saṃsāra and also attain the state of liberation and omniscience—he intended this, for the Saṃcayagāthā says: 'Those endowed with minds attached to saṃsāra cycle permanently;

[2-154] translation already produced for this document:
Having explained that the extremely subtle particle is not established by its own nature, demonstrating that the coarse forms accumulated from them are also not established by their own nature is as follows: The Tathāgata has spoken of even that great three-thousandfold world system as not being ultimately established as a world system; therefore, it is called 'the great three-thousandfold world system' merely conventionally by name. By this, both the environment and its inhabitants are illustrated. If such a world system of environment and inhabitants were to ultimately exist, it would have to be established and apprehended as a single coarse whole without depending on being collected and gathered; and if it were established in that way, the Tathāgata would also have had to see it. Because the Tathāgata did not see such world systems of environment and inhabitants as being established as a single partless coarse whole that is not collected and gathered, regarding the statement 'whatever grasping as being established as a single partless solid coarse whole in the world was spoken of, that grasping is also not ultimately established as grasping'—the former is the apprehended object, and this is explained as demonstrating that the apprehending subject is also ultimately established. If this latter one is treated from the perspective of demonstrating the world of the inhabitants, the bodies of the sentient beings who are the inhabitants are coarse forms arising from the accumulation of extremely subtle particles; that refutes apprehending them as a single partless coarse whole by their own essence, without depending on the collecting and gathering of minute particles. Although it is easy to ascertain that the coarse forms accumulated from the extremely subtle are false things that are collected and gathered, due to it being somewhat difficult to ascertain the extremely subtle particle as false, there have also occurred assertions of it as partless, permanent, and ultimately true.

heading: རྡུལ་རགས་པ་བརྩམ་ཚུལ།
translation: the self and the dharmas of the self are both unreal and empty, yet childish beings themselves cast knots in space. For example, due to a suspicious perception of pervasive poison, even though that poison has not gone inside, one faints. Likewise, childish beings who assert a self and what belongs to a self, through the unreal conception of perceiving that self, are born and destroyed. Just as there is grasping, thus thorough affliction is taught; not apprehending a self or what belongs to a self is spoken of as purification'; and: 'However many sentient beings there are—inferior, middling, and supreme—the Sugata has spoken of them all as arising from ignorance. When conditions gather, the machine of suffering thoroughly arises; that machine of ignorance is without exhaustion and without increase. However many gateways of the method of pristine awareness and roots there are, they all arise from the supreme prajñāpāramitā. When conditions gather, the machine of pristine awareness thoroughly arises; in the prajñāpāramitā there is no exhaustion and no increase.' In short, the prajñā that realizes selflessness is the chief of all causes that produce the attainment of liberation, because without it, it is impossible to attain the liberation of being freed from saṃsāra, for the Samādhirāja says: 'If one discriminates selflessness in dharmas, and whoever meditates having discriminated that, that is the cause of the result of attaining the liberation of nirvāṇa; whatever other causes there are, they will not bring peace.' Just as this states, there are many other sources as well, and it is extremely important.

[2-154] translation already produced for this document:
Having explained that the extremely subtle particle is not established by its own nature, demonstrating that the coarse forms accumulated from them are also not established by their own nature is as follows: The Tathāgata has spoken of even that great three-thousandfold world system as not being ultimately established as a world system; therefore, it is called 'the great three-thousandfold world system' merely conventionally by name. By this, both the environment and its inhabitants are illustrated. If such a world system of environment and inhabitants were to ultimately exist, it would have to be established and apprehended as a single coarse whole without depending on being collected and gathered; and if it were established in that way, the Tathāgata would also have had to see it. Because the Tathāgata did not see such world systems of environment and inhabitants as being established as a single partless coarse whole that is not collected and gathered, regarding the statement 'whatever grasping as being established as a single partless solid coarse whole in the world was spoken of, that grasping is also not ultimately established as grasping'—the former is the apprehended object, and this is explained as demonstrating that the apprehending subject is also ultimately established. If this latter one is treated from the perspective of demonstrating the world of the inhabitants, the bodies of the sentient beings who are the inhabitants are coarse forms arising from the accumulation of extremely subtle particles; that refutes apprehending them as a single partless coarse whole by their own essence, without depending on the collecting and gathering of minute particles. Although it is easy to ascertain that the coarse forms accumulated from the extremely subtle are false things that are collected and gathered, due to it being somewhat difficult to ascertain the extremely subtle particle as false, there have also occurred assertions of it as partless, permanent, and ultimately true.

Then the Bhagavān said to Subhūti: 'That very grasping as a whole exists in worldly convention and does not ultimately exist; and although that dharma which is the apprehended object is ultimately inexpressible, ordinary childish beings have grasped it by adhering to it as being ultimately expressible.' By these, both the profound and the extensive aspects have been explained. However, in order to excellently know the manner in which it is ultimately inexpressible, one appears to need to excellently know this manner in which expressing sounds do not engage with their own objects by the power of real entities, but engage by the power of intention and the power of convention.

translation: Considering it to be important in that way, the conclusion by way of demonstrating the benefits is: 'Subhūti, more than if any bodhisattva mahāsattva were to fill measureless world systems with the seven precious substances like gold, silver, pearls, and so forth, and give them as a gift, if any son of noble family or daughter of noble family, let alone completely, having written down even as little as a stanza of four lines pointing out the profound of this text of the prajñāpāramitā, memorizes it, or reads the volume, or holds the entire volume in hand, or comprehends, that is, knows all its words and meanings, or, just as they themselves know the words and meanings, correctly explains them extensively to other sentient beings as well—that very person, on the basis of having done that, would generate much more merit, meaning benefits, countless and measureless.' What is called 'merit' indicates both the accumulations of merit and pristine awareness, and from the three—generosity, ethical discipline, and patience—primarily the accumulation of merit is gathered, while from the two—concentration and prajñā—primarily the accumulation of pristine awareness is gathered, and from joyous effort, both arise. Therefore, doing hearing, reflection, and so forth on the prajñāpāramitā is primarily the gathering of the accumulation of pristine awareness. 'Well then, in the occasions of explaining the benefits in this text, how is it that what is called "heap of merit" appears so often?' That does not intend merely the accumulation of merit which is differentiated as one of the pair of the two accumulations, but refers to benefits by the name 'merit'.

'For what reason is that? Subhūti, what is called the perception of a dharma, is because the Tathāgata has spoken of the object of perception and the perception itself as ultimately not existing as perception; therefore, it is called the perception of a dharma conventionally.' Regarding both 'de ci'i phyir zhe na' and 'de ci'i slad du zhe na', 'phyir' and 'slad du' indicate the logic or reason, and although their original term is identical as 'atha', the former is the Teacher's speech and has no honorific, while the latter is Subhūti's speech and is translated with an honorific. Thus, having repeatedly explained the absence of true existence, grasping at true existence is emphatically refuted. As for the manner of refuting it, it is refuted by demonstrating logical invalidation to its adhered object, just as it is apprehended by grasping at true existence, but it is not like extracting a thorn; for Āryadeva said, 'If one sees the lack of self in objects, the seed of existence will be stopped,' and the Pramāṇavārttika says, 'Without invalidating its object, one is unable to abandon it.' As for the reason for refuting it, it is because grasping at true existence is ignorance, and by its power one cycles in saṃsāra, and to abandon grasping at true existence one must realize the lack of true existence, and having realized it, through the power of meditation one will be liberated from saṃsāra and also attain the state of liberation and omniscience—he intended this, for the Saṃcayagāthā says: 'Those endowed with minds attached to saṃsāra cycle permanently;

the self and the dharmas of the self are both unreal and empty, yet childish beings themselves cast knots in space. For example, due to a suspicious perception of pervasive poison, even though that poison has not gone inside, one faints. Likewise, childish beings who assert a self and what belongs to a self, through the unreal conception of perceiving that self, are born and destroyed. Just as there is grasping, thus thorough affliction is taught; not apprehending a self or what belongs to a self is spoken of as purification'; and: 'However many sentient beings there are—inferior, middling, and supreme—the Sugata has spoken of them all as arising from ignorance. When conditions gather, the machine of suffering thoroughly arises; that machine of ignorance is without exhaustion and without increase. However many gateways of the method of pristine awareness and roots there are, they all arise from the supreme prajñāpāramitā. When conditions gather, the machine of pristine awareness thoroughly arises; in the prajñāpāramitā there is no exhaustion and no increase.' In short, the prajñā that realizes selflessness is the chief of all causes that produce the attainment of liberation, because without it, it is impossible to attain the liberation of being freed from saṃsāra, for the Samādhirāja says: 'If one discriminates selflessness in dharmas, and whoever meditates having discriminated that, that is the cause of the result of attaining the liberation of nirvāṇa; whatever other causes there are, they will not bring peace.' source: གཞུང་འདི་སྟོན་ཚུལ་ཇི་ལྟར་བྱ་བ་ནི། ཇི་ལྟར་ཡང་དག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་སྟོན་ཅེ་ན། དེ་ཡང་བརྗོད་ཅིང་སྟོན་པ་དང་གོ་བ་རྣམས་ནི་ཐ་སྙད་ཙམ་དུ་འཇོག་ཅིང་། དོན་དམ་པར་བརྗོད་བྱ་རྗོད་བྱེད་སོགས་མེད་པས་དོན་ཇི་ལྟར་ཡང་དག་པར་རམ་དོན་དམ་པར་རམ་རབ་ཏུ་མི་སྟོན་ཀྱང་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་སྟོན་པ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ། འདིར་ཡང་ཐ་སྙད་ཙམ་དུ་ཚིག་དང་དོན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་ཡང་དག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་སྟོན་ཏེ། རྒྱུ་མཚན་དེས་ན། ཡང་དག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་སྟོན་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །འདི་ལེགས་པར་ཤེས་པ་ནི། རྗོད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་སྒྲ་རྣམས་ནི་རང་ཡུལ་ལ་བརྡ་དང་ཐ་སྙད་ཀྱི་དབང་གིས་འཇུག་ཅིང་། དངོས་པོའི་དབང་གིས་མི་འཇུག་པའི་ཚུལ་ལེགས་པར་ཤེས་དགོས་ཏེ་གོང་དུ་མཚོན་ཙམ་ཞིག་བཤད་ཀྱང་། འདིར་ཡང་དངོས་པོའི་དབང་གིས་མི་འཇུག་པའི་རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་དོན་གཅིག་ལའང་མིང་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་བརྗོད་ཆོག་པ་ལྟ་བུ་སྟེ། དཔེར་ན་རྟ་ལྟ་བུ་གཅིག་ལ་ཡང་རྒྱ་གར་རྒྱ་ནག་བོད་སོག་པོ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་རང་རང་གི་ཡུལ་སྐད་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱི་མིང་གིས་བརྗོད་པ་བཞིན་དང་། ཤེར་ཕྱིན་བྱམས་པས་ཞུས་པ་ལས་གཟུགས་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་ཡང་མིང་གློ་བུར་དུ་བཏགས་པར་གསུངས་པས་མིང་འཇུག་པ་ནི་བརྡའི་དབང་ཡིན་གྱི། དངོས་པོའི་དབང་གིས་མིན་ནོ། །དེས་ན་མིང་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་དོན་གོ་བ་ཡང་བརྡ་སྦྱར་དགོས་པའི་དབང་གིས་ཡིན་གྱི། བརྡ་མ་སྦྱར་ན་དོན་གོ་མི་ནུས་ཏེ། དཔེར་ན་བྱིས་པ་ཆུང་ངུ་བརྡ་མི་ཤེས་པ་ལ་མིང་དེ་དང་དེ་བརྗོད་ཀྱང་སྒྲ་ཙམ་ཞིག་ཐོས་པར་འགྱུར་ཞིང་། དོན་དེ་དང་དེ་མི་གོ་བ་ལྟར་རོ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་གཞན་ཀུན་གྱིས་ཀྱང་དོན་དེ་གོ་བ་ནི་བརྡའི་དབང་གིས་ཡིན་གྱི། བརྡ་མེད་ན་བྱིས་པ་ཆུང་ངུ་ལྟར་སྒྲ་ཙམ་ཞིག་ཐོས་པར་འགྱུར་གྱི་དོན་གོ་བར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཆོས་རྣམས་དོན་དམ་དཔྱོད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་རིགས་པས་དཔྱད་མི་བཟོད་ཅིང་། འཕགས་པའི་མཉམ་བཞག་གི་གཟིགས་ངོར་གཉིས་སྣང་གི་སྤྲོས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཉེ་བར་ཞི་བས་དེའི་ངོར་སྤྲོས་བཅས་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་དུ་བརྗོད་མི་ནུས་པ་ནི་སྔ་མ་ལས་ཀྱང་ཟབ་སྟེ། སྨྲ་བསམ་བརྗོད་མེད་ཤེས་རབ་ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །
translation: As for the manner of explaining this text: 'How does one correctly explain it?' The expression, explanation, and understanding are established as merely conventional, and because ultimately there are no expressed meaning, expressing words, and so forth, although in reality it is not correctly or ultimately explained, just as it is explained conventionally, here too one correctly explains the words and meanings unmistakably on a merely conventional level; for that reason, it is called 'correctly explaining'. As for understanding this well: one must well understand the manner in which expressing sounds engage with their own objects by the power of convention and terminology, and do not engage by the power of the things themselves; although this was briefly indicated above, here again the reason they do not engage by the power of the things themselves is like the fact that even one object can be designated with diverse names; for example, just as a single horse is designated with names in diverse regional languages by Indians, Chinese, Tibetans, Mongolians, and so forth, and in the Prajñāpāramitā Requested by Maitreya it is said that names are adventitiously imputed upon all dharmas such as form; thus, the engagement of names is by the power of convention, and not by the power of the things themselves. Therefore, understanding the meaning based on the name is also by the power of needing to apply convention, and if convention is not applied, one is unable to understand the meaning; for example, even if such and such names are spoken to a small child who does not know conventions, they will hear mere sounds, but they do not understand such and such meanings. Similarly, the understanding of that meaning by all others is also by the power of convention, and without convention, like a small child, they would hear mere sounds but would not understand the meaning. Dharmas cannot withstand analysis by reasoning that analyzes the ultimate, and in the perspective of the ārya's meditative equipoise all elaborations of dualistic appearance are thoroughly pacified, so being unable to express them in an elaborated manner in that perspective is even more profound than the former, for as it is said, 'Prajñāpāramitā, inexpressible, inconceivable, unutterable.'

Then, wishing to conclude, the Bhagavān said: 'Subhūti, here, those who have correctly entered the bodhisattva vehicle should know, view, and resolve upon all dharmas by applying them just as they were explained'; regarding this, 'knowing' is the prajñā of hearing, 'viewing' is the prajñā of reflection, and 'resolving' means one should generate the prajñā of meditation. 'For what reason is that? Subhūti, what is called the perception of a dharma, is because the Tathāgata has spoken of the object of perception and the perception itself as ultimately not existing as perception; therefore, it is called the perception of a dharma conventionally.' Regarding both 'de ci'i phyir zhe na' and 'de ci'i slad du zhe na', 'phyir' and 'slad du' indicate the logic or reason, and although their original term is identical as 'atha', the former is the Teacher's speech and has no honorific, while the latter is Subhūti's speech and is translated with an honorific. Thus, having repeatedly explained the absence of true existence, grasping at true existence is emphatically refuted. As for the manner of refuting it, it is refuted by demonstrating logical invalidation to its adhered object, just as it is apprehended by grasping at true existence, but it is not like extracting a thorn; for Āryadeva said, 'If one sees the lack of self in objects, the seed of existence will be stopped,' and the Pramāṇavārttika says, 'Without invalidating its object, one is unable to abandon it.' As for the reason for refuting it, it is because grasping at true existence is ignorance, and by its power one cycles in saṃsāra, and to abandon grasping at true existence one must realize the lack of true existence, and having realized it, through the power of meditation one will be liberated from saṃsāra and also attain the state of liberation and omniscience—he intended this, for the Saṃcayagāthā says: 'Those endowed with minds attached to saṃsāra cycle permanently;

source: དེ་ནས་འདུས་བྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་རང་བཞིན་མེད་ཅིང་མི་རྟག་པར་བསྟན་ནས་མཇུག་བསྡུ་བ་ནི། སྐར་མ་རབ་རིབ་མར་མེ་དང་། །ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔ་སོགས་ལ་མཚོན་ན། དཔེར་ཇི་ལྟར་ན། སྐར་མ་རྣམས་ནི་མཚན་མོར་སྣང་ཞིང་། ཉིན་མོར་མི་སྣང་བ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཕུང་སོགས་ཀྱི་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ནི་མ་རིག་པའི་མུན་པ་ཡོད་ན་དོན་དམ་པར་སྣང་གི །བདེན་མེད་རྟོགས་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཉི་མ་ཤར་བ་ན་དོན་དམ་པར་མི་སྣང་བས་སྐར་མ་བཞིན་དུ་བལྟའོ། །རྡུལ་སོགས་རབ་རིབ་ཀྱིས་མིག་བསྒྲིབས་པའི་ཚེ་དོན་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་དུ་མི་སྣང་བར་གཞན་དུ་མཐོང་བ་ལྟར་མ་རིག་ པའི་རབ་རིབ་ཀྱིས་བློ་མིག་བསྒྲིབས་པའི་ངོར་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་དོན་གཞན་དུ་སྣང་ངོ་། །མར་མེ་ནི་སྡོང་བུ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་མྱུར་དུ་སྐྱེ་ཞིང་འཇིག་པ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ནི་རང་རང་གི་རྒྱུ་རྐྱེན་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་མྱུར་དུ་སྐྱེ་འཇིག་བྱེད་དོ། །སྒྱུ་མ་ནི་དོན་གཞན་དུ་སྣང་བ་ལྟར་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ནི་བློ་འཁྲུལ་བའི་ངོར་བདེན་པར་སྣང་ངོ་། །ཟིལ་པ་ནི་མྱུར་དུ་འཇིག་པ་ལྟར་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ནི་རང་གི་དུས་གཉིས་པར་མི་སྡོད་པར་མྱུར་དུ་འཇིག་གོ །ཆུ་བུར་ནི་ཆུ་འཁྲུགས་པ་སོགས་ལས་གློ་བུར་དུ་འབྱུང་ཞིང་འཇིག་པ་ལྟར་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ནི་རྐྱེན་ཚོགས་ན་གློ་བུར་དུ་འབྱུང་ཞིང་འཇིག་གོ །རྨི་ལམ་ནི་གཉིད་ཀྱིས་བསླད་པའི་ཚེ་འཁྲུལ་སྣང་ཡིན་པ་ལྟར་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ནི་མ་རིག་པས་བསླད་པའི་ངོར་བདེན་སྣང་དུ་འཆར་རོ། །གློག་ནི་མྱུར་དུ་འབྱུང་ཞིང་འཇིག་པ་ལྟར་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ནི་རྐྱེན་ཚོགས་ན་མྱུར་དུ་འབྱུང་ཞིང་འཇུག་གོ །སྤྲིན་ནི་ཀླུ་སོགས་ཀྱི་བསམ་པའི་དབང་གིས་མཁའ་ལ་སྐྱེ་ཞིང་འཇིག་པ་ལྟར་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ནི། ཐུན་མོང་དང་ཐུན་མོང་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ལས་དབང་གིས་སྐྱེ་འཇིག་བྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་ཞེས་པའི་དཔེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་འདུས་བྱས་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་མེད་དུ་བཤད་དོ། །དེ་དག་ནི་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ལ་ཐུན་མོང་དུ་སྦྱར་ནས་བཤད་པ་སྟེ། མདོ་ལས་ནི། གཟུགས་ནི་དབུ་བ་བརྡོས་པ་འདྲ། །ཚོར་བ་ཆུ་ཡི་ཆུ་བུར་བཞིན། །འདུ་ཤེས་སྨིག་རྒྱུ་ལྟ་བུ་སྟེ། །འདུ་བྱེད་རྣམས་ནི་ཆུ་ཤིང་བཞིན། །རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟར། །ཉི་མའི་གཉེན་གྱིས་བཀའ་བསྩལ་ཏོ། །ཞེས་།བཤད་ཅེས་མགོན་པོ་ཀླུ་སྒྲུབ་གསུང་ངོ་། །སློབ་དཔོན་ཀཱ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལས་ནི་ཕྱི་མ་གསུམ་དུས་གསུམ་དང་སྦྱར་ནས་སྔ་མ་ལས་མི་འདྲ་བར་བཤད་ཀྱང་མི་འགལ་ལོ། །མདོར་ན་འདུས་བྱས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་གོང་དུ་བཤད་པའི་དཔེ་དགུ་པོ་དེ་ལྟར་མི་རྟག་པ་དང་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་བལྟ་བོ་ཞེས་སོ། །འདིས་ཀྱང་གང་ཟག་དང་ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདག་མེད་པ་གཉིས་ཀ་བསྟན་པར་བཟུང་ངོ་། །
translation: Then, having demonstrated that conditioned dharmas are lacking in nature and impermanent, the conclusion is: it is stated, 'A star, a visual aberration, a butter lamp...' To illustrate with the five aggregates, such as form, and so forth: For example, just as stars appear at night and do not appear during the day, similarly, conditioned things such as the aggregates appear ultimately if the darkness of ignorance is present, but when the sun of pristine awareness realizing lack of true existence has arisen, they do not appear ultimately, so they should be viewed like a star. Just as when the eye is obscured by visual aberrations like dust and so forth, objects do not appear as they are but are seen as something else, in the perspective where the eye of the mind is obscured by the visual aberration of ignorance, conditioned things also appear as something else. Just as a butter lamp quickly arises and is destroyed in dependence on a wick, similarly, conditioned things quickly arise and are destroyed in dependence on their own causes and conditions. Just as an illusion appears as something else, conditioned things appear as true in the perspective of a mistaken mind. Just as a dewdrop is quickly destroyed, conditioned things are quickly destroyed without remaining into their own second moment. Just as a water bubble suddenly arises and is destroyed from the agitation of water and so forth, conditioned things suddenly arise and are destroyed when conditions come together. Just as a dream is a mistaken appearance when tainted by sleep, conditioned things dawn as a true appearance in a perspective tainted by ignorance. Just as lightning quickly arises and is destroyed, conditioned things quickly arise and are destroyed when conditions come together. Just as clouds arise and are destroyed in the sky by the power of the intentions of nāgas and so forth, conditioned things undergo arising and destruction by the power of common and uncommon karma—by these examples as well, all conditioned things are explained as being without true existence. Those were explained by applying them to conditioned things in common; whereas in the sūtra it is said: 'Form is like a mass of foam, feeling is like a water bubble, perception is like a mirage, formations are like a plantain tree, consciousness is like an illusion, so the Kinsman of the Sun has declared'—so the protector Nāgārjuna says. Master Kamalaśīla explains the latter three by applying them to the three times in a manner different from the former, yet there is no contradiction. In short, it is said that all conditioned things as well should be viewed as impermanent and lacking in nature like those nine examples explained above. One should hold that this too demonstrates both the selflessness of persons and of dharmas.

དེ་ལྟར་གལ་ཆེ་བ་ལ་དགོངས་ཏེ་ཕན་ཡོན་བསྟན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་མཇུག་བསྡུ་བ་ནི། རབ་འབྱོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་གང་གིས་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པ་དག་གསེར་དངུལ་མུ་ཏིག་སོགས་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྣ་བདུན་གྱིས་གང་བར་བྱས་ཏེ་སྦྱིན་པ་བྱིན་པ་བས་ཀྱང་། རིགས་ཀྱི་བུའམ། རིགས་ཀྱི་བུ་མོ་གང་གིས་གཞུང་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་འདི་རྫོགས་པར་ལྟ་ཞོག །ཐ་ན་ཟབ་མོ་སྟོན་པའི་ཚིག་རྐང་པ་བཞི་པའི་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པ་ཙམ་བྲིས་ནས་བློ་ལ་འཛིན་ཏམ། གླེགས་བམ་ཀློག་གམ། གླེགས་བམ་ཡོངས་རྫོགས་ལག་ཏུ་འཆང་ངམ། དེའི་ཚིག་དོན་རྣམས་ཀུན་ཆུབ་པ་སྟེ་ཤེས་པར་བྱེད་དམ། རང་གིས་ཚིག་དོན་ཤེས་པ་ལྟར་སེམས་ཅན་གཞན་དག་ལ་ཡང་རྒྱ་ཆེར་ཡང་དག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་ན། གང་ཟག་དེ་ཉིད་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་བྱས་པའི་གཞི་དེ་ལས་བསོད་ནམས་ཏེ་དོན་ལ་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེས་མང་དུ་གྲངས་མེད་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པ་བསྐྱེད་དོ། །བསོད་ནམས་ཞེས་པ་ནི་བསོད་ནམས་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་གཉིས་ཀ་མཚོན་ཞིང་། སྦྱིན་པ་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་བཟོད་པ་གསུམ་ལས་ནི་གཙོ་བོར་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་གསོག་ལ། བསམ་གཏན་ཤེས་རབ་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་ནི་གཙོ་བོར་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་གསོག་ཅིང་། བརྩོན་འགྲུས་ལས་ནི་དེ་གཉིས་ཀ་འབྱུང་ངོ་། དེས་ན་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལ་ཐོས་བསམ་སོགས་བྱེད་པ་ནི་ཡེ་ཤེས་གྱི་ཚོགས་གསོག་པ་གཙོ་ཆེའོ།འོ་ན་གཞུང་འདིར་ཕན་ཡོན་འཆད་པའི་སྐབས་རྣམས་སུ་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ཞེས་པ་མང་དུ་འབྱུང་བ་ཇི་ལྟར་ཡིན་ཞེ་ན། དེ་ནི་ཚོགས་གཉིས་ཀྱི་ཟླས་ཕྱེ་བའི་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཙམ་ལ་དགོངས་པ་མ་ཡིན་གྱི། ཕན་ཡོན་ལ་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་མིང་གིས་བརྗོད་པའོ། །

Considering it to be important in that way, the conclusion by way of demonstrating the benefits is: 'Subhūti, more than if any bodhisattva mahāsattva were to fill measureless world systems with the seven precious substances like gold, silver, pearls, and so forth, and give them as a gift, if any son of noble family or daughter of noble family, let alone completely, having written down even as little as a stanza of four lines pointing out the profound of this text of the prajñāpāramitā, memorizes it, or reads the volume, or holds the entire volume in hand, or comprehends, that is, knows all its words and meanings, or, just as they themselves know the words and meanings, correctly explains them extensively to other sentient beings as well—that very person, on the basis of having done that, would generate much more merit, meaning benefits, countless and measureless.' What is called 'merit' indicates both the accumulations of merit and pristine awareness, and from the three—generosity, ethical discipline, and patience—primarily the accumulation of merit is gathered, while from the two—concentration and prajñā—primarily the accumulation of pristine awareness is gathered, and from joyous effort, both arise. Therefore, doing hearing, reflection, and so forth on the prajñāpāramitā is primarily the gathering of the accumulation of pristine awareness. 'Well then, in the occasions of explaining the benefits in this text, how is it that what is called "heap of merit" appears so often?' That does not intend merely the accumulation of merit which is differentiated as one of the pair of the two accumulations, but refers to benefits by the name 'merit'.

གཞུང་འདི་སྟོན་ཚུལ་ཇི་ལྟར་བྱ་བ་ནི། ཇི་ལྟར་ཡང་དག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་སྟོན་ཅེ་ན། དེ་ཡང་བརྗོད་ཅིང་སྟོན་པ་དང་གོ་བ་རྣམས་ནི་ཐ་སྙད་ཙམ་དུ་འཇོག་ཅིང་། དོན་དམ་པར་བརྗོད་བྱ་རྗོད་བྱེད་སོགས་མེད་པས་དོན་ཇི་ལྟར་ཡང་དག་པར་རམ་དོན་དམ་པར་རམ་རབ་ཏུ་མི་སྟོན་ཀྱང་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་སྟོན་པ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ། འདིར་ཡང་ཐ་སྙད་ཙམ་དུ་ཚིག་དང་དོན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་ཡང་དག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་སྟོན་ཏེ། རྒྱུ་མཚན་དེས་ན། ཡང་དག་པར་རབ་ཏུ་སྟོན་པ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །འདི་ལེགས་པར་ཤེས་པ་ནི། རྗོད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་སྒྲ་རྣམས་ནི་རང་ཡུལ་ལ་བརྡ་དང་ཐ་སྙད་ཀྱི་དབང་གིས་འཇུག་ཅིང་། དངོས་པོའི་དབང་གིས་མི་འཇུག་པའི་ཚུལ་ལེགས་པར་ཤེས་དགོས་ཏེ་གོང་དུ་མཚོན་ཙམ་ཞིག་བཤད་ཀྱང་། འདིར་ཡང་དངོས་པོའི་དབང་གིས་མི་འཇུག་པའི་རྒྱུ་མཚན་ནི་དོན་གཅིག་ལའང་མིང་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱིས་བརྗོད་ཆོག་པ་ལྟ་བུ་སྟེ། དཔེར་ན་རྟ་ལྟ་བུ་གཅིག་ལ་ཡང་རྒྱ་གར་རྒྱ་ནག་བོད་སོག་པོ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་རང་རང་གི་ཡུལ་སྐད་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཀྱི་མིང་གིས་བརྗོད་པ་བཞིན་དང་། ཤེར་ཕྱིན་བྱམས་པས་ཞུས་པ་ལས་གཟུགས་སོགས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་ཡང་མིང་གློ་བུར་དུ་བཏགས་པར་གསུངས་པས་མིང་འཇུག་པ་ནི་བརྡའི་དབང་ཡིན་གྱི། དངོས་པོའི་དབང་གིས་མིན་ནོ། །དེས་ན་མིང་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་དོན་གོ་བ་ཡང་བརྡ་སྦྱར་དགོས་པའི་དབང་གིས་ཡིན་གྱི། བརྡ་མ་སྦྱར་ན་དོན་གོ་མི་ནུས་ཏེ། དཔེར་ན་བྱིས་པ་ཆུང་ངུ་བརྡ་མི་ཤེས་པ་ལ་མིང་དེ་དང་དེ་བརྗོད་ཀྱང་སྒྲ་ཙམ་ཞིག་ཐོས་པར་འགྱུར་ཞིང་། དོན་དེ་དང་དེ་མི་གོ་བ་ལྟར་རོ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་གཞན་ཀུན་གྱིས་ཀྱང་དོན་དེ་གོ་བ་ནི་བརྡའི་དབང་གིས་ཡིན་གྱི། བརྡ་མེད་ན་བྱིས་པ་ཆུང་ངུ་ལྟར་སྒྲ་ཙམ་ཞིག་ཐོས་པར་འགྱུར་གྱི་དོན་གོ་བར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཆོས་རྣམས་དོན་དམ་དཔྱོད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་རིགས་པས་དཔྱད་མི་བཟོད་ཅིང་། འཕགས་པའི་མཉམ་བཞག་གི་གཟིགས་ངོར་གཉིས་སྣང་གི་སྤྲོས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཉེ་བར་ཞི་བས་དེའི་ངོར་སྤྲོས་བཅས་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་དུ་བརྗོད་མི་ནུས་པ་ནི་སྔ་མ་ལས་ཀྱང་ཟབ་སྟེ། སྨྲ་བསམ་བརྗོད་མེད་ཤེས་རབ་ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་རོ། །

As for the manner of explaining this text: 'How does one correctly explain it?' The expression, explanation, and understanding are established as merely conventional, and because ultimately there are no expressed meaning, expressing words, and so forth, although in reality it is not correctly or ultimately explained, just as it is explained conventionally, here too one correctly explains the words and meanings unmistakably on a merely conventional level; for that reason, it is called 'correctly explaining'. As for understanding this well: one must well understand the manner in which expressing sounds engage with their own objects by the power of convention and terminology, and do not engage by the power of the things themselves; although this was briefly indicated above, here again the reason they do not engage by the power of the things themselves is like the fact that even one object can be designated with diverse names; for example, just as a single horse is designated with names in diverse regional languages by Indians, Chinese, Tibetans, Mongolians, and so forth, and in the Prajñāpāramitā Requested by Maitreya it is said that names are adventitiously imputed upon all dharmas such as form; thus, the engagement of names is by the power of convention, and not by the power of the things themselves. Therefore, understanding the meaning based on the name is also by the power of needing to apply convention, and if convention is not applied, one is unable to understand the meaning; for example, even if such and such names are spoken to a small child who does not know conventions, they will hear mere sounds, but they do not understand such and such meanings. Similarly, the understanding of that meaning by all others is also by the power of convention, and without convention, like a small child, they would hear mere sounds but would not understand the meaning. Dharmas cannot withstand analysis by reasoning that analyzes the ultimate, and in the perspective of the ārya's meditative equipoise all elaborations of dualistic appearance are thoroughly pacified, so being unable to express them in an elaborated manner in that perspective is even more profound than the former, for as it is said, 'Prajñāpāramitā, inexpressible, inconceivable, unutterable.'

source: གསུམ་པ་མཇུག་གི་རིམ་པ་ནི། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་དེ་སྐད་ཅེས་བཀའ་བསྩལ་ནས། དེ་ལ་གནས་བརྟན་རབ་འབྱོར་དང་། དེ་ལས་གཞན་པའི་དགེ་སློང་སྟོང་ཉིས་བརྒྱ་ལྔ་བཅུ་པོ་དེ་དག་དང་།བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་དག་དང་། དགེ་སློང་ཕ་དང་། དགེ་སློང་མ་དང་། དགེ་བསྙེན་ཕ་དང་། དགེ་བསྙེན་མའི་འཁོར་རྣམ་པ་བཞི་པོ་དང་། གཞན་ཡང་ལྷ་དང་མི་དང་ལྷ་མ་ཡིན་དང་དྲི་ཟར་བཅས་པའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཡི་རང་ཞིང་དགའ་སྟེ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱིས་ཇི་སྐད་གསུངས་པ་ལ་མངོན་པར་བསྟོད་དོ་ཞེས་སོ། །
translation: Third, the concluding sequence: After the Bhagavan had spoken those words, the elder Subhūti and those other one thousand two hundred and fifty monks, and those bodhisattvas, and the fourfold retinue of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, and the beings of the world including gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced and were delighted, and they highly praised what the Bhagavan had said.

དེ་ནས་འདུས་བྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་རང་བཞིན་མེད་ཅིང་མི་རྟག་པར་བསྟན་ནས་མཇུག་བསྡུ་བ་ནི། སྐར་མ་རབ་རིབ་མར་མེ་དང་། །ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔ་སོགས་ལ་མཚོན་ན། དཔེར་ཇི་ལྟར་ན། སྐར་མ་རྣམས་ནི་མཚན་མོར་སྣང་ཞིང་། ཉིན་མོར་མི་སྣང་བ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཕུང་སོགས་ཀྱི་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ནི་མ་རིག་པའི་མུན་པ་ཡོད་ན་དོན་དམ་པར་སྣང་གི །བདེན་མེད་རྟོགས་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཉི་མ་ཤར་བ་ན་དོན་དམ་པར་མི་སྣང་བས་སྐར་མ་བཞིན་དུ་བལྟའོ། །རྡུལ་སོགས་རབ་རིབ་ཀྱིས་མིག་བསྒྲིབས་པའི་ཚེ་དོན་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་དུ་མི་སྣང་བར་གཞན་དུ་མཐོང་བ་ལྟར་མ་རིག་ པའི་རབ་རིབ་ཀྱིས་བློ་མིག་བསྒྲིབས་པའི་ངོར་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱང་དོན་གཞན་དུ་སྣང་ངོ་། །མར་མེ་ནི་སྡོང་བུ་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་མྱུར་དུ་སྐྱེ་ཞིང་འཇིག་པ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ནི་རང་རང་གི་རྒྱུ་རྐྱེན་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་མྱུར་དུ་སྐྱེ་འཇིག་བྱེད་དོ། །སྒྱུ་མ་ནི་དོན་གཞན་དུ་སྣང་བ་ལྟར་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ནི་བློ་འཁྲུལ་བའི་ངོར་བདེན་པར་སྣང་ངོ་། །ཟིལ་པ་ནི་མྱུར་དུ་འཇིག་པ་ལྟར་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ནི་རང་གི་དུས་གཉིས་པར་མི་སྡོད་པར་མྱུར་དུ་འཇིག་གོ །ཆུ་བུར་ནི་ཆུ་འཁྲུགས་པ་སོགས་ལས་གློ་བུར་དུ་འབྱུང་ཞིང་འཇིག་པ་ལྟར་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ནི་རྐྱེན་ཚོགས་ན་གློ་བུར་དུ་འབྱུང་ཞིང་འཇིག་གོ །རྨི་ལམ་ནི་གཉིད་ཀྱིས་བསླད་པའི་ཚེ་འཁྲུལ་སྣང་ཡིན་པ་ལྟར་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ནི་མ་རིག་པས་བསླད་པའི་ངོར་བདེན་སྣང་དུ་འཆར་རོ། །གློག་ནི་མྱུར་དུ་འབྱུང་ཞིང་འཇིག་པ་ལྟར་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ནི་རྐྱེན་ཚོགས་ན་མྱུར་དུ་འབྱུང་ཞིང་འཇུག་གོ །སྤྲིན་ནི་ཀླུ་སོགས་ཀྱི་བསམ་པའི་དབང་གིས་མཁའ་ལ་སྐྱེ་ཞིང་འཇིག་པ་ལྟར་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ནི། ཐུན་མོང་དང་ཐུན་མོང་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ལས་དབང་གིས་སྐྱེ་འཇིག་བྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་ཞེས་པའི་དཔེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་འདུས་བྱས་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་མེད་དུ་བཤད་དོ། །དེ་དག་ནི་འདུས་བྱས་རྣམས་ལ་ཐུན་མོང་དུ་སྦྱར་ནས་བཤད་པ་སྟེ། མདོ་ལས་ནི། གཟུགས་ནི་དབུ་བ་བརྡོས་པ་འདྲ། །ཚོར་བ་ཆུ་ཡི་ཆུ་བུར་བཞིན། །འདུ་ཤེས་སྨིག་རྒྱུ་ལྟ་བུ་སྟེ། །འདུ་བྱེད་རྣམས་ནི་ཆུ་ཤིང་བཞིན། །རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟར། །ཉི་མའི་གཉེན་གྱིས་བཀའ་བསྩལ་ཏོ། །ཞེས་།བཤད་ཅེས་མགོན་པོ་ཀླུ་སྒྲུབ་གསུང་ངོ་། །སློབ་དཔོན་ཀཱ་མ་ལ་ཤཱི་ལས་ནི་ཕྱི་མ་གསུམ་དུས་གསུམ་དང་སྦྱར་ནས་སྔ་མ་ལས་མི་འདྲ་བར་བཤད་ཀྱང་མི་འགལ་ལོ། །མདོར་ན་འདུས་བྱས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱང་གོང་དུ་བཤད་པའི་དཔེ་དགུ་པོ་དེ་ལྟར་མི་རྟག་པ་དང་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་བལྟ་བོ་ཞེས་སོ། །འདིས་ཀྱང་གང་ཟག་དང་ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདག་མེད་པ་གཉིས་ཀ་བསྟན་པར་བཟུང་ངོ་། །
[2-163] translation already produced for this document:
Then, having demonstrated that conditioned dharmas are lacking in nature and impermanent, the conclusion is: it is stated, 'A star, a visual aberration, a butter lamp...' To illustrate with the five aggregates, such as form, and so forth: For example, just as stars appear at night and do not appear during the day, similarly, conditioned things such as the aggregates appear ultimately if the darkness of ignorance is present, but when the sun of pristine awareness realizing lack of true existence has arisen, they do not appear ultimately, so they should be viewed like a star. Just as when the eye is obscured by visual aberrations like dust and so forth, objects do not appear as they are but are seen as something else, in the perspective where the eye of the mind is obscured by the visual aberration of ignorance, conditioned things also appear as something else. Just as a butter lamp quickly arises and is destroyed in dependence on a wick, similarly, conditioned things quickly arise and are destroyed in dependence on their own causes and conditions. Just as an illusion appears as something else, conditioned things appear as true in the perspective of a mistaken mind. Just as a dewdrop is quickly destroyed, conditioned things are quickly destroyed without remaining into their own second moment. Just as a water bubble suddenly arises and is destroyed from the agitation of water and so forth, conditioned things suddenly arise and are destroyed when conditions come together. Just as a dream is a mistaken appearance when tainted by sleep, conditioned things dawn as a true appearance in a perspective tainted by ignorance. Just as lightning quickly arises and is destroyed, conditioned things quickly arise and are destroyed when conditions come together. Just as clouds arise and are destroyed in the sky by the power of the intentions of nāgas and so forth, conditioned things undergo arising and destruction by the power of common and uncommon karma—by these examples as well, all conditioned things are explained as being without true existence. Those were explained by applying them to conditioned things in common; whereas in the sūtra it is said: 'Form is like a mass of foam, feeling is like a water bubble, perception is like a mirage, formations are like a plantain tree, consciousness is like an illusion, so the Kinsman of the Sun has declared'—so the protector Nāgārjuna says. Master Kamalaśīla explains the latter three by applying them to the three times in a manner different from the former, yet there is no contradiction. In short, it is said that all conditioned things as well should be viewed as impermanent and lacking in nature like those nine examples explained above. One should hold that this too demonstrates both the selflessness of persons and of dharmas.

heading: མཇུག་གི་རིམ་པ།
source: འདིའི་མཇུག་ཏུ་རྡོ་རྗེ་གཅོད་པའི་སྙིང་པོའི་སྔགས་ཞེས་པ་ཞིག་འབྱུང་བ་འདི་མདོ་རྒྱུད་ན་ཡོད་པར་མ་མཐོང་བས། གཞན་ཞིག་གིས་བྱས་ནས་བཅུག་པར་ངེས་སོ། །དེར་མ་ཟད་སྙིང་པོ་འདི་ལན་གཅིག་བརྗོད་པས་རྡོར་གཅོད་ཚར་ཁྲི་དགུ་སྟོང་བཀླག་པ་དང་མཉམ་མོ་ཞེས་པ་ནི་བསྔགས་བརྗོད་ཧ་ཅང་ཐལ་བ་སྟེ། འོན་ཀྱང་ཏོན་མི་ཆོག་པ་ནི་མིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟར་གསུང་རབ་འདི་ལ་སོགས་པ་གཞུང་མང་པོའི་ དགོངས་འགྲེལ་འབད་པས་བྱས་པ་ནི། གསང་བ་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་པའི་མདོ་ལས། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་ཀྱི་བསོད་ནམས་དང་། །དམ་ཆོས་འཛིན་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་གང་། །སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ལ་མོས་པ་ཡི། །བཅུ་དྲུག་ཆར་ཡང་མི་ཕོད་དོ། །ཞེས་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་འཆད་ཅིང་མོས་པ་ལས་ཕན་ཡོན་ཆེན་པོ་འབྱུང་བར་གསུངས་པ་དང་། ལྷའི་བུ་བློ་གྲོས་རབ་གནས་ཀྱིས་ཞུས་པའི་མདོ་ལས། ཆོས་རྣམས་ཐམས་ཅད་བཀའ་བསྟན་གཉིས་སུ་འདུ། །ལེགས་པར་བཤད་དང་དེ་ཡི་དགོངས་འགྲེལ་བ། །དེ་ཡི་དབང་གིས་ཤཱཀྱའི་བསྟན་པ་ཡང་། །འཇིག་རྟེན་ཁམས་འདིར་ཡུན་རིང་གནས་པར་འགྱུར། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར་ཐུབ་པའི་བསྟན་པ་ལ་ཕན་ཅུང་ཟད་རེ་ཨེ་ཐོགས་བསམས་ནས་ཡིན་གྱི་གཞན་མིན་ནོ། །སྟོན་པས་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་བྱང་ཕྱོགས་ནས་བྱང་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུད་དུ་དར་བར་འགྱུར་ཞེས་ལུང་བསྟན་འདུག་པ་བཞིན། བྱང་ཕྱོགས་འདིར་རྗེ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་འཕགས་པ་ཡབ་སྲས་ཀྱི་དགོངས་པ་ལྟར་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་སྙིང་པོ་ལྟ་བ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་གསལ་བར་མཛད་པའི་སྲོལ་དུ་ཞུགས་ནས། ཁོ་བོས་ཀྱང་རྗེའི་དགོངས་པ་འགྲེལ་པའི་ལྟ་བའི་རྣམ་གཞག་དུ་མ་བྱས་པ་རྣམས་ཕྱོགས་མང་པོར་དར་ཞིང་། ཁྱད་པར་དུ་རྩ་འཇུག་གཉིས་ཀྱི་འགྲེལ་པ་དང་། ཤེར་སྙིང་དང་ཟབ་མོའི་གཞུང་འདིའི་དགོངས་པ་བློས་ཅི་ནུས་སུ་བཀྲལ་བ་འདི་དག་ཀྱང་། རྒྱལ་བས་ལུང་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱོགས་སུ་འགྲོའམ་སྙམ་ནས་ཡིན་པས། དེའི་ཕྱིར་ཚུལ་འདི་ལ་འབད་པ་ནི་དོན་མཆིས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ།།
translation: At the end of this, there occurs what is called the 'mantra of the essence of the Vajracchedikā'; since I have not seen this existing in the sūtras or tantras, it is certain that someone else composed and inserted it. Not only that, but the claim that 'reciting this essence once is equal to reading the Vajracchedikā ninety thousand times' is an extreme exaggeration of praise; however, it is not that one is not allowed to recite it. Thus, making an effort to compose commentaries on the intent of many texts such as this scripture was done because the Sūtra of Inconceivable Secrets says: 'The merit of bodhicitta / And whatever merit there is in upholding the true dharma / Cannot match even a sixteenth part / Of being inspired by emptiness,' thereby stating that great benefits arise from explaining and being inspired by the meaning of emptiness, and because the Sūtra Requested by the Devaputra Susthitamati says: 'All dharmas are included in two teachings: / The excellent speech and the commentaries on its intent. / By the power of those, the teaching of the Śākya as well / Will remain for a long time in this world system.' Thinking that this might be of some slight benefit to the Sage's teaching, I did this, and for no other reason. Just as the Teacher prophesied that the prajñāpāramitā would spread from the north to the northern region, in this northern direction, the Lord himself entered the tradition of illuminating the completely pure view, the essence of the prajñāpāramitā, according to the intent of the Noble Father and Son; following this, the numerous presentations of the view that I too composed commenting on the Lord's intent have spread in many directions. In particular, I composed commentaries on both the Root and the Entry, and these explanations of the intent of the Heart of Prajñā and this profound text according to the best of my intellectual ability, thinking that they might go in the direction prophesied by the Victor in that way; therefore, making an effort in this method is meaningful.

Then, having demonstrated that conditioned dharmas are lacking in nature and impermanent, the conclusion is: it is stated, 'A star, a visual aberration, a butter lamp...' To illustrate with the five aggregates, such as form, and so forth: For example, just as stars appear at night and do not appear during the day, similarly, conditioned things such as the aggregates appear ultimately if the darkness of ignorance is present, but when the sun of pristine awareness realizing lack of true existence has arisen, they do not appear ultimately, so they should be viewed like a star. Just as when the eye is obscured by visual aberrations like dust and so forth, objects do not appear as they are but are seen as something else, in the perspective where the eye of the mind is obscured by the visual aberration of ignorance, conditioned things also appear as something else. Just as a butter lamp quickly arises and is destroyed in dependence on a wick, similarly, conditioned things quickly arise and are destroyed in dependence on their own causes and conditions. Just as an illusion appears as something else, conditioned things appear as true in the perspective of a mistaken mind. Just as a dewdrop is quickly destroyed, conditioned things are quickly destroyed without remaining into their own second moment. Just as a water bubble suddenly arises and is destroyed from the agitation of water and so forth, conditioned things suddenly arise and are destroyed when conditions come together. Just as a dream is a mistaken appearance when tainted by sleep, conditioned things dawn as a true appearance in a perspective tainted by ignorance. Just as lightning quickly arises and is destroyed, conditioned things quickly arise and are destroyed when conditions come together. Just as clouds arise and are destroyed in the sky by the power of the intentions of nāgas and so forth, conditioned things undergo arising and destruction by the power of common and uncommon karma—by these examples as well, all conditioned things are explained as being without true existence. Those were explained by applying them to conditioned things in common; whereas in the sūtra it is said: 'Form is like a mass of foam, feeling is like a water bubble, perception is like a mirage, formations are like a plantain tree, consciousness is like an illusion, so the Kinsman of the Sun has declared'—so the protector Nāgārjuna says. Master Kamalaśīla explains the latter three by applying them to the three times in a manner different from the former, yet there is no contradiction. In short, it is said that all conditioned things as well should be viewed as impermanent and lacking in nature like those nine examples explained above. One should hold that this too demonstrates both the selflessness of persons and of dharmas.

heading: མཇུག་གི་རིམ་པ།
translation: Let it be said: You, the twice-born bird flying in the sky of profound meaning, having vigorously flapped the wing-feathers of scripture and reasoning by the wind-force of previously accumulated good conduct and extensive hearing, have you not fallen into the abyss of meaningless, mistaken error? If there are any faulty explanations in this presentation, I confess and ask for forgiveness in the presence of the Lord of Sages himself; by your compassionate mind, having cleansed the stains of my faults, may you accept me until enlightenment. By the virtue of explaining the meaning of the most profound, profound sūtra, may I, an intelligent one who has heard many, many texts, find the basis for accomplishing the omniscient path in all my lifetimes, completely perfect the accumulations, and quickly attain perfect buddhahood! This 'Sun that Illuminates the Profound Meaning of the Excellent Path for Travelling to Freedom, a Commentary on the Vajracchedikā' was composed by the Śākya monk Drakpa Shedrup in his seventieth year, the wood-mouse year of the twelfth sexagenary cycle, with faith, at the monastery of Chone itself; the scribe was Tayi Lalung Lozang Dondrup. Mangalam.

Then, having demonstrated that conditioned dharmas are lacking in nature and impermanent, the conclusion is: it is stated, 'A star, a visual aberration, a butter lamp...' To illustrate with the five aggregates, such as form, and so forth: For example, just as stars appear at night and do not appear during the day, similarly, conditioned things such as the aggregates appear ultimately if the darkness of ignorance is present, but when the sun of pristine awareness realizing lack of true existence has arisen, they do not appear ultimately, so they should be viewed like a star. Just as when the eye is obscured by visual aberrations like dust and so forth, objects do not appear as they are but are seen as something else, in the perspective where the eye of the mind is obscured by the visual aberration of ignorance, conditioned things also appear as something else. Just as a butter lamp quickly arises and is destroyed in dependence on a wick, similarly, conditioned things quickly arise and are destroyed in dependence on their own causes and conditions. Just as an illusion appears as something else, conditioned things appear as true in the perspective of a mistaken mind. Just as a dewdrop is quickly destroyed, conditioned things are quickly destroyed without remaining into their own second moment. Just as a water bubble suddenly arises and is destroyed from the agitation of water and so forth, conditioned things suddenly arise and are destroyed when conditions come together. Just as a dream is a mistaken appearance when tainted by sleep, conditioned things dawn as a true appearance in a perspective tainted by ignorance. Just as lightning quickly arises and is destroyed, conditioned things quickly arise and are destroyed when conditions come together. Just as clouds arise and are destroyed in the sky by the power of the intentions of nāgas and so forth, conditioned things undergo arising and destruction by the power of common and uncommon karma—by these examples as well, all conditioned things are explained as being without true existence. Those were explained by applying them to conditioned things in common; whereas in the sūtra it is said: 'Form is like a mass of foam, feeling is like a water bubble, perception is like a mirage, formations are like a plantain tree, consciousness is like an illusion, so the Kinsman of the Sun has declared'—so the protector Nāgārjuna says. Master Kamalaśīla explains the latter three by applying them to the three times in a manner different from the former, yet there is no contradiction. In short, it is said that all conditioned things as well should be viewed as impermanent and lacking in nature like those nine examples explained above. One should hold that this too demonstrates both the selflessness of persons and of dharmas.
